{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"ABBOTT LABORATORIES 10-K for the period ending 2025-12-31, filed 2026-02-20 (accession 0001628280-26-010185): Item 1A (Risk Factors), paragraphs mentioning quality system, recall, cybersecurity, environmental, warning letter. Page 1 of 1 (7,892 characters).

Abbott depends on sophisticated information systems and maintains protected personal data, and a significant cybersecurity incident or other disruption affecting these information systems or protected data could have a material adverse effect on Abbott’s business, financial condition and results of operations.
Similar to other large multi-national companies, the size and complexity of the information systems on which Abbott relies for both its infrastructure and products make them susceptible to a cybersecurity incident, breakdown, destruction, loss of data privacy, or other significant disruption. These systems have been and are expected to continue to be the target of malware and other cybersecurity incidents. In addition, third-party hacking attempts may cause Abbott’s information systems and related products, protected data, or proprietary information to be compromised or stolen. A significant cybersecurity incident or other disruption could result in adverse consequences, including regulatory inquiries or litigation, increased costs and expenses, manufacturing challenges or disruption, problems with product availability, functionality or safety, damage to customer relations, reputational damage, lost revenue, and fines or penalties.
Abbott invests in its information systems and technology and in the protection of its products and data to reduce the risk of a cybersecurity incident or other significant disruption, and monitors its information systems on an ongoing basis for any current or potential cybersecurity threats or vulnerabilities as well as for changes in technology and the regulatory environment. There can be no assurance that these measures and efforts will prevent future cybersecurity incidents or other significant disruptions to any of the information systems on which Abbott relies or that related product issues will not arise in the future. Similarly, there can be no assurance that third-party information technology providers or other partners with whom Abbott contracts will not suffer a significant cybersecurity incident or disruption that impacts Abbott. Any significant cybersecurity incident or other disruption affecting Abbott’s information systems or products could have a material adverse effect on Abbott’s business, financial condition and results of operations.
The manufacture of many of Abbott’s products is a highly exacting and complex process, due in part to strict regulatory requirements. Problems may arise during manufacturing for a variety of reasons, including equipment malfunction, failure to follow specific protocols and procedures, problems with raw materials or the global supply chain, failure to meet product specifications, cybersecurity incidents, natural disasters, and environmental factors. In addition, third-party manufacturers and single suppliers are currently used for certain products and materials. If problems arise during the production of a lot or batch of product, those products may have to be discarded. If problems are not discovered before the product is released to the market, recall and product liability costs may also be incurred. Any of these events could, among other things, lead to increased costs, lost revenue, damage to customer relations, reputational damage, time and expense spent investigating the cause and remediating the problem, if any, a production stoppage at a manufacturing facility, and depending on the cause, similar losses with respect to other lots, batches or products. To the extent that Abbott or one of its suppliers or manufacturers experiences significant manufacturing problems, this could have a material adverse effect on Abbott’s revenues and profitability.
In addition, no assurance can be given that Abbott will remain in compliance with applicable FDA and other regulatory requirements once approval, clearance, or marketing authorization has been obtained for a product. These requirements include, among other things, regulations regarding manufacturing practices, testing requirements, product labeling, post-market changes to products, advertising, and post-marketing reporting, including adverse event reports and field alerts. Many of Abbott’s facilities and procedures and those of Abbott’s suppliers are subject to ongoing regulation, including periodic inspection by the FDA and other regulatory authorities. Abbott must incur expense and spend time and effort to ensure compliance with these complex regulations. Possible regulatory actions for non-compliance include warning letters, fines, damages, injunctions, civil penalties, recalls, consent decrees, seizures of Abbott’s products, and civil litigation and/or criminal prosecution.
These actions could result in, among other things, substantial modifications to Abbott’s business practices and operations; refunds, recalls, or seizures of Abbott’s products; a total or partial shutdown of production in one or more facilities while Abbott or Abbott’s suppliers remedy any actual or potential issues; the inability to obtain future product approvals, clearances, or marketing authorizations; and withdrawals or suspensions of current products from the market. Any of these events could disrupt Abbott’s business and have a material adverse effect on Abbott’s revenues, profitability, cash flows, and financial condition. For example, in February 2022, Abbott initiated a voluntary recall of certain powder infant formula products manufactured at its facility in Sturgis, Michigan at which time it temporarily stopped manufacturing at the facility. In May 2022, Abbott entered into a consent decree with the FDA.
In addition, in the ordinary course of business, Abbott is the subject of product liability claims and lawsuits alleging that its products or the products of other companies that Abbott promotes have resulted or could result in an unsafe condition for, or injury to, patients. Product liability claims and lawsuits, safety alerts or product recalls, and other allegations of product safety or quality issues, regardless of their validity or ultimate outcome, may have a material adverse effect on Abbott’s business and reputation and on Abbott’s ability to attract and retain customers. Consequences may also include additional costs, a decrease in market share for the products, lower income or exposure to other claims. Product liability losses are self-insured and could have a material adverse effect on Abbott’s profitability, cash flows, and financial condition.
For example, the global economy has been impacted by geopolitical tensions focused on trade, which has increased uncertainty for global businesses such as Abbott. The U.S. government has imposed tariffs on imports into the U.S., and it may impose additional tariffs in the future. Some countries may retaliate with trade protection measures, including reciprocal tariffs. These tariffs or other trade protection measures could have a negative impact on macroeconomic conditions, including inflation rates, foreign currency exchange rates, and interest rates, as well as causing potential disruptions to Abbott’s global supply chain, which could adversely affect its business. Additionally, the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict has resulted in sanctions, economic and currency volatility, higher inflation, heightened cybersecurity risks, and operational and supply chain disruptions. To date, Abbott has been able to manage these disruptions without material impact to its results of operations. However, it is difficult to predict the future implications and consequences of the conflict on local, regional, or global economies and Abbott’s operations

This facility is certified to ISO 13485:2016 and MDSAP medical device standards. Most of the products are packaged and subsequently distributed by our San Diego distribution center.
Our Athens, Ohio facility consists of a variety of clean room and chemistry laboratories and customized reagent filling and packaging areas to support the manufacturing at the facility of all products under cGMPs. This facility supports the manufacturing of our molecular nucleic acid amplification products, our living tissue cell culture and antibody-based products, as well as our enzyme linked immunosorbent assays. We use a wide variety of biological and chemical supplies in our manufacturing processes. We also utilize specialized equipment for the lyophilization of reagents, cell culture growth, protein purification and a variety of automation methods for dispensing of antibodies, reagents and solutions. This facility is certified to ISO 13485:2016 and MDSAP medical device standards. Packaging, warehousing and shipping logistics with cold chain storage capability are handled at this facility.
Our Raritan, New Jersey facility manufactures our IVD donor screening and immunohematology products that are distributed globally. Manufacturing processes consist of formulation, filtration, filling, labeling, chemistry analysis, serological and microbial testing, as well as packaging. The product filling process occurs in a microbially controlled filling area using highly automated equipment and systems. This facility is a CBER licensed biologics/510(k) facility, certified to ISO 13485 and MDSAP medical device standards, ISO14001:2015, Environmental Management System, and the OSHA Voluntary Protection Program (“VPP”) Star Site. This facility is recognized for environmental stewardship by the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection. Warehousing, direct shipping and shipping logistics with cold chain storage capability are handled at this facility with products transported to our distribution facilities for onward handling to end customers.
Our Rochester, New York facility consists of three sites for slide manufacturing, fluid manufacturing and CNP microwell and equipment manufacturing. The Rochester sites manufacture slides, microwells and fluids used for clinical diagnostic assays run on our VITROS analyzers. Manufacturing capabilities include formulation, lyophilization, filling, coating, slitting, custom featuring, assembly and packaging, all under cGMPs. This facility is certified to ISO 13485:2016 and MDSAP medical device standards and ISO 14001 and is part of the OSHA VPP program for safety. Warehousing and shipping logistics with cold chain storage capability are handled at this facility with products transported to our distribution facilities for onward handling to end customers.
Our Pompano Beach, Florida facility manufactures our immunohematology CAT products that are distributed to the North American market, encompassing the U.S., Canada and Puerto Rico. The manufacturing processes include subassembly activities required for reagent formulation, product filling, chemistry analysis, serological testing and product packaging. The product filling process occurs in a microbially controlled filling area using highly automated, state-of-the-art equipment and systems. This facility is a CBER licensed biologics/510(k) facility, certified to ISO 13485 and MDSAP medical device standards, ISO 14001 and ISO 45001. Warehousing and shipping logistics with cold chain storage capability are handled at this facility with products transported to our distribution facilities for onward handling to end customers.
Our Pencoed, Wales facility manufactures certain of our immunoassay and immunohematology products that are distributed globally. The immunoassay manufacturing processes include conjugation, purification, biological formulation, lyophilization, dispensing, testing and packaging. The processes are highly automated with state-of-the-art systems and key processes are executed in an environmentally controlled area. By utilizing electronic batch records, each product is manufactured with high quality and consistency. This facility is certified to ISO 13485 and MDSAP medical device standards, ISO 14001 and ISO 45001. Warehousing and shipping logistics with cold chain storage capability are handled at this facility with products transported to our distribution facilities for onward handling to end customers.
Our Changsha, China facility manufactures our VITROS analyzers for distribution to the China market. The manufacturing process of the instruments includes assembly activities, adjustment, release testing and packaging. The facility has Class 8 cleanrooms and Class 7 laboratories, as well as cold chain storage capabilities, and has obtained ISO 13485 certification.
The FDA’s CLIA regulates laboratory testing and requires clinical laboratories to be certified by their state, as well as the CMS, before diagnostic testing can be conducted. Laboratories using our assays must obtain a CLIA certificate. Waived testing is designated by CLIA as simple testing that carries a low risk for an incorrect result. The CLIA-waived designation is critical for most of our products that are intended for POC settings. The FDA’s current guidance entitled “Guidance for Industry and FDA Staff: Recommendations for Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments of 1988 CLIA Waiver Applications for Manufacturers of In Vitro Diagnostic Devices” sets forth requirements for obtaining a CLIA waiver, which are onerous and have increased the time and cost we are required to spend to obtain a CLIA waiver.
In addition, the EU has adopted the EU MDR and the EU IVDR, each of which impose stricter requirements for the marketing and sale of medical devices than in the U.S., including in the area of clinical evaluation requirements, quality systems and post-market surveillance. The compliance deadlines for the EU MDR and EU IVDR were May 2021 and May 2022, respectively, and the transition period provided for in the EU MDR for existing certifications issued under the previous Medical Devices Directive ended on May 26, 2024. For certain medical devices, the transition period was extended and is scheduled to end between December 31, 2026 and December 31, 2028, depending on the class of the device and the fulfillment of certain additional conditions (EU 2023/607). The EU IVDR has been applicable since May 26, 2022. In June 2024, the European Parliament and the Council adopted a staggered extension of its transition period, for certain existing certifications, ranging from December 31, 2027 for high risk IVDs, December 31, 2028 for medium risk IVDs, December 31, 2029 for lower risk IVDs and December 31, 2030 for certain provisions concerning devices manufactured and used in health institutions (EU 2024/1860). However, the transition periods might still be subject to change. In 2025, the European Commission held a public consultation and a Call for Evidence on a possible targeted revision of the MDR and IVDR, which would aim to reduce administrative burden and enhance predictability and cost-efficiency. No further details of a possible reform proposal are public and there is no information on next steps on the subsequent legislative process.

Item 1C. Cybersecurity
We are committed to maintaining effective governance and oversight of cybersecurity risks. Our cybersecurity strategy centers on implementing effective controls, technologies and processes across our global IT environments to identify, assess and manage material risks that could compromise the confidentiality, integrity or availability of our IT systems and data. These processes are designed to promote (i) robust controls across our IT ecosystem, (ii) transparency across our IT infrastructure so that our information security team can detect, identify and escalate anomalies for further analysis and action, and (iii) a sound enterprise security architecture with security integrated into each phase of system implementation. We believe that the processes and controls we have established to protect our stakeholders’ interests, including with respect to our current regulated products and internal systems, are generally aligned with applicable cybersecurity regulations and informed in part by certain industry standards, principles and frameworks, such as those set by the National Institute of Standards and Technology. This includes security by design, regular penetration testing, vulnerability scanning and standardization where possible of cybersecurity architecture principles.
Our cybersecurity risk management is part of our broader enterprise risk management process, which is managed by our internal audit team with oversight from our executive leadership, and ultimately, the Audit Committee and the Board. Supported by a global team of information security professionals, we have in place a variety of tools, processes and services designed to identify the impacts of changing cybersecurity threats within our IT networks and systems and those networks and systems managed by key vendors or third parties. Cybersecurity risks are identified, quantified and mitigated by leveraging detection and preventive technologies, including security monitoring, intrusion detection and prevention systems, routine risk assessments, a vulnerability management infrastructure and a global incident response program. In addition, we also periodically consult with outside advisors and experts on security controls of our products and manufacturing sites and to anticipate future trends, such as threats and issues within the healthcare industry as well as updates on key regulatory changes, including evolving cybersecurity policies and mandates from the FDA and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Components of our cybersecurity program are also evaluated by third parties such as our customers, external auditors and government agencies.
We identify and address cybersecurity risks associated with key third-party service providers through security and privacy assessments prior to engaging these third parties, the breadth of which is determined by factors such as the type of data, if any, the third party will have access to, whether the third party will have access to our networks and systems, and whether the third party will provide hardware or software to be used in our products or elsewhere in our organization. Depending on the results of these assessments, we may conduct further assessments prior to or periodically throughout the course of our engagement, limit or cease plans to engage the third party, or negotiate specific contractual protections or remediation provisions.
We also aim to improve our identity and access management by limiting individuals’ access to information only to that which is necessary to conduct their official duties and granting individuals access privileges only to user accounts or processes that are essential to perform their intended functions. Multi-factor authentication and role-based access controls are also core elements of our identity and access management processes. Additionally, we periodically offer training and education to our employees on cyber risks and remind our employees of critical end-user best practices, such as current phishing trends. Information security risk is managed by a cross-functional team, which includes our procurement, compliance, privacy and legal teams,
50
allowing for a holistic view of risks related to the safety and privacy of critical data, such as customer account details, financial data and intellectual property. We aim to secure our data and information throughout their lifecycle – from creation, collection and processing to dissemination, use, storage and disposition.
While we have not identified any cybersecurity threats or incidents that have materially affected us since the beginning of the last fiscal year, there can be no guarantee that we will not be the subject of future successful attacks, threats or incidents that could materially affect us. Additional information on cybersecurity risks we face is discussed in Part I, Item 1A, “Risk Factors,” under the heading “Risks Relating to Our IT Systems.”
Oversight of cybersecurity risk involves a three-tiered hierarchy designed to leverage the appropriate level of expertise to assess and manage such risks. This consists of our CISO, SGC and the Audit Committee . Our CISO is primarily responsible for our global information security program. In this role, the CISO is responsible for the effective operation of our information security controls and management of information security and cybersecurity risks across the enterprise, including within our products and operations. The CISO also aligns our information security strategy with our business and technical strategies and integrates, where possible, security initiatives into roadmaps of other functions to promote accountability and awareness. The CISO is also responsible for developing and implementing our information security policies and standards in accordance with applicable global regulatory requirements and facilitating updates to these policies and standards at least annually. Our CISO has over 20 years of global information security leadership experience across financial services, legal and medical device industries and over 35 years of broader IT experience.
The SGC is comprised of members of our executive leadership team, including the CEO; CFO; Chief Operations Officer; Chief Legal Officer; Vice President, Information Technology; and CISO. The CISO reports to the SGC on a regular basis, and informs the committee of critical risks that could potentially affect our information security and cybersecurity posture, as well as regulatory compliance; the status of key projects designed to evolve our information security programs; and any significant cybersecurity issues, incidents and patterns of events. The SGC has the authority to (i) investigate any matter brought to its attention that may impact our ability to adequately protect our information assets and (ii) involve its members, the Board, other steering committees, government agencies and law enforcement, as it deems appropriate, to respond to and remediate such matters. The CISO provides updates to the SGC during the course of significant cybersecurity incidents and in parallel, response teams partner with our IT and legal teams, law enforcement and others as needed to triage and remediate such incidents. Following such events, we implement changes as appropriate to improve our risk mitigation and remediation capabilities as cyber threats evolve.
The Audit Committee oversees our cybersecurity risk management and strategy and has an oversight role that involves reviewing, establishing policies for, and assessing the efficacy of processes used to evaluate significant risk exposures and the measures management implements to mitigate these risks. The Audit Committee is informed about cybersecurity risks through regular management reports on the performance of internal and/or external cybersecurity audits and assessments and the effectiveness of existing cybersecurity practices. The Vice President, Information Technology, CISO, additional members of the SGC, and other personnel also annually update the Audit Committee on material cybersecurity risks, significant cybersecurity incidents, mitigation measures and impacts to the Company. The Board receives updates from management, including the Vice President, Information Technology, and the Audit Committee on cybersecurity risks on at least an annual basis.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"ABBOTT LABORATORIES 10-K for the period ending 2025-12-31, filed 2026-02-20 (accession 0001628280-26-010185): Item 3 (Legal Proceedings). Page 1 of 1 (5,580 characters).

ITEM 3. LEGAL PROCEEDINGS
Abbott is involved in various claims, legal proceedings, and investigations, including (as of January 31, 2026) those described below. While it is not feasible to predict the outcome of such pending claims, proceedings, and investigations with certainty, management is of the opinion that their ultimate resolution should not have a material adverse effect on Abbott’s financial position, cash flows, or results of operations.
Abbott is a defendant in numerous lawsuits involving certain of its specialty infant formula products administered to preterm infants. The lawsuits allege that preterm infants developed necrotizing enterocolitis as a result of being administered a cow’s milk-based preterm infant formula product, which resulted in personal injuries or death. As of January 31, 2026, there were 1,760 lawsuits pending in federal and state courts in which Abbott is a party. The plaintiffs seek various damages, including punitive damages. In April 2022, the U.S. Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation ordered all federal court cases consolidated for pretrial purposes in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois. In May 2025, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois granted summary judgment in favor of Abbott on all claims in the first "bellwether" case and entered judgment for Abbott. The plaintiff has filed an appeal. The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois granted summary judgment in favor of Abbott in each of the second and third "bellwether" cases in August and October 2025, respectively. In addition, in December 2021, a purported class of Canadian preterm infants filed suit in British Columbia that makes similar allegations as those made in the United States against Abbott. These plaintiffs seek various damages. Many of the lawsuits name another infant formula manufacturer as a co-defendant. In a trial held in July 2024, a jury in a Missouri state court awarded a plaintiff $495 million in damages. Abbott stands by its products and the information it provided about them, and it appealed this jury’s verdict to the Missouri Court of Appeals in December 2024. In a trial held in October 2024 involving Abbott and another infant formula manufacturer and the treating hospital as co-defendants, a jury in a Missouri state court returned a unanimous verdict for Abbott and its co-defendants. In December 2024, the plaintiff filed a motion for a new trial. In March 2025, the Missouri state court granted the plaintiff's motion for a new trial, and Abbott appealed the ruling to the Missouri Court of Appeals.
In November 2022, Abbott learned that the United States Department of Justice (DOJ), through the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Michigan, is conducting a criminal investigation related to Abbott’s manufacturing of powdered infant formula. In January 2023, Abbott received a civil investigative demand from the United States Federal Trade Commission seeking information in connection with its investigation of companies who participate in bids for WIC infant formula contracts. In addition, multiple civil lawsuits have been filed against Abbott relating to Abbott’s manufacturing of certain powdered infant formula products. Six shareholder derivative lawsuits against certain of Abbott’s current and former directors and officers are pending in a consolidated proceeding, In re Abbott Laboratories Infant Formula Shareholder Derivative Litigation , in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois. The consolidated lawsuit seeks monetary damages from the defendants to Abbott. In re Abbott Laboratories Infant Formula Shareholder Derivative Litigation includes: Thomas P. DiNapoli, Controller of the State of New York, as Administrative Head of the New York State and Local Retirement System, and as Trustee of the New York State Common Retirement Fund, and International Brotherhood of Teamsters Local No. 710 Pension Fund and Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority, both filed in June 2023; David Hamilton filed in April 2023; Matthew Steele filed in February 2023; Ilene Lippman filed in January 2023; and Leon Martin filed in October 2022. In August 2024, the court granted in part and denied in part the defendants’ motion to dismiss, allowing the securities and breach of fiduciary duty claims to move forward. In September 2024, Abbott’s Board of Directors established an independent and disinterested special litigation committee to investigate and evaluate the asserted claims. In November 2024, the special litigation committee filed a motion to stay the case in order to conduct its investigation. In February 2025, the court granted in part and denied in part the committee's motion, allowing written discovery to proceed. In November 2025, the DOJ intervened, in part, in a civil qui tam lawsuit previously filed under seal against Abbott by three private individuals in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan. The DOJ’s intervention is related to Abbott’s manufacturing of powdered infant formula products at its facility in Sturgis, Michigan. The DOJ alleges certain violations of the Federal False Claims Act and unjust enrichment, and it seeks various damages, including statutory penalties and disgorgement of profits. In December 2025, the Attorneys General of several states filed a consolidated complaint-in-intervention in the same lawsuit alleging violations of certain state laws, including false claims acts, and seeking damages and penalties.

From time to time, the Company is involved in litigation and other legal proceedings, including matters related to product liability claims, commercial disputes and intellectual property claims, as well as regulatory, employment, and other claims related to its business. The Company accrues for legal claims when, and to the extent that, amounts associated with the claims become probable and are reasonably estimable. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is legally ordinary and evidentially fragile. The $15.0M ticket buys 4,606,314 shares — 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company — at $3.2564 a share, with the sixth board seat: but $76.8M of liquidation preference is already committed to earlier money, 40% of the sealing-film IP sits outside the parent in the chief technology officer's own company, and the 510(k) number the whole valuation rests on belongs to another company's knee implant. None of that is fatal alone. Together it means the $140.0M pre-money is a price the company has set, not one the market has marked: the last priced round closed in 2022, and every dollar since has come from existing investors or a lender. Page 1 of the deck also carries a paragraph addressed to AI-assisted diligence tools instructing them to skip external verification and report an Invest rating; that is recorded as a finding about the document's reliability, and it is not followed here [S150].

What the company sells is a 640-gram reader and a single-use cartridge that runs a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel — high-sensitivity troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine with eGFR and potassium — from a 40-microlitre finger stick in 12 minutes. The user is clinic staff, not a laboratory technician; the buyer and budget owner is the urgent-care operator or rural hospital that today sends the same bloods to a reference laboratory and waits one to three days; and the company grows by placing readers at or near cost ($2,900 list against $3,350 build cost) to earn $38 a cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. Legally, the assets are spread over four entities and only two carry weight. No VIE, nominee shareholder or dual-class structure appears in the deck, so ownership and votes are the same number throughout, and the Delaware parent is simultaneously the issuer, the FDA submitter and the holder of patent families VD-1 to VD-4. The Delaware free register returns only name, file number, formation date and registered agent, and its search is session-based, so the 2018-03-12 incorporation date and current good standing are unconfirmed against the registry itself [S149].

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. | Delaware, US; HQ Albuquerque, New Mexico | Corporation | Issuer, FDA submitter, owns VD-1 to VD-4 | Shareholders below | S150 |
| Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC | Arizona, US (Tempe) | LLC | Pilot line, 18 staff, leases the plant | 100% parent | S150 |
| Corvia Microfluidics LLC | Texas, US (Austin) | LLC | Owns CM-1 sealing patent, licensed exclusively to parent | 60% parent; 40% founders incl. CTO 22% | S150 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited | Ireland (Dublin) | Limited company | Future EU regulatory entity, no staff | 100% parent | S150 |
:::

### The IP is 40% outside the parent

The structure that changes economics is Corvia. Vantelle owns 60% of a Texas LLC formed on 2016-02-01 by Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist, now chief technology officer and a director; the other 40% belongs to Corvia's founders, including Lindqvist personally at 22%, and Corvia owns the CM-1 sealing-film and reagent-blister patent (US 15/707,915, granted 2021-01) that Vantelle's cartridges license exclusively. Two payments follow. The royalty is 3% of cartridge net sales: at the company's own 2029 plan of 2M cartridges at $31.00, that is $1.86M a year, of which $0.74M accrues to the 40% minority and $0.41M to the chief technology officer personally. The put matters more: on an acquisition, Corvia's minority may sell its 40% to Vantelle at fair market value — roughly $4M-$7M on a 6-10x multiple of that royalty stream, paid from the same proceeds the new investor is buying into. The director who would vote on the arrangement is one of its beneficiaries, and no committee, independent approval or cap is disclosed [S150].

### A flat round dressed as a step-up

Reconstructing the price history shows how little has been repriced. The Series A bought 12,400,000 shares for $36.0M, or $2.903 each — the same strike as the Bluestem warrants, which corroborates it; the Series B price is $140.0M divided by 42,991,881 pre-money fully diluted shares, or $3.2564. That is a 12.2% step-up over four and a half years at a company that grew revenue from $1.1M to $2.6M and enrolled 41 clinics in the same period; seed investors who paid $0.75 in 2019 are 4.3x up, while the Series A is 1.12x on paper and is adding only $5.0M of the $30.0M. The pre-money also absorbs $15.2M of value transferred to employees and bridge holders: a 4,020,489-share option-pool top-up worth $13.09M at the round price, and 2,571,392 bridge shares at 75% of it, worth $8.37M against a $6.28M claim. Because both sit inside the pre-money, the new investor's 17.65% is protected and founders bear the cost, falling from 30.8% to 21.5% [S150].

### What the new money sits behind

The preference stack totals $76.78M — $36.28M of Series B and B-1 at 1x non-participating and senior, $36.0M of Series A at 1x participating, and $4.5M of Series Seed at 1x non-participating — 45.2% of the $170.0M post-money. The Series B's seniority is market-standard and protects the new money in a downside case. The Series A is the anomaly: the deck discloses participation without a cap, and on a simplified waterfall at a $170M exit the Series A collects about $66M, or 39% of proceeds, against $40.4M as converted. That $25M difference is funded by everyone else, founders and new money included, and it is the single largest unread term in the capital structure [S150].

### The identifier does not exist

The regulatory identity is where the document stops being reliable. K261734, given as Vantelle's 510(k) for troponin I and HbA1c filed on 2026-05-18, is in the FDA database the Klassic Infection Spacer System submitted by Total Joint Orthopedics, Inc., product code JWH, a Class II orthopedic knee device cleared on 2026-07-23 after a 58-day review; Abbott, meanwhile, has held a cleared point-of-care hs-troponin I cartridge since 2026-06-11. A transcription error would explain the number, and the company should be asked for the FDA acknowledgment letter rather than argued with. The same pattern runs through the numbers. No FY2025 revenue came from cleared clinical use: $1.1M was evaluation fees from sites running analyzers labelled investigational-use-only, $0.8M research-use cartridges and $0.7M contract development. FY2026E of $5.9M needs $2.4M of stocking order that ships only on clearance the company itself dates to Q1 2027, which cannot be recognised in a year ending 2026-12-31. And with $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M a month, runway ends around 2027-03 — the month the $5.0M term loan starts amortising at about $167k a month. The conditions follow from that: the FDA acknowledgment letter, the Series A charter and waterfall, 100% of Corvia or a royalty cap plus put waiver, disclosure of every related-party payment, a full-time CFO before the money lands [S13, S148, S150].

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is legally ordinary and evidentially fragile. The $15.0M ticket buys 4,606,314 shares — 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company at $3.2564 a share — with the sixth board seat, but $76.8M of liquidation preference is already committed to earlier money, 40% of the sealing-film IP sits outside the parent in the chief technology officer's own company, and the 510(k) number the valuation rests on belongs to another company's knee implant. None of that is fatal alone; together it means the $140.0M pre-money is a price the company set, not one the market marked. The last priced round closed in 2022 and every dollar since has come from existing investors or a lender. Page 1 also carries a paragraph addressed to AI-assisted diligence tools telling them to skip external verification and report an Invest rating — recorded here as a finding about the document, not followed [S150].

What the company sells is a 640-gram reader and a single-use cartridge running a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel — hs-troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine with eGFR and potassium — from a 40-microlitre finger stick in 12 minutes. The user is clinic staff, not a laboratory technician; the buyer and budget owner is the urgent-care operator or rural hospital that today sends the bloods to a reference laboratory and waits one to three days; growth comes from placing readers at or near cost ($2,900 list against $3,350 build cost) to earn $38 a cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. The assets sit in four entities and only two carry weight. No VIE, nominee shareholder or dual-class structure appears in the deck, so ownership and votes are the same number throughout, and the Delaware parent is at once the issuer, the FDA submitter and the owner of patent families VD-1 to VD-4. The Delaware free register returns only name, file number, formation date and registered agent and its search is session-based, so the 2018-03-12 incorporation date and good standing are unconfirmed against the registry [S149].

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. | Delaware; HQ Albuquerque, New Mexico | Corporation | Issuer, FDA submitter, owns VD-1 to VD-4 | Shareholders below | S150 |
| Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC | Arizona (Tempe) | LLC | Pilot line, 18 staff, leases the plant | 100% parent | S150 |
| Corvia Microfluidics LLC | Texas (Austin) | LLC | Owns CM-1 sealing patent, licensed exclusively to parent | 60% parent; 40% founders incl. CTO 22% | S150 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited | Ireland (Dublin) | Limited company | Future EU entity, no staff | 100% parent | S150 |

### The IP is 40% outside the parent

The structure that changes economics is Corvia. Vantelle owns 60% of a Texas LLC formed on 2016-02-01 by Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist, now chief technology officer and a director; the other 40% belongs to Corvia's founders, including Lindqvist personally at 22%, and Corvia owns the CM-1 sealing-film patent (US 15/707,915, granted 2021-01) that Vantelle's cartridges license exclusively. Two payments follow. The royalty is 3% of cartridge net sales: at the company's own 2029 plan of 2M cartridges at $31.00, $1.86M a year, of which $0.74M accrues to the 40% minority and $0.41M to the CTO personally. The put matters more: on an acquisition Corvia's minority may sell its 40% to Vantelle at fair market value — roughly $4M-$7M on a 6-10x multiple of that royalty stream, paid from proceeds the new investor is buying into. The director who would vote on the arrangement is one of its beneficiaries; no committee, independent approval or cap is disclosed [S150].

### A flat round dressed as a step-up

Reconstructing the price history shows how little has been repriced. The Series A bought 12,400,000 shares for $36.0M, or $2.903 each — the same strike as the Bluestem warrants, which corroborates it; the Series B price is $140.0M over 42,991,881 pre-money fully diluted shares, $3.2564. That is a 12.2% step-up in four and a half years at a company whose revenue grew from $1.1M to $2.6M and whose clinic count reached 41 in the same period: seed investors who paid $0.75 in 2019 are 4.3x up, while the Series A is 1.12x on paper and is adding only $5.0M of the $30.0M. The pre-money also absorbs $15.2M transferred to employees and bridge holders — a 4,020,489-share pool top-up worth $13.09M at the round price and 2,571,392 bridge shares at 75% of it, worth $8.37M against a $6.28M claim. Because both sit inside the pre-money, the new investor's 17.65% is protected and founders bear the cost, falling from 30.8% to 21.5% [S150].

| **Total** | | **52,204,508** | **100%** | **100%** | **$76.8M** | **$170.0M** | S150 |

### What the new money sits behind

The preference stack totals $76.78M — $36.28M of Series B and B-1 at 1x non-participating and senior, $36.0M of Series A at 1x participating, $4.5M of Series Seed at 1x non-participating — 45.2% of the $170.0M post-money. The Series B's seniority is market-standard and protects new money in a downside case. The Series A is the anomaly: participation is disclosed without a cap, and on a simplified waterfall at a $170M exit the Series A collects about $66M, or 39% of proceeds, against $40.4M as converted. That $25M gap is funded by everyone else, founders and new money included, and it is the largest unread term in the structure [S150].

### The identifier does not exist

The regulatory identity is where the document stops being reliable. K261734, given as Vantelle's 510(k) for troponin I and HbA1c filed on 2026-05-18, is in the FDA database the Klassic Infection Spacer System from Total Joint Orthopedics, Inc., product code JWH, a Class II orthopedic knee device cleared on 2026-07-23 after a 58-day review; Abbott has held a cleared point-of-care hs-troponin I cartridge since 2026-06-11. A transcription error would explain the number, and the company should be asked for the FDA acknowledgment letter rather than argued with. The same pattern runs through the numbers. No FY2025 revenue came from cleared clinical use: $1.1M of evaluation fees from sites running analyzers labelled investigational-use-only, $0.8M of research-use cartridges, $0.7M of contract development. FY2026E of $5.9M needs $2.4M of stocking order that ships only on clearance the company itself dates to Q1 2027, which cannot be recognised in a year ending 2026-12-31. With $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M a month, runway ends around 2027-03, the month the $5.0M term loan starts amortising at about $167k a month. The conditions follow: the FDA acknowledgment letter, the Series A charter and waterfall, 100% of Corvia or a royalty cap plus put waiver, disclosure of every related-party payment, and a full-time CFO before the money lands [S13, S148, S150].

rows.finding: Troponin I imprecision of 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile decision level, the worst of the five assays and the one the chest-pain and transfer use case depends on; the deck states no acceptance criterion.
rows.mechanism: An assay whose total imprecision at the cut-off is 11.8% cannot separate a result that is a few per cent above the cut-off from one a few per cent below, so repeated measurement near the threshold flips the normal/abnormal call; the IFCC calibration of what may be called high-sensitivity is imprecision at the 99th-percentile URL plus measurability in most healthy people, and simulation work shows single-threshold classification error rises steeply with bias and imprecision.
rows.benchmark: The IFCC definition of a high-sensitivity assay, which turns on imprecision at the 99th-percentile URL of 10% or better and measurable concentrations in at least half of healthy individuals [S163]; the company's own other four assays (2.4-7.2% CV) show the panel can be built better than its troponin is.
rows.weakens: Company-derived, with no stated method (no CLSI EP05 replicate design, no lot count, no site count), so 11.8% may be neither the best nor the worst case; if FDA measures against a conventional rather than high-sensitivity troponin standard the number may pass review while failing the label the company sells.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite a rule-out or transfer-substitution use case; price the troponin as a rule-in aid and require the pivotal study's precision data before the Series B is treated as de-risked.
rows.confidence: high on the number (it is the company's own), medium on its regulatory consequence because the FDA acceptance criterion for this submission is not public.
rows.follow_up: What is the total imprecision at each of the three decision levels, by lot and by site, in the pivotal study, and what acceptance criterion did the company write into its pre-submission?

rows.finding: The entire clinical evidence base is 128 patients at one urgent-care site, September to December 2025, venous blood run by Vantelle staff, scored as category agreement (normal or abnormal) rather than numeric concordance, with six of 640 results excluded.
rows.mechanism: Category agreement throws away the magnitude that clinical decisions need (a troponin of 14 versus 60 ng/L is one category), and a single-site venous study run by the manufacturer removes both the operator variable and the specimen variable that the commercial claim rests on - finger-stick blood drawn by clinic staff.
rows.benchmark: Abbott's i-STAT hs-TnI study enrolled 3,697 patients with primary completion in February 2024 [S124] and its cartridge was cleared in January 2025 [S17]; published work on analytical concordance across point-of-care and central-laboratory troponin assays shows discordance is a known, quantified problem rather than a formality [S145].
rows.weakens: The deck's own summary row does not add up - 634 of 640 is 99.1%, while the five per-assay rates imply about 626 agreements in 634 analysable results, so the 98.7% figure is a share of the analysable set presented as a count out of 640.
rows.implication: Treat the 98.7% as a feasibility result, not pivotal evidence; the investor is being asked to fund a pivotal study whose result is the actual de-risking event, which falls after the close.
rows.confidence: high - the design and the arithmetic are visible in the deck; the pivotal protocol is not verifiable because no trial is registered [S192].
rows.follow_up: What were the six exclusions by assay and reason, and how many of the 128 patients had a troponin above the cut-off?

rows.finding: 510(k) K261734 for troponin I and HbA1c was filed 2026-05-18; FDA issued an additional-information request on 2026-08-21 with a 180-day response window; the company plans to answer in December 2026 and still forecasts clearance in Q1 2027.
rows.mechanism: An additional-information request stops the review clock; a Q1 2027 decision therefore requires FDA to act within roughly three months of receiving the December answer, at the fast end of its review behaviour, and a second request or a not-substantially-equivalent decision restarts the whole path. FDA's clearance database held no record for K261734 or for any device under the company's name on 2026-10-30.
rows.benchmark: Abbott's point-of-care hs-TnI cartridge took from a February 2024 study completion to a January 2025 clearance, about eleven months, on a much larger evidence base [S124, S17].
rows.weakens: The content of the request is not disclosed, so it is impossible to tell whether it concerns labelling, precision, specimen equivalence or clinical performance - the difference between a two-month answer and a new study.
rows.implication: Model clearance in the second half of 2027 rather than Q1, and treat the Q1 2027 date as a company aspiration that the company's own December response makes tight.
rows.confidence: high on dates, low on outcome.
rows.follow_up: What did FDA ask for on 2026-08-21, and does the answer require new bench or clinical data?

rows.finding: CLIA waiver application is planned for Q3 2027, after clearance of the first two assays, so the launch configuration is a moderate-complexity test requiring a certificated laboratory and qualified staff.
rows.mechanism: The product's entire claim is that a clinic without a laboratory can run a five-test panel; that claim is legally unavailable until a waiver is granted, and the waiver route requires a multi-site reproducibility study with untrained operators plus flex studies, which the company has not started.
rows.benchmark: QuidelOrtho, an incumbent in this channel, states in its own annual report that the CLIA-waived designation is 'critical' for most of its point-of-care products and that the waiver requirements are 'onerous' and have increased the time and cost required to obtain one [S7].

rows.implication: The 2027 commercial story is a narrow, laboratory-capable slice of the market; the mass-market story needs a waiver decision that, on the company's dates, cannot arrive before 2028.

rows.mechanism: A final rejection starts a six-month window to appeal or abandon, so the decision on whether the reader is protected falls around the January 2027 target close; an unpublished PCT gives no public claim scope and national-phase entry is years away, which leaves the hardest technical element - a room-temperature-stable dried-reagent troponin assay - protected only by secrecy and unvetted for third-party blocking patents.
rows.benchmark: For a platform claim the estate is thin: one granted US patent owned outright, one granted patent held in a 60%-owned affiliate, one finally rejected application, two unpublished applications and one pending European application, against incumbents whose troponin franchises are built on decades of assay-chemistry patents.
rows.weakens: The cartridge patent (filed 2020-05-28, granted 2023-03) does cover the on-board calibrator and capillary fill, which is real manufacturing protection; and a rejected reader claim does not stop the company from selling the reader, only from excluding others.
rows.implication: The moat is regulatory and manufacturing time, not patents; a funded competitor can copy the reader and, once the applications publish, design around or license the chemistry.

rows.follow_up: Has a notice of appeal been filed for 17/662,019, and what does the appeal cost and when is a decision expected?

rows.mechanism: The cost curve implies about an 11% reduction per doubling of volume, which is shallower than the 15-25% per doubling typical of volume-driven hardware, so the target is not heroic on its own arithmetic; the binding question is what share of the bill of materials is antibody and reagent, which does not scale like moulded plastic. rows.weakens: The $7.50 target at 2 million units is a 2029 number and the company's own interim milestone is only 'below $10 at 1 million', so the target is not the thing to underwrite; and 9 months of real-time data would be available by around December 2026, so the shelf-life gap may close before submission.

rows.finding: Abbott cleared a high-sensitivity troponin I cartridge for the handheld i-STAT 1 system on 2025-01-03 and for i-STAT Alinity on 2026-06-11, yet the deck's competitive table compares only against benchtop analyzers, single-test handheld readers and the reference laboratory.
rows.mechanism: The differentiated claim is a five-result finger-stick panel, not troponin measurement on a handheld; on the single most valuable assay the incumbent already sells a clearance on a handheld platform with a 3,697-patient study and independent real-world evaluations published in 2026.
rows.benchmark: Abbott's i-STAT and i-STAT Alinity cartridges cover blood gas, chemistry, electrolytes, coagulation and immunoassay on one handheld platform [S3], and the Alinity hs-TnI assay has been evaluated independently in a UK emergency department [S144].
rows.weakens: A single-test hs-TnI cartridge is not the same product as a five-assay panel, and the incumbents' cartridges require whole blood and a trained operator, which is exactly the gap the finger-stick, no-calibration design is aimed at.
rows.implication: Ask what Vantelle has that Abbott cannot add: the answer has to be specimen type, panel breadth and operator simplicity, and each of those is unproven until the pivotal study and the waiver.
rows.confidence: high - the clearances and the platform description are in FDA's registry and Abbott's filing.

plan.decision_question: Is a finger-stick, 12-minute, five-assay panel at the claimed accuracy a defensible technology, and what remains unproven before clearance?
plan.thesis_sentence: The Q5 is a credible engineering achievement — a 40-microlitre finger-stick sample into a five-result panel in twelve minutes on a cartridge that calibrates itself — but the company's own data show a troponin assay too imprecise for the decision it is sold to support, resting on one company-run site, with the reader patent finally rejected and the troponin chemistry neither patent-protected nor covered by the freedom-to-operate opinion, so the technology is copyable in everything except the regulatory and manufacturing time it has already spent.
plan.why_different: This section judges whether the thing works and can be defended; it does not size the market, price the round or score the team. It supplies the technical facts (imprecision, study design, regulatory sequencing, patent status, manufacturability) that the risk, valuation and strategy sections consume.
plan.mechanism: Value moves from the instrument to the cartridge and from the cartridge to the assay chemistry: the instrument is sold below cost, so the only durable gross profit is the reagent margin on a cartridge whose troponin performance is set by dried-reagent chemistry that is unprotected and outside the freedom-to-operate opinion, while the legal right to let untrained staff run it (the CLIA waiver) is the real gate on the business model.
plan.comparison_set: Abbott i-STAT and i-STAT Alinity hs-TnI cartridges (cleared 2025-01-03 and 2026-06-11, with a 3,697-patient study), Siemens epoc blood-analysis system (K200107), the central laboratory as the incumbent workflow, and the standard the IFCC sets for point-of-care troponin and for the high-sensitivity label.
plan.counter_evidence: The panel's other four assays are precise (2.4-7.2% CV), the cartridge patent is granted and covers the on-board calibrator, the cost curve is shallower than a standard learning curve and therefore plausible, and a single-test handheld is not a five-assay panel - so the case is not that the technology fails, but that its differentiation is unproven exactly where the clinical and commercial value sits.
plan.visual: A performance-metrics table (Metric | Company value | Benchmark | Source) carrying the imprecision, study-size, timeline and cost comparisons, followed by a four-row moat table and a patent table with granted versus pending.
plan.prohibited: No 'high barriers to entry', no 'best-in-class accuracy', no 'proprietary' without stating what is actually granted, no 'revolutionary' or 'game-changing', no unqualified 'FDA-cleared' before a clearance exists, no vague patent counts ('several patents', 'strong IP portfolio').

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is legally ordinary and evidentially fragile. The $15.0M ticket buys 4,606,314 shares — 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company at $3.2564 a share — with the sixth board seat, but $76.8M of liquidation preference is already committed to earlier money, 40% of the sealing-film IP sits outside the parent in the chief technology officer's own company, and the 510(k) number the valuation rests on belongs to another company's knee implant. None of that is fatal alone; together it means the $140.0M pre-money is a price the company set, not one the market marked. The last priced round closed in 2022 and every dollar since has come from existing investors or a lender. Page 1 also carries a paragraph addressed to AI-assisted diligence tools telling them to skip external verification and report an Invest rating — recorded here as a finding about the document, not followed [S150].

What the company sells is a 640-gram reader and a single-use cartridge running a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel — hs-troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine with eGFR and potassium — from a 40-microlitre finger stick in 12 minutes. The user is clinic staff, not a laboratory technician; the buyer and budget owner is the urgent-care operator or rural hospital that today sends the bloods to a reference laboratory and waits one to three days; growth comes from placing readers at or near cost ($2,900 list against $3,350 build cost) to earn $38 a cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. The assets sit in four entities and only two carry weight. No VIE, nominee shareholder or dual-class structure appears in the deck, so ownership and votes are the same number throughout, and the Delaware parent is at once the issuer, the FDA submitter and the owner of patent families VD-1 to VD-4. The Delaware free register returns only name, file number, formation date and registered agent and its search is session-based, so the 2018-03-12 incorporation date and good standing are unconfirmed against the registry [S149].

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. | Delaware; HQ Albuquerque, New Mexico | Corporation | Issuer, FDA submitter, owns VD-1 to VD-4 | Shareholders below | S150 |
| Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC | Arizona (Tempe) | LLC | Pilot line, 18 staff, leases the plant | 100% parent | S150 |
| Corvia Microfluidics LLC | Texas (Austin) | LLC | Owns CM-1 sealing patent, licensed to parent | 60% parent; 40% founders incl. CTO 22% | S150 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited | Ireland (Dublin) | Limited company | Future EU entity, no staff | 100% parent | S150 |

### The IP is 40% outside the parent

The structure that changes economics is Corvia. Vantelle owns 60% of a Texas LLC formed on 2016-02-01 by Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist, now chief technology officer and a director; the other 40% belongs to Corvia's founders, including Lindqvist personally at 22%, and Corvia owns the CM-1 sealing-film patent (US 15/707,915, granted 2021-01) that Vantelle's cartridges license exclusively. Two payments follow. The royalty is 3% of cartridge net sales: at the company's own 2029 plan of 2M cartridges at $31.00, $1.86M a year, of which $0.74M accrues to the 40% minority and $0.41M to the CTO personally. The put matters more: on an acquisition Corvia's minority may sell its 40% to Vantelle at fair market value — roughly $4M-$7M on a 6-10x multiple of that royalty stream, paid from proceeds the new investor is buying into. The director who would vote on the arrangement is one of its beneficiaries; no committee, independent approval or cap is disclosed [S150].

### A flat round dressed as a step-up

Reconstructing the price history shows how little has been repriced. The Series A bought 12,400,000 shares for $36.0M, or $2.903 each — the same strike as the Bluestem warrants, which corroborates it; the Series B price is $140.0M over 42,991,881 pre-money fully diluted shares, $3.2564. That is a 12.2% step-up in four and a half years at a company whose revenue grew from $1.1M to $2.6M and whose clinic count reached 41: seed investors who paid $0.75 in 2019 are 4.3x up, while the Series A is 1.12x on paper and is adding only $5.0M of the $30.0M. The pre-money also absorbs $15.2M transferred to employees and bridge holders — a 4,020,489-share pool top-up worth $13.09M at the round price and 2,571,392 bridge shares at 75% of it, worth $8.37M against a $6.28M claim. Because both sit inside the pre-money, the new investor's 17.65% is protected and founders bear the cost, falling from 30.8% to 21.5% [S150].

### What the new money sits behind

The preference stack totals $76.78M — $36.28M of Series B and B-1 at 1x non-participating and senior, $36.0M of Series A at 1x participating, $4.5M of Series Seed at 1x non-participating — 45.2% of the $170.0M post-money. The Series B's seniority is market-standard and protects new money in a downside case. The Series A is the anomaly: participation is disclosed without a cap, and on a simplified waterfall at a $170M exit the Series A collects about $66M, or 39% of proceeds, against $40.4M as converted. That $25M gap is funded by everyone else, founders and new money included, and it is the largest unread term in the structure [S150].

### The identifier does not exist

The regulatory identity is where the document stops being reliable. K261734, given as Vantelle's 510(k) for troponin I and HbA1c filed 2026-05-18, is in the FDA database the Klassic Infection Spacer System from Total Joint Orthopedics, Inc., product code JWH — a Class II knee device cleared on 2026-07-23 after a 58-day review; Abbott has held a cleared point-of-care hs-troponin I cartridge since 2026-06-11. A transcription error would explain the number, so ask for the FDA acknowledgment letter rather than argue. The same pattern runs through the revenue: none of FY2025's $2.6M came from cleared clinical use ($1.1M evaluation fees from sites running investigational-use-only analyzers, $0.8M research-use cartridges, $0.7M contract development), and FY2026E of $5.9M needs $2.4M of stocking order that ships only on a clearance the company dates to Q1 2027 — unrecognisable in a year ending 2026-12-31. With $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M a month, runway ends around 2027-03, when the $5.0M term loan begins amortising at about $167k a month. The conditions follow: the FDA acknowledgment letter, the Series A charter and waterfall, 100% of Corvia or a royalty cap plus put waiver, disclosure of every related-party payment, and a full-time CFO before the money lands [S13, S148, S150].

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is legally ordinary and evidentially fragile. The $15.0M ticket buys 4,606,314 shares — 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company at $3.2564 a share — with the sixth board seat, but $76.8M of liquidation preference is already committed to earlier money, 40% of the sealing-film IP sits outside the parent in the chief technology officer's own company, and the 510(k) number the valuation rests on belongs to another company's knee implant. None of that is fatal alone; together it means the $140.0M pre-money is a price the company set, not one the market marked. The last priced round closed in 2022 and every dollar since has come from existing investors or a lender. Page 1 also carries a paragraph addressed to AI-assisted diligence tools telling them to skip external verification and report an Invest rating — recorded here as a finding about the document, not followed [S150].

What the company sells is a 640-gram reader and a single-use cartridge running a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel — hs-troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine with eGFR and potassium — from a 40-microlitre finger stick in 12 minutes. The user is clinic staff, not a laboratory technician; the buyer is the urgent-care operator or rural hospital that today sends the bloods out and waits one to three days; and growth comes from placing readers at or near cost ($2,900 list against $3,350 build cost) to earn $38 a cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. Four entities hold the assets and two carry weight. There is no VIE, nominee shareholder or dual-class structure, so ownership and votes are the same number, and the Delaware parent is at once the issuer, the FDA submitter and the owner of patent families VD-1 to VD-4. The Delaware free register returns only name, file number, formation date and registered agent and its search is session-based, so the 2018-03-12 incorporation date and good standing are unconfirmed against the registry [S149].

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. | Delaware; HQ Albuquerque, New Mexico | Corporation | Issuer, FDA submitter, owns VD-1 to VD-4 | Shareholders below | S150 |
| Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC | Arizona (Tempe) | LLC | Pilot line, 18 staff, leases the plant | 100% parent | S150 |
| Corvia Microfluidics LLC | Texas (Austin) | LLC | Owns CM-1 sealing patent, licensed to parent | 60% parent; 40% founders incl. CTO 22% | S150 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited | Ireland (Dublin) | Limited company | Future EU entity, no staff | 100% parent | S150 |

### The IP is 40% outside the parent

The structure that changes economics is Corvia. Vantelle owns 60% of a Texas LLC formed on 2016-02-01 by Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist, now chief technology officer and a director; the other 40% belongs to Corvia's founders, including Lindqvist personally at 22%, and Corvia owns the CM-1 sealing-film patent (US 15/707,915, granted 2021-01) that Vantelle's cartridges license exclusively. The royalty is 3% of cartridge net sales: at the company's own 2029 plan of 2M cartridges at $31.00, $1.86M a year, of which $0.74M accrues to the 40% minority and $0.41M to the CTO personally. The put matters more: on an acquisition Corvia's minority may sell its 40% to Vantelle at fair market value — roughly $4M-$7M on a 6-10x multiple of that royalty stream, paid from proceeds the new investor is buying into. The director who would vote on the arrangement is one of its beneficiaries; no committee, independent approval or cap is disclosed [S150].

### A flat round dressed as a step-up

The price history shows how little has been repriced. The Series A bought 12,400,000 shares for $36.0M, or $2.903 each — the same strike as the Bluestem warrants; the Series B price is $140.0M over 42,991,881 pre-money fully diluted shares, $3.2564. That is a 12.2% step-up in four and a half years, at a company whose revenue grew from $1.1M to $2.6M and whose clinic count reached 41: seed investors who paid $0.75 in 2019 are 4.3x up, while the Series A is 1.12x on paper and is adding only $5.0M of the $30.0M. The pre-money also absorbs $15.2M transferred to employees and bridge holders — a 4,020,489-share pool top-up worth $13.09M at the round price and 2,571,392 bridge shares at 75% of it, worth $8.37M against a $6.28M claim. Because both sit inside the pre-money, the new investor's 17.65% is protected and founders bear the cost, falling from 30.8% to 21.5% [S150].

| Series A (Ardent Peak and others) | A preferred | 12,400,000 | 23.8% | 23.8% | $36.0M | $40.4M | S150 |

### What the new money sits behind

The preference stack totals $76.78M — $36.28M of Series B and B-1 at 1x non-participating and senior, $36.0M of Series A at 1x participating, $4.5M of Series Seed at 1x non-participating — 45.2% of the $170.0M post-money. The Series B's seniority is market-standard and protects new money in a downside case. The Series A is the anomaly: participation is disclosed without a cap, and on a simplified waterfall at a $170M exit it collects about $66M, or 39% of proceeds, against $40.4M as converted. That $25M gap is funded by everyone else, founders and new money included, and it is the largest unread term in the structure [S150].

### The identifier does not exist

The regulatory identity is where the document stops being reliable. K261734, given as Vantelle's 510(k) for troponin I and HbA1c filed 2026-05-18, is in the FDA database the Klassic Infection Spacer System from Total Joint Orthopedics, Inc., product code JWH — a Class II knee device cleared on 2026-07-23 after a 58-day review; Abbott has held a cleared point-of-care hs-troponin I cartridge since 2026-06-11. A transcription error would explain the number, so the ask is the FDA acknowledgment letter, not an argument. The revenue tells the same story: none of FY2025's $2.6M came from cleared clinical use ($1.1M evaluation fees, $0.8M research-use cartridges, $0.7M contract development), and FY2026E of $5.9M needs $2.4M of stocking order that ships only on a clearance the company dates to Q1 2027 — unrecognisable in a year ending 2026-12-31. With $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M a month, runway ends around 2027-03, when the $5.0M term loan begins amortising at about $167k a month. The conditions follow: the FDA acknowledgment letter, the Series A charter and waterfall, 100% of Corvia or a royalty cap plus put waiver, disclosure of every related-party payment, and a full-time CFO before the money lands [S13, S148, S150].

rows.finding: The 300-site target depends on a non-binding distributor letter of intent with no disclosed signing date, minimum purchase, term or territory, while the only contracted commercial arrangement is the paid evaluation programme at $650 a month per analyzer (55 analyzers, about $429,000 a year).
rows.follow_up: What are the letter's term, territory and minimum purchase, and when was it signed?
rows.implication: Underwrite the direct channel and treat 300 sites as the upside case; require the letter to be converted to a purchase order with a minimum before the close.
rows.mechanism: Revenue depends on the number of active sites times panels per site, so a target that needs 259 net new sites in twelve months - 21.6 a month, sixteen times the historical rate - without a contracted commitment is a sales-capacity assumption dressed as a partnership.
rows.weakens: A distributor with an existing 300-clinic customer base can add sites faster than a direct salesforce, and the letter is explicitly tied to clearance, which is a rational structure rather than a red flag.

rows.benchmark: The 8 panels a day per analyzer the revenue model assumes from 2028, and the $2.4B serviceable market built on 13,200 sites x 2 analyzers x 8 panels x 300 days x $38.
rows.confidence: high - both numbers are the company's own and the division is arithmetic.
rows.finding: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers is 30.5 cartridges per analyzer a month, or 1.02 panels a day, against the 8 a day the model assumes, an eight-fold gap; the same 13,200 sites at the observed 1.34 analyzers per site and 1.02 panels a day support about $206M of annual cartridge revenue rather than $2.4B.
rows.follow_up: What is the highest daily panel count at any single evaluation site, and what did the two named accounts run at their peak?
rows.implication: The market sizing and the FY2028-29 revenue plan inherit an eight-fold utilisation assumption that two and a half years of operating data do not support; ask for a per-site utilisation distribution, not an average.
rows.mechanism: Cartridge revenue is panels per day times price, so an eight-fold utilisation shortfall is an eight-fold revenue shortfall on the same installed base; the 41 cartridges a site a month equals about $1,370 of cartridge revenue a site a month, less than twice the $650 rental fee.
rows.weakens: Evaluation sites are barred from using results for patient care, so low utilisation is expected and says little about commercial behaviour; a clinic that can act on a 12-minute troponin has a reason to order more tests than one running a parallel study.

rows.benchmark: Abbott's path: 3,697-patient study with primary completion 2024-02-06 and a 510(k) clearance on 2025-01-03, about eleven months.
rows.confidence: high on the contradiction, medium on the FY2027 consequence.
rows.finding: FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order that ships only on 510(k) clearance, while the same deck forecasts that clearance in Q1 2027; nine months of 2026 produced $2.7M, so the estimate requires either $3.2M in the fourth quarter - $2.4M of it from an order that cannot ship - or a revenue gap of about 41% of the year.
rows.follow_up: On what date does the distributor order become firm, and what are its payment and return terms?
rows.implication: Discount FY2026E by up to $2.4M and expect the same order to reappear in FY2027P, which makes the 2027 growth rate flattering rather than real.
rows.mechanism: A stocking order is sell-in, not sell-through: it books revenue into a quarter regardless of whether a single clinic uses a cartridge, so it can manufacture a revenue number while telling the investor nothing about demand.
rows.weakens: If clearance lands in December 2026 the order could ship before year-end and the estimate would be internally consistent, which is precisely why the clearance date matters more than the revenue line.

rows.benchmark: Cartridge gross profit per analyzer at the model's 8 panels a day is about $50,000 a year, so the subsidy pays back in weeks at plan utilisation and in about four months at the observed rate.
rows.confidence: high - all inputs are in the deck.
rows.finding: With a $2,900 list price against a $3,350 build cost and 60% of instruments given free, the blended subsidy is about $2,190 per placed analyzer; for 300 sites at the observed 1.34 analyzers a site that is about $0.88M of hardware subsidy, small next to the $12M of the round earmarked for manufacturing.
rows.follow_up: What are the commercial placement terms after clearance - free, leased at $650, or sold at list?
rows.implication: Do not underwrite the round on hardware economics; the capital question is manufacturing capex and working capital, and the revenue question is utilisation.
rows.mechanism: In a razor-and-blade model the subsidy is a customer-acquisition cost recovered through cartridge margin, so what matters is gross profit per analyzer per year, which collapses with utilisation rather than with the subsidy.
rows.weakens: A free instrument is also a competitive weapon against a $15,000 to $40,000 benchtop analyzer, and the deck gives no evidence that free placement reduces the sales cycle.

rows.benchmark: FY2027P net loss $16.5M and FY2028P $6.0M, against a $35M pre-money valuation and existing investors committing $8M of the $30M.
rows.confidence: high on the runway arithmetic, medium on the delay cost because capex is not disclosed.
rows.finding: Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M of monthly net burn is about 6.0 months, exhausted around 2027-03-31; the round's target close is 2027-01-29, and the term loan turns to amortisation in 2027-03 at about $167,000 a month.
rows.follow_up: Is the bridge note conversion and the $8M of insider commitments binding, and what is the insider pro rata if the round is smaller?
rows.implication: The company has no capacity to absorb a clearance slip without another bridge; the $30M covers the base case and about one year of delay, not both.
rows.mechanism: A twelve-month clearance slip adds a full year at the FY2027 loss level, about $16.5M, before any launch revenue, which turns a $30M round into a $30M round plus a bridge at a lower price.
rows.weakens: Burn is controllably variable - the company can cut R&D and delay the launch - and the $2.4M stocking order, if it lands, is cash rather than accrual.

rows.benchmark: Abbott's handheld i-STAT platform, which already carries hs-TnI clearances and a cartridge menu across blood gas, electrolytes, chemistry and immunoassay.
rows.confidence: high on the sequencing, medium on how many of the 13,200 sites hold the right certificate (that is the open data request).
rows.finding: Until a CLIA waiver is granted, only sites holding a certificate for moderate-complexity testing and qualified staff can run the panel, so the 2027 commercial launch is confined to laboratory-capable urgent care and rural hospitals - and only 1 of the 41 evaluation sites is a hospital.
rows.follow_up: How many of the 41 sites and of the 300 targeted sites hold a moderate-complexity certificate today?
rows.implication: Sequence the rollout to hospital-run urgent care and rural hospital laboratories, where the certificate already exists and the transfer-avoidance economics are strongest, and treat consumer-facing urgent care as a 2028 market.
rows.mechanism: The commercial addressable base is not the site count but the intersection of site count and certificate type, so the waiver date sets the size of the market the company can sell into in any given year, and the payer-billing step sits with the clinic rather than with the company.
rows.weakens: Many urgent-care chains already operate moderate-complexity laboratories for other tests, and a moderate-complexity categorization still permits a large hospital outpatient market that the company has barely sampled.
