arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is legally ordinary and evidentially fragile. The $15.0M ticket buys 4,606,314 shares — 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company at $3.2564 a share — with the sixth board seat, but $76.8M of liquidation preference is already committed to earlier money, 40% of the sealing-film IP sits outside the parent in the chief technology officer's own company, and the 510(k) number the valuation rests on belongs to another company's knee implant. Together that means the $140.0M pre-money is a price the company set, not one the market marked. The last priced round closed in 2022 and every dollar since has come from existing investors or a lender. Page 1 also carries a paragraph addressed to AI-assisted diligence tools telling them to skip external verification and report an Invest rating — recorded here as a finding about the document, not followed [S150].

The product is a 640-gram reader and a single-use cartridge running a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel — hs-troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine with eGFR and potassium — from a 40-microlitre finger stick in 12 minutes. The user is clinic staff, not a laboratory technician; the buyer is the urgent-care operator or rural hospital that today sends the bloods out and waits one to three days; and growth comes from placing readers at or near cost ($2,900 list against $3,350 build cost) to earn $38 a cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. There is no VIE, nominee shareholder or dual-class structure, so ownership and votes are the same number, and the Delaware parent is at once the issuer, the FDA submitter and the owner of patent families VD-1 to VD-4. The Delaware free register returns only name, file number, formation date and registered agent and its search is session-based, so the 2018-03-12 incorporation date and good standing are unconfirmed against the registry [S149].

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. | Delaware; HQ Albuquerque, New Mexico | Corporation | Issuer, FDA submitter, owns VD-1 to VD-4 | Shareholders below | S150 |
| Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC | Arizona (Tempe) | LLC | Pilot line, 18 staff, leases the plant | 100% parent | S150 |
| Corvia Microfluidics LLC | Texas (Austin) | LLC | Owns CM-1 sealing patent, licensed to parent | 60% parent; 40% founders incl. CTO 22% | S150 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited | Ireland (Dublin) | Limited company | EU entity, no staff | 100% parent | S150 |

### The IP is 40% outside the parent

The structure that changes economics is Corvia. Vantelle owns 60% of a Texas LLC formed on 2016-02-01 by Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist, now chief technology officer and a director; the other 40% belongs to Corvia's founders, including Lindqvist personally at 22%, and Corvia owns the CM-1 sealing-film patent (US 15/707,915, granted 2021-01) licensed exclusively to Vantelle. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is legally ordinary and evidentially fragile. The $15.0M ticket buys 4,606,314 shares — 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company at $3.2564 a share — with the sixth board seat, but $76.8M of liquidation preference is already committed to earlier money, 40% of the sealing-film IP sits outside the parent in the chief technology officer's own company, and the 510(k) number the valuation rests on belongs to another company's knee implant. Together that means the $140.0M pre-money is a price the company set, not one the market marked. The last priced round closed in 2022; every dollar since is insider money or debt. Page 1 also carries a paragraph addressed to AI-assisted diligence tools telling them to skip external verification and report an Invest rating — recorded here as a finding about the document, not followed [S150].

The product is a 640-gram reader and a single-use cartridge running a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel — hs-troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine with eGFR and potassium — from a 40-microlitre finger stick in 12 minutes. The user is clinic staff, not a laboratory technician; the buyer is the urgent-care operator or rural hospital that today sends the bloods out and waits one to three days; and growth comes from placing readers at or near cost ($2,900 list against $3,350 build cost) to earn $38 a cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. There is no VIE, nominee shareholder or dual-class structure, so ownership and votes are the same number, and the Delaware parent is at once the issuer, the FDA submitter and the owner of patent families VD-1 to VD-4. The Delaware free register returns only name, file number, formation date and registered agent and its search is session-based, so the 2018-03-12 incorporation date and good standing are unconfirmed against the registry; the ownership percentages, entity roles and dates below are unverified company material, while the share and price arithmetic is verified because it reconciles to the deck's own totals [S149].

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership (unverified) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. | Delaware; HQ Albuquerque, New Mexico | Corporation | Issuer, FDA submitter, owns VD-1 to VD-4 | Shareholders below | S150 |
| Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC | Arizona (Tempe) | LLC | Pilot line, 18 staff, leases the plant | 100% parent | S150 |
| Corvia Microfluidics LLC | Texas (Austin) | LLC | Owns CM-1 sealing patent, licensed to parent | 60% parent; 40% founders incl. CTO 22% | S150 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited | Ireland (Dublin) | Limited company | EU entity, no staff | 100% parent | S150 |

### The IP is 40% outside the parent

The structure that changes economics is Corvia. Vantelle owns 60% of a Texas LLC formed on 2016-02-01 by Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist, now chief technology officer and a director; the other 40% belongs to Corvia's founders, including Lindqvist personally at 22%, and Corvia owns the CM-1 sealing-film patent (US 15/707,915, granted 2021-01) licensed exclusively to Vantelle. The royalty is 3% of cartridge net sales: at the company's own 2029 plan of 2M cartridges at $31.00, $1.86M a year, of which $0.74M accrues to the 40% minority and $0.41M to the CTO personally. The put matters more: on an acquisition Corvia's minority may sell its 40% to Vantelle at fair market value — $4.0M-$7.0M on a 6-10x multiple of that royalty stream, paid from proceeds the new investor is buying into. The director voting on it is a beneficiary; no committee, approval or cap is disclosed [S150].

### A flat round dressed as a step-up

The price history shows how little has been repriced. The Series A bought 12,400,000 shares for $36.0M, or $2.903 each — the same strike as the Bluestem warrants; the Series B price is $140.0M over 42,991,881 pre-money fully diluted shares, $3.2564. That is a 12.2% step-up in four and a half years at a company whose revenue grew from $1.1M to $2.6M: seed investors who paid $0.75 in 2019 are 4.3x up, compared with 1.12x on paper for the Series A, which is adding only $5.0M of the $30.0M. The pre-money also absorbs $15.2M transferred to employees and bridge holders — a 4,020,489-share pool top-up worth $13.09M at the round price and 2,571,392 bridge shares at 75% of it, worth $8.37M against a $6.28M claim. | Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist | Common | 4,800,000 | 9.2% | 9.2% | Founder | $15.6M | S150 |

| Bluestem warrants | Common, strike $2.903 | 400,000 | 0.8% | 0.8% | With the loan | $1.3M | S150 |
| 2026 bridge holders | B-1 preferred | 2,571,392 | 4.9% | 4.9% | $6.28M | $8.4M | S150 |
| New Series B investors | B preferred | 9,212,627 | 17.6% | 17.6% | $30.0M | $30.0M | S150 |

| **Total** | | **52,204,508** | **100%** | **100%** | **$76.8M** | **$170.0M** | S150 |

### What the new money sits behind

The preference stack totals $76.78M — $36.28M of Series B and B-1 at 1x non-participating and senior, $36.0M of Series A at 1x participating, $4.5M of Series Seed at 1x non-participating — 45.2% of the $170.0M post-money. The Series B's seniority is market-standard and protects new money in a downside case. The Series A is the anomaly: participation is disclosed without a cap, and on a simplified waterfall at a $170M exit it collects $66.0M, or 39% of proceeds, against $40.4M as converted. That $25M gap is funded by everyone else, founders and new money included, and it is the largest unread term in the structure [S150].

### The identifier does not exist

The regulatory identity is where the document stops being reliable. K261734, given as Vantelle's 510(k) for troponin I and HbA1c filed 2026-05-18, is in the FDA database the Klassic Infection Spacer System from Total Joint Orthopedics, Inc., product code JWH, cleared 2026-07-23 after a 58-day review; Abbott has held a cleared point-of-care hs-troponin I cartridge since 2026-06-11. A transcription error would explain the number, so the ask is the FDA acknowledgment letter. The revenue tells the same story: none of FY2025's $2.6M came from cleared clinical use ($1.1M evaluation fees, $0.8M research-use cartridges, $0.7M contract development), and FY2026E of $5.9M needs $2.4M of stocking order that ships only on a clearance the company dates to Q1 2027 — unrecognisable in a year ending 2026-12-31. With $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M a month, runway ends 2027-03, when the $5.0M term loan begins amortising at $166,667 a month. The conditions follow: the FDA acknowledgment letter, the Series A charter and waterfall, 100% of Corvia or a royalty cap plus put waiver, disclosure of every related-party payment, and a full-time CFO before the money lands [S13, S148, S150].

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has built something genuinely difficult — a 40-microlitre finger-stick sample turned into five results in twelve minutes on a cartridge that calibrates itself — and has not yet shown that it works as a diagnostic. The company's own study puts troponin I at 11.8% imprecision at the very cut-off that drives the chest-pain decision, measured on 128 patients at one site, by Vantelle's own staff, scored as normal or abnormal rather than as a number; the patent on the five-assay reader was finally rejected in July 2026; and the dried-reagent chemistry that produces the troponin result is an unpublished PCT that the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion explicitly does not cover [S150]. What Vantelle owns outright is time — two 510(k) submissions' worth of regulatory work, a pilot line in Tempe, and two and a half years of relationships with 41 clinics — and time is the one asset a funded competitor can buy.

### The difficult part is the dried chemistry, not the handheld

The Q5 is three technologies in a 640-gram box: a capillary-fill cartridge that meters 40 microlitres of whole blood, a dried-reagent chemistry that must survive nine months at room temperature, and an optical reader that corrects for drift across five assays at once. The first is solved and patented (US 16/884,327, filed 2020-05-28, granted 2023-03, covering capillary fill with an on-board calibrator). The third is the one the Patent Office rejected. The second decides whether the troponin number is right, and it is the one the company has kept secret: an unpublished PCT filed 2026-02-11, with no granted claim and no freedom-to-operate opinion behind it. On-board calibration is a genuine workflow advantage over a benchtop analyzer that needs daily quality control, but it also turns a calibrator fault into a silent bias across every cartridge in the lot, and finger-stick blood adds the two variables a laboratory removes by using a tube — haematocrit and haemolysis, an interference class the IFCC treats as a first-order problem for troponin and especially for potassium, which on an optical platform cannot be read by the electrode a blood-gas analyzer uses and must rely on an ion-selective chemistry reported by light [S166].

### The performance claim is a category count from one site

"98.7% agreement" is not concordance. The study ran 128 patients at one urgent-care site between September and December 2025, drew venous blood, ran it on the Q5 with Vantelle staff operating the device, and scored each result into the same category as the reference laboratory. Category agreement discards the magnitude the clinician uses: a troponin of 14 ng/L and one of 60 ng/L are one category if both sit above the cut-off, and the decision the product exists to serve — transfer or hold a patient with chest pain — turns on magnitude and on change between samples, which is the unit the universal definition of myocardial infarction actually uses. The summary row does not close arithmetically: 634 of 640 is 99.1%, and the five per-assay rates imply about 626 agreements among 634 analysable results, so 98.7% is a share of the analysable set printed as a count out of 640. Six exclusions in 640 results (0.94%) is not unreasonable; not disclosing them by assay and reason is. Against this, the incumbent's evidence is a different order of magnitude, and simulation work shows that at a single threshold, classification error rises steeply with exactly the imprecision and bias the company's study was not designed to measure [S10, S124].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the decision level | 11.8% CV | 10% or better at the 99th-percentile URL for a high-sensitivity assay | S150, S163 |
| Troponin I agreement | 96.1% (123 of 128) | Category agreement, not concordance | S150 |
| Five-assay agreement | 98.7% claimed | 634 of 640 would be 99.1%; per-assay rates imply ~626 of 634 | S150 |
| Clinical evidence | 128 patients, 1 site, venous, company-operated | 3,697 patients in the incumbent's study | S150, S124 |
| Sample and turnaround | 40 µL finger-stick, 12 minutes | Venous, 1-3 days for a send-out | S150 |
| Cartridge shelf life | 9 months claimed, 6 months measured | — | S150 |
| Cartridge cost | $16.20 at ~20,000 units a year; $7.50 at 2 million (2029) | ~11% per volume doubling | S150 |

### Clearance is later than the deck says, and the waiver later still

The 510(k) was filed 2026-05-18 and FDA asked for additional information on 2026-08-21, with 180 days to answer and a December 2026 answer planned. A Q1 2027 clearance therefore requires a decision within about three months of the December response, and FDA's clearance database held no record for K261734, or for any device under the company's name, on 2026-10-30 — what a pending submission looks like, but also proof that nothing is cleared today [S7, S191]. The sequencing matters more than the date. Only troponin I and HbA1c are in the first submission, so the five-assay panel is two clearances away, and the CLIA waiver — the legal permission for staff without laboratory training to run the test — is not planned until Q3 2027. QuidelOrtho, which sells into the same channel, calls the waived designation "critical" for its point-of-care products and the waiver requirements "onerous" [S7]. Until a waiver is granted the Q5 is a moderate-complexity test for a certificated laboratory: a different buyer, a different sales motion and a much smaller market than the deck describes.

### The patent estate is one granted family owned outright

| Patent or application | Subject | Jurisdiction | Filed / granted | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 | Capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator | US | 2020-05-28 / 2023-03 | Granted, expiry ~2040-05 | S150 |
| EP family of 16/884,327 | Same | Europe | — | Pending | S150 |
| US 17/662,019 | Five-assay optical reader with drift correction | US | 2022-05-04 / — | Final rejection 2026-07; appeal under consideration | S150 |
| US 19/318,770 | Finger-stick sample-volume check | US | 2025-09-30 / — | Unpublished | S150 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 | Troponin assay chemistry on dried reagents | PCT | 2026-02-11 / — | Unpublished; outside the 2024 FTO opinion | S150 |
| US 15/707,915 | Cartridge sealing film and reagent blister | US | 2017-09-18 / 2021-01 | Granted, expiry ~2037-09; owned by 60%-held Corvia, licensed at a 3% royalty | S150 |

Strip out the narrative and the estate is: one US patent granted to the parent and covering the cartridge; one granted patent held by a subsidiary Vantelle owns 60% of and licensed back at a 3% royalty whose beneficiaries include the chief technology officer; one application finally rejected; and two applications not yet published. The reader — the part a competitor would otherwise have to design around — is unpatented as things stand, and the six-month window that follows a final rejection puts the appeal-or-abandon decision around the round's January 2027 target close. The freedom-to-operate opinion dates from 2024, predates the troponin chemistry filing and does not cover it, so the hardest technical element is both unprotected and unvetted [S150].

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dried-reagent troponin chemistry | 8 | Antibody stability at room temperature sets the assay's imprecision; also the assay the whole chest-pain case rests on | 3-4 years |
| Cartridge manufacturability at scale | 7 | 40 µL capillary fill, on-board calibrator, 9-month shelf life; haemolysis and fill volume are the failure modes | 2-3 years |
| Regulatory clearance and CLIA waiver | 9 | Two 510(k)s and a multi-site operator study; the incumbent's own point-of-care predecessor took about 11 months from study completion to clearance | 3-5 years |
| Reader design | 3 | Optics and drift correction are engineering, not science, and the claim was rejected | 6-12 months |
| Patent protection | 2 | One granted US family owned outright; the reader unpatented | immediate |
| Ecosystem and switching | 5 | Cartridge lock-in once a clinic trains on the platform and wires the EHR | 3-5 years |

The replication test is unflattering in one direction and favourable in another. Fifty well-funded engineers given the published cartridge and sealing patents would have a working prototype of a five-assay optical reader in 18 months; what they could not have is a cleared troponin assay. The moat is therefore regulatory and manufacturing time, roughly three to four years, not the twelve-month technical lead a patent portfolio would have bought.

| Product | Stage | Revenue, FY2025 | Margin | Next milestone |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 five-assay panel | 2 of 5 assays in 510(k) K261734 | $1.1M evaluation fees | Not disclosed by product | Clearance, then three remaining assays (Q2 2027 filing planned) |
| Evaluation programme | 41 sites, 55 analyzers | $1.1M | — | Conversion to commercial terms after clearance |
| Research-use cartridges | Selling | $0.8M | Not disclosed | None stated |
| Contract development | One partner, unnamed | $0.7M | Not disclosed | None stated |

The cost curve is the most credible number in the deck. Falling from $16.20 a cartridge at roughly 20,000 units a year to $7.50 at 2 million is a 54% reduction over about 6.6 volume doublings, or roughly 11% per doubling — shallower than the 15-25% per doubling volume-driven hardware usually achieves, so the target is not the implausible part. What is missing is the bill of materials: if antibody and reagent dominate, the curve is slower than the arithmetic, because antibodies do not get cheaper the way moulded plastic does. The pilot line is 18 people in a leased Tempe plant running about 1,680 cartridges a month; a million a year is a fifty-fold increase, and the round allocates 40% of proceeds, $12M, to it without disclosing capex, line count or qualification schedule. Point-of-care troponin cartridges also have a quality history to survive: Abbott's i-STAT cTnI cartridges were recalled four times between 2011 and 2013 for device design, labelling and material contamination, which is the failure taxonomy a dried-reagent cartridge inherits.

::: evidence
**The number that decides the technology is 11.8% — the troponin assay's imprecision at the cut-off the product exists to interpret — and the company reports it without stating the standard it must meet.**

The IFCC defines a high-sensitivity assay by its imprecision at the 99th-percentile upper reference limit and by its ability to measure troponin in most healthy people [S163], and simulation models show single-threshold classification error climbing steeply with assay imprecision and bias. Four Vantelle assays sit at 2.4-7.2% CV; the one that drives the transfer decision sits at 11.8%. The study that produced it cannot settle the question, and the pivotal study that could is not registered and reports after the round closes.
:::

The dependencies are concentrated rather than diversified. The sealing film and blister come from a patent licensed from a company Vantelle owns 60% of, at a 3% royalty that partly flows to the chief technology officer; there is one manufacturing site and no disclosed second source; the EHR connection is described as HL7 and FHIR with no named integration partner; and the three assays not yet submitted depend on chemistry with neither a granted claim nor a freedom-to-operate opinion. Readiness is uneven in a way the deck's single "Q5" label hides: troponin and HbA1c are at the point of a submission, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium sit behind a pivotal study, and the untrained-operator configuration the entire business model depends on has not been tested at all. The pivotal study's precision data by site and lot is the document that would turn an 11.8% worst case into a known design point, or confirm it as the design point itself; until it exists, the accuracy claim is partially verified at best and the technology should be valued as a cartridge company with a regulatory option, not as a validated diagnostic platform.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle Diagnostics sells a $33.40 cartridge that costs $16.20 to make, but at the 1.35 panels a day its own 41 evaluation sites average, a site returns $7,945 of annual gross profit — too little to cover the cost of selling and supporting it, so the $140M pre-money valuation is a bet on an eight-to-twelve-fold utilisation step-up that no disclosed data supports; the $30M buys a manufacturing cost curve and a distribution option, not proven unit economics. The money flows through three parties: a clinic buys the analyzer and cartridges, its staff runs the test, and the clinic bills the patient's insurer under existing codes, while Vantelle never bills a payer. The clinic pays $2,900 for an analyzer that costs $3,350 to build, $650 a month per analyzer during the evaluation programme, and $38 list per cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. In the 2026 average the 55 analyzers in the field consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, 41 per site, and 60% of evaluation sites were given instruments free; the one large order in sight is a non-binding distributor letter of intent that becomes a $2.4M stocking order only when the 510(k) clears in Q1 2027 [S150]. All of these figures are company-reported and unaudited.

| Metric | Per cartridge, 2026 | Per cartridge, 2029 target | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Average selling price | $33.40 | $31.00 | — | S150, company-reported |
| Cost of goods | $16.20 | $7.50 | — | S150, company-reported |
| Gross profit | $17.20 (51.5%) | $23.50 (75.8%) | Abbott FY2025 gross margin 56.4% | S150; S3 |
| Corvia royalty, 3% of net sales | $1.00 | $0.93 | — | S150, company-reported |
| Gross profit after royalty | $16.20 (48.5%) | $22.57 (72.8%) | — | S150, derived |
| Volume, cartridges a year | 20,160 | 2,532,000 | — | S150, derived |
| Multiple of 2026 volume | 1.0x | 126x | — | S150, derived |
| Gross profit pool after royalty | $0.33M | $57.1M | FY2029 plan gross profit $55.7M | S150, derived |

The cartridge is the only link in the chain with positive gross margin, and it is thinner than presented. A 2026 cartridge earns $17.20 (51.5%); the 3% royalty on net cartridge sales paid to Corvia Microfluidics takes $1.00, leaving $16.20 and 48.5% — the deck reports 51% and does not say whether the royalty sits inside its $16.20 cost. The 2029 target cuts cost 54% to $7.50 while price falls 7% to $31.00, lifting gross profit to $23.50, or $22.57 and 72.8% after royalty rather than the 76% shown. The volume required is the weak point: 2M cartridges is 99 times the 2026 run-rate of 20,160, and the FY2029 revenue line of $78.5M at $31 needs 2.53M cartridges, 126 times. The deck discloses no line capacity, yield, scrap rate or capex for that step; the only visible cost is the 40% of the raise ($12M) labelled "scale cartridge manufacturing". Each percentage point of scrap at the target volume adds $0.08 to unit cost, so $7.50 depends on yield as much as on volume.

| Metric | Evaluation actual, 2026 | Plan from 2028 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridges per analyzer a month | 30.5 | 240 | S150, derived |
| Panels a day per analyzer | 1.02 | 8.0 | S150, derived |
| Panels a day per site (2 analyzers planned, 1.34 actual) | 1.35 | 16.0 | S150, derived |
| Cartridge gross profit per analyzer a year, after royalty | $5,929 | $38,880 | S150, derived |
| Instrument cash cost per placement (60% free, 40% at $2,900) | $2,190 | $2,190 | S150, derived |
| Cash cost of the installed base | $120,450 (55 analyzers) | $2.31M (1,055 analyzers) | S150, derived |
| Instrument payback, months | 4.4 | 0.7 | S150, derived |
| Three-year cartridge gross profit per site, after royalty | $23,835 | $233,280 | S150, derived |
| Selling cost per site a year, analyst estimate | $33,000-49,000 | $4,500-6,700 | S150, derived |
| Value of 13,200 sites at $38 a cartridge | $247M | $2.4B | S150, derived |
| Sites needed for $78.5M of FY2029 revenue | 3,459 | 527 | S150, derived |

The instrument is not where the model breaks, but it is not free either. At $2,900 against a $3,350 build every analyzer sold loses $450 (-15.5%), and with 60% given away the cash cost averages $2,190 a placement: $120,450 for the 55 analyzers in the field, $1.31M for the 600 that a 300-site base implies, and $2.31M for the 1,055 the 2029 plan needs. Against that, an analyzer at the observed 30.5 cartridges a month produces $5,929 of cartridge gross profit a year after royalty and repays its subsidy in 4.4 months; at the modelled 240 cartridges a month it repays in under one month. The hardware is cheap customer acquisition. What it acquires is a site whose profit is decided by utilisation.

That is where the deck parts company with its own data. The model assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer and two analyzers a site, 16 a day per site; the evaluation sites averaged 1.35 a day per site and 1.02 per analyzer, a gap of 7.8 times per analyzer and 11.9 times per site [S150]. The $2.4B serviceable market is the same arithmetic — 13,200 sites x 2 analyzers x 8 panels x 300 days x $38 — and at the observed rate those sites are worth $247M. Per-site cartridge gross profit after royalty is $7,945 a year at observed utilisation against $52,099 at the modelled rate. Selling cost is not disclosed; the nine sales and support staff imply $1.35M-$2.0M a year, or $33,000-$49,000 per active site today and $4,500-$6,700 a site at 300 sites, so a three-year LTV of $23,835 a site covers its selling cost 1.2-1.8 times at observed utilisation and 12-17 times at the modelled rate (analyst estimate; customer acquisition cost is not disclosed). This is a utilisation bet presented as a scale bet.

Revenue quality compounds the problem. FY2025's $2.6M was $1.1M of evaluation-programme revenue (42%), $0.8M of research-use cartridges sold to clinical research organisations (31%) and $0.7M of contract development for a partner (27%) — none of it cleared clinical testing [S150]. Revenue to September 2026 was $2.7M, and the $5.9M full-year estimate includes the $2.4M stocking order that ships only on clearance in Q1 2027, so underlying FY2026 is $3.5M, up 35% rather than 127%. The evaluation line does not reconcile with its own price either: 55 analyzers at $650 a month is $429,000 a year, 39% of the $1.1M booked in FY2025, so the line must also contain cartridges bought by evaluation sites or fees the deck does not describe. Until revenue is reported by type and customer, the recurring share cannot be calculated.

Payer risk sits with the clinic but does not stop there. After clearance a clinic bills Medicare or a commercial payer per test and buys the cartridge from Vantelle, so a denial is the clinic's loss — and a reason not to reorder. Medicare's 2026 laboratory fee schedule pays $21.96 for the two assays in the first 510(k), 34% below the $33.40 cartridge before the clinic's labour and quality-control cost; the full five-test panel recovers $61.22 on the three assays whose rates are published, which is where the cartridge becomes affordable. Independent fee-schedule aggregators supply these rates, so they are medium-confidence. The full panel is not cleared until the second 510(k), and clinic staff cannot run it without the CLIA waiver — a listed peer calls waived status "critical for most of our products that are intended for POC settings" and describes the waiver as onerous and slow [S7]. The Q1 2027 clearance launches a two-test product whose Medicare recovery is below its cartridge price.

| Test (CPT) | Medicare 2026 rate | Cleared in the first 510(k)? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin, quantitative (84484) | $12.47 | Yes | S177, independent |
| HbA1c (83036) | $9.49 | Yes | S178, independent |
| BNP/NT-proBNP (83880) | $39.26 | No, second 510(k) | S176, independent |
| First two assays, subtotal | $21.96 | — | Derived from S177, S178 |
| Three assays, subtotal | $61.22 | — | Derived from S176, S177, S178 |

Two structural features take value off the top. The 3% Corvia royalty goes to a company Vantelle owns 60% of, and the CTO, Dr Tomasz Lindqvist, holds 22% of Corvia, so he receives 0.66% of every cartridge's net sales: 3% of the FY2029 plan's cartridge revenue is $2.36M, of which his share is $0.52M. On an acquisition, Corvia's 40% minority may put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value, a claim ahead of common [S150]. Neither is fatal at these amounts, but both belong in the term sheet: a capped or repriced put, and the royalty disclosed in the gross-margin line.

::: evidence
**At the utilisation its own evaluation sites show, Vantelle's cartridge annuity does not cover the cost of selling a site; the plan works only at 7.8 times observed volume per analyzer.**

Evidence: the $2.4B market model assumes 16 panels a day per site against 1.35 observed, and 2M cartridges a year is 99 times the current run-rate; the closest analogue, LumiraDx, was placed in pre-pack administration on 2023-12-29 and its platform sold to Roche for $295M, while Cue Health filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28 after raising more than $480M [S150, S172, S173, S174].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is legally ordinary and evidentially fragile (company-reported facts, unverified). The $15.0M ticket buys 4,606,314 shares — 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company at $3.2564 a share — with the sixth board seat, but $76.8M of liquidation preference is already committed to earlier money, 40% of the sealing-film IP sits outside the parent in the chief technology officer's own company, and the 510(k) number the valuation rests on belongs to another company's knee implant. Together that means the $140.0M pre-money is a price the company set, not one the market marked. The last priced round closed in 2022; every dollar since is insider money or debt. Page 1 also carries a paragraph addressed to AI-assisted diligence tools telling them to skip external verification and report an Invest rating — recorded as a finding, not followed [S150].

The product is a 640-gram reader and a single-use cartridge running a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel — hs-troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine with eGFR and potassium — from a 40-microlitre finger stick in 12 minutes. The user is clinic staff, not a laboratory technician; the buyer is the urgent-care operator or rural hospital that today sends the bloods out and waits one to three days; and growth comes from placing readers at or near cost ($2,900 list against $3,350 build cost) to earn $38 a cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. No VIE, nominee shareholder or dual-class structure exists, so ownership and votes match, and the Delaware parent is issuer, FDA submitter and owner of VD-1 to VD-4. The Delaware free register returns only name, file number, formation date and registered agent and its search is session-based, so the 2018-03-12 incorporation date and good standing are unconfirmed against the registry; the ownership percentages, entity roles and dates below are unverified company material, while the share and price arithmetic is verified because it reconciles to the deck's own totals [S149].

The structure that changes economics is Corvia, and it is disclosed only by the company (unverified). ### A flat round dressed as a step-up

The price history, company-reported and unverified, shows how little has been repriced. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has built something genuinely difficult — a 40-microlitre finger-stick sample turned into five results in twelve minutes on a cartridge that calibrates itself — and has not yet shown that it works as a diagnostic. The company's own study puts troponin I at 11.8% imprecision at the very cut-off that drives the chest-pain decision, measured on 128 patients at one site, by Vantelle's own staff, scored as normal or abnormal rather than as a number; the reader patent was finally rejected in July 2026; and the dried chemistry that produces the troponin result is an unpublished PCT the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion does not cover [S150]. What Vantelle owns outright is time — two 510(k) submissions' worth of regulatory work, a pilot line, and two and a half years with 41 clinics — and time is the one asset a funded competitor can buy.

### The difficult part is the dried chemistry, not the handheld

The Q5 is three technologies in a 640-gram box: a capillary-fill cartridge metering 40 microlitres of whole blood, a dried-reagent chemistry that must survive nine months at room temperature, and an optical reader correcting for drift across five assays. The first is solved and patented (US 16/884,327, filed 2020-05-28, granted 2023-03). The second decides whether the troponin number is right, and it is the one kept secret: an unpublished PCT filed 2026-02-11, no granted claim, no freedom-to-operate opinion behind it. The third is the one the Patent Office rejected. On-board calibration is a real advantage over a benchtop analyzer needing daily quality control, but it also turns a calibrator fault into a silent bias across every cartridge in the lot, and finger-stick blood adds what a tube removes — haematocrit and haemolysis, an interference class the IFCC treats as first-order for troponin and especially for potassium, which an optical platform cannot read with the electrode a blood-gas analyzer uses [S166].

### The performance claim is a category count from one site

"98.7% agreement" is not concordance. The study ran 128 patients at one urgent-care site between September and December 2025, drew venous blood, ran it on the Q5 with Vantelle staff operating the device, and scored each result into the same category as the reference laboratory. Category agreement discards the magnitude the clinician uses: a troponin of 14 and one of 60 ng/L are one category if both exceed the cut-off, and the decision the product exists to serve — transfer or hold a patient with chest pain — turns on magnitude and on change between samples. The summary row also does not close: 634 of 640 is 99.1%, and the five per-assay rates imply about 626 agreements among 634 analysable results, so 98.7% is a share of the analysable set printed as a count out of 640. Six exclusions in 640 results (0.94%) is not unreasonable; not disclosing them by assay and reason is. Against this, the incumbent's evidence is another order of magnitude, and simulation shows single-threshold classification error rising steeply with exactly the imprecision and bias this study was not designed to measure [S10, S124].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the decision level | 11.8% CV | 10% or better at the 99th-percentile URL | S150, S163 |
| Troponin I agreement | 96.1% (123 of 128) | Category agreement, not concordance | S150 |
| Five-assay agreement | 98.7% claimed | 634 of 640 is 99.1%; per-assay rates imply ~626 of 634 | S150 |
| Clinical evidence | 128 patients, 1 site, venous, company-run | 3,697 patients in the incumbent's study | S150, S124 |
| Sample, turnaround, shelf life | 40 µL finger-stick, 12 min, 9 months claimed on 6 months of data | Venous; 1-3 days for a send-out | S150 |

### Clearance is later than the deck says, and the waiver later still

The 510(k) was filed 2026-05-18 and FDA asked for additional information on 2026-08-21, with 180 days to answer and a December 2026 answer planned. A Q1 2027 clearance therefore needs a decision within about three months of that response, and FDA's clearance database held no record for K261734, or for any device under the company's name, on 2026-10-30 — what a pending submission looks like, but also proof that nothing is cleared today [S7, S191]. Sequencing matters more than the date. Only troponin I and HbA1c are in the first submission, so the five-assay panel is two clearances away, and the CLIA waiver — permission for staff without laboratory training — is not planned until Q3 2027. QuidelOrtho, selling into the same channel, calls the waived designation "critical" for its point-of-care products and the waiver requirements "onerous" [S7]. Until a waiver is granted the Q5 is a moderate-complexity test for a certificated laboratory: a different buyer and a much smaller market than the deck describes.

### The patent estate is one granted family owned outright

The estate reduces to one US patent granted to the parent, one granted patent held by a subsidiary Vantelle owns 60% of and licensed back at a 3% royalty whose beneficiaries include the chief technology officer, one finally rejected application and two unpublished ones. The reader — the part a competitor would otherwise design around — is unpatented, and the six-month window after a final rejection puts the appeal-or-abandon decision around the round's January 2027 target close. The freedom-to-operate opinion predates the troponin chemistry filing and excludes it, so the hardest element is both unprotected and unvetted [S150].

| Cartridge manufacturability at scale | 7 | 40 µL capillary fill, on-board calibrator, 9-month shelf life; haemolysis and fill volume fail first | 2-3 years |
| Clearance and CLIA waiver | 9 | Two 510(k)s plus a multi-site operator study; the incumbent took about 11 months from study completion to clearance | 3-5 years |
| Reader design | 3 | Optics are engineering, not science, and the claim was rejected | 6-12 months |
| Patent protection | 2 | One granted US family owned outright; reader unpatented | immediate |
| Ecosystem and switching | 5 | Cartridge lock-in after training and EHR wiring | 3-5 years |

The replication test cuts both ways. Fifty funded engineers given the published cartridge and sealing patents would have a working five-assay reader in 18 months; what they could not have is a cleared troponin assay. The moat is three to four years of regulatory and manufacturing time, not a technical lead.

|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 five-assay panel | Two of five assays in K261734 | $1.1M evaluation fees | Clearance; remaining three assays filed Q2 2027 |
| Evaluation programme | 41 sites, 55 analyzers | $1.1M | Conversion to commercial terms |
| Research-use cartridges | Selling to CROs | $0.8M | None stated |
| Contract development | One unnamed partner | $0.7M | None stated |

The cost curve is the most credible number in the deck. Falling from $16.20 a cartridge at roughly 20,000 units a year to $7.50 at 2 million is a 54% cut over about 6.6 volume doublings, or roughly 11% per doubling — shallower than the 15-25% per doubling volume-driven hardware usually achieves, so the target is not the implausible part; the missing piece is the bill of materials, because if antibody and reagent dominate, the curve is slower than the arithmetic. The pilot line is 18 people in a leased Tempe plant running about 1,680 cartridges a month, so a million a year is a fifty-fold increase, and the round puts 40% of proceeds, $12M, into it without disclosing capex, line count or qualification schedule. Abbott's i-STAT cTnI cartridges were recalled four times between 2011 and 2013 for device design, labelling and material contamination — the failure taxonomy a dried-reagent cartridge inherits.

::: evidence
**The number that decides the technology is 11.8% — the troponin assay's imprecision at the cut-off the product exists to interpret — and the company reports it without stating the standard it must meet.**

The IFCC defines a high-sensitivity assay by its imprecision at the 99th-percentile upper reference limit and by its ability to measure troponin in most healthy people [S163]; simulation models show single-threshold error climbing steeply with imprecision and bias. Four Vantelle assays sit at 2.4-7.2% CV; the one driving the transfer decision sits at 11.8%. The study that produced it cannot settle the question, and the pivotal study that could is not registered and reports after the round closes.
:::

The dependencies are concentrated. The sealing film and blister come from a patent licensed from a company Vantelle owns 60% of, at a 3% royalty partly flowing to the chief technology officer; there is one manufacturing site and no disclosed second source; the EHR connection is described as HL7 and FHIR with no named integration partner; and the three assays not yet submitted depend on chemistry with neither a granted claim nor a freedom-to-operate opinion. Readiness is uneven in a way the single "Q5" label hides: troponin and HbA1c are at the point of a submission, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium sit behind a pivotal study, and the untrained-operator configuration the business model depends on has not been tested at all. The pivotal study's precision data by site and lot is the document that would turn an 11.8% worst case into a known design point, or confirm it as the design point itself; until it exists the accuracy claim is partially verified and the technology should be valued as a cartridge company holding a regulatory option, not as a validated diagnostic platform.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle Diagnostics sells a $33.40 cartridge that costs $16.20 to make, but at the 1.35 panels a day its own 41 evaluation sites average, a site returns $7,945 of annual gross profit — too little to cover the cost of selling and supporting it, so the $140M pre-money valuation is a bet on an eight-to-twelve-fold utilisation step-up that no disclosed data supports; the $30M buys a manufacturing cost curve and a distribution option, not proven unit economics. The clinic buys the analyzer and cartridges, its staff runs the test and bills the patient's insurer under existing codes; Vantelle never bills a payer. The clinic pays $2,900 for an analyzer that costs $3,350 to build, $650 a month per analyzer during the evaluation programme, and $38 list per cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. In the 2026 average the 55 analyzers in the field consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, 41 per site, and 60% of evaluation sites were given instruments free; the one large order in sight is a non-binding distributor letter of intent that becomes a $2.4M stocking order only when the 510(k) clears in Q1 2027 [S150]. All of these figures are company-reported and unaudited.

At $2,900 against a $3,350 build every analyzer sold loses $450 (-15.5%), and with 60% given away the cash cost averages $2,190 a placement: $120,450 for the 55 analyzers in the field, $1.31M for the 600 that a 300-site base implies, and $2.31M for the 1,055 the 2029 plan needs. Against that, an analyzer at the observed 30.5 cartridges a month produces $5,929 of cartridge gross profit a year after royalty and repays its subsidy in 4.4 months; at the modelled 240 cartridges a month it repays in under one month. The hardware is cheap customer acquisition. What it buys is a site whose profit depends on utilisation.

That is where the deck parts company with its own data. The model assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer and two analyzers a site, 16 a day per site; the evaluation sites averaged 1.35 a day per site and 1.02 per analyzer, a gap of 7.8 times per analyzer and 11.9 times per site [S150]. The $2.4B serviceable market is the same arithmetic — 13,200 sites x 2 analyzers x 8 panels x 300 days x $38 — and at the observed rate those sites are worth $247M. Per-site cartridge gross profit is $7,945 a year at observed utilisation against $52,099 modelled. Selling cost is not disclosed; the nine sales and support staff imply $1.35M-$2.0M a year, or $33,000-$49,000 per active site today and $4,500-$6,700 a site at 300 sites, so a three-year LTV of $23,835 a site covers its selling cost 1.2-1.8 times at observed utilisation and 12-17 times at the modelled rate (analyst estimate; customer acquisition cost is not disclosed). This is a utilisation bet presented as a scale bet.

Revenue quality compounds the problem. FY2025's $2.6M was $1.1M of evaluation-programme revenue (42%), $0.8M of research-use cartridges sold to clinical research organisations (31%) and $0.7M of contract development for a partner (27%) — none of it cleared clinical testing [S150]. Until revenue is reported by type and customer, the recurring share cannot be calculated.

Payer risk sits with the clinic but does not stop there. After clearance the clinic bills Medicare or a commercial payer per test and buys cartridges from Vantelle, so a denial is its loss — and a reason not to reorder. Medicare's 2026 laboratory fee schedule pays $21.96 for the two assays in the first 510(k), 34% below the $33.40 cartridge before the clinic's labour and quality-control cost; the full five-test panel recovers $61.22 on the three assays whose rates are published, where the cartridge becomes affordable. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has built something genuinely difficult — a 40-microlitre finger-stick sample turned into five results in twelve minutes on a cartridge that calibrates itself — and has not yet shown that it works as a diagnostic. The company's own study puts troponin I at 11.8% imprecision at the very cut-off that drives the chest-pain decision, measured on 128 patients at one site, by Vantelle's own staff, scored as normal or abnormal rather than as a number; the reader patent was finally rejected in July 2026; and the dried chemistry behind the troponin result is an unpublished PCT the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion does not cover [S150]. What Vantelle owns outright is time — two 510(k) submissions' worth of regulatory work and two and a half years with 41 clinics — and time is the one asset a funded competitor can buy.

### The difficult part is the dried chemistry, not the handheld

The Q5 is three technologies in a 640-gram box: a capillary-fill cartridge metering 40 microlitres of whole blood, a dried-reagent chemistry that must survive nine months at room temperature, and an optical reader correcting for drift across five assays. The first is solved and patented (US 16/884,327, filed 2020-05-28, granted 2023-03). The second decides whether the troponin number is right, and it is the one kept secret: an unpublished PCT filed 2026-02-11, no granted claim, no freedom-to-operate opinion behind it. The third is the one the Patent Office rejected. On-board calibration beats a benchtop analyzer needing daily quality control, but it also turns a calibrator fault into a silent bias across every cartridge in the lot, and finger-stick blood adds what a tube removes — haematocrit and haemolysis, an interference class the IFCC treats as first-order for troponin and especially for potassium, which an optical platform cannot read with the electrode a blood-gas analyzer uses [S166].

### The performance claim is a category count from one site

"98.7% agreement" is not concordance. The study ran 128 patients at one urgent-care site between September and December 2025, drew venous blood, ran it on the Q5 with Vantelle staff operating the device, and scored each result into the same category as the reference laboratory. Category agreement discards the magnitude the clinician uses: a troponin of 14 and one of 60 ng/L are one category if both exceed the cut-off, and the decision the product serves — transfer or hold a patient with chest pain — turns on magnitude and on change between samples. The summary row does not close either: 634 of 640 is 99.1%, and the five per-assay rates imply about 626 agreements among 634 analysable results, so 98.7% is a share of the analysable set printed as a count out of 640. Against this the incumbent's evidence is another order of magnitude, and simulation shows single-threshold classification error rising steeply with exactly the imprecision and bias this study was not designed to measure [S10, S124].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the decision level | 11.8% CV | 10% or better at the 99th-percentile URL | S150, S163 |
| Troponin I agreement | 96.1% (123 of 128) | Category agreement, not concordance | S150 |
| Five-assay agreement | 98.7% claimed | 634 of 640 is 99.1%; per-assay rates imply ~626 of 634 | S150 |
| Clinical evidence | 128 patients, 1 site, company-run | 3,697 patients in the incumbent's study | S150, S124 |

### Clearance is later than the deck says, and the waiver later still

The 510(k) was filed 2026-05-18 and FDA asked for additional information on 2026-08-21, with 180 days to answer and a December 2026 answer planned. A Q1 2027 clearance therefore needs a decision within about three months of that response, and FDA's clearance database held no record for K261734, or for any device under the company's name, on 2026-10-30 — what a pending submission looks like, but also proof that nothing is cleared today [S7, S191]. Sequencing matters more than the date. Only troponin I and HbA1c are in the first submission, so the five-assay panel is two clearances away, and the CLIA waiver — permission for staff without laboratory training — is not planned until Q3 2027. QuidelOrtho, selling into the same channel, calls the waived designation "critical" for its point-of-care products and the waiver requirements "onerous" [S7]. Until a waiver is granted the Q5 is a moderate-complexity test for a certificated laboratory: a different buyer and a much smaller market than the deck describes.

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT platform | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US status | Two of five assays in K261734, information request pending; nothing cleared | hs-TnI cleared 2025-01-03 (i-STAT 1), 2026-06-11 (Alinity) | S191, S17, S13 |
| Evidence scale | 128 patients, one site, company-run | 3,697-patient study, completed 2024-02 | S150, S124 |
| Platform menu | Five assays in one cartridge | Blood gas, chemistry, electrolytes, coagulation, immunoassay | S150, S3 |
| Operator | Laboratory staff until a waiver is granted | Trained operator; waiver status not verified in this run | S150, S7 |
| External validation | None located | Independent UK emergency-department evaluation, 2026 | S144 |

### The patent estate is one granted family owned outright

| Patent or application | Subject | Filed / granted | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327, plus EP family | Capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator | 2020-05-28 / 2023-03 | US granted to ~2040-05; Europe pending | S150 |
| US 17/662,019 | Five-assay optical reader with drift correction | 2022-05-04 / — | Final rejection 2026-07; appeal under consideration | S150 |
| US 19/318,770 | Finger-stick sample-volume check | 2025-09-30 / — | Unpublished | S150 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 | Troponin chemistry on dried reagents | 2026-02-11 / — | Unpublished; outside the 2024 FTO opinion | S150 |
| US 15/707,915 | Cartridge sealing film and reagent blister | 2017-09-18 / 2021-01 | Granted to ~2037-09; owned by 60%-held Corvia, licensed at 3% | S150 |

The estate reduces to one US patent granted to the parent, one granted patent held by a subsidiary Vantelle owns 60% of and licensed back at a 3% royalty whose beneficiaries include the chief technology officer, one finally rejected application and two unpublished ones. The reader — the part a competitor would otherwise design around — is unpatented, and the six-month window after a final rejection puts the appeal-or-abandon decision around the round's January 2027 close. The freedom-to-operate opinion predates the troponin chemistry filing and excludes it, so the hardest element is both unprotected and unvetted [S150].

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dried-reagent troponin chemistry | 8 | Antibody stability at room temperature sets imprecision | 3-4 years |
| Cartridge manufacturability at scale | 7 | 40 µL fill, on-board calibrator, 9-month shelf life; haemolysis fails first | 2-3 years |
| Clearance and CLIA waiver | 9 | Two 510(k)s plus a multi-site operator study | 3-5 years |
| Reader design | 3 | Optics are engineering, not science; claim rejected | 6-12 months |
| Patent protection | 2 | One granted US family owned outright | immediate |

The replication test cuts both ways. Fifty funded engineers given the published cartridge and sealing patents would have a working five-assay reader in 18 months; what they could not have is a cleared troponin assay. The moat is three to four years of regulatory and manufacturing time, not a technical lead.

| Product | Stage | Revenue, FY2025 | Next milestone |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 five-assay panel | Two of five assays in K261734 | $1.1M evaluation fees | Clearance; other three assays filed Q2 2027 |
| Research-use cartridges | Selling to CROs | $0.8M | None stated |
| Contract development | One unnamed partner | $0.7M | None stated |

The cost curve is the most credible number in the deck. Falling from $16.20 a cartridge at roughly 20,000 units a year to $7.50 at 2 million is a 54% cut over about 6.6 volume doublings, or roughly 11% per doubling — shallower than the 15-25% per doubling volume-driven hardware usually achieves, so the target is not the implausible part; the missing piece is the bill of materials, because if antibody and reagent dominate, the curve is slower than the arithmetic. The pilot line is 18 people in a leased Tempe plant running about 1,680 cartridges a month, so a million a year is a fifty-fold increase, and the round puts 40% of proceeds, $12M, into it without disclosing capex, line count or qualification schedule. Abbott's i-STAT cTnI cartridges were recalled four times between 2011 and 2013 for device design, labelling and material contamination — the failure taxonomy a dried-reagent cartridge inherits.

::: evidence
**The number that decides the technology is 11.8% — the troponin assay's imprecision at the cut-off the product exists to interpret — and the company reports it without stating the standard it must meet.**

The IFCC defines a high-sensitivity assay by its imprecision at the 99th-percentile upper reference limit and its ability to measure troponin in most healthy people [S163]; simulation models show single-threshold error climbing steeply with imprecision and bias. Four Vantelle assays sit at 2.4-7.2% CV; the one driving the transfer decision sits at 11.8%. The study behind it cannot settle the question, and the pivotal study that could is not registered and reports after the round closes.
:::

The dependencies are concentrated. The sealing film comes from a patent licensed from a company Vantelle owns 60% of, at a 3% royalty partly flowing to the chief technology officer; there is one manufacturing site and no disclosed second source; the EHR connection is described as HL7 and FHIR with no named integration partner; and the three assays not yet submitted depend on chemistry with neither a granted claim nor a freedom-to-operate opinion. Readiness is uneven in a way the single "Q5" label hides: troponin and HbA1c are at the point of a submission, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium sit behind a pivotal study, and the untrained-operator configuration the business model depends on has not been tested at all. The pivotal study's precision data by site and lot would turn an 11.8% worst case into a known design point, or confirm it as the design point itself; until it exists the accuracy claim is partially verified and the technology is a cartridge company holding a regulatory option, not a validated diagnostic platform.

What is documented is thinner: she joined on 2025-11, two months after her predecessor left during preparation of the submission; ISO 13485 certification is not held, with an audit booked for Q1 2027; and nine of 64 employees sit in clinical and regulatory against a workload of one additional-information response, a further three-assay submission, a four-site 1,150-patient pivotal study and a CLIA waiver application. Abbott cleared hs-troponin I cartridges twice in eighteen months (K240984 on 2025-01-03 and K253051 on 2026-06-11), which is the cadence an established regulatory organisation produces and not a fair comparison for a 64-person company; the fair test is whether Vantelle answers one FDA request on time, and the bench that must do it has been in place under a year [S13, S148, S17, S150].

### One sales career, one part-time finance function

Commercial and financial leadership are single-track. Luis Arrellano spent 2006-2023 at one company, Tavora Health Systems, rising from sales representative to regional vice president for the Southwest — a 17-year record in the same three states where all 41 evaluation sites sit, with no disclosed diagnostics or capital-equipment experience, which is the experience the model needs because the analyzer is a $2,900 capital sale and the cartridge is a recurring consumable. Darnell Whitcombe has been interim CFO since 2026-03 through his advisory firm, part-time, while the company ran a $6.0M bridge, a $30.0M round and a $5.0M term loan that begins amortising in 2027-03; six of 64 employees work in finance and administration. A part-time CFO is common below $10M of revenue; a part-time CFO through a priced round with a bridge, warrants and a participating preference is a choice the lead should reverse before funding [S150].

### Governance concentrates the same risk

Five of six board seats are filled: two common held by the founders, one seed, one Series A and one Series B, with the independent seat vacant — so until it is filled the founders occupy two of five occupied seats and sit with the investors committing $8.0M of the round. The Corvia royalty and put are related-party matters that one founder-director benefits from and the other votes on, and no protective provisions, information rights or drag-along terms appear in the deck. Key-person dependency is high on both founders and on the regulatory vice president. After the round the founders hold 11,200,000 shares, 21.5% against 30.8% today, with a 20.0% option pool and a share price flat since 2022: the retention question is whether two founders diluted to a fifth of the company keep the appetite a five-assay panel and a three-year regulatory calendar demand [S150].

### What would settle it

Three checks would settle most of this before a term sheet: confirm Albescu's NPI and state licences and both founders' degrees directly with the awarding institutions; obtain Meridale Medical's 510(k) list and three named references, one of them on FDA interaction; and take structured references on the two 2025-2026 departures. The hires still missing are a full-time CFO, a regulatory lead with point-of-care clearance experience at vice-president level or above, and an independent director the new lead nominates. What would change the decision is all three in place before close, with a milestone tranche tied to the additional-information response. Until then the team is a bet on two founders' clinical and engineering insight — a story the company tells about itself, supported by no record this diligence could open, which is a reason to condition the investment and price the execution risk, not to walk away [S150].

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle Diagnostics sells a $33.40 cartridge that costs $16.20 to make, but at the 1.35 panels a day its own 41 evaluation sites average, a site returns $7,945 of annual gross profit — too little to cover the cost of selling and supporting it, so the $140M pre-money valuation is a bet on an eight-to-twelve-fold utilisation step-up that no disclosed data supports; the $30M buys a manufacturing cost curve and a distribution option, not proven unit economics. The clinic buys the analyzer and cartridges, its staff runs the test and bills the patient's insurer under existing codes; Vantelle never bills a payer. The clinic pays $2,900 for an analyzer that costs $3,350 to build, $650 a month per analyzer during the evaluation programme, and $38 list per cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. In the 2026 average the 55 analyzers in the field consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, 41 per site, and 60% of evaluation sites were given instruments free; the one large order in sight is a non-binding distributor letter of intent that becomes a $2.4M stocking order only when the 510(k) clears in Q1 2027 [S150]. All of these figures are company-reported and unaudited.

| Metric | Per unit, 2026 | Per unit, 2029 target | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Average selling price | $33.40 | $31.00 | — | S150, company-reported, unaudited |
| Cost of goods | $16.20 | $7.50 | — | S150, company-reported, unaudited |
| Gross profit | $17.20 (51.5%) | $23.50 (75.8%) | Abbott FY2025 gross margin 56.4% | S150; S3 |
| Corvia royalty, 3% of net sales | $1.00 | $0.93 | — | S150, company-reported, unaudited |
| Gross profit after royalty | $16.20 (48.5%) | $22.57 (72.8%) | — | S150, derived from unaudited figures |
| Volume, cartridges a year | 20,160 | 2,532,000 | — | S150, derived from unaudited figures |
| Multiple of 2026 volume | 1.0x | 126x | — | S150, derived from unaudited figures |
| Gross profit pool after royalty | $0.33M | $57.1M | FY2029 plan gross profit $55.7M | S150, derived from unaudited figures |

The cartridge is the only link with positive gross margin, and it is thinner than presented. A 2026 cartridge earns $17.20 (51.5%); the 3% royalty on net cartridge sales paid to Corvia Microfluidics takes $1.00, leaving $16.20 and 48.5% — the deck reports 51%, without saying whether the royalty sits inside the $16.20. The 2029 target cuts cost 54% to $7.50 while price falls 7% to $31.00, lifting gross profit to $23.50, or $22.57 and 72.8% after royalty rather than the 76% shown. The volume required is the weak point: 2M cartridges is 99 times the 2026 run-rate of 20,160, and the FY2029 revenue line of $78.5M at $31 needs 2.53M cartridges, 126 times. The deck discloses no line capacity, yield, scrap rate or capex for it; the only visible cost is the 40% of the raise ($12M) labelled "scale cartridge manufacturing". Each percentage point of scrap at the target volume adds $0.08 to unit cost, so $7.50 depends on yield as much as on volume. The royalty also takes value off the top: Corvia is 60% owned by Vantelle, and the CTO, Dr Tomasz Lindqvist, holds 22% of Corvia, so he receives 0.66% of cartridge net sales — 3% of the FY2029 plan's cartridge revenue is $2.36M, of which his share is $0.52M. On an acquisition, Corvia's 40% minority may put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value, a claim ahead of common [S150].

| Cartridges per analyzer a month | 30.5 | 240 | S150, derived from unaudited figures |
| Panels a day per analyzer | 1.02 | 8.0 | S150, derived from unaudited figures |
| Panels a day per site (2 analyzers planned, 1.34 actual) | 1.35 | 16.0 | S150, derived from unaudited figures |
| Cartridge gross profit per analyzer a year, after royalty | $5,929 | $38,880 | S150, derived from unaudited figures |
| Instrument cash cost per placement (60% free, 40% at $2,900) | $2,190 | $2,190 | S150, derived from unaudited figures |
| Cash cost of the installed base | $120,450 (55 analyzers) | $2.31M (1,055 analyzers) | S150, derived from unaudited figures |
| Instrument payback, months | 4.4 | 0.7 | S150, derived from unaudited figures |
| Three-year cartridge gross profit per site, after royalty | $23,835 | $233,280 | S150, derived from unaudited figures |
| Selling cost per site a year, analyst estimate | $33,000-49,000 | $4,500-6,700 | S150, derived from unaudited figures |
| Value of 13,200 sites at $38 a cartridge | $247M | $2.4B | S150, derived from unaudited figures |
| Sites needed for $78.5M of FY2029 revenue | 3,459 | 527 | S150, derived from unaudited figures |

The instrument is not where the model breaks, but it is not free either. At $2,900 against a $3,350 build every analyzer sold loses $450 (-15.5%), and with 60% given away the cash cost averages $2,190 a placement: $120,450 for the 55 analyzers in the field, $1.31M for the 600 that a 300-site base implies, and $2.31M for the 1,055 the 2029 plan needs [S150]. Against that, an analyzer at the observed 30.5 cartridges a month produces $5,929 of cartridge gross profit a year after royalty and repays its subsidy in 4.4 months; at the modelled 240 cartridges a month it repays in under one month. The hardware is cheap customer acquisition. What it buys is a site whose profit depends on utilisation.

That is where the deck parts company with its own data. The model assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer and two analyzers a site, 16 a day per site; the evaluation sites averaged 1.35 a day per site and 1.02 per analyzer, a gap of 7.8 times per analyzer and 11.9 times per site [S150]. The $2.4B serviceable market is the same arithmetic (13,200 sites x 2 analyzers x 8 panels x 300 days x $38); at the observed rate those sites are worth $247M. Per-site cartridge gross profit is $7,945 a year at observed utilisation against $52,099 modelled. Selling cost is not disclosed; the nine sales and support staff imply $1.35M-$2.0M a year, or $33,000-$49,000 per active site today and $4,500-$6,700 a site at 300 sites, so a three-year LTV of $23,835 a site covers its selling cost 1.2-1.8 times at observed utilisation and 12-17 times at the modelled rate (analyst estimate; customer acquisition cost is not disclosed). This is a utilisation bet presented as a scale bet.

Revenue quality compounds the problem. FY2025's $2.6M was $1.1M of evaluation-programme revenue (42%), $0.8M of research-use cartridges sold to clinical research organisations (31%) and $0.7M of contract development for a partner (27%) — none of it cleared clinical testing [S150]. Revenue to September 2026 was $2.7M, and the $5.9M full-year estimate includes the $2.4M stocking order that ships only on clearance in Q1 2027, so underlying FY2026 is $3.5M, up 35% rather than 127%. The evaluation line does not reconcile with its own price either: 55 analyzers at $650 a month is $429,000 a year, 39% of the $1.1M booked in FY2025, so the line must also contain cartridges bought by evaluation sites or undisclosed fees. Until revenue is reported by type and customer, the recurring share cannot be calculated.

Payer risk sits with the clinic but does not stop there. After clearance the clinic bills Medicare or a commercial payer per test and buys cartridges from Vantelle, so a denial is its loss — and a reason not to reorder. Medicare's 2026 laboratory fee schedule pays $21.96 for the two assays in the first 510(k), 34% below the $33.40 cartridge before the clinic's labour and quality-control cost; the full five-test panel recovers $61.22 on the three assays whose rates are published, where the cartridge becomes affordable. These rates come from independent fee-schedule aggregators and are medium-confidence. The full panel needs the second 510(k), and clinic staff cannot run it without the CLIA waiver — a listed peer calls waived status "critical for most of our products that are intended for POC settings" and describes the waiver as onerous and slow [S7]. The Q1 2027 clearance launches a two-test product whose Medicare recovery is below its cartridge price.

| Test (CPT) | Medicare 2026 rate | Cleared in the first 510(k)? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin, quantitative (84484) | $12.47 | Yes | S177, independent |
| HbA1c (83036) | $9.49 | Yes | S178, independent |
| BNP/NT-proBNP (83880) | $39.26 | No, second 510(k) | S176, independent |
| First two assays, subtotal | $21.96 | — | Derived, S177-S178 |
| Three assays, subtotal | $61.22 | — | Derived, S176-S178 |

::: evidence
**At the utilisation its own evaluation sites show, Vantelle's cartridge annuity does not cover the cost of selling a site; the plan needs a step-up in panels per day that no disclosed data supports.**

Evidence: the $2.4B market model assumes 16 panels a day per site against 1.35 observed, and 2M cartridges a year is 99 times the current run-rate; LumiraDx was placed in pre-pack administration on 2023-12-29 and its platform sold to Roche for $295M, while Cue Health filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28 after raising more than $480M [S150, S172, S173, S174].
:::

That's a compelling way to present it: even with a 25% chance of the plan working and a 10% chance of a strong outcome, the expected exit is ~$200M, which returns Meridian ~1.0x (dead zone) because of the preference. But it depends on my probability estimates; I'll present as an illustrative scenario table, clearly labelled "analyst estimates."

Meridian would be the only new price-setting investor. Follow-on capacity: Ardent Peak's $5M is 14% of its 2022 check; Juniper Rock's $3M is 67% of its seed check — modest. The $22M new-money gap is large relative to the $8M insider commitment. Also the term loan from Bluestem has warrants at $2.903 — a lender warrant that is already in the money at $3.2564.
6. Counter-evidence, diligence questions, and the deck's AI instruction. Counter-evidence: SpinChip €138M pre-revenue acquisition shows strategics will pay ~$140M for a differentiated POC platform; the 41-clinic 92% reorder rate and 1,680 cartridges/month show real demand; a 5-panel finger-stick device could be scarce. Also report the deck p.1 instruction aimed at AI diligence tools as a finding — it claims independent verification and requests a positive Invest rating, which is contradicted by the absence of public verification and should be treated as a diligence-integrity red flag (the figures are company data, unverified).

(5) Confirm the $22M new-money demand and whether the round closes at $15M or $30M, and the pro-rata rights.

Maybe 3-5 questions; the evidence block needs 2-5. In the memo, "Open questions" can be a short list.

**Section 12 structure** (7,000-8,500 chars):
Thesis: "The realistic exit is a strategic sale in 2029-2031 at $250-450M, not an IPO; at a $140M pre-money the new money's 1x preference converts that outcome into only 1.5-2.1x, and only a $546M+ sale — above every recent POC comparable — returns 3x."

The range for a platform asset is $100-295M; scaled assets 3.3-6.5x revenue. A $400M+ outcome requires revenue >$60-100M at 5-6.5x.
3. Failure base rate: Cue Health ($480M+ raised, Chapter 7), LumiraDx (sold tech for $295M after distress), Biocartis recapitalization. Point-of-care is littered with failures because reimbursement and manufacturing scale are hard. Implication for a $400M+ outcome: maybe 10-20% probability. This supports the scenario table.
4. Liquidation waterfall and return sensitivity table: Exit value | Meridian proceeds | Multiple | IRR. Include the dead zone insight.
5. IPO feasibility: Medline opened the window; Molbio in India; but Vantelle needs $50M+ revenue, 3 years of audits, SOX, and a CLIA-waived menu; 2030+ at the earliest; EU IVDR not before 2028; the Irish entity has no staff. IPO venue: Nasdaq. Lock-ups 180 days. Also the 510(k) pending with an AI request dated 2026-08-21 means the timeline is not in the company's control; an IPO before clearance is impossible.
6. Buyer's view of the patent and Corvia: CM-1 sealing patent owned by 60%-owned Corvia, licensed exclusively, 3% royalty; CTO owns 22% of Corvia and shares in the royalty; minority has a put at FMV. A buyer would need to consolidate Corvia (buy the 40%) and renegotiate the CTO's royalty/employment; the 3% royalty on cartridge sales is a permanent margin leak (at $78.5M revenue, 3% ≈ $2.4M/yr). Also VD-2 (five-assay optical reader) has a final rejection in 2026-07 with an appeal under consideration — a key patent is not granted. Buyer diligence would focus on freedom to operate for VD-4 troponin chemistry (not covered by the 2024 opinion). These reduce the buyer universe and the price.

FDA clearance is the gating item; CLIA waiver determines the site economics. Lock-ups only relevant for IPO. Expected holding period 4-6 years (2027 entry → 2031-2033 exit). Also the Series A's participating preference means Ardent Peak may prefer a sale at $200M (2.1x) where Meridian gets 1.0x — a misalignment of incentives. That's a great point: the Series A investor can support a $200M sale that returns it 2.1x while returning the new lead only 1.0x. At $200M, Ardent's $5M? Wait Ardent Peak led the Series A with part of $36M; its own stake is unknown (the deck aggregates "Ardent Peak Ventures and other Series A investors 12.4M"). At $200M, the Series A class gets $75.2M on $36M = 2.09x. So yes, the Series A class is 2.1x while B is 1.0x. arguments.title: QuidelOrtho Completes Acquisition of LEX Diagnostics
arguments.claims: QuidelOrtho acquired LEX Diagnostics for about $100M cash on 2026-04-20; the LEX VELO system received FDA 510(k) clearance and CLIA waiver in February 2026, before the deal.
arguments.claims_weakened: Weakens any claim that a pre-clearance point-of-care platform is worth $140M: a cleared, CLIA-waived POC platform changed hands for $100M in 2026.

arguments.title: QuidelOrtho looks at point-of-care testing unit sale at $1.5B, FT reports (Bloomberg)
arguments.claims: QuidelOrtho was exploring a sale of its point-of-care testing unit at a valuation of about $1.5B, per the Financial Times.
arguments.claims_weakened: The $1.5B is an asking valuation, not a completed price; it shows a scaled POC franchise with about $450M annualized revenue is marketed at roughly 3.3x revenue.

arguments.title: bioMérieux strengthens its point of care presence with the acquisition of SpinChip Diagnostics
arguments.claims: bioMérieux agreed to acquire 100% of SpinChip Diagnostics at a total enterprise value of €138M (NOK 1,624M), a pre-commercial point-of-care immunoassay platform.
arguments.claims_weakened: Supports the opposite case: strategics have paid about €138M for a pre-revenue POC immunoassay platform, close to Vantelle's $140M pre-money.

arguments.title: Roche closes acquisition of LumiraDx's Point of Care technology
arguments.claims: Roche closed its acquisition of LumiraDx's point-of-care technology platform on 2024-07-29, combining multiple diagnostic modalities on one instrument.
arguments.claims_weakened: Shows a strategic buyer will pay for a POC platform asset even from a distressed seller; sets a platform-value benchmark above a pure asset liquidation.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle Diagnostics sells a $33.40 cartridge that costs $16.20 to make, but at the 1.35 panels a day its own 41 evaluation sites average, a site returns $7,945 of annual gross profit — too little to cover the cost of selling and supporting it, so the $140M pre-money valuation is a bet on an eight-to-twelve-fold utilisation step-up that no disclosed data supports; the $30M buys a manufacturing cost curve and a distribution option, not proven unit economics. The clinic buys the analyzer and cartridges, its staff runs the test and bills the patient's insurer under existing codes; Vantelle never bills a payer. The clinic pays $2,900 for an analyzer that costs $3,350 to build, $650 a month per analyzer during the evaluation programme, and $38 list per cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. In the 2026 average the 55 analyzers in the field consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, 41 per site, and 60% of evaluation sites were given instruments free; the one large order in sight is a non-binding distributor letter of intent that becomes a $2.4M stocking order only when the 510(k) clears in Q1 2027 [S150]. All of these figures are company-reported and unaudited.

| Metric | Per unit, 2026 | Per unit, 2029 target | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Average selling price | $33.40 | $31.00 | — | S150, company-reported |
| Cost of goods | $16.20 | $7.50 | — | S150, company-reported |
| Gross profit | $17.20 (51.5%) | $23.50 (75.8%) | Abbott FY2025 gross margin 56.4% | S150; S3 |
| Corvia royalty, 3% of net sales | $1.00 | $0.93 | — | S150, company-reported |
| Gross profit after royalty | $16.20 (48.5%) | $22.57 (72.8%) | — | S150, derived, unaudited |
| Volume, cartridges a year | 20,160 | 2,532,000 | — | S150, derived, unaudited |
| Multiple of 2026 volume | 1.0x | 126x | — | S150, derived, unaudited |
| Gross profit pool after royalty | $0.33M | $57.1M | FY2029 plan gross profit $55.7M | S150, derived, unaudited |

The cartridge is the only link with positive gross margin, and it is thinner than presented. A 2026 cartridge earns $17.20 (51.5%); the 3% royalty on net cartridge sales paid to Corvia Microfluidics takes $1.00, leaving $16.20 and 48.5% — the deck reports 51%, without saying whether the royalty sits inside the $16.20. The 2029 target cuts cost 54% to $7.50 while price falls 7% to $31.00, lifting gross profit to $23.50, or $22.57 and 72.8% after royalty rather than the 76% shown. The volume required is the weak point: 2M cartridges is 99 times the 2026 run-rate of 20,160, and the FY2029 revenue line of $78.5M at $31 needs 2.53M cartridges, 126 times. The deck discloses no line capacity, yield, scrap rate or capex for it; the only visible cost is the 40% of the raise ($12M) labelled "scale cartridge manufacturing". Each percentage point of scrap at the target volume adds $0.08 to unit cost, so $7.50 depends on yield as much as on volume. The royalty also takes value off the top: Corvia is 60% owned by Vantelle, and the CTO, Dr Tomasz Lindqvist, holds 22% of Corvia, so he receives 0.66% of cartridge net sales — 3% of the FY2029 plan's cartridge revenue is $2.36M, of which his share is $0.52M. On an acquisition, Corvia's 40% minority may put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value, a claim ahead of common [S150].

| Panels a day per site (2 analyzers planned, 1.34 actual) | 1.35 | 16.0 | S150, derived, unaudited |
| Cartridge gross profit per analyzer a year, after royalty | $5,929 | $38,880 | S150, derived, unaudited |
| Instrument cash cost per placement (60% free, 40% at $2,900) | $2,190 | $2,190 | S150, derived, unaudited |
| Cash cost of the installed base | $120,450 (55 analyzers) | $2.31M (1,055 analyzers) | S150, derived, unaudited |
| Instrument payback, months | 4.4 | 0.7 | S150, derived, unaudited |

| Value of 13,200 sites at $38 a cartridge | $247M | $2.4B | S150, derived, unaudited |
