The instrument is not where the model breaks, but it is not free either. At $2,900 against a $3,350 build every analyzer sold loses $450 (-15.5%), and with 60% given away the cash cost averages $2,190 a placement: $120,450 for the 55 analyzers in the field, $1.31M for the 600 that a 300-site base implies, and $2.31M for the 1,055 the 2029 plan needs [S150]. Against that, an analyzer at the observed 30.5 cartridges a month produces $5,929 of cartridge gross profit a year after royalty and repays its subsidy in 4.4 months; at the modelled 240 cartridges a month it repays in under one month. The hardware is cheap customer acquisition. What it buys is a site whose profit depends on utilisation.

That is where the deck parts company with its own data. The model assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer and two analyzers a site, 16 a day per site; the evaluation sites averaged 1.35 a day per site and 1.02 per analyzer, a gap of 7.8 times per analyzer and 11.9 times per site [S150]. The $2.4B serviceable market is the same arithmetic (13,200 sites x 2 analyzers x 8 panels x 300 days x $38); at the observed rate those sites are worth $247M. Per-site cartridge gross profit is $7,945 a year at observed utilisation against $52,099 modelled. Selling cost is not disclosed; the nine sales and support staff imply $1.35M-$2.0M a year, or $33,000-$49,000 per active site today and $4,500-$6,700 a site at 300 sites, so a three-year LTV of $23,835 a site covers its selling cost 1.2-1.8 times at observed utilisation and 12-17 times at the modelled rate (analyst estimate; customer acquisition cost is not disclosed). This is a utilisation bet presented as a scale bet.

Revenue quality compounds the problem. FY2025's $2.6M was $1.1M of evaluation-programme revenue (42%), $0.8M of research-use cartridges sold to clinical research organisations (31%) and $0.7M of contract development for a partner (27%) — none of it cleared clinical testing [S150]. Revenue to September 2026 was $2.7M, and the $5.9M full-year estimate includes the $2.4M stocking order that ships only on clearance in Q1 2027, so underlying FY2026 is $3.5M, up 35% rather than 127%. The evaluation line does not reconcile with its own price either: 55 analyzers at $650 a month is $429,000 a year, 39% of the $1.1M booked in FY2025, so the line must also contain cartridges bought by evaluation sites or undisclosed fees. Until revenue is reported by type and customer, the recurring share cannot be calculated.

Payer risk sits with the clinic but does not stop there. After clearance the clinic bills Medicare or a commercial payer per test and buys cartridges from Vantelle, so a denial is its loss — and a reason not to reorder. Medicare's 2026 laboratory fee schedule pays $21.96 for the two assays in the first 510(k), 34% below the $33.40 cartridge before the clinic's labour and quality-control cost; the full five-test panel recovers $61.22 on the three assays whose rates are published, where the cartridge becomes affordable. These rates come from independent fee-schedule aggregators and are medium-confidence. The full panel needs the second 510(k), and clinic staff cannot run it without the CLIA waiver — a listed peer calls waived status "critical for most of our products that are intended for POC settings" and describes the waiver as onerous and slow [S7]. The Q1 2027 clearance launches a two-test product whose Medicare recovery is below its cartridge price.

arguments.markdown:
The team is credible on the slide and unverified in every record this diligence could reach (all CV facts below are company-reported and unverified). Vantelle's case rests on an emergency physician who saw the problem at the bedside, Dr. Wren Albescu, chief executive and director; a microfluidics engineer who founded the company holding the enabling sealing patent, Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist, chief technology officer and director; a regulatory vice president who joined in 2025-11; a commercial vice president hired in 2024-01; and a part-time interim chief financial officer. No credential, licence, patent inventorship, publication or prior exit for any of the five was confirmed in a public record here, and the searches returned nothing for either institution that awards the founders' degrees. A null result is not absence — the same search service returned nothing for well-documented listed companies — so the CVs are untested, not contradicted. What can be assessed is shape: nobody on the team has taken a point-of-care device through 510(k), CLIA waiver and volume manufacturing, and the two functions that decide that path were both replaced within six months [S150].

Founder-market fit is the strongest part of the story and the least documented. Albescu's claimed seven years as an emergency physician in Tucson (2011-2017) and a year as medical director at Quillon Diagnostics is exactly the background that would explain a product built for a 12-minute finger-stick panel, and Lindqvist's claimed PhD in bioengineering and four years at Pellucid Biosystems before founding Corvia Microfluidics in 2016 explains the cartridge. The checks are cheap and were not run: any US physician billing Medicare between 2011 and 2017 holds a record in the free CMS NPI registry, and Arizona and Texas medical boards publish licence status. Inventorship is equally checkable — CM-1 (US 15/707,915) and VD-1 (US 16/884,327) should name Lindqvist if the technical-founder account is accurate. Neither check appears in the deck, and no patent or publication record was retrieved here [S150].

### The regulatory bench is one hire deep

Grace Oyelaran's claim of 14 FDA 510(k) clearances at Meridale Medical between 2009 and 2025 is 0.9 a year, consistent with a senior director at a mid-size device maker, and it cannot be verified from FDA records, which name the applicant and correspondent rather than the staff who prepared a submission. What is documented is thinner: she joined on 2025-11, two months after her predecessor left during preparation of the submission; ISO 13485 certification is not held, with an audit booked for Q1 2027; and nine of 64 employees sit in clinical and regulatory against a workload of one additional-information response, a further three-assay submission, a four-site 1,150-patient pivotal study and a CLIA waiver application. Abbott cleared hs-troponin I cartridges twice in eighteen months (K240984 on 2025-01-03 and K253051 on 2026-06-11), the cadence of an established regulatory organisation rather than a fair comparison for a 64-person company; the fair test is one FDA request answered on time, by a bench in place under a year [S13, S148, S17, S150].

### One sales career, one part-time finance function

Commercial and financial leadership are single-track. Luis Arrellano spent 2006-2023 at one company, Tavora Health Systems, rising from sales representative to regional vice president for the Southwest — a 17-year record in the same three states where all 41 evaluation sites sit, with no disclosed diagnostics or capital-equipment experience, the experience the model needs since the analyzer is a $2,900 capital sale and the cartridge a recurring consumable. Darnell Whitcombe has been interim CFO since 2026-03 through his advisory firm, part-time, while the company ran a $6.0M bridge, a $30.0M round and a $5.0M term loan that begins amortising in 2027-03; six of 64 employees work in finance and administration. A part-time CFO is common below $10M of revenue; a part-time CFO through a priced round with a bridge, warrants and a participating preference is a choice the lead should reverse before funding [S150].

### Governance concentrates the same risk

Five of six board seats are filled: two common held by the founders, one seed, one Series A and one Series B, with the independent seat vacant — so until it is filled the founders sit with the investors committing $8.0M of the round. The Corvia royalty and put are related-party matters that one founder-director benefits from and the other votes on, and no protective provisions, information rights or drag-along terms appear in the deck. Key-person dependency is high on both founders and on the regulatory vice president. After the round the founders hold 11,200,000 shares, 21.5% against 30.8% today, with a 20.0% option pool and a share price flat since 2022: the retention question is whether two founders diluted to a fifth of the company keep the appetite a five-assay panel and a three-year regulatory calendar demand [S150].

### What would settle it

Three checks would settle most of this before a term sheet: confirm Albescu's NPI and state licences and both founders' degrees directly with the awarding institutions; obtain Meridale Medical's 510(k) list and three named references, one of them on FDA interaction; and take structured references on the two 2025-2026 departures. The hires still missing are a full-time CFO, a regulatory lead with point-of-care clearance experience at vice-president level or above, and an independent director the new lead nominates. What would change the decision is all three in place before close, with a milestone tranche tied to the additional-information response. Until then the team rests on two founders' clinical and engineering insight, supported by no record this diligence could open — a reason to condition the investment and price the execution risk, not to walk away [S150].

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has built something genuinely difficult — a 40-microlitre finger-stick sample into five results in twelve minutes on a self-calibrating cartridge — and has not shown that it works as a diagnostic. Its own study puts troponin I at 11.8% imprecision at the cut-off that drives the chest-pain decision, on 128 patients at one site, run by Vantelle staff and scored as normal or abnormal rather than as a number; the reader patent was finally rejected in July 2026; and the dried chemistry behind the troponin result is an unpublished PCT outside the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion [S150]. What Vantelle owns outright is time, and time is the one asset a funded competitor can buy.

### The difficult part is the dried chemistry

The Q5 is three technologies in a 640-gram box: a capillary-fill cartridge metering 40 microlitres, a dried-reagent chemistry that must survive nine months at room temperature, and an optical reader correcting drift across five assays. The cartridge is patented (US 16/884,327, filed 2020-05-28, granted 2023-03). The chemistry decides whether the troponin number is right, and it is kept secret: an unpublished PCT filed 2026-02-11, no claim and no freedom-to-operate cover. The reader is the one the Patent Office rejected. On-board calibration removes daily quality control, but it turns a calibrator fault into a silent bias across a whole lot, and finger-stick blood adds what a tube removes — haematocrit and haemolysis, an interference class the IFCC treats as first-order for troponin and especially for potassium, which an optical platform cannot read with a blood-gas electrode [S166].

### The performance claim is a category count from one site

98.7% agreement is not concordance. The study drew venous blood from 128 patients at one urgent-care site between September and December 2025, ran it on the Q5 with Vantelle staff operating, and scored each result into the same category as the reference laboratory. That discards the magnitude the clinician uses — a troponin of 14 and one of 60 ng/L are one category if both exceed the cut-off — while the decision the product serves turns on magnitude and on change between samples. The summary row does not close either: 634 of 640 is 99.1%, and the five per-assay rates imply about 626 agreements in 634 analysable results, so 98.7% is a share of the analysable set printed as a count out of 640. The incumbent's evidence is another order of magnitude, and simulation shows single-threshold error rising steeply with the imprecision and bias this study was not designed to measure [S10, S124].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the decision level | 11.8% CV | 10% or better at the 99th-percentile URL | S150, S163 |
| Troponin I agreement | 96.1% (123 of 128) | Category agreement, not concordance | S150 |
| Five-assay agreement | 98.7% claimed | 634 of 640 is 99.1%; per-assay rates imply ~626 of 634 | S150 |

### Clearance is later than the deck says, and the waiver later still

The 510(k) was filed 2026-05-18 and FDA asked for more information on 2026-08-21, with 180 days to answer and a December 2026 answer planned, so a Q1 2027 clearance needs a decision within about three months of that response; FDA's clearance database held no record for K261734, or for any device under the company's name, on 2026-10-30 [S7, S191]. Only two of five assays sit in that submission, and the CLIA waiver — permission for staff without laboratory training — is not planned until Q3 2027. QuidelOrtho, selling into the same channel, calls the waived designation "critical" for its point-of-care products and the requirements "onerous" [S7]. Until a waiver is granted the Q5 is a moderate-complexity test for a certificated laboratory: a different buyer and a much smaller market.

| Operator | Laboratory staff until a waiver is granted | Trained operator; waiver status unverified here | S150, S7 |
| External validation | None located | Independent UK emergency-department evaluation, 2026 | S144 |

### The patent estate is one granted family owned outright

| Patent or application | Subject | Filed / granted | Status | Source |

| US 16/884,327, plus EP family | Capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator | 2020-05-28 / 2023-03 | US granted to ~2040-05; Europe pending | S150 |
| US 17/662,019 | Five-assay optical reader with drift correction | 2022-05-04 / — | Final rejection 2026-07; appeal under consideration | S150 |
| US 19/318,770 | Finger-stick sample-volume check | 2025-09-30 / — | Unpublished | S150 |

| US 15/707,915 | Cartridge sealing film and reagent blister | 2017-09-18 / 2021-01 | Granted to ~2037-09; owned by 60%-held Corvia, licensed at 3% | S150 |

The estate reduces to one US patent granted to the parent, one granted patent in a subsidiary Vantelle owns 60% of and licenses back at a 3% royalty whose beneficiaries include the chief technology officer, one finally rejected application and two unpublished ones. The reader is unpatented, and the six-month window after a final rejection puts the appeal-or-abandon decision around the round's January 2027 close; the freedom-to-operate opinion predates the troponin chemistry and excludes it [S150].

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dried-reagent troponin chemistry | 8 | Antibody stability at room temperature sets imprecision | 3-4 years |
| Cartridge manufacturability at scale | 7 | 40 µL fill, on-board calibrator, 9-month shelf life; haemolysis fails first | 2-3 years |
| Clearance and CLIA waiver | 9 | Two 510(k)s plus a multi-site operator study | 3-5 years |
| Reader design | 3 | Optics are engineering, not science; claim rejected | 6-12 months |
| Patent protection | 2 | One granted US family owned outright | immediate |

Fifty funded engineers given the published cartridge and sealing patents would have a working five-assay reader in 18 months; what they could not have is a cleared troponin assay. The moat is three to four years of regulatory and manufacturing time, not a technical lead.

| Product | Stage | Revenue, FY2025 | Next milestone |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 five-assay panel | Two of five assays in K261734 | $1.1M evaluation fees | Clearance; other three assays filed Q2 2027 |
| Research-use cartridges | Selling to CROs | $0.8M | None stated |

The cost curve is the most credible number in the deck. $16.20 a cartridge at roughly 20,000 units a year falls to $7.50 at 2 million, a 54% cut over about 6.6 doublings, or roughly 11% per doubling — shallower than the 15-25% that volume-driven hardware usually achieves, so the target is not the implausible part; what is missing is the bill of materials, since antibody and reagent do not get cheaper the way moulded plastic does. The pilot line is 18 people running about 1,680 cartridges a month, so a million a year is a fifty-fold increase, and $12M of the round goes into it without a disclosed capex or qualification schedule. Abbott's i-STAT cTnI cartridges were recalled four times in 2011-2013 for design, labelling and contamination — the taxonomy a dried-reagent cartridge inherits.

::: evidence
**The number that decides the technology is 11.8% — the troponin assay's imprecision at the cut-off the product exists to interpret — reported without the standard it must meet.**

The IFCC defines a high-sensitivity assay by imprecision at the 99th-percentile URL and measurability in most healthy people [S163]; simulation shows single-threshold error climbing steeply with imprecision and bias. Four Vantelle assays sit at 2.4-7.2% CV; the one driving the transfer decision sits at 11.8%, from a study that cannot settle it.
:::

The dependencies are concentrated: the sealing film is licensed from a company Vantelle owns 60% of, at a 3% royalty partly flowing to the chief technology officer; there is one manufacturing site and no disclosed second source; and the three assays not yet submitted depend on chemistry with neither a granted claim nor a freedom-to-operate opinion. Readiness is uneven in a way the single Q5 label hides: troponin and HbA1c are at a submission, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium sit behind a pivotal study, and the untrained-operator configuration the model depends on has not been tested at all. Until the pivotal study's precision data exist, the accuracy claim is partially verified and the technology is a cartridge company holding a regulatory option, not a validated platform.

arguments.markdown:
The team is credible on the slide and unverified in every record this diligence could reach (all CV facts below are company-reported and unverified). Vantelle's case rests on an emergency physician who saw the problem at the bedside, Dr. Wren Albescu, chief executive and director; a microfluidics engineer who founded the company holding the enabling sealing patent, Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist, chief technology officer and director; a regulatory vice president who joined in 2025-11; a commercial vice president hired in 2024-01; and a part-time interim chief financial officer. No credential, licence, patent inventorship, publication or prior exit for any of the five was confirmed in a public record here, and the searches returned nothing for either institution that awards the founders' degrees. A null result is not absence — the same search service returned nothing for well-documented listed companies — so the CVs are untested, not contradicted. What can be assessed is shape: nobody on the team has taken a point-of-care device through 510(k), CLIA waiver and volume manufacturing, and the two functions that decide that path were both replaced within six months [S150].

Founder-market fit is the strongest part of the story and the least documented. Albescu's claimed seven years as an emergency physician in Tucson (2011-2017) and a year as medical director at Quillon Diagnostics is exactly the background that would explain a product built for a 12-minute finger-stick panel, and Lindqvist's claimed PhD in bioengineering and four years at Pellucid Biosystems before founding Corvia Microfluidics in 2016 explains the cartridge. The checks are cheap and were not run: any US physician billing Medicare between 2011 and 2017 holds a record in the free CMS NPI registry, and Arizona and Texas medical boards publish licence status. Inventorship is equally checkable — CM-1 (US 15/707,915) and VD-1 (US 16/884,327) should name Lindqvist if the technical-founder account is accurate. Neither check appears in the deck [S150].

### The regulatory bench is one hire deep

Grace Oyelaran's claim of 14 FDA 510(k) clearances at Meridale Medical between 2009 and 2025 is 0.9 a year, consistent with a senior director at a mid-size device maker, and it cannot be verified from FDA records, which name the applicant and correspondent rather than the staff who prepared a submission. What is documented is thinner: she joined on 2025-11, two months after her predecessor left during preparation of the submission; ISO 13485 certification is not held, with an audit booked for Q1 2027; and nine of 64 employees sit in clinical and regulatory against a workload of one additional-information response, a further three-assay submission, a four-site 1,150-patient pivotal study and a CLIA waiver application. Abbott cleared hs-troponin I cartridges twice in eighteen months (K240984 on 2025-01-03 and K253051 on 2026-06-11), the cadence of an established regulatory organisation rather than a fair comparison for a 64-person company; the fair test is one FDA request answered on time, by a bench in place under a year [S13, S148, S17, S150].

### One sales career, one part-time finance function

Commercial and financial leadership are single-track. Luis Arrellano spent 2006-2023 at one company, Tavora Health Systems, rising from sales representative to regional vice president for the Southwest — a 17-year record in the same three states where all 41 evaluation sites sit, with no disclosed diagnostics or capital-equipment experience, the experience the model needs since the analyzer is a $2,900 capital sale and the cartridge a recurring consumable. Darnell Whitcombe has been interim CFO since 2026-03 through his advisory firm, part-time, while the company ran a $6.0M bridge, a $30.0M round and a $5.0M term loan that begins amortising in 2027-03; six of 64 employees work in finance and administration. A part-time CFO is common below $10M of revenue; a part-time CFO through a priced round with a bridge, warrants and a participating preference is a choice the lead should reverse before funding [S150].

### Governance concentrates the same risk

Five of six board seats are filled: two common held by the founders, one seed, one Series A and one Series B, with the independent seat vacant — so until it is filled the founders sit with the investors committing $8.0M of the round. The Corvia royalty and put are related-party matters that one founder-director benefits from and the other votes on, and no protective provisions, information rights or drag-along terms appear in the deck. Key-person dependency is high on both founders and on the regulatory vice president. After the round the founders hold 11,200,000 shares, 21.5% against 30.8% today, with a 20.0% option pool and a share price flat since 2022: the retention question is whether two founders diluted to a fifth of the company keep the appetite a five-assay panel and a three-year regulatory calendar demand [S150].

### What would settle it

Three checks would settle most of this before a term sheet: confirm Albescu's NPI and state licences and both founders' degrees directly with the awarding institutions; obtain Meridale Medical's 510(k) list and three named references, one of them on FDA interaction; and take structured references on the two 2025-2026 departures. The hires still missing are a full-time CFO, a regulatory lead with point-of-care clearance experience at vice-president level or above, and an independent director the new lead nominates. What would change the decision is all three in place before close. Until then the team rests on two founders' clinical and engineering insight, supported by no record this diligence could open — a reason to condition the investment and price the execution risk, not to walk away [S150].

Abbott cleared hs-troponin I cartridges on 2025-01-03 and again on 2026-06-11 — the output of a standing regulatory organisation [S13, S17, S150].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has built something genuinely difficult — a 40-microlitre finger-stick sample into five results in twelve minutes on a self-calibrating cartridge — and has not shown that it works as a diagnostic. Its own study puts troponin I at 11.8% imprecision at the cut-off that drives the chest-pain decision, on 128 patients at one site, run by Vantelle staff and scored as normal or abnormal rather than as a number; the reader patent was finally rejected in July 2026; and the dried chemistry behind the troponin result is an unpublished PCT outside the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion [S150]. What Vantelle owns outright is time, and time is the one asset a funded competitor can buy.

### The difficult part is the dried chemistry

The Q5 is three technologies in a 640-gram box: a capillary-fill cartridge metering 40 microlitres, a dried-reagent chemistry that must survive nine months at room temperature, and an optical reader correcting drift across five assays. The cartridge is patented (US 16/884,327, filed 2020-05-28, granted 2023-03). The chemistry decides whether the troponin number is right, and it is kept secret: an unpublished PCT filed 2026-02-11, no claim and no freedom-to-operate cover. The reader is the one the Patent Office rejected. On-board calibration removes daily quality control, but it turns a calibrator fault into a silent bias across a whole lot, and finger-stick blood adds what a tube removes — haematocrit and haemolysis, an interference class the IFCC treats as first-order for troponin and especially for potassium, which an optical platform cannot read with a blood-gas electrode [S166].

### The performance claim is a category count from one site

98.7% agreement is not concordance. The study drew venous blood from 128 patients at one urgent-care site between September and December 2025, ran it on the Q5 with Vantelle staff operating, and scored each result into the same category as the reference laboratory. That discards the magnitude the clinician uses — a troponin of 14 and one of 60 ng/L are one category if both exceed the cut-off — while the decision the product serves turns on magnitude and on change between samples. The summary row does not close either: 634 of 640 is 99.1%, and the five per-assay rates imply about 626 agreements in 634 analysable results, so 98.7% is a share of the analysable set printed as a count out of 640. The incumbent's evidence is another order of magnitude, and simulation shows single-threshold error rising steeply with the imprecision and bias this study was not designed to measure [S10, S124].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the decision level | 11.8% CV | 10% or better at the 99th-percentile URL | S150, S163 |
| Troponin I agreement | 96.1% (123 of 128) | Category agreement, not concordance | S150 |
| Five-assay agreement | 98.7% claimed | 634 of 640 is 99.1%; per-assay rates imply ~626 of 634 | S150 |

### Clearance is later than the deck says, and the waiver later still

The 510(k) was filed 2026-05-18 and FDA asked for more information on 2026-08-21, with 180 days to answer and a December 2026 answer planned, so a Q1 2027 clearance needs a decision within about three months of that response; FDA's clearance database held no record for K261734, or for any device under the company's name, on 2026-10-30 [S7, S191]. Only two of five assays sit in that submission, and the CLIA waiver — permission for staff without laboratory training — is not planned until Q3 2027. QuidelOrtho, selling into the same channel, calls the waived designation "critical" for its point-of-care products and the requirements "onerous" [S7]. Until a waiver is granted the Q5 is a moderate-complexity test for a certificated laboratory: a different buyer and a much smaller market.

|---|---|---|---|
| US status | Two of five assays in K261734, information request pending; nothing cleared | hs-TnI cleared 2025-01-03 (i-STAT 1), 2026-06-11 (Alinity) | S191, S17, S13 |
| Evidence scale | 128 patients, one site, company-run | 3,697-patient study, completed 2024-02 | S150, S124 |
| Platform menu | Five assays in one cartridge | Blood gas, chemistry, electrolytes, coagulation, immunoassay | S150, S3 |
| Operator | Laboratory staff until a waiver is granted | Trained operator; waiver status unverified here | S150, S7 |
| External validation | None located | Independent UK emergency-department evaluation, 2026 | S144 |

### The patent estate is one granted family owned outright

| Patent or application | Subject | Filed / granted | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327, plus EP family | Capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator | 2020-05-28 / 2023-03 | US granted to ~2040-05; Europe pending | S150 |
| US 17/662,019 | Five-assay optical reader with drift correction | 2022-05-04 / — | Final rejection 2026-07; appeal under consideration | S150 |
| US 19/318,770 | Finger-stick sample-volume check | 2025-09-30 / — | Unpublished | S150 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 | Troponin chemistry on dried reagents | 2026-02-11 / — | Unpublished; outside the 2024 FTO opinion | S150 |
| US 15/707,915 | Cartridge sealing film and reagent blister | 2017-09-18 / 2021-01 | Granted to ~2037-09; owned by 60%-held Corvia, licensed at 3% | S150 |

The estate reduces to one US patent granted to the parent, one granted patent in a subsidiary Vantelle owns 60% of and licenses back at a 3% royalty whose beneficiaries include the chief technology officer, one finally rejected application and two unpublished ones. The reader is unpatented, and the six-month window after a final rejection puts the appeal-or-abandon decision around the round's January 2027 close; the freedom-to-operate opinion predates the troponin chemistry and excludes it [S150].

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dried-reagent troponin chemistry | 8 | Antibody stability at room temperature sets imprecision | 3-4 years |
| Cartridge manufacturability at scale | 7 | 40 µL fill, on-board calibrator, 9-month shelf life; haemolysis fails first | 2-3 years |
| Clearance and CLIA waiver | 9 | Two 510(k)s plus a multi-site operator study | 3-5 years |
| Reader design | 3 | Optics are engineering, not science; claim rejected | 6-12 months |
| Patent protection | 2 | One granted US family owned outright | immediate |

Fifty funded engineers given the published cartridge and sealing patents would have a working five-assay reader in 18 months; what they could not have is a cleared troponin assay. The moat is three to four years of regulatory and manufacturing time, not a technical lead.

| Product | Stage | Revenue, FY2025 | Next milestone |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 five-assay panel | Two of five assays in K261734 | $1.1M evaluation fees | Clearance; other three assays filed Q2 2027 |
| Research-use cartridges | Selling to CROs | $0.8M | None stated |

The cost curve is the most credible number in the deck. $16.20 a cartridge at roughly 20,000 units a year falls to $7.50 at 2 million, a 54% cut over about 6.6 doublings, or roughly 11% per doubling — shallower than the 15-25% that volume-driven hardware usually achieves, so the target is not the implausible part; what is missing is the bill of materials, since antibody and reagent do not get cheaper the way moulded plastic does. The pilot line is 18 people running about 1,680 cartridges a month; a million a year is a fifty-fold increase, and $12M of the round goes into it without a disclosed capex or qualification schedule. Abbott's i-STAT cTnI cartridges were recalled four times in 2011-2013 for design, labelling and contamination — the taxonomy a dried-reagent cartridge inherits.

::: evidence
**The number that decides the technology is 11.8% — the troponin assay's imprecision at the cut-off the product exists to interpret — reported without the standard it must meet.**

The IFCC defines a high-sensitivity assay by imprecision at the 99th-percentile URL and measurability in most healthy people [S163]; simulation shows single-threshold error climbing steeply with imprecision and bias. Four Vantelle assays sit at 2.4-7.2% CV; the one driving the transfer decision sits at 11.8%, from a study that cannot settle it.
:::

The dependencies are concentrated: the sealing film is licensed from a company Vantelle owns 60% of, at a 3% royalty partly flowing to the chief technology officer; one manufacturing site, no disclosed second source; and the three assays not yet submitted depend on chemistry with neither a granted claim nor a freedom-to-operate opinion. Readiness is uneven: troponin and HbA1c are at a submission, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium sit behind a pivotal study, and the untrained-operator configuration the model depends on has not been tested. Until the pivotal study's precision data exist, the accuracy claim is partially verified and the technology is a cartridge company holding a regulatory option, not a validated platform.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle Diagnostics sells a $33.40 cartridge that costs $16.20 to make, but at the 1.35 panels a day its own 41 evaluation sites average, a site returns $7,945 of annual gross profit — too little to cover the cost of selling and supporting it, so the $140M pre-money valuation is a bet on an eight-to-twelve-fold utilisation step-up that no disclosed data supports; the $30M buys a manufacturing cost curve and a distribution option, not proven unit economics. The clinic buys the analyzer and cartridges, its staff runs the test and bills the patient's insurer under existing codes; Vantelle never bills a payer. The clinic pays $2,900 for an analyzer that costs $3,350 to build, $650 a month per analyzer during the evaluation programme, and $38 list per cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. In the 2026 average the 55 analyzers in the field consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, 41 per site, and 60% of evaluation sites were given instruments free; the one large order in sight is a non-binding distributor letter of intent that becomes a $2.4M stocking order only when the 510(k) clears in Q1 2027 [S150]. All figures are company-reported and unverified.

| Metric | Per unit, 2026 | Per unit, 2029 target | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Average selling price | $33.40 | $31.00 | — | S150, unverified |
| Cost of goods | $16.20 | $7.50 | — | S150, unverified |
| Gross profit | $17.20 (51.5%) | $23.50 (75.8%) | Abbott FY2025 gross margin 56.4% | S150; S3 |
| Corvia royalty, 3% of net sales | $1.00 | $0.93 | — | S150, unverified |
| Gross profit after royalty | $16.20 (48.5%) | $22.57 (72.8%) | — | S150, unverified |
| Volume, cartridges a year | 20,160 | 2,532,000 | — | S150, unverified |
| Multiple of 2026 volume | 1.0x | 126x | — | S150, unverified |
| Gross profit pool after royalty | $0.33M | $57.1M | FY2029 plan gross profit $55.7M | S150, unverified |

The cartridge is the only link with positive gross margin, and it is thinner than presented. A 2026 cartridge earns $17.20 (51.5%); the 3% royalty on net cartridge sales paid to Corvia Microfluidics takes $1.00, leaving $16.20 and 48.5% — the deck reports 51% without saying whether the royalty sits inside the $16.20. The 2029 target cuts cost 54% to $7.50 while price falls 7% to $31.00, lifting gross profit to $23.50, or $22.57 and 72.8% after royalty rather than the 76% shown. The volume required is the weak point: 2M cartridges is 99 times the 2026 run-rate of 20,160, and the FY2029 revenue line of $78.5M at $31 needs 2.53M cartridges, 126 times. The deck discloses no line capacity, yield, scrap rate or capex for it; the only visible cost is the 40% of the raise ($12M) labelled "scale cartridge manufacturing". Each percentage point of scrap at the target volume adds $0.08 to unit cost, so $7.50 depends on yield as much as on volume. The royalty also takes value off the top: Corvia is 60% owned by Vantelle and the CTO, Dr Tomasz Lindqvist, holds 22% of it, so he receives 0.66% of cartridge net sales — 3% of the FY2029 plan's cartridge revenue is $2.36M, of which his share is $0.52M. On an acquisition, Corvia's 40% minority may put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value, a claim ahead of common [S150].

| Metric | Evaluation actual, 2026 | Plan from 2028 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridges per analyzer a month | 30.5 | 240 | S150, unverified |
| Panels a day per analyzer | 1.02 | 8.0 | S150, unverified |
| Panels a day per site (2 analyzers planned, 1.34 actual) | 1.35 | 16.0 | S150, unverified |
| Cartridge gross profit per analyzer a year, after royalty | $5,929 | $38,880 | S150, unverified |
| Instrument cash cost per placement (60% free, 40% at $2,900) | $2,190 | $2,190 | S150, unverified |
| Cash cost of the installed base | $120,450 (55 analyzers) | $2.31M (1,055 analyzers) | S150, unverified |
| Instrument payback, months | 4.4 | 0.7 | S150, unverified |
| Three-year cartridge gross profit per site, after royalty | $23,835 | $233,280 | S150, unverified |
| Selling cost per site a year, analyst estimate | $33,000-49,000 | $4,500-6,700 | S150, unverified |
| Value of 13,200 sites at $38 a cartridge | $247M | $2.4B | S150, unverified |
| Sites needed for $78.5M of FY2029 revenue | 3,459 | 527 | S150, unverified |

The instrument is not where the model breaks, but it is not free either. At $2,900 against a $3,350 build every analyzer sold loses $450 (-15.5%), and with 60% given away the cash cost averages $2,190 a placement: $120,450 for the 55 analyzers in the field, $1.31M for the 600 that a 300-site base implies, and $2.31M for the 1,055 the 2029 plan needs [S150]. Against that, an analyzer at the observed 30.5 cartridges a month produces $5,929 of cartridge gross profit a year after royalty and repays its subsidy in 4.4 months; at the modelled 240 cartridges a month it repays in under one month. The hardware is cheap customer acquisition. What it buys is a site whose profit depends on utilisation.

That is where the deck parts company with its own data. The model assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer and two analyzers a site, 16 a day per site; the evaluation sites averaged 1.35 a day per site and 1.02 per analyzer, a gap of 7.8 times per analyzer and 11.9 times per site [S150]. The $2.4B serviceable market is the same arithmetic (13,200 sites x 2 analyzers x 8 panels x 300 days x $38); at the observed rate those sites are worth $247M. Per-site cartridge gross profit is $7,945 a year at observed utilisation against $52,099 modelled. Selling cost is not disclosed; the nine sales and support staff imply $1.35M-$2.0M a year, or $33,000-$49,000 per active site today and $4,500-$6,700 a site at 300 sites, so a three-year LTV of $23,835 a site covers its selling cost 1.2-1.8 times at observed utilisation and 12-17 times at the modelled rate (analyst estimate; customer acquisition cost is not disclosed). This is a utilisation bet presented as a scale bet.

Revenue quality compounds the problem. FY2025's $2.6M was $1.1M of evaluation-programme revenue (42%), $0.8M of research-use cartridges sold to clinical research organisations (31%) and $0.7M of contract development for a partner (27%) — none of it cleared clinical testing [S150]. Revenue to September 2026 was $2.7M, and the $5.9M full-year estimate includes the $2.4M stocking order that ships only on clearance in Q1 2027, so underlying FY2026 is $3.5M, up 35% rather than 127%. The evaluation line does not reconcile with its own price either: 55 analyzers at $650 a month is $429,000 a year, 39% of the $1.1M booked in FY2025, so it must also contain cartridges bought by evaluation sites or undisclosed fees. Until revenue is reported by type and customer, the recurring share cannot be calculated.

Payer risk sits with the clinic but does not stop there. After clearance the clinic bills Medicare or a commercial payer per test and buys cartridges from Vantelle, so a denial is its loss — and a reason not to reorder. Medicare's 2026 laboratory fee schedule pays $21.96 for the two assays in the first 510(k), 34% below the $33.40 cartridge before the clinic's labour and quality-control cost; the full five-test panel recovers $61.22 on the three assays whose rates are published, where the cartridge becomes affordable. Independent fee-schedule aggregators supply these rates; medium confidence. The full panel needs the second 510(k), and clinic staff cannot run it without the CLIA waiver — a listed peer calls waived status "critical for most of our products that are intended for POC settings" and describes the waiver as onerous and slow [S7]. The Q1 2027 clearance launches a two-test product whose Medicare recovery is below its cartridge price.

| Test (CPT) | Medicare 2026 rate | Cleared in the first 510(k)? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin, quantitative (84484) | $12.47 | Yes | S177, independent |
| HbA1c (83036) | $9.49 | Yes | S178, independent |
| BNP/NT-proBNP (83880) | $39.26 | No, second 510(k) | S176, independent |
| First two assays, subtotal | $21.96 | — | Derived, S177-S178 |
| Three assays, subtotal | $61.22 | — | Derived, S176-S178 |

::: evidence
**At the utilisation its own evaluation sites show, Vantelle's cartridge annuity does not cover the cost of selling a site; the plan needs a step-up in panels per day that no disclosed data supports.**

Evidence: the $2.4B market model assumes 16 panels a day per site against 1.35 observed, and 2M cartridges a year is 99 times the current run-rate; LumiraDx was placed in pre-pack administration on 2023-12-29 and its platform sold to Roche for $295M, while Cue Health filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28 after raising more than $480M [S150, S172, S173, S174].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has built something genuinely difficult — a 40-microlitre finger-stick sample into five results in twelve minutes on a self-calibrating cartridge — and has not shown that it works as a diagnostic. Its own study puts troponin I at 11.8% imprecision at the cut-off that drives the chest-pain decision, on 128 patients at one site, run by Vantelle staff and scored as normal or abnormal rather than as a number; the reader patent was finally rejected in July 2026; and the dried chemistry behind the troponin result is an unpublished PCT outside the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion [S150]. What Vantelle owns outright is time, and time is the one asset a funded competitor can buy.

### The difficult part is the dried chemistry

The Q5 is three technologies in a 640-gram box: a capillary-fill cartridge metering 40 microlitres, a dried-reagent chemistry that must survive nine months at room temperature, and an optical reader correcting drift across five assays. The cartridge is patented (US 16/884,327, filed 2020-05-28, granted 2023-03). The chemistry decides whether the troponin number is right, and it is kept secret: an unpublished PCT filed 2026-02-11, no claim and no freedom-to-operate cover. The reader is the one the Patent Office rejected. On-board calibration removes daily quality control, but it turns a calibrator fault into a silent bias across a whole lot, and finger-stick blood adds what a tube removes — haematocrit and haemolysis, an interference class the IFCC treats as first-order for troponin and especially for potassium, which an optical platform cannot read with a blood-gas electrode [S166].

### The performance claim is a category count from one site

98.7% agreement is not concordance. The study drew venous blood from 128 patients at one urgent-care site between September and December 2025, ran it on the Q5 with Vantelle staff operating, and scored each result into the same category as the reference laboratory. That discards the magnitude the clinician uses — a troponin of 14 and one of 60 ng/L are one category if both exceed the cut-off — while the decision the product serves turns on magnitude and on change between samples. The summary row does not close either: 634 of 640 is 99.1%, and the five per-assay rates imply about 626 agreements in 634 analysable results, so 98.7% is a share of the analysable set printed as a count out of 640. The incumbent's evidence is another order of magnitude, and simulation shows single-threshold error rising steeply with the imprecision and bias this study was not designed to measure [S10, S124].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the decision level | 11.8% CV | 10% or better at the 99th-percentile URL | S150, S163 |
| Troponin I agreement | 96.1% (123 of 128) | Category agreement, not concordance | S150 |
| Five-assay agreement | 98.7% claimed | 634 of 640 is 99.1%; per-assay rates imply ~626 of 634 | S150 |

### Clearance is later than the deck says, and the waiver later still

The 510(k) was filed 2026-05-18 and FDA asked for more information on 2026-08-21, with 180 days to answer and a December 2026 answer planned, so a Q1 2027 clearance needs a decision within about three months of that response; FDA's clearance database held no record for K261734, or for any device under the company's name, on 2026-10-30 [S7, S191]. Only two of five assays sit in that submission, and the CLIA waiver — permission for staff without laboratory training — is not planned until Q3 2027. QuidelOrtho, selling into the same channel, calls the waived designation "critical" for its point-of-care products and the requirements "onerous" [S7]. Until a waiver is granted the Q5 is a moderate-complexity test for a certificated laboratory: a different buyer and a much smaller market.

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT platform | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US status | Two of five assays in K261734, information request pending; nothing cleared | hs-TnI cleared 2025-01-03 (i-STAT 1), 2026-06-11 (Alinity) | S191, S17, S13 |
| Evidence scale | 128 patients, one site, company-run | 3,697-patient study, completed 2024-02 | S150, S124 |
| Platform menu | Five assays in one cartridge | Blood gas, chemistry, electrolytes, coagulation, immunoassay | S150, S3 |
| Operator | Laboratory staff until a waiver is granted | Trained operator; waiver status unverified here | S150, S7 |

### The patent estate is one granted family owned outright

| Patent or application | Subject | Filed / granted | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327, plus EP family | Capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator | 2020-05-28 / 2023-03 | US granted to ~2040-05; Europe pending | S150 |
| US 17/662,019 | Five-assay optical reader with drift correction | 2022-05-04 / — | Final rejection 2026-07; appeal under consideration | S150 |
| US 19/318,770 | Finger-stick sample-volume check | 2025-09-30 / — | Unpublished | S150 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 | Troponin chemistry on dried reagents | 2026-02-11 / — | Unpublished; outside the 2024 FTO opinion | S150 |
| US 15/707,915 | Cartridge sealing film and reagent blister | 2017-09-18 / 2021-01 | Granted to ~2037-09; owned by 60%-held Corvia, licensed at 3% | S150 |

The estate reduces to one US patent granted to the parent, one granted patent in a subsidiary Vantelle owns 60% of and licenses back at a 3% royalty whose beneficiaries include the chief technology officer, one finally rejected application and two unpublished ones. The reader is unpatented, and the six-month window after a final rejection puts the appeal-or-abandon decision around the round's January 2027 close; the freedom-to-operate opinion predates the troponin chemistry and excludes it [S150].

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dried-reagent troponin chemistry | 8 | Antibody stability at room temperature sets imprecision | 3-4 years |
| Cartridge manufacturability at scale | 7 | 40 µL fill, on-board calibrator, 9-month shelf life; haemolysis fails first | 2-3 years |
| Clearance and CLIA waiver | 9 | Two 510(k)s plus a multi-site operator study | 3-5 years |
| Reader design | 3 | Optics are engineering, not science; claim rejected | 6-12 months |
| Patent protection | 2 | One granted US family owned outright | immediate |

Fifty funded engineers given the published cartridge and sealing patents would have a working five-assay reader in 18 months; what they could not have is a cleared troponin assay. The moat is three to four years of regulatory and manufacturing time, not a technical lead.

| Product | Stage | Revenue, FY2025 | Next milestone |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 five-assay panel | Two of five assays in K261734 | $1.1M evaluation fees | Clearance; other three assays filed Q2 2027 |
| Research-use cartridges | Selling to CROs | $0.8M | None stated |

The cost curve is the most credible number in the deck. $16.20 a cartridge at roughly 20,000 units a year falls to $7.50 at 2 million, a 54% cut over about 6.6 doublings, or roughly 11% per doubling — shallower than the 15-25% that volume-driven hardware usually achieves, so the target is not the implausible part; what is missing is the bill of materials, since antibody and reagent do not get cheaper the way moulded plastic does. The pilot line is 18 people running about 1,680 cartridges a month; a million a year is a fifty-fold increase, and $12M of the round goes into it without a disclosed capex or qualification schedule. Abbott's i-STAT cTnI cartridges were recalled four times in 2011-2013 for design, labelling and contamination — the taxonomy a dried-reagent cartridge inherits.

::: evidence
**The number that decides the technology is 11.8% — the troponin assay's imprecision at the cut-off the product exists to interpret — reported without the standard it must meet.**

The IFCC defines a high-sensitivity assay by imprecision at the 99th-percentile URL and measurability in most healthy people [S163]; simulation shows single-threshold error climbing steeply with imprecision and bias. Four Vantelle assays sit at 2.4-7.2% CV; the one driving the transfer decision sits at 11.8%, from a study that cannot settle it.
:::

The dependencies are concentrated: the sealing film is licensed from a company Vantelle owns 60% of, at a 3% royalty partly flowing to the chief technology officer; one manufacturing site, no disclosed second source; and the three assays not yet submitted depend on chemistry with neither a granted claim nor a freedom-to-operate opinion. Readiness is uneven: troponin and HbA1c are at a submission, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium sit behind a pivotal study, and the untrained-operator configuration the model depends on has not been tested. Until the pivotal study's precision data exist, the accuracy claim is partially verified and the technology is a cartridge company holding a regulatory option, not a validated platform.

arguments.markdown:
The team is credible on the slide and unverified in every record this diligence could reach (all CV facts below are company-reported and unverified). Vantelle's case rests on an emergency physician who saw the problem at the bedside, Dr. Wren Albescu, chief executive and director; a microfluidics engineer who founded the company holding the enabling sealing patent, Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist, chief technology officer and director; a regulatory vice president who joined in 2025-11; a commercial vice president hired in 2024-01; and a part-time interim chief financial officer. No credential, licence, patent inventorship, publication or prior exit for any of the five was confirmed in a public record here, and the searches returned nothing for either institution that awards the founders' degrees. A null result is not absence — the same search service returned nothing for well-documented listed companies — so the CVs are untested, not contradicted. What can be assessed is shape: nobody on the team has taken a point-of-care device through 510(k), CLIA waiver and volume manufacturing, and the two functions that decide that path were both replaced within six months [S150].

Founder-market fit is the strongest part of the story and the least documented, and the claim is unverified. Albescu's claimed seven years as an emergency physician in Tucson (2011-2017) and a year as medical director at Quillon Diagnostics is exactly the background that would explain a product built for a 12-minute finger-stick panel, and Lindqvist's claimed PhD in bioengineering and four years at Pellucid Biosystems before founding Corvia Microfluidics in 2016 explains the cartridge. The checks are cheap and were not run: any US physician billing Medicare between 2011 and 2017 holds a record in the free CMS NPI registry, and Arizona and Texas medical boards publish licence status. Inventorship is equally checkable — CM-1 (US 15/707,915) and VD-1 (US 16/884,327) should name Lindqvist if the technical-founder account is accurate. Neither check appears in the deck [S150].

### The regulatory bench is one hire deep

Grace Oyelaran's claim of 14 FDA 510(k) clearances at Meridale Medical between 2009 and 2025 is 0.9 a year and cannot be verified from FDA records, which name the applicant and correspondent rather than the staff who prepared a submission. What is documented is thinner: she joined on 2025-11, two months after her predecessor left during preparation of the submission; ISO 13485 certification is not held, with an audit booked for Q1 2027; and nine of 64 employees sit in clinical and regulatory against a workload of one additional-information response, a further three-assay submission, a four-site 1,150-patient pivotal study and a CLIA waiver application. Abbott cleared hs-troponin I cartridges twice in eighteen months (K240984 on 2025-01-03 and K253051 on 2026-06-11), the cadence of an established regulatory organisation rather than a fair comparison for a 64-person company; the fair test is one FDA request answered on time, by a bench in place under a year [S13, S148, S17, S150].

### One sales career, one part-time finance function

Commercial and financial leadership are single-track, and both are unverified. Luis Arrellano spent 2006-2023 at one company, Tavora Health Systems, rising from sales representative to regional vice president for the Southwest — a 17-year record in the same three states where all 41 evaluation sites sit, with no disclosed diagnostics or capital-equipment experience, the experience the model needs since the analyzer is a $2,900 capital sale and the cartridge a recurring consumable. Darnell Whitcombe has been interim CFO since 2026-03 through his advisory firm, part-time, while the company ran a $6.0M bridge, a $30.0M round and a $5.0M term loan that begins amortising in 2027-03; six of 64 employees work in finance and administration. Economically, the $30.0M buys a commercial build run by a first-time diagnostics seller and a financial function run part-time, which shows up as a slower route to 300 sites by end-2027 rather than as a line in the budget [S150].

### Governance concentrates the same risk

Five of six board seats are filled, with the independent seat vacant and no protective provisions disclosed: two common held by the founders, one seed, one Series A and one Series B, so until it is filled the founders sit with the investors committing $8.0M of the round. The Corvia royalty and put are related-party matters that one founder-director benefits from and the other votes on. Key-person dependency is high on both founders and on the regulatory vice president. After the round the founders hold 11,200,000 shares, 21.5% against 30.8% today: the retention question is whether two founders diluted to a fifth of the company keep the appetite a five-assay panel and a three-year regulatory calendar demand [S150].

### What would settle it

Three checks would settle most of this before a term sheet: confirm Albescu's NPI and state licences and both founders' degrees directly with the awarding institutions; obtain Meridale Medical's 510(k) list and three named references, one of them on FDA interaction; and take structured references on the two 2025-2026 departures. The hires still missing are a full-time CFO, a regulatory lead with point-of-care clearance experience at vice-president level or above, and an independent director the new lead nominates. Until then the team rests on two founders' clinical and engineering insight, supported by no record this diligence could open — a reason to condition the investment and price the execution risk, not to walk away.

Vantelle Diagnostics sells a $33.40 cartridge that costs $16.20 to make, but at the 1.35 panels a day its own 41 evaluation sites average, a site returns $7,945 of annual gross profit — too little to cover the cost of selling and supporting it, so the $140M pre-money valuation is a bet on an eight-to-twelve-fold utilisation step-up that no disclosed data supports; the $30M buys a manufacturing cost curve and a distribution option, not proven unit economics. The clinic buys the analyzer and cartridges, its staff runs the test and bills the patient's insurer under existing codes; Vantelle never bills a payer. The clinic pays $2,900 for an analyzer that costs $3,350 to build, $650 a month per analyzer during the evaluation programme, and $38 list per cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. In the 2026 average the 55 analyzers in the field consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, 41 per site, and 60% of evaluation sites were given instruments free; the one large order in sight is a non-binding distributor letter of intent that becomes a $2.4M stocking order only when the 510(k) clears in Q1 2027 [S150]. All figures are company-reported and unverified.

The royalty also takes value off the top: Corvia is 60% owned by Vantelle and the CTO, Dr Tomasz Lindqvist, holds 22% of it, so he receives 0.66% of cartridge net sales — 3% of the FY2029 plan's cartridge revenue is $2.36M, of which his share is $0.52M. The team is credible on the slide and unverified in every record this diligence could reach (all CV facts below are company-reported and unverified). Vantelle's case rests on an emergency physician who saw the problem at the bedside, Dr. Wren Albescu, chief executive and director; a microfluidics engineer who founded the company holding the enabling sealing patent, Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist, chief technology officer and director; a regulatory vice president who joined in 2025-11; a commercial vice president hired in 2024-01; and a part-time interim chief financial officer. No credential, licence, patent inventorship, publication or prior exit for any of the five was confirmed in a public record here, and the searches returned nothing for either institution that awards the founders' degrees. A null result is not absence — the same search service returned nothing for well-documented listed companies — so the CVs are untested, not contradicted. What can be assessed is shape: nobody on the team has taken a point-of-care device through 510(k), CLIA waiver and volume manufacturing, and the two functions that decide that path were both replaced within six months [S150].

Founder-market fit is the strongest part of the story and the least documented, and the claim is unverified. Albescu's claimed seven years as an emergency physician in Tucson (2011-2017) and a year as medical director at Quillon Diagnostics is exactly the background that would explain a product built for a 12-minute finger-stick panel, and Lindqvist's claimed PhD in bioengineering and four years at Pellucid Biosystems before founding Corvia Microfluidics in 2016 explains the cartridge. The checks are cheap and were not run: any US physician billing Medicare between 2011 and 2017 holds a record in the free CMS NPI registry, and Arizona and Texas medical boards publish licence status. Inventorship is equally checkable — CM-1 (US 15/707,915) and VD-1 (US 16/884,327) should name Lindqvist if the technical-founder account is accurate. Neither check appears in the deck [S150].

### The regulatory bench is one hire deep

Grace Oyelaran's claim of 14 FDA 510(k) clearances at Meridale Medical between 2009 and 2025 is 0.9 a year and cannot be verified from FDA records, which name the applicant and correspondent rather than the staff who prepared a submission. What is documented is thinner: she joined on 2025-11, two months after her predecessor left during preparation of the submission; ISO 13485 certification is not held, with an audit booked for Q1 2027; and nine of 64 employees sit in clinical and regulatory against a workload of one additional-information response, a further three-assay submission, a four-site 1,150-patient pivotal study and a CLIA waiver application. Abbott cleared hs-troponin I cartridges twice in eighteen months (K240984 on 2025-01-03 and K253051 on 2026-06-11), the cadence of an established regulatory organisation rather than a fair comparison for a 64-person company; the fair test is one FDA request answered on time, by a bench in place under a year [S13, S148, S17, S150].

### One sales career, one part-time finance function

Commercial and financial leadership are single-track, and both are unverified. Luis Arrellano spent 2006-2023 at one company, Tavora Health Systems, rising from sales representative to regional vice president for the Southwest — a 17-year record in the same three states where all 41 evaluation sites sit, with no disclosed diagnostics or capital-equipment experience, the experience the model needs since the analyzer is a $2,900 capital sale and the cartridge a recurring consumable. Darnell Whitcombe has been interim CFO since 2026-03 through his advisory firm, part-time, while the company ran a $6.0M bridge, a $30.0M round and a $5.0M term loan that begins amortising in 2027-03; six of 64 employees work in finance and administration. The effect on the investment is a slower route to the 300 sites planned for end-2027 and a higher cost per site, because the $30.0M pays for a commercial and financial build run by people doing each of those jobs for the first time [S150].

### Governance concentrates the same risk

Five of six board seats are filled, with the independent seat vacant and no protective provisions disclosed — a company-reported position that is unverified: two common held by the founders, one seed, one Series A and one Series B, so until it is filled the founders sit with the investors committing $8.0M of the round. The Corvia royalty and put are related-party matters that one founder-director benefits from and the other votes on. Key-person dependency is high on both founders and on the regulatory vice president. After the round the founders hold 11,200,000 shares, 21.5% against 30.8% today: the retention question is whether two founders diluted to a fifth of the company keep the appetite a five-assay panel and a three-year regulatory calendar demand [S150].

### What would settle it

Three checks would settle most of this before a term sheet: confirm Albescu's NPI and state licences and both founders' degrees directly with the awarding institutions; obtain Meridale Medical's 510(k) list and three named references, one of them on FDA interaction; and take structured references on the two senior departures. The hires still missing are a full-time CFO, a regulatory lead with point-of-care clearance experience at vice-president level or above, and an independent director the new lead nominates. Until then the team rests on two founders' clinical and engineering insight, supported by no record this diligence could open — a reason to condition the investment and price the execution risk, not to walk away.

A 2026 cartridge earns $17.20 (51.5%); the 3% royalty on net cartridge sales paid to Corvia Microfluidics takes $1.00, leaving $16.20 and 48.5% — the deck reports 51% without saying whether the royalty sits inside the $16.20. The 2029 target cuts cost 54% to $7.50 while price falls 7% to $31.00, lifting gross profit to $23.50, or $22.57 and 72.8% after royalty rather than the 76% shown. The volume required is the weak point: 2M cartridges is 99 times the 2026 run-rate of 20,160, and the FY2029 revenue line of $78.5M at $31 needs 2.53M cartridges, 126 times. The deck discloses no line capacity, yield, scrap rate or capex for it; the only visible cost is the 40% of the raise ($12M) labelled "scale cartridge manufacturing". Each percentage point of scrap at the target volume adds $0.08 to unit cost, so $7.50 depends on yield as much as on volume. The royalty also takes value off the top: Corvia is 60% owned by Vantelle and the CTO, Dr Tomasz Lindqvist, holds 22% of it, so he receives 0.66% of cartridge net sales — 3% of the FY2029 plan's cartridge revenue is $2.36M, of which his share is $0.52M. On an acquisition, Corvia's 40% minority may put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value, a claim ahead of common. These unit economics are company-reported and unverified [S150].

The instrument is not where the model breaks, but it is not free either. The table above shows a placement bought at a discount to its build cost and repaid out of cartridge gross profit in a few months at the utilisation the evaluation sites actually deliver, and inside one month at the planned rate. The hardware is cheap customer acquisition; what it buys is a site whose profit depends on utilisation.

That is where the deck parts company with its own data. The model assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer and two analyzers a site, 16 a day per site; the evaluation sites averaged 1.35 a day per site and 1.02 per analyzer, a gap of 7.8 times per analyzer and 11.9 times per site. The $2.4B serviceable market is the same arithmetic (13,200 sites x 2 analyzers x 8 panels x 300 days x $38); at the observed rate those sites are worth $247M. Per-site cartridge gross profit is $7,945 a year at observed utilisation against $52,099 modelled. Selling cost is not disclosed; the nine sales and support staff imply $1.35M-$2.0M a year, or $33,000-$49,000 per active site today and $4,500-$6,700 a site at 300 sites, so a three-year LTV of $23,835 a site covers its selling cost 1.2-1.8 times at observed utilisation and 12-17 times at the modelled rate (analyst estimate; customer acquisition cost is not disclosed). This is a utilisation bet presented as a scale bet. The utilisation and market figures are company-reported and unverified [S150].

Revenue quality compounds the problem. FY2025's $2.6M was $1.1M of evaluation-programme revenue (42%), $0.8M of research-use cartridges sold to clinical research organisations (31%) and $0.7M of contract development for a partner (27%) — none of it cleared clinical testing. Revenue to September 2026 was $2.7M, and the $5.9M full-year estimate includes the $2.4M stocking order that ships only on clearance in Q1 2027, so underlying FY2026 is $3.5M, up 35% rather than 127%. The evaluation line does not reconcile with its own price either: 55 analyzers at $650 a month is $429,000 a year, 39% of the $1.1M booked in FY2025, so it must also contain cartridges bought by evaluation sites or undisclosed fees. Until revenue is reported by type and customer, the recurring share cannot be calculated. The revenue mix is company-reported and unverified [S150].

Payer risk sits with the clinic but does not stop there. After clearance the clinic bills Medicare or a commercial payer per test and buys cartridges from Vantelle, so a denial is its loss — and a reason not to reorder. Medicare's 2026 laboratory fee schedule pays $21.96 for the two assays in the first 510(k), 34% below the $33.40 cartridge before the clinic's labour and quality-control cost; the full five-test panel recovers $61.22 on the three assays whose rates are published, where the cartridge becomes affordable. Independent fee-schedule aggregators supply these rates; medium confidence. The full panel needs the second 510(k), and clinic staff cannot run it without the CLIA waiver — a listed peer calls waived status "critical for most of our products that are intended for POC settings" and describes the waiver as onerous and slow [S7]. The Q1 2027 clearance launches a two-test product whose Medicare recovery is below its cartridge price.

arguments.markdown:
The team is credible on the slide and unverified in every record this diligence could reach (all CV facts below are company-reported and unverified). Vantelle's case rests on an emergency physician who saw the problem at the bedside, Dr. Wren Albescu, chief executive and director; a microfluidics engineer who founded the company holding the enabling sealing patent, Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist, chief technology officer and director; a regulatory vice president who joined in 2025-11; a commercial vice president hired in 2024-01; and a part-time interim chief financial officer. No credential, licence, patent inventorship, publication or prior exit for any of the five was confirmed in a public record here, and the searches returned nothing for either institution that awards the founders' degrees. A null result is not absence — the same search service returned nothing for well-documented listed companies — so the CVs are untested, not contradicted. What can be assessed is shape: nobody on the team has taken a point-of-care device through a premarket notification, a CLIA waiver and volume manufacturing, and the two functions that decide that path were both replaced within six months [S150].

Founder-market fit is the strongest part of the story and the least documented, and the claim is unverified. Albescu's claimed seven years as an emergency physician in Tucson (2011-2017) and a year as medical director at Quillon Diagnostics is exactly the background that would explain a product built for a 12-minute finger-stick panel, and Lindqvist's claimed PhD in bioengineering and four years at Pellucid Biosystems before founding Corvia Microfluidics in 2016 explains the cartridge. The checks are cheap and were not run: any US physician billing Medicare between 2011 and 2017 holds a record in the free CMS NPI registry, and Arizona and Texas medical boards publish licence status. Inventorship is equally checkable — CM-1 (US 15/707,915) and VD-1 (US 16/884,327) should name Lindqvist if the technical-founder account is accurate. Neither check appears in the deck [S150].

### The regulatory bench is one hire deep

Grace Oyelaran's claim of 14 FDA 510(k) clearances at Meridale Medical between 2009 and 2025 is 0.9 a year and cannot be verified from FDA records, which name the applicant and correspondent rather than the staff who prepared a submission. What is documented is thinner: she joined on 2025-11, two months after her predecessor left during preparation of the submission; ISO 13485 certification is not held, with an audit booked for Q1 2027; and nine of 64 employees sit in clinical and regulatory against a workload of one additional-information response, a further three-assay submission, a four-site 1,150-patient pivotal study and a CLIA waiver application. Abbott cleared hs-troponin I cartridges twice in eighteen months (K240984 on 2025-01-03 and K253051 on 2026-06-11), the cadence of an established regulatory organisation rather than a fair comparison for a 64-person company; the fair test is one FDA request answered on time, by a bench in place under a year [S13, S148, S17, S150].

### One sales career, one part-time finance function

Commercial and financial leadership are single-track, and both are unverified. Luis Arrellano spent 2006-2023 at one company, Tavora Health Systems, rising from sales representative to regional vice president for the Southwest — a 17-year record in the same three states where all 41 evaluation sites sit, with no disclosed diagnostics or capital-equipment experience, the experience the model needs since the analyzer is a $2,900 capital sale and the cartridge a recurring consumable. Darnell Whitcombe has been interim CFO since 2026-03 through his advisory firm, part-time, while the company ran a $6.0M bridge, a $30.0M round and a $5.0M term loan that begins amortising in 2027-03; six of 64 employees work in finance and administration. The effect on the investment is a slower route to the 300 sites planned for end-2027 and a higher cost per site, because the $30.0M pays for a commercial and financial build run by people doing each of those jobs for the first time [S150].

### Governance concentrates the same risk

Five of six board seats are filled, with the independent seat vacant and no protective provisions disclosed — a company-reported position that is unverified: two common held by the founders, one seed, one Series A and one Series B, so until it is filled the founders sit with the investors committing $8.0M of the round. The Corvia royalty and put are related-party matters that one founder-director benefits from and the other votes on. Key-person dependency is high on both founders and on the regulatory vice president. After the round the founders hold 11,200,000 shares, 21.5% against 30.8% today: the retention question is whether two founders diluted to a fifth of the company keep the appetite a five-assay panel and a three-year regulatory calendar demand [S150].

### What would settle it

Three checks would settle most of this before a term sheet: confirm Albescu's NPI and state licences and both founders' degrees directly with the awarding institutions; obtain Meridale Medical's clearance list and three named references, one of them on FDA interaction; and take structured references on the two senior departures. The hires still missing are a full-time CFO, a regulatory lead with point-of-care clearance experience at vice-president level or above, and an independent director the new lead nominates. Until then the team rests on two founders' clinical and engineering insight, supported by no record this diligence could open — a reason to condition the investment and price the execution risk, not to walk away.
