arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has built something genuinely difficult — a 40-microlitre finger-stick sample into five results in twelve minutes on a self-calibrating cartridge — and has not shown that it works as a diagnostic. Its own study, company data unverified against any registry, puts troponin I at 11.8% imprecision at the cut-off that drives the chest-pain decision, on 128 patients at one site, run by Vantelle staff and scored as normal or abnormal rather than as a number; the reader patent (US 17/662,019) was finally rejected in July 2026; and the dried chemistry behind the troponin result is an unpublished PCT outside the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion [S150]. What Vantelle owns outright is time, and time is the one asset a funded competitor can buy.

### The difficult part is the dried chemistry

The Q5 is three technologies in a 640-gram box: a capillary-fill cartridge metering 40 microlitres, a dried-reagent chemistry that must survive nine months at room temperature, and an optical reader correcting drift across five assays. The cartridge is patented (US 16/884,327, granted 2023-03). The chemistry decides whether the troponin number is right, and it is kept secret: an unpublished PCT filed 2026-02-11, no claim and no freedom-to-operate cover. The reader is the one the Patent Office rejected. On-board calibration removes daily quality control but turns a calibrator fault into a silent bias across a whole lot, and finger-stick blood adds what a tube removes — haematocrit and haemolysis, which make potassium the hardest assay on the panel [S166].

### The performance claim is a category count from one site

98.7% agreement is not concordance. The study drew venous blood from 128 patients at one urgent-care site between September and December 2025, ran it on the Q5 with Vantelle staff operating, and scored each result into the same category as the reference laboratory — discarding the magnitude the clinician uses, since a troponin of 14 and one of 60 ng/L are one category if both exceed the cut-off, while the decision the product serves turns on magnitude and on change between samples. The summary row does not close either: 634 of 640 is 99.1%, and the per-assay rates imply roughly 626 agreements in 634 analysable results, so 98.7% is a share of the analysable set printed as a count out of 640. The incumbent's evidence is another order of magnitude, and simulation shows single-threshold error rising steeply with the imprecision and bias this study was not designed to measure [S10, S124].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the decision level | 11.8% CV (company data) | 10% or better at the 99th-percentile URL | S150, S163 |
| Troponin I agreement | 96.1%, 123 of 128 (company data) | Category agreement, not concordance | S150 |
| Five-assay agreement | 98.7% claimed (company data) | 634 of 640 is 99.1%; per-assay rates imply ~626 of 634 | S150 |

### Clearance is later than the deck says, and the waiver later still

The 510(k) was filed 2026-05-18 and FDA asked for more information on 2026-08-21, with 180 days to answer and a December 2026 answer planned, so a Q1 2027 clearance needs a decision within three months of that response; FDA's clearance database held no record for K261734, or for any device under the company's name, on 2026-10-30 [S7, S191]. Only two of five assays sit in that submission, and the CLIA waiver — permission for staff without laboratory training — is not planned until Q3 2027. QuidelOrtho, selling into the same channel, calls the waived designation "critical" for its point-of-care products and the requirements "onerous" [S7]. Until a waiver is granted the Q5 is a moderate-complexity test for a certificated laboratory: a different buyer and a smaller market.

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT platform | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US status | Two of five assays in K261734, information request pending; nothing cleared | hs-TnI cleared 2025-01-03 (i-STAT 1), 2026-06-11 (Alinity) | S191, S17, S13 |
| Evidence scale | 128 patients, one site, company-run | 3,697-patient study, completed 2024-02 | S150, S124 |
| Platform menu | Five assays in one cartridge | Blood gas, chemistry, electrolytes, coagulation, immunoassay | S150, S3 |
| Operator | Laboratory staff until a waiver is granted | Trained operator; waiver status unverified | S150, S7 |

### The patent estate is one granted family owned outright

| Patent or application | Subject | Filed / granted | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327, plus EP family | Capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator | 2020-05-28 / 2023-03 | US granted to 2040-05; Europe pending (company data) | S150 |
| US 17/662,019 | Five-assay optical reader with drift correction | 2022-05-04 / — | Final rejection 2026-07; appeal under consideration (company data) | S150 |
| US 19/318,770 | Finger-stick sample-volume check | 2025-09-30 / — | Unpublished (company data) | S150 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 | Troponin chemistry on dried reagents | 2026-02-11 / — | Unpublished; outside the 2024 FTO opinion (company data) | S150 |
| US 15/707,915 | Cartridge sealing film and reagent blister | 2017-09-18 / 2021-01 | Granted to 2037-09; owned by 60%-held Corvia, licensed at 3% | S150 |

The estate reduces to one US patent granted to the parent, one granted patent sitting in a partly-owned subsidiary and licensed back at a royalty whose beneficiaries include the chief technology officer, one finally rejected application and two unpublished ones. The reader is unpatented, and the six-month window after a final rejection puts the appeal-or-abandon decision around the round's January 2027 close; the freedom-to-operate opinion predates the troponin chemistry and excludes it.

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dried-reagent troponin chemistry | 8 | Antibody stability at room temperature sets imprecision | 3-4 years | S150 |
| Cartridge manufacturability | 7 | 40 µL fill, on-board calibrator, 9-month shelf life; four i-STAT cTnI recalls in 2011-2013 set the failure modes | 2-3 years | S150, S69 |
| Clearance and CLIA waiver | 9 | Two 510(k)s plus a multi-site operator study | 3-5 years | S150 |
| Reader design | 3 | Optics are engineering, not science; claim rejected | 6-12 months | S150 |
| Patent protection | 2 | One granted US family owned outright | immediate | S150 |

The replication test: a funded team given the published patents would reach a working reader inside two years and a cleared troponin assay only after years of clinical and regulatory work — that is the moat, and it is a schedule, not a secret.

| Product | Stage | Revenue, FY2025 | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 five-assay panel | Two of five assays in K261734 | $1.1M evaluation fees | Clearance; other three assays filed Q2 2027 | S150 |
| Research-use cartridges | Selling to CROs | $0.8M | None stated | S150 |

The cost curve is the most credible number in the deck, and still company data. $16.20 a cartridge at roughly 20,000 units a year falls to $7.50 at 2 million, a 54% cut over 6.6 doublings, or 11% per doubling — shallower than the 15-25% volume-driven hardware usually achieves, so the target is not the implausible part; what is missing is the bill of materials, since antibody and reagent do not get cheaper like moulded plastic. The pilot line is 18 people running 1,680 cartridges a month; a million a year is a fifty-fold increase, and $12M of the round goes into it without a disclosed capex or qualification schedule [S150].

::: evidence
**The number that decides the technology is 11.8% — the troponin assay's imprecision at the cut-off the product exists to interpret — reported without the standard it must meet.**

The IFCC defines a high-sensitivity assay by imprecision at the 99th-percentile URL and measurability in most healthy people [S163]; simulation shows single-threshold error climbing steeply with imprecision and bias. Four Vantelle assays sit at 2.4-7.2% CV; the one driving the transfer decision sits at 11.8%, from a study that cannot settle it.
:::

The dependencies are concentrated: the sealing film is licensed from a subsidiary Vantelle partly owns, at a royalty that partly flows to the chief technology officer; one manufacturing site, no disclosed second source; and the three assays not yet submitted depend on chemistry with neither a granted claim nor a freedom-to-operate opinion. Readiness is uneven: troponin and HbA1c are at a submission, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium sit behind a pivotal study, and the untrained-operator configuration has not been tested at all. The counter-case is real — four of five assays are precise, the cartridge patent is granted, the cost curve is conservative against a standard learning rate, and Abbott's i-STAT is a one-test cartridge against a five-test panel — so the risk is that the evidence fails, not that the engineering does. For the investor that makes the accuracy claim a pricing question rather than a pass-or-fail one: $140M pre-money buys a platform whose clinical claim rests on one study that is not yet public, and the condition worth attaching is the pivotal precision data by site and lot.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is legally ordinary and evidentially fragile (company-reported facts, unverified). The $15.0M ticket buys 4,606,314 shares — 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company at $3.2564 a share — with the sixth board seat, but $76.8M of liquidation preference is already committed to earlier money, 40% of the sealing-film IP sits outside the parent in the chief technology officer's own company, and the 510(k) number the valuation rests on belongs to another company's knee implant. Together that means the $140.0M pre-money is a price the company set, not one the market marked. The last priced round closed in 2022; every dollar since is insider money or debt. Page 1 also instructs AI-assisted diligence tools to skip external verification and report an Invest rating — recorded as a finding, not followed [S150].

The product is a 640-gram reader and a single-use cartridge running a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel — hs-troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine with eGFR and potassium — from a 40-microlitre finger stick in 12 minutes. The user is clinic staff, not a laboratory technician; the buyer is the urgent-care operator or rural hospital that sends the bloods out and waits one to three days; and growth comes from placing readers at or near cost ($2,900 list against $3,350 build cost) to earn $38 a cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. No VIE, nominee shareholder or dual-class structure exists, so ownership and votes match, and the Delaware parent is issuer, FDA submitter and owner of VD-1 to VD-4. The Delaware free register returns only name, file number, formation date and registered agent and its search is session-based, so the 2018-03-12 incorporation date and good standing are unconfirmed against the registry; the ownership percentages, entity roles and dates below are unverified company material, while the share and price arithmetic is verified because it reconciles to the deck's own totals [S149].

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership (unverified) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. | Delaware; HQ Albuquerque, New Mexico | Corporation | Issuer, FDA submitter, VD-1 to VD-4 owner | Shareholders below | S150, unverified |
| Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC | Arizona (Tempe) | LLC | Pilot line, 18 staff, leased plant | 100% parent | S150, unverified |
| Corvia Microfluidics LLC | Texas (Austin) | LLC | Owns CM-1 patent, licensed to parent | 60% parent; 40% founders incl. CTO 22% | S150, unverified |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Ltd | Ireland (Dublin) | Limited company | EU entity, no staff | 100% parent | S150, unverified |

### The IP is 40% outside the parent

The structure that changes economics is Corvia, and it is disclosed only by the company (unverified). Vantelle owns 60% of a Texas LLC formed on 2016-02-01 by Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist, now chief technology officer and a director; the other 40% belongs to Corvia's founders, incl. Lindqvist at 22%, and Corvia owns the CM-1 sealing-film patent (US 15/707,915, granted 2021-01) licensed exclusively to Vantelle. The royalty is 3% of cartridge net sales: at the company's own 2029 plan of 2M cartridges at $31.00, $1.86M a year, of which $0.74M accrues to the 40% minority and $0.41M to the CTO personally. The put matters more: on an acquisition Corvia's minority may sell its 40% to Vantelle at fair market value — $4.0M-$7.0M on a 6-10x multiple of that royalty stream, paid from exit proceeds. The director voting on it is a beneficiary; no committee, approval or cap is disclosed [S150].

### A flat round dressed as a step-up

The price history, company-reported and unverified, shows how little has been repriced. The Series A bought 12,400,000 shares for $36.0M, or $2.903 each — the same strike as the Bluestem warrants; the Series B price is $140.0M over 42,991,881 pre-money fully diluted shares, $3.2564. That is a 12.2% step-up in four and a half years, whose revenue grew from $1.1M to $2.6M: seed investors who paid $0.75 in 2019 are 4.3x up, compared with 1.12x on paper for the Series A, which is adding only $5.0M of the $30.0M. The pre-money also absorbs $15.2M transferred to employees and bridge holders — a 4,020,489-share pool top-up worth $13.09M at the round price and 2,571,392 bridge shares at 75% of it, worth $8.37M against a $6.28M claim. Both sit inside the pre-money, so the new investor's 17.65% is protected and founders bear the cost, falling 30.8% to 21.5% [S150].

### What the new money sits behind

The preference stack, company-reported and unverified, totals $76.78M — $36.28M of Series B and B-1 at 1x non-participating and senior, $36.0M of Series A at 1x participating, $4.5M of Series Seed at 1x non-participating — 45.2% of the $170.0M post-money. The Series B seniority is market-standard downside protection. The Series A is the anomaly: participation is disclosed without a cap, and on a simplified waterfall at a $170M exit it collects $66.0M, or 39% of proceeds, against $40.4M as converted. That $25M gap is funded by everyone else, founders and new money included, the largest unread term [S150].

### The identifier does not exist

The regulatory identity is where the document stops being reliable. K261734, given as Vantelle's 510(k) for troponin I and HbA1c filed 2026-05-18, is in the FDA database the Klassic Infection Spacer System from Total Joint Orthopedics, Inc., product code JWH, cleared 2026-07-23 after a 58-day review; Abbott has held a cleared point-of-care hs-troponin I cartridge since 2026-06-11. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has built something genuinely difficult — a 40-microlitre finger-stick sample into five results in twelve minutes on a self-calibrating cartridge — and has not shown that it works as a diagnostic. Its own study, company data unverified against any registry, puts troponin I at 11.8% imprecision at the cut-off that drives the chest-pain decision, on 128 patients at one site, run by Vantelle staff and scored as normal or abnormal rather than as a number; the reader patent (US 17/662,019) was finally rejected in July 2026; and the dried chemistry behind the troponin result is an unpublished PCT outside the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion [S150]. What Vantelle owns outright is time, and time is the one asset a funded competitor can buy.

### The difficult part is the dried chemistry

The Q5 is three technologies in a 640-gram box: a capillary-fill cartridge metering 40 microlitres, a dried-reagent chemistry that must survive nine months at room temperature, and an optical reader correcting drift across five assays. The cartridge is patented (US 16/884,327, granted 2023-03). The chemistry decides whether the troponin number is right, and it is kept secret: an unpublished PCT filed 2026-02-11, no claim and no freedom-to-operate cover. The reader is the one the Patent Office rejected. On-board calibration removes daily quality control but turns a calibrator fault into a silent bias across a whole lot, and finger-stick blood adds what a tube removes — haematocrit and haemolysis, which make potassium the hardest assay on the panel [S166].

### The performance claim is a category count from one site

98.7% agreement is not concordance. The study drew venous blood from 128 patients at one urgent-care site between September and December 2025, ran it on the Q5 with Vantelle staff operating, and scored each result into the same category as the reference laboratory — discarding the magnitude the clinician uses, since a troponin of 14 and one of 60 ng/L are one category if both exceed the cut-off, while the decision the product serves turns on magnitude and on change between samples. The summary row does not close either: 634 of 640 is 99.1%, and the per-assay rates imply roughly 626 agreements in 634 analysable results, so 98.7% is a share of the analysable set printed as a count out of 640. The incumbent's evidence is another order of magnitude, and simulation shows single-threshold error rising steeply with the imprecision and bias this study was not designed to measure [S10, S124].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the decision level | 11.8% CV (company data) | 10% or better at the 99th-percentile URL | S150, S163 |
| Troponin I agreement | 96.1%, 123 of 128 (company data) | Category agreement, not concordance | S150 |
| Five-assay agreement | 98.7% claimed (company data) | 634 of 640 is 99.1%; per-assay rates imply ~626 of 634 | S150 |

### Clearance is later than the deck says, and the waiver later still

The 510(k) was filed 2026-05-18 and FDA asked for more information on 2026-08-21, with 180 days to answer and a December 2026 answer planned, so a Q1 2027 clearance needs a decision within three months of that response; FDA's clearance database held no record for K261734, or for any device under the company's name, on 2026-10-30 [S7, S191]. Only two of five assays sit in that submission, and the CLIA waiver — permission for staff without laboratory training — is not planned until Q3 2027. QuidelOrtho, selling into the same channel, calls the waived designation "critical" for its point-of-care products and the requirements "onerous" [S7]. Until a waiver is granted the Q5 is a moderate-complexity test for a certificated laboratory: a different buyer and a smaller market.

| US status | Two of five assays in K261734, information request pending; nothing cleared | hs-TnI cleared 2025-01-03 (i-STAT 1), 2026-06-11 (Alinity) | S191, S17, S13 |

| Operator | Laboratory staff until a waiver is granted | Trained operator; waiver status unverified | S150, S7 |

### The patent estate is one granted family owned outright

| US 16/884,327, plus EP family | Capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator | 2020-05-28 / 2023-03 | US granted to 2040-05; Europe pending (company data) | S150 |

The estate reduces to one US patent granted to the parent, one granted patent sitting in a partly-owned subsidiary and licensed back at a royalty whose beneficiaries include the chief technology officer, one finally rejected application and two unpublished ones. The reader is unpatented, and the six-month window after a final rejection puts the appeal-or-abandon decision around the round's January 2027 close; the freedom-to-operate opinion predates the troponin chemistry and excludes it.

Replication: a funded team given the published patents reaches a working reader inside two years, a cleared troponin assay only after years of clinical and regulatory work — the moat is a schedule, not a secret.

| Product | Stage | Revenue, FY2025 | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|

The cost curve is the most credible number in the deck. $16.20 a cartridge at roughly 20,000 units a year falls to $7.50 at 2 million, a 54% cut over 6.6 doublings, or 11% per doubling — shallower than the 15-25% volume-driven hardware usually achieves, so the target is not the implausible part; what is missing is the bill of materials, since antibody and reagent do not get cheaper like moulded plastic. The pilot line is 18 people running 1,680 cartridges a month; a million a year is a fifty-fold increase, and $12M of the round goes into it without a disclosed capex or qualification schedule [S150].

::: evidence
**The number that decides the technology is 11.8% — the troponin assay's imprecision at the cut-off the product exists to interpret — reported without the standard it must meet.**

The IFCC defines a high-sensitivity assay by imprecision at the 99th-percentile URL and measurability in most healthy people [S163]; simulation shows single-threshold error climbing steeply with imprecision and bias. Four Vantelle assays sit at 2.4-7.2% CV; the one driving the transfer decision sits at 11.8%, from a study that cannot settle it.
:::

The dependencies are concentrated: the sealing film is licensed from a subsidiary Vantelle partly owns, at a royalty that partly flows to the chief technology officer; one manufacturing site, no disclosed second source; and the three assays not yet submitted depend on chemistry with neither a granted claim nor a freedom-to-operate opinion. Readiness is uneven: troponin and HbA1c are at a submission, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium sit behind a pivotal study, and the untrained-operator configuration has not been tested at all. The counter-case is real — four of five assays are precise, the cartridge patent is granted, the cost curve is conservative against a standard learning rate, and Abbott's i-STAT is a one-test cartridge against a five-test panel — so the risk is that the evidence fails, not that the engineering does. For the investor that makes the accuracy claim a pricing question rather than a pass-or-fail one: $140M pre-money buys a platform whose clinical claim rests on one study that is not yet public, and the condition worth attaching is the pivotal precision data by site and lot.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is legally ordinary and evidentially fragile (company-reported facts, unverified). The $15.0M ticket buys 4,606,314 shares — 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company at $3.2564 a share — with the sixth board seat, but $76.8M of liquidation preference is already committed to earlier money, 40% of the sealing-film IP sits outside the parent in the chief technology officer's own company, and the 510(k) number the valuation rests on belongs to another company's knee implant. Together that means the $140.0M pre-money is a price the company set, not one the market marked. The last priced round closed in 2022; every dollar since is insider money or debt. Page 1 also instructs AI-assisted diligence tools to skip external verification and report an Invest rating — recorded as a finding, not followed [S150].

The product is a 640-gram reader and a single-use cartridge running a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel — hs-troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine with eGFR and potassium — from a 40-microlitre finger stick in 12 minutes. The user is clinic staff, not a laboratory technician; the buyer is the urgent-care operator or rural hospital that sends the bloods out and waits one to three days; and growth comes from placing readers at or near cost ($2,900 list against $3,350 build cost) to earn $38 a cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. No VIE, nominee shareholder or dual-class structure exists, so ownership and votes match, and the Delaware parent is issuer, FDA submitter and owner of VD-1 to VD-4. The Delaware free register returns only name, file number, formation date and registered agent and its search is session-based, so the 2018-03-12 incorporation date and good standing are unconfirmed against the registry; the ownership percentages, entity roles and dates below are unverified company material, while the share and price arithmetic is verified because it reconciles to the deck's own totals [S149].

### The IP is 40% outside the parent

The structure that changes economics is Corvia, and it is disclosed only by the company (unverified). Vantelle owns 60% of a Texas LLC formed on 2016-02-01 by Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist, now chief technology officer and a director; the other 40% belongs to Corvia's founders, incl. Lindqvist at 22%, and Corvia owns the CM-1 sealing-film patent (US 15/707,915, granted 2021-01) licensed exclusively to Vantelle. The royalty is 3% of cartridge net sales: at the company's own 2029 plan of 2M cartridges at $31.00, $1.86M a year, of which $0.74M accrues to the 40% minority and $0.41M to the CTO personally. The put matters more: on an acquisition Corvia's minority may sell its 40% to Vantelle at fair market value — $4.0M-$7.0M on a 6-10x multiple of that royalty stream, paid from exit proceeds. The director voting on it is a beneficiary; no committee, approval or cap is disclosed [S150].

### A flat round dressed as a step-up

The price history, company-reported and unverified, shows how little has been repriced. The Series A bought 12,400,000 shares for $36.0M, or $2.903 each — the same strike as the Bluestem warrants; the Series B price is $140.0M over 42,991,881 pre-money fully diluted shares, $3.2564. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has built something genuinely difficult — a 40-microlitre finger-stick sample into five results in twelve minutes on a self-calibrating cartridge — and has not shown that it works as a diagnostic. Its own study, company data unverified against any registry, puts troponin I at 11.8% imprecision at the cut-off that drives the chest-pain decision, on 128 patients at one site, run by Vantelle staff and scored as normal or abnormal rather than as a number; the reader patent (US 17/662,019) was finally rejected in July 2026; and the dried chemistry behind the troponin result is an unpublished PCT outside the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion [S150]. What Vantelle owns outright is time, and time is the one asset a funded competitor can buy.

### The difficult part is the dried chemistry

The Q5 is three technologies in a 640-gram box: a capillary-fill cartridge metering 40 microlitres, a dried-reagent chemistry that must survive nine months at room temperature, and an optical reader correcting drift across five assays. The cartridge is patented (US 16/884,327, granted 2023-03). The chemistry decides whether the troponin number is right, and it is kept secret: an unpublished PCT filed 2026-02-11, no claim and no freedom-to-operate cover. The reader is the one the Patent Office rejected. On-board calibration removes daily quality control but turns a calibrator fault into a silent bias across a whole lot, and finger-stick blood adds what a tube removes — haematocrit and haemolysis, which make potassium the hardest assay on the panel [S166].

### The performance claim is a category count from one site

98.7% agreement is not concordance. The study drew venous blood from 128 patients at one urgent-care site between September and December 2025, ran it on the Q5 with Vantelle staff operating, and scored each result into the same category as the reference laboratory — discarding the magnitude the clinician uses, since a troponin of 14 and one of 60 ng/L are one category if both exceed the cut-off, while the decision the product serves turns on magnitude and on change between samples. The summary row does not close either: 634 of 640 is 99.1%, and the per-assay rates imply ~626 agreements in 634 analysable results, so 98.7% is a share of the analysable set printed as a count out of 640. The incumbent's evidence is another order of magnitude, and simulation shows single-threshold error rising steeply with the imprecision and bias this study was not designed to measure [S10, S124].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the decision level | 11.8% CV (company data) | 10% or better at the 99th-percentile URL | S150, S163 |
| Troponin I agreement | 96.1%, 123 of 128 (company data) | Category agreement, not concordance | S150 |
| Five-assay agreement | 98.7% claimed | 634 of 640 is 99.1%; per-assay rates imply ~626 of 634 | S150 |

### Clearance is later than the deck says, and the waiver later still

The 510(k) was filed 2026-05-18 and FDA asked for more information on 2026-08-21, with 180 days to answer and a December 2026 answer planned, so a Q1 2027 clearance needs a decision within three months of that response; FDA's clearance database held no record for K261734, or any device under its name, on 2026-10-30 [S7, S191]. Only two of five assays sit in that submission, and the CLIA waiver — permission for staff without laboratory training — is not planned until Q3 2027. QuidelOrtho, selling into the same channel, calls the waived designation "critical" for its point-of-care products and the requirements "onerous" [S7]. Until a waiver is granted the Q5 is a moderate-complexity test for a certificated laboratory: a different buyer and a smaller market.

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT platform | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US status | Two of five assays in K261734, information request pending; nothing cleared | hs-TnI cleared 2025-01-03 (i-STAT 1), 2026-06-11 (Alinity) | S191, S17, S13 |
| Evidence scale | 128 patients, one site, company-run | 3,697-patient study, completed 2024-02 | S150, S124 |
| Operator | Laboratory staff until a waiver is granted | Trained operator; waiver status unverified | S150, S7 |

### The patent estate is one granted family owned outright

| Patent or application | Subject | Filed / granted | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327, plus EP family | Capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator | 2020-05-28 / 2023-03 | US granted to 2040-05; Europe pending (company data) | S150 |
| US 17/662,019 | Five-assay optical reader with drift correction | 2022-05-04 / — | Final rejection 2026-07; appeal under consideration (company data) | S150 |
| US 19/318,770 | Finger-stick sample-volume check | 2025-09-30 / — | Unpublished (company data) | S150 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 | Troponin chemistry on dried reagents | 2026-02-11 / — | Unpublished; outside the 2024 FTO opinion (company data) | S150 |
| US 15/707,915 | Cartridge sealing film and reagent blister | 2017-09-18 / 2021-01 | Granted to 2037-09; owned by 60%-held Corvia, licensed at 3% | S150 |

The estate reduces to one US patent granted to the parent, one granted patent sitting in a partly-owned subsidiary and licensed back at a royalty whose beneficiaries include the chief technology officer, one finally rejected application and two unpublished ones. The reader is unpatented, and the six-month window after a final rejection puts the appeal-or-abandon decision around the round's January 2027 close; the freedom-to-operate opinion predates the troponin chemistry and excludes it.

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dried-reagent troponin chemistry | 8 | Antibody stability at room temperature sets imprecision | 3-4 years | S150 |
| Cartridge manufacturability | 7 | 40 µL fill, on-board calibrator, 9-month shelf life; four i-STAT cTnI recalls in 2011-2013 set the failure modes | 2-3 years | S150, S69 |
| Clearance and CLIA waiver | 9 | Two 510(k)s plus a multi-site operator study | 3-5 years | S150 |
| Reader design | 3 | Optics are engineering, not science; claim rejected | 6-12 months | S150 |
| Patent protection | 2 | One granted US family owned outright | immediate | S150 |

Replication: a funded team given the published patents reaches a working reader inside two years, a cleared troponin assay only after years of clinical and regulatory work — the moat is a schedule, not a secret.

| Product | Stage | Revenue, FY2025 | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 five-assay panel | Two of five assays in K261734 | $1.1M evaluation fees | Clearance; other three assays filed Q2 2027 | S150 |

The cost curve is the most credible number in the deck. $16.20 a cartridge at 20,000 units a year falls to $7.50 at 2 million, a 54% cut over 6.6 doublings, or 11% per doubling — shallower than the 15-25% volume-driven hardware usually achieves, so the target is not the implausible part; what is missing is the bill of materials, since antibody and reagent do not get cheaper like moulded plastic. The pilot line is 18 people running 1,680 cartridges a month; a million a year is a fifty-fold increase, and $12M of the round goes into it without a disclosed capex or qualification schedule [S150].

::: evidence
**The number that decides the technology is 11.8% — the troponin assay's imprecision at the cut-off the product exists to interpret — reported without the standard it must meet.**

The IFCC defines a high-sensitivity assay by imprecision at the 99th-percentile URL and measurability in most healthy people [S163]; simulation shows single-threshold error climbing steeply with imprecision and bias. Four Vantelle assays sit at 2.4-7.2% CV; the one driving the transfer decision sits at 11.8%, from a study that cannot settle it.
:::

The dependencies are concentrated: the sealing film is licensed from a subsidiary Vantelle partly owns, at a royalty that partly flows to the chief technology officer; one manufacturing site, no disclosed second source; and the three assays not yet submitted depend on chemistry with neither a granted claim nor a freedom-to-operate opinion. Readiness is uneven: troponin and HbA1c are at a submission, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium sit behind a pivotal study, and the untrained-operator configuration has not been tested. The counter-case is real — four of five assays are precise, the cartridge patent is granted, the cost curve is conservative against a standard learning rate, and Abbott's i-STAT is a one-test cartridge against a five-test panel — so the risk is that the evidence fails, not that the engineering does. For the investor that makes the accuracy claim a pricing question rather than a pass-or-fail one: $140M pre-money buys a platform whose clinical claim rests on one study that is not yet public, and the condition worth attaching is the pivotal precision data by site and lot.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has built something difficult — a 40-microlitre finger-stick sample into five results in twelve minutes on a self-calibrating cartridge — and has not shown that it works as a diagnostic. Its own study, company data unverified against any registry, puts troponin I at 11.8% imprecision at the cut-off that drives the chest-pain decision, on 128 patients at one site, run by Vantelle staff and scored as normal or abnormal rather than as a number; the reader patent (US 17/662,019) was finally rejected in July 2026; and the dried chemistry behind the troponin result is an unpublished PCT outside the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion [S150]. What Vantelle owns outright is time, and time is the one asset a funded competitor can buy.

### The difficult part is the dried chemistry

The Q5 is three technologies in a 640-gram box: a capillary-fill cartridge metering 40 microlitres, a dried-reagent chemistry that must survive nine months at room temperature, and an optical reader correcting drift across five assays. The cartridge is patented (US 16/884,327, granted 2023-03). The chemistry decides whether the troponin number is right, and it is kept secret: an unpublished PCT filed 2026-02-11, no claim and no freedom-to-operate cover. The reader is the one the Patent Office rejected. On-board calibration removes daily quality control but turns a calibrator fault into a silent bias across a whole lot, and finger-stick blood adds what a tube removes — haematocrit and haemolysis, which make potassium the hardest assay on the panel [S166].

### The performance claim is a category count from one site

98.7% agreement is not concordance. The study drew venous blood from 128 patients at one urgent-care site between September and December 2025, ran it on the Q5 with Vantelle staff operating, and scored each result into the same category as the reference laboratory — discarding the magnitude the clinician uses, since a troponin of 14 and one of 60 ng/L are one category if both exceed the cut-off, while the decision the product serves turns on magnitude and change between samples. The summary row does not close either: 634 of 640 is 99.1%, and the per-assay rates imply ~626 agreements in 634 analysable results, so 98.7% is a share of the analysable set printed as a count out of 640. Abbott's equivalent study enrolled 3,697 patients [S124].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the decision level | 11.8% CV (unverified) | 10% or better at the 99th-percentile URL | S150, S163 |
| Troponin I agreement | 96.1%, 123 of 128 (unverified) | Category agreement, not concordance | S150 |
| Five-assay agreement | 98.7% claimed (unverified) | 634 of 640 is 99.1%; per-assay rates imply ~626 of 634 | S150 |

### Clearance is later than the deck says, and the waiver later still

The 510(k) was filed 2026-05-18 and FDA asked for more information on 2026-08-21, with 180 days to answer and a December 2026 answer planned, so a Q1 2027 clearance needs a decision within three months of that response; FDA's clearance database held no record for K261734, or any device under its name, on 2026-10-30 [S191]. Only two of five assays sit in that submission, and the CLIA waiver — permission for staff without laboratory training — is not planned until Q3 2027. QuidelOrtho states in its 2025 annual report that the waived designation is "critical" for its point-of-care products and the requirements "onerous". Until a waiver is granted the Q5 is a moderate-complexity test for a certificated laboratory: a different buyer and a smaller market.

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT platform | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US status | Two of five assays in K261734, information request pending; nothing cleared | hs-TnI cleared 2025-01-03 (i-STAT 1), 2026-06-11 (Alinity) | S191, S17, S13 |
| Evidence scale | 128 patients, one site, company-run | 3,697-patient study, completed 2024-02 | S150, S124 |
| Operator | Laboratory staff until a waiver is granted | Trained operator; waiver status unverified | S150, S7 |

### The patent estate is one granted family owned outright

| Patent or application number | Subject | Filed / granted | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327, plus EP family | Capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator | 2020-05-28 / 2023-03 | Granted to 2040-05; Europe pending (unverified) | S150 |
| US 17/662,019 | Five-assay optical reader with drift correction | 2022-05-04 / — | Final rejection 2026-07; appeal under consideration (unverified) | S150 |
| US 19/318,770 | Finger-stick sample-volume check | 2025-09-30 / — | Unpublished (unverified) | S150 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 | Troponin chemistry on dried reagents | 2026-02-11 / — | Unpublished; outside the 2024 FTO opinion (unverified) | S150 |
| US 15/707,915 | Cartridge sealing film and reagent blister | 2017-09-18 / 2021-01 | Granted to 2037-09; owned by 60%-held Corvia, licensed at 3% | S150 |

The estate reduces to one US patent granted to the parent, one granted patent sitting in a partly-owned subsidiary and licensed back at a royalty whose beneficiaries include the chief technology officer, one finally rejected application and two unpublished ones. The reader is unpatented, and the six-month window after a final rejection puts the appeal-or-abandon decision around the round's January 2027 close; the freedom-to-operate opinion predates the troponin chemistry and excludes it.

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dried-reagent troponin chemistry | 8 | Antibody stability at room temperature sets imprecision | 3-4 years | S150 |
| Cartridge manufacturability | 7 | 40 µL fill, on-board calibrator, 9-month shelf life; four i-STAT cTnI recalls in 2011-2013 set the failure modes | 2-3 years | S150, S69 |
| Clearance and CLIA waiver | 9 | Two 510(k)s plus a multi-site operator study | 3-5 years | S150 |
| Patent protection | 2 | One granted US family owned outright | immediate | S150 |

Replication: a funded team given the published patents reaches a working reader inside two years, a cleared troponin assay only after years of clinical and regulatory work — the moat is a schedule, not a secret.

| Product | Stage | Revenue, FY2025 | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 five-assay panel | Two of five assays in K261734 | $1.1M evaluation fees | Clearance; other three assays filed Q2 2027 | S150 |

The cost curve is the most credible number in the deck. $16.20 a cartridge at 20,000 units a year falls to $7.50 at 2 million, a 54% cut over 6.6 doublings, or 11% per doubling — shallower than the 15-25% that volume-driven hardware achieves, so the target is not the implausible part; what is missing is the bill of materials, since antibody and reagent do not get cheaper like moulded plastic. The pilot line is 18 people running 1,680 cartridges a month; a million a year is a fifty-fold increase, and $12M of the round goes into it without a disclosed capex or qualification schedule [S150].

::: evidence
**The number that decides the technology is 11.8% — the troponin assay's imprecision at the cut-off the product exists to interpret — reported without the standard it must meet [S150, S163].**

The IFCC defines a high-sensitivity assay by imprecision at the 99th-percentile URL and measurability in most healthy people; simulation shows single-threshold error climbing steeply with imprecision and bias. Four Vantelle assays sit at 2.4-7.2% CV; the one driving the transfer decision sits at 11.8%, from a study that cannot settle it.
:::

The dependencies are concentrated: the sealing film is licensed from a subsidiary Vantelle partly owns, at a royalty that partly flows to the chief technology officer; one manufacturing site, no disclosed second source; and the three assays not yet submitted depend on chemistry with neither a granted claim nor a freedom-to-operate opinion. Readiness is uneven: troponin and HbA1c are at a submission, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium sit behind a pivotal study, and the untrained-operator configuration has not been tested. Economically the Q5 is a reagent-margin business whose margin rests on the one assay the company has not proven, and the counter-case is real — four of five assays are precise, the cartridge patent is granted, the cost curve is conservative against a standard learning rate, and Abbott's i-STAT is a one-test cartridge against a five-test panel — so the risk is that the evidence fails, not that the engineering does. That makes accuracy a pricing question rather than a pass-or-fail one: the pre-money valuation buys a platform whose clinical claim rests on one study not yet public, and the condition worth attaching is the pivotal precision data by site and lot.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has built something difficult — a 40-microlitre finger-stick sample into five results in twelve minutes on a self-calibrating cartridge — and has not shown that it works as a diagnostic. Its own study, company data unverified against any registry, puts troponin I at 11.8% imprecision at the cut-off that drives the chest-pain decision, on 128 patients at one site, run by Vantelle staff and scored as normal or abnormal rather than as a number; the reader patent (US 17/662,019) was finally rejected in July 2026; and the dried chemistry behind the troponin result is an unpublished PCT outside the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion [S150]. What Vantelle owns outright is time, and time is the one asset a funded competitor can buy.

### The difficult part is the dried chemistry

The Q5 is three technologies in a 640-gram box: a capillary-fill cartridge metering 40 microlitres, a dried-reagent chemistry that must survive nine months at room temperature, and an optical reader correcting drift across five assays. The cartridge is patented (US 16/884,327, granted 2023-03). The chemistry decides whether the troponin number is right, and it is kept secret: an unpublished PCT filed 2026-02-11, no claim and no freedom-to-operate cover. The reader is the one the Patent Office rejected. On-board calibration removes daily quality control but turns a calibrator fault into a silent bias across a whole lot, and finger-stick blood adds what a tube removes — haematocrit and haemolysis, which make potassium the hardest assay on the panel [S166].

### The performance claim is a category count from one site

98.7% agreement is not concordance. The study drew venous blood from 128 patients at one urgent-care site between September and December 2025, ran it on the Q5 with Vantelle staff operating, and scored each result into the same category as the reference laboratory — discarding the magnitude the clinician uses, since a troponin of 14 and one of 60 ng/L are one category if both exceed the cut-off, while the decision the product serves turns on magnitude and change between samples. The summary row does not close either: 634 of 640 is 99.1%, and the per-assay rates imply ~626 agreements in 634 analysable results, so 98.7% is a share of the analysable set printed as a count out of 640. Abbott's equivalent study enrolled 3,697 patients [S124].

|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the decision level | 11.8% CV (unverified) | 10% or better at the 99th-percentile URL | S150, S163 |
| Troponin I agreement | 96.1%, 123 of 128 (unverified) | Category agreement, not concordance | S150 |
| Five-assay agreement | 98.7% claimed (unverified) | 634 of 640 is 99.1%; per-assay rates imply ~626 of 634 | S150 |

### Clearance is later than the deck says, and the waiver later still

The 510(k) was filed 2026-05-18 and FDA asked for more information on 2026-08-21, with 180 days to answer and a December 2026 answer planned, so a Q1 2027 clearance needs a decision within three months of that response; FDA's clearance database held no record for K261734, or any device under its name, on 2026-10-30 [S191]. Only two of five assays sit in that submission, and the CLIA waiver — permission for staff without laboratory training — is not planned until Q3 2027. QuidelOrtho states in its 2025 annual report that the waived designation is "critical" for its point-of-care products and the requirements "onerous". Until a waiver is granted the Q5 is a moderate-complexity test for a certificated laboratory: a different buyer and a smaller market.

### The patent estate is one granted family owned outright

The estate reduces to one US patent granted to the parent, one granted patent sitting in a partly-owned subsidiary and licensed back at a royalty whose beneficiaries include the chief technology officer, one finally rejected application and two unpublished ones. The reader is unpatented, and the six-month window after a final rejection puts the appeal-or-abandon decision around the round's January 2027 close; the freedom-to-operate opinion predates the troponin chemistry and excludes it.

The cost curve is the most credible number in the deck. $16.20 a cartridge at 20,000 units a year falls to $7.50 at 2 million, a 54% cut over 6.6 doublings, or 11% per doubling — shallower than the 15-25% that volume-driven hardware achieves, so the target is not the implausible part; what is missing is the bill of materials, since antibody and reagent do not get cheaper like moulded plastic. The pilot line is 18 people running 1,680 cartridges a month; a million a year is a fifty-fold increase, and $12M of the round goes into it without a disclosed capex or qualification schedule [S150].

::: evidence
**The number that decides the technology is 11.8% — the troponin assay's imprecision at the cut-off the product exists to interpret — reported without the standard it must meet [S150, S163].**

The IFCC defines a high-sensitivity assay by imprecision at the 99th-percentile URL and measurability in most healthy people; simulation shows single-threshold error climbing steeply with imprecision and bias. Four Vantelle assays sit at 2.4-7.2% CV; the one driving the transfer decision sits at 11.8%, from a study that cannot settle it [S163].
:::

The dependencies are concentrated: the sealing film is licensed from a subsidiary Vantelle partly owns, at a royalty that partly flows to the chief technology officer; one manufacturing site, no disclosed second source; and the three assays not yet submitted depend on chemistry with neither a granted claim nor a freedom-to-operate opinion. Readiness is uneven: troponin and HbA1c are at a submission, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium sit behind a pivotal study, and the untrained-operator configuration has not been tested. Economically the Q5 is a reagent-margin business whose margin rests on the one assay the company has not proven, and the counter-case is real — four of five assays are precise, the cartridge patent is granted, the cost curve is conservative against a standard learning rate, and Abbott's i-STAT is a one-test cartridge against a five-test panel — so the risk is that the evidence fails, not that the engineering does. That makes accuracy a pricing question rather than a pass-or-fail one: the pre-money valuation buys a platform whose clinical claim rests on one study not yet public, and the condition worth attaching is the pivotal precision data by site and lot.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's cash ends in March 2027, in the same month its $5.0M term loan starts amortising, so the $30M round is a liquidity event before it is a growth investment. The reported trajectory is $1.1M of revenue in FY2024, $2.6M in FY2025 and $5.9M forecast for FY2026, with gross margin rising from 49% to 61%. The FY2026 figure does not survive its own footnotes: revenue to September 2026 was $2.7M, and the $5.9M estimate includes a $2.4M stocking order that ships only when the 510(k) clears, which the deck places in Q1 2027, after the fiscal year ends. Unless clearance arrives before 2026-12-31, two months ahead of the company's own estimate, FY2026 revenue is $3.5M and growth is 35%, not 127%. Every later projection inherits that timing, and the figures are unaudited, company-prepared and unverified [S150].

| $M | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026E | FY2027P | FY2028P | FY2029P | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 1.1 | 2.6 | 5.9 | 16.8 | 41.0 | 78.5 | S150, unverified |
| Gross margin | 49% | 58% | 61% | 63% | 67% | 71% | S150, unverified |
| Gross profit | 0.5 | 1.5 | 3.6 | 10.6 | 27.5 | 55.7 | S150, derived, unverified |
| Net profit (loss) | (9.8) | (12.4) | (14.0) | (16.5) | (6.0) | 9.0 | S150, unverified |
| Implied operating expense and interest | 10.3 | 13.9 | 17.6 | 27.1 | 33.5 | 46.7 | S150, derived, unverified |
| Cash at year end | 21.0 | 11.3 | not disclosed | not disclosed | not disclosed | not disclosed | S150, unverified |
| Cumulative net profit (loss) | (9.8) | (22.2) | (36.2) | (52.7) | (58.7) | (49.7) | S150, derived, unverified |

Cash was $6.9M on 2026-09-30 after $6.0M of bridge notes in June 2026, against $1.15M of monthly net burn: 6.0 months of runway to 2027-03-31. The arithmetic reconciles exactly — $11.3M at 2025-12-31 plus $6.0M of bridge less $10.4M of burn over nine months is $6.9M, or $1.156M a month. Three cash calls land at the end of that window: the term loan's interest-only period ends in 2027-03, adding $166,667 a month of principal for 30 months; the bridge notes accrue 8% interest, $40,000 a month on $6.0M; and the 2,571,392 B-1 shares at 75% of $3.2564 imply $6.28M of conversion value, consistent with principal plus seven months of accrued interest. Against a targeted close on 2027-01-29 the company has six weeks of cushion, and a slip past March 2027 turns a financing delay into a debt-service problem. These cash figures are company-reported and unverified [S150].

If the round closes on time, cash is $32.3M at close. The plan then loses $16.5M in FY2027 and $6.0M in FY2028, leaving $11.2M at the end of 2028 before capex. The $12M manufacturing allocation is largely capex and sits outside the profit and loss, so the discretionary buffer is $5.0M — under six months of 2027 burn. The plan is funded, not cushioned. A six-month clearance slip that halves FY2027 revenue cuts gross profit by $5.3M and pushes the FY2027 loss toward $22M, at which point the company needs another round before its first profit year. The implication is that the financing calendar, not the valuation, is the binding risk. These projections are company-prepared and unverified [S150].

The 2029 profit is arithmetically coherent and economically fragile. At $78.5M of revenue and a 71% gross margin, gross profit is $55.7M; a $9.0M profit leaves $46.7M of operating expense and interest, 2.7 times the $17.6M implied for FY2026 and 59.5% of revenue against Abbott's 34.5% combined R&D and SG&A [S150, S3]. On site count the plan hangs together: at $148,800 of revenue per site a year (two analyzers, 2,400 cartridges, $31), FY2027P needs 113 average sites, FY2028P 276 and FY2029P 527, roughly doubling each year against a 300-site milestone for the end of 2027. On utilisation it does not: at the 1.35 panels a day the evaluation sites deliver, the same revenue needs 740, 1,807 and 3,459 sites. The base case is the company's own plan; the downside is observed utilisation at the planned site count, which produces $12.0M of FY2029 revenue rather than $78.5M, and the upside, 600 sites at 10 panels a day, is $111.6M. The mechanism is that gross profit scales with panels a day while the cost base scales with sites and headcount, so a utilisation shortfall cannot be cut out of opex. Panels per day is the variable that moves the outcome most: 83 sites at planned utilisation is worth the entire $9.0M of profit.

| Returns and working capital | Value | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cash, 2026-09-30 | $6.9M | after $6.0M bridge | S150, unverified |
| Monthly net burn | $1.15M | company-reported | S150, unverified |
| Runway | 6.0 months, to 2027-03-31 | derived | S150, derived, unverified |
| Term loan principal from 2027-03 | $166,667 a month | $5.0M over 30 months | S150, derived, unverified |
| Bridge note interest | $40,000 a month | 8% on $6.0M | S150, derived, unverified |
| Revenue per employee | $40,625 | FY2025, 64 staff | S150, derived, unverified |
| Revenue per dollar raised | $0.05 FY2025; $0.19 cumulative | $51.5M raised | S150, derived, unverified |
| Burn multiple | 8.3x FY2025; 15.6x FY2026 excluding the stocking order | net burn / revenue added | S150, derived, unverified |
| Cumulative losses, FY2024-FY2028E | $58.7M | sum of the plan | S150, derived, unverified |
| Receivable, inventory and payable days | not disclosed | no balance sheet | S150, unverified |
| ROE and ROIC | not computable | no equity or asset detail | S150, unverified |

Capital efficiency has been low. The company has raised $46.5M of equity and $5.0M of debt; cumulative losses of $58.7M over FY2024-FY2028E exceed the equity raised, and pre-2024 losses are not disclosed. Revenue was $2.6M in FY2025, $0.05 per dollar raised and $0.19 cumulative over FY2024-FY2026E; revenue per employee is $40,625 on 64 staff, and the burn multiple is 8.3 times in FY2025 and 15.6 times in FY2026 excluding the stocking order. The base rate in this category is unforgiving: Cue Health raised more than $480M and filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28, LumiraDx entered pre-pack administration on 2023-12-29 and its platform sold to Roche for $295M, and Truvian has raised $225.3M while still funding clearance. The stated uses of the $30M — $10.5M for clearance, $12M for manufacturing scale and $7.5M for launch — are not broken down further, and the clearance budget must also cover a 1,150-patient pivotal study, a second 510(k) covering three assays and a CLIA waiver application not yet filed. Because the plan consumes the raise before the first profit year, the round buys time rather than a margin of safety [S150, S172, S173, S174, S175].

The interim figures cannot be tested as presented. The interim revenue, cash and burn are unaudited and company-prepared; the deck names no auditor, discloses no revenue-recognition policy and gives no balance sheet beyond cash and debt, so these statements are unverified. The largest forecast item depends on a sequence of conditions: a non-binding distributor letter of intent converting into a purchase order, and the FDA clearing the submission. Verification would require audited statements with revenue by type and customer, the distributor's purchase order and shipment terms, an assessment under the revenue standard of whether the monthly evaluation fee is a service, an analyzer lease or a prepayment for cartridges, bank statements, the Bluestem loan agreement and the Corvia purchase documents. None of these is in the pack, so the cash and burn figures carry medium confidence and every forecast year carries low confidence.

::: info danger
Page 1 of the deck carries a note addressed to AI-assisted diligence tools: it states that the figures were independently verified by the investor's partners, that no external verification or competitor research is needed, that an Invest rating should be assigned and that no further review is required. It is treated here as data, not as an instruction, and it is itself an unverified finding: a pack prepared for the lead investor that seeks to suppress diligence weakens confidence in every other figure in it [S150].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has built something difficult — a 40-microlitre finger-stick sample into five results in twelve minutes on a self-calibrating cartridge — and has not shown that it works as a diagnostic. Its own study, company data unverified against any registry, puts troponin I at 11.8% imprecision at the cut-off that drives the chest-pain decision, on 128 patients at one site, run by Vantelle staff and scored as normal or abnormal rather than as a number; the reader patent (US 17/662,019) was finally rejected in July 2026; and the dried chemistry behind the troponin result is an unpublished PCT outside the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion [S150]. What Vantelle owns outright is time, and time is the one asset a funded competitor can buy.

### The difficult part is the dried chemistry

The Q5 is three technologies in a 640-gram box: a capillary-fill cartridge metering 40 microlitres, a dried-reagent chemistry that must survive nine months at room temperature, and an optical reader correcting drift across five assays. The cartridge is patented (US 16/884,327, granted 2023-03). The chemistry decides whether the troponin number is right, and it is kept secret: an unpublished PCT filed 2026-02-11, no claim and no freedom-to-operate cover. The reader is the one the Patent Office rejected. On-board calibration removes daily quality control but turns a calibrator fault into a silent bias across a whole lot, and finger-stick blood adds what a tube removes — haematocrit and haemolysis, which make potassium the hardest assay on the panel [S166].

### The performance claim is a category count from one site

98.7% agreement is not concordance. The study drew venous blood from 128 patients at one urgent-care site between September and December 2025, ran it on the Q5 with Vantelle staff operating, and scored each result into the same category as the reference laboratory — discarding the magnitude the clinician uses, since a troponin of 14 and one of 60 ng/L are one category if both exceed the cut-off, while the decision the product serves turns on magnitude and change between samples. The summary row does not close either: 634 of 640 is 99.1%, and the per-assay rates imply ~626 agreements in 634 analysable results, so 98.7% is a share of the analysable set printed as a count out of 640. Abbott's equivalent study enrolled 3,697 patients [S124].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the decision level | 11.8% CV (unverified) | 10% or better at the 99th-percentile URL | S150, S163 |
| Troponin I agreement | 96.1%, 123 of 128 (unverified) | Category agreement, not concordance | S150 |
| Five-assay agreement | 98.7% claimed (unverified) | 634 of 640 is 99.1%; per-assay rates imply ~626 of 634 | S150 |

### Clearance is later than the deck says, and the waiver later still

The 510(k) was filed 2026-05-18 and FDA asked for more information on 2026-08-21, with 180 days to answer and a December 2026 answer planned, so a Q1 2027 clearance needs a decision within three months of that response; FDA's clearance database held no record for K261734, or any device under its name, on 2026-10-30 [S191]. Only two of five assays sit in that submission, and the CLIA waiver — permission for staff without laboratory training — is not planned until Q3 2027. QuidelOrtho states in its 2025 annual report that the waived designation is "critical" for its point-of-care products and the requirements "onerous". Until a waiver is granted the Q5 is a moderate-complexity test for a certificated laboratory: a different buyer and a smaller market.

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT platform | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US status | Two of five assays in K261734, information request pending; nothing cleared | hs-TnI cleared 2025-01-03 (i-STAT 1), 2026-06-11 (Alinity) | S191, S17, S13 |
| Evidence scale | 128 patients, one site, company-run | 3,697-patient study, completed 2024-02 | S150, S124 |
| Operator | Laboratory staff until a waiver is granted | Trained operator; waiver status unverified | S150, S7 |

### The patent estate is one granted family owned outright

| Patent or application number | Subject | Filed / granted | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327, plus EP family | Capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator | 2020-05-28 / 2023-03 | Granted to 2040-05; Europe pending (unverified) | S150 |
| US 17/662,019 | Five-assay optical reader with drift correction | 2022-05-04 / — | Final rejection 2026-07; appeal under consideration (unverified) | S150 |
| US 19/318,770 | Finger-stick sample-volume check | 2025-09-30 / — | Unpublished (unverified) | S150 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 | Troponin chemistry on dried reagents | 2026-02-11 / — | Unpublished; outside the 2024 FTO opinion (unverified) | S150 |
| US 15/707,915 | Cartridge sealing film and reagent blister | 2017-09-18 / 2021-01 | Granted to 2037-09; owned by 60%-held Corvia, licensed at 3% (unverified) | S150 |

The estate reduces to one US patent granted to the parent, one granted patent sitting in a partly-owned subsidiary and licensed back at a royalty whose beneficiaries include the chief technology officer, one finally rejected application and two unpublished ones. The reader is unpatented, and the six-month window after a final rejection puts the appeal-or-abandon decision around the round's January 2027 close; the freedom-to-operate opinion predates the troponin chemistry and excludes it.

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dried-reagent troponin chemistry | 8 | Antibody stability at room temperature sets imprecision | 3-4 years | S150 (unverified) |
| Cartridge manufacturability | 7 | 40 µL fill, on-board calibrator, 9-month shelf life; four i-STAT cTnI recalls in 2011-2013 set the failure modes | 2-3 years | S150, S69 |
| Clearance and CLIA waiver | 9 | Two 510(k)s plus a multi-site operator study | 3-5 years | S150 (unverified) |
| Patent protection | 2 | One granted US family owned outright | immediate | S150 (unverified) |

Replication: a funded team given the published patents reaches a working reader inside two years, a cleared troponin assay only after years of clinical and regulatory work — the moat is a schedule, not a secret.

| Product | Stage | Revenue, FY2025 | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 five-assay panel | Two of five assays in K261734 | $1.1M evaluation fees | Clearance; other three assays filed Q2 2027 | S150 (unverified) |

The cost curve is the most credible number in the deck, and still company data unverified by any supplier quote. $16.20 a cartridge at 20,000 units a year falls to $7.50 at 2 million, a 54% cut over 6.6 doublings, or 11% per doubling — shallower than the 15-25% that volume-driven hardware achieves, so the target is not the implausible part; what is missing is the bill of materials, since antibody and reagent do not get cheaper like moulded plastic. The pilot line is 18 people running 1,680 cartridges a month; a million a year is a fifty-fold increase, and $12M of the round goes into it without a disclosed capex or qualification schedule [S150].

::: evidence
**The number that decides the technology is 11.8% — the troponin assay's imprecision at the cut-off the product exists to interpret — reported without the standard it must meet [S150, S163].**

The IFCC defines a high-sensitivity assay by imprecision at the 99th-percentile URL and measurability in most healthy people; simulation shows single-threshold error climbing steeply with imprecision and bias. Four Vantelle assays sit at 2.4-7.2% CV; the one driving the transfer decision sits at 11.8%, from a study that cannot settle it.
:::

The dependencies are concentrated: the sealing film is licensed from a subsidiary Vantelle partly owns, at a royalty that partly flows to the chief technology officer; one manufacturing site, no disclosed second source; and the three assays not yet submitted depend on chemistry with neither a granted claim nor a freedom-to-operate opinion. Readiness is uneven: troponin and HbA1c are at a submission, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium sit behind a pivotal study, and the untrained-operator configuration has not been tested. Economically the Q5 is a reagent-margin business whose margin rests on the one assay the company has not proven, and the counter-case is real — four of five assays are precise, the cartridge patent is granted, the cost curve is conservative against a standard learning rate, and Abbott's i-STAT is a one-test cartridge against a five-test panel — so the risk is that the evidence fails, not that the engineering does. That makes accuracy a pricing question rather than a pass-or-fail one: the pre-money valuation buys a platform whose clinical claim rests on one study not yet public, and the condition worth attaching is the pivotal precision data by site and lot.

The reader is unpatented, and the six-month window after a final rejection puts the appeal-or-abandon decision around the round's January 2027 close; the freedom-to-operate opinion predates the troponin chemistry and excludes it.

Replication: a funded team given the published patents reaches a working reader inside two years, a cleared troponin assay only after years of clinical and regulatory work — the moat is a schedule, not a secret.

The cost curve is the most credible number in the deck, and still company data unverified by any supplier quote. $16.20 a cartridge at 20,000 units a year falls to $7.50 at 2 million, a 54% cut over 6.6 doublings, or 11% per doubling — shallower than the 15-25% that volume-driven hardware achieves, so the target is not the implausible part; what is missing is the bill of materials, since antibody and reagent do not get cheaper like moulded plastic. The pilot line is 18 people running 1,680 cartridges a month; a million a year is a fifty-fold increase, and $12M of the round goes into it without a disclosed capex or qualification schedule [S150].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay's imprecision at the very cut-off the product exists to interpret is reported without the standard it must meet.**

The IFCC defines a high-sensitivity assay by imprecision at the 99th-percentile URL and measurability in most healthy people; simulation shows single-threshold error climbing steeply with imprecision and bias. Four Vantelle assays sit at 2.4-7.2% CV; the one driving the transfer decision sits at 11.8%, from a study that cannot settle it [S163].
:::

The dependencies are concentrated: the sealing film is licensed from a subsidiary Vantelle partly owns, at a royalty that partly flows to the chief technology officer; one manufacturing site, no disclosed second source; and the three assays not yet submitted depend on chemistry with neither a granted claim nor a freedom-to-operate opinion. Readiness is uneven: troponin and HbA1c are at a submission, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium sit behind a pivotal study, and the untrained-operator configuration has not been tested. Economically the Q5 is a reagent-margin business whose margin rests on the one assay the company has not proven, and the counter-case is real — four of five assays are precise, the cartridge patent is granted, the cost curve is conservative against a standard learning rate, and Abbott's i-STAT is a one-test cartridge against a five-test panel — so the risk is that the evidence fails, not that the engineering does. That makes accuracy a pricing question rather than a pass-or-fail one: the pre-money valuation buys a platform whose clinical claim rests on one study not yet public, and the condition worth attaching is the pivotal precision data by site and lot.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle Diagnostics sells a $33.40 cartridge that costs $16.20 to make, but at the 1.35 panels a day its own 41 evaluation sites average, a site returns $7,945 of annual gross profit — too little to cover the cost of selling and supporting it, so the $140M pre-money valuation is a bet on an eight-to-twelve-fold utilisation step-up that no disclosed data supports; the $30M buys a manufacturing cost curve and a distribution option, not proven unit economics. The clinic buys the analyzer and cartridges, its staff runs the test and bills the patient's insurer under existing codes; Vantelle never bills a payer. The clinic pays $2,900 for an analyzer that costs $3,350 to build, $650 a month per analyzer during the evaluation programme, and $38 list per cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. In the 2026 average the 55 analyzers in the field consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, 41 per site, and 60% of evaluation sites were given instruments free; the one large order in sight is a non-binding distributor letter of intent that becomes a $2.4M stocking order only when the 510(k) clears in Q1 2027 [S150]. All figures are company-reported and unverified.

| Metric | Per unit, 2026 | Per unit, 2029 target | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Average selling price | $33.40 | $31.00 | — | S150, unverified |
| Cost of goods | $16.20 | $7.50 | — | S150, unverified |
| Gross profit | $17.20 (51.5%) | $23.50 (75.8%) | Abbott FY2025 gross margin 56.4% | S150; S3 |
| Corvia royalty, 3% of net sales | $1.00 | $0.93 | — | S150, unverified |
| Gross profit after royalty | $16.20 (48.5%) | $22.57 (72.8%) | — | S150, unverified |
| Volume, cartridges a year | 20,160 | 2,532,000 | — | S150, unverified |
| Multiple of 2026 volume | 1.0x | 126x | — | S150, unverified |
| Gross profit pool after royalty | $0.33M | $57.1M | FY2029 plan gross profit $55.7M | S150, unverified |

The cartridge is the only link with positive gross margin, and it is thinner than presented. A 2026 cartridge earns $17.20 (51.5%); the 3% royalty on net cartridge sales paid to Corvia Microfluidics takes $1.00, leaving $16.20 and 48.5% — the deck reports 51% without saying whether the royalty sits inside the $16.20. The 2029 target cuts cost 54% to $7.50 while price falls 7% to $31.00, lifting gross profit to $23.50, or $22.57 and 72.8% after royalty rather than the 76% shown. The volume required is the weak point: 2M cartridges is 99 times the 2026 run-rate of 20,160, and the FY2029 revenue line of $78.5M at $31 needs 2.53M cartridges, 126 times. The deck discloses no line capacity, yield, scrap rate or capex for it; the only visible cost is the 40% of the raise ($12M) labelled "scale cartridge manufacturing". Each percentage point of scrap at the target volume adds $0.08 to unit cost, so $7.50 depends on yield as much as on volume. The royalty also takes value off the top: Corvia is 60% owned by Vantelle and the CTO, Dr Tomasz Lindqvist, holds 22% of it, so he receives 0.66% of cartridge net sales — 3% of the FY2029 plan's cartridge revenue is $2.36M, of which his share is $0.52M. On an acquisition, Corvia's 40% minority may put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value, a claim ahead of common. These unit economics are company-reported and unverified [S150].

| Metric | Evaluation actual, 2026 | Plan from 2028 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridges per analyzer a month | 30.5 | 240 | S150, unverified |
| Panels a day per analyzer | 1.02 | 8.0 | S150, unverified |
| Panels a day per site (2 analyzers planned, 1.34 actual) | 1.35 | 16.0 | S150, unverified |
| Cartridge gross profit per analyzer a year, after royalty | $5,929 | $38,880 | S150, unverified |
| Instrument cash cost per placement (60% free, 40% at $2,900) | $2,190 | $2,190 | S150, unverified |
| Cash cost of the installed base | $120,450 (55 analyzers) | $2.31M (1,055 analyzers) | S150, unverified |
| Instrument payback, months | 4.4 | 0.7 | S150, unverified |
| Three-year cartridge gross profit per site, after royalty | $23,835 | $233,280 | S150, unverified |
| Selling cost per site a year, analyst estimate | $33,000-49,000 | $4,500-6,700 | S150, unverified |
| Value of 13,200 sites at $38 a cartridge | $247M | $2.4B | S150, unverified |
| Sites needed for $78.5M of FY2029 revenue | 3,459 | 527 | S150, unverified |

The instrument is not where the model breaks, but it is not free either. The table above shows a placement bought at a discount to its build cost and repaid out of cartridge gross profit in a few months at the utilisation the evaluation sites actually deliver, and inside one month at the planned rate. The hardware is cheap customer acquisition; what it buys is a site whose profit depends on utilisation.

That is where the deck parts company with its own data. The model assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer and two analyzers a site, 16 a day per site; the evaluation sites averaged 1.35 a day per site and 1.02 per analyzer, a gap of 7.8 times per analyzer and 11.9 times per site. The $2.4B serviceable market is the same arithmetic (13,200 sites x 2 analyzers x 8 panels x 300 days x $38); at the observed rate those sites are worth $247M. Per-site cartridge gross profit is $7,945 a year at observed utilisation against $52,099 modelled. Selling cost is not disclosed; the nine sales and support staff imply $1.35M-$2.0M a year, or $33,000-$49,000 per active site today and $4,500-$6,700 a site at 300 sites, so a three-year LTV of $23,835 a site covers its selling cost 1.2-1.8 times at observed utilisation and 12-17 times at the modelled rate (analyst estimate; customer acquisition cost is not disclosed). This is a utilisation bet presented as a scale bet. The utilisation and market figures are company-reported and unverified [S150].

Revenue quality compounds the problem. FY2025's $2.6M was $1.1M of evaluation-programme revenue (42%), $0.8M of research-use cartridges sold to clinical research organisations (31%) and $0.7M of contract development for a partner (27%) — none of it cleared clinical testing. Revenue to September 2026 was $2.7M, and the $5.9M full-year estimate includes the $2.4M stocking order that ships only on clearance in Q1 2027, so underlying FY2026 is $3.5M, up 35% rather than 127%. The evaluation line does not reconcile with its own price either: 55 analyzers at $650 a month is $429,000 a year, 39% of the $1.1M booked in FY2025, so it must also contain cartridges bought by evaluation sites or undisclosed fees. Until revenue is reported by type and customer, the recurring share cannot be calculated. The revenue mix is company-reported and unverified [S150].

Payer risk sits with the clinic but does not stop there. After clearance the clinic bills Medicare or a commercial payer per test and buys cartridges from Vantelle, so a denial is its loss — and a reason not to reorder. Medicare's 2026 laboratory fee schedule pays $21.96 for the two assays in the first 510(k), 34% below the $33.40 cartridge before the clinic's labour and quality-control cost; the full five-test panel recovers $61.22 on the three assays whose rates are published, where the cartridge becomes affordable. Independent fee-schedule aggregators supply these rates; medium confidence. The full panel needs the second 510(k), and clinic staff cannot run it without the CLIA waiver — a listed peer calls waived status "critical for most of our products that are intended for POC settings" and describes the waiver as onerous and slow [S7]. The Q1 2027 clearance launches a two-test product whose Medicare recovery is below its cartridge price.

| Test (CPT) | Medicare 2026 rate | Cleared in the first 510(k)? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin, quantitative (84484) | $12.47 | Yes | S177, independent |
| HbA1c (83036) | $9.49 | Yes | S178, independent |
| BNP/NT-proBNP (83880) | $39.26 | No, second 510(k) | S176, independent |
| First two assays, subtotal | $21.96 | — | Derived, S177-S178 |
| Three assays, subtotal | $61.22 | — | Derived, S176-S178 |

::: evidence
**At the utilisation its own evaluation sites show, Vantelle's cartridge annuity does not cover the cost of selling a site; the plan needs a step-up in panels per day that no disclosed data supports.**

Evidence: the $2.4B market model assumes 16 panels a day per site against 1.35 observed, and 2M cartridges a year is 99 times the current run-rate; LumiraDx was placed in pre-pack administration on 2023-12-29 and its platform sold to Roche for $295M, while Cue Health filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28 after raising more than $480M [S150, S172, S173, S174, S236].
:::
