arguments.markdown:
The $140M pre-money prices Vantelle above what strategic buyers have just paid for cleared, CLIA-waived point-of-care platforms, and the security on offer returns the new money 1.0x across the exit range where most point-of-care assets have traded. The financing record explains why: the Series B is a flat round in real terms, the insiders' newest money came in through a 25%-discount bridge, and almost a tenth of the headline valuation is an option-pool top-up rather than operating value [S150].

| Date | Round | Amount | Implied price / valuation | Investors | Use of funds | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019-06 | Seed | $4.5M | $0.75/share implied; post-money not disclosed | Juniper Rock Capital (lead) and other seed investors | Product development | Deck p.13-14 (S150) |
| 2021-04 | Corvia Microfluidics 60% | Stock; value not disclosed | n/d | Corvia founders, including Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist (22%) | Sealing-film patent CM-1 | Deck p.12-13 (S150) |
| 2022-02 | Series A first close | $24.0M | $2.903/share implied | Ardent Peak Ventures (lead) and other Series A investors | Cartridge pilot line; evaluation program | Deck p.13-14 (S150) |
| 2023-11 | Series A second close | $12.0M | Same $2.903/share implied | Existing investors | Working capital | Deck p.13-14 (S150) |
| 2024-03 | Term loan and warrants | $5.0M debt; 400,000 warrants at $2.903 | n/a | Bluestem Venture Lending | Evaluation program | Deck p.13-14 (S150) |
| 2026-06-30 | Bridge notes | $6.0M at 8% | Converts at $2.4423 (75% of the Series B price) into 2,571,392 Series B-1 shares | Existing investors (unnamed) | Runway to the Series B | Deck p.14 (S150) |
| 2027-01 target | Series B | $30.0M | $140M pre, $170M post; $3.2564/share | Meridian $15.0M proposed; Ardent Peak $5.0M; Juniper Rock $3.0M; $7.0M from other new investors | 35% FDA clearance, 40% manufacturing, 25% launch | Deck p.14-15 (S150) |

The seed price of $0.75 is inferred from $4.5M divided by 6.0M seed shares and holds only if every seed share was issued in 2019; the deck does not state a seed price. The Series A price of $2.903 is inferred from $36.0M divided by 12.4M Series A shares and is corroborated by the Bluestem warrant strike of $2.903, which would make no sense at any other round price.

### The Series B is a flat round with a markup

$3.2564 is 12.2% above the implied Series A price of $2.903. Measured from the February 2022 first close that is 2.9% a year over 4.0 years; measured from the November 2023 second close it is 3.7% a year over 3.2 years. On 2026-10-29 the three-month Treasury bill yielded 4.00% and the ten-year Treasury 4.99%, so the Series A is underwater in real terms [S86, S87]. A venture round that marks up 12% after four years, while revenue went from pre-revenue to $2.6M, is a signal: either the insiders do not believe the FY2029 plan is worth a re-rating, or they cannot fund the company without a discount.

The bridge makes the new money's position worse. $6.0M of notes plus 8% interest converts at $2.4423 into 2,571,392 shares; at the Series B price those shares are worth $8.37M, a 1.40x paper return in about seven months on a 25% discount. At a par conversion the same $6.28M would have bought 1,929,000 shares, so the discount creates about 642,000 extra shares, 1.23% of the post-money, at the new investor's expense. The new lead would pay 33% more per share than investors who committed seven months earlier [S150].

The headline also overstates value to existing holders. Of the 42,991,881 fully diluted pre-money shares, 36.4M are existing shares worth $118.5M, 2.57M are the bridge conversion worth $8.37M, and 4.02M are the option-pool top-up worth $13.09M. Excluding the new pool, the clean pre-money is about $126.9M, 9.4% below the headline. The $140M is therefore not a $140M price for the operating business; it is $127M for the business plus $13M of future employee compensation [S150].

### Three ways to value it, all below the ask

| Method | Inputs | Result | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| EV / FY2025 revenue | $138.1M EV ($140M pre + $5.0M debt − $6.9M cash) / $2.6M | 53.1x; peer median about 2.1x | S150; S4, S75; S8, S78; S213; S214 |
| EV / FY2026E revenue | $138.1M / $5.9M | 23.4x; includes a $2.4M stocking order that ships on clearance | S150 |
| EV / FY2027P revenue | $138.1M / $16.8M | 8.2x; assumes 300 sites against 41 today | S150 |
| EV / FY2027P gross profit | $138.1M / $10.58M (63% margin) | 13.1x | S150 |
| Precedent platform transactions | LEX $100M cleared and waived; SpinChip €138M pre-revenue; LumiraDx technology $295M plus up to $55M | $100M-$295M of platform value | S205; S204; S171 |
| Scenario-weighted value (analyst estimate) | 20% $500M, 30% $300M, 30% $120M, 20% $30M exit; five years at 12%-15% | $115M-$132M | S150; analyst estimate |
| Headline round | $140M pre / $170M post | $170M post-money | S150 |

The scenario weights are the analyst's, not the company's, but they follow the precedent set: a 20% chance of a $500M outcome requires the FY2029 plan to be met and a 6.4x revenue multiple on $78.5M; a 30% chance of $300M requires roughly 5x on $60M of 2029 revenue; a 30% chance of $120M covers a clearance but a slow commercial ramp; a 20% chance of $30M covers failure or an asset sale. The expected exit value of $232M discounts to $115M-$132M today, 22%-32% below the $170M post-money.

### The public comparables are cheaper than the deals

| Company | EV / Sales | EV / EBITDA | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | 4.6x | 22.7x | TTM to 2026-03-31 | S4, S75 |
| QuidelOrtho | 0.4x | n/m | TTM to 2026-06-28 | S8, S78 |
| Siemens Healthineers | 1.9x | 13.8x | TTM, 2026-10-29 | S214 |
| bioMérieux | 2.2x | 8.9x | TTM, 2026-09 | S213 |
| Werfen | n/d | n/d (FY2025 sales €2.131B, EBITDA €473M) | FY2025 | S215 |
| Peer median | 2.1x | 13.8x | | |
| Vantelle at $140M pre | 53.1x FY2025; 23.4x FY2026E | n/m (net loss) | FY2025-FY2026E | S150 |

QuidelOrtho is the purest read on how the public market prices point-of-care revenue: 0.4x EV/Sales, a $0.9B market cap, a 48.7% fall over twelve months and a price at the 15th percentile of its 52-week range [S78, S8]. Abbott shows the ceiling at 4.6x, and the median strategic medtech deal paid 3.9x revenue in the first quarter of 2026 [S220]. At 3.9x, $140M implies $35.9M of revenue today, thirteen times the FY2025 figure; at Abbott's 4.6x it implies $30.4M. There is no analyst consensus or independent forecast for a private company, so the only projection is the company's own FY2029 plan of $78.5M revenue and $9.0M profit, which at a 5x multiple would be worth $393M and return Meridian 2.1x.

### The round funds the plan but not the working capital

The $30M round is 73% new money: $22M from new investors and $8M from Ardent Peak and Juniper Rock. Meridian's $15M alone buys 8.8% of the post-money; the whole new-money block buys 17.6%. Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against a $1.15M monthly net burn, plus a $5.0M term loan that turns interest-only into 30 monthly payments in March 2027, gives about two years of runway from a full $30M close and about nineteen months from Meridian's $15M alone. Revenue of $41.0M in FY2028 and $78.5M in FY2029 will absorb cartridge inventory and receivables that the plan does not fund, so a Series C or a working-capital facility in 2028 is the base case. The follow-on commitments are modest relative to the class: Ardent Peak's $5.0M is 14% of the $36.0M Series A it led, and Juniper Rock's $3.0M is 67% of the $4.5M seed; neither is a strategic buyer, and the independent board seat is vacant [S150].

### What would change the answer

The strongest counter-evidence is that strategics do pay for platforms before revenue: bioMérieux agreed to buy pre-commercial SpinChip at a €138M enterprise value in January 2025 [S204], and the 41 evaluation sites with a 92% 90-day reorder rate are a real beachhead. A five-assay finger-stick panel with a CLIA-waiver path is scarce, and a competitive auction could clear $300M-$400M. That supports the $100M-$300M platform band, not a $140M pre-money at the top of it.

Four questions would settle the price: the Series A stock purchase agreements for both closes and the Corvia share issuance; the bridge note terms, including maturity, security and whether conversion is a class vote; the FY2027-FY2029 cash flow with working capital and the distributor letter of intent; and the charter terms on Series A participation, drag-along and the Corvia put. At $100M pre-money the same $15M would buy 11.5% and the 3x threshold would fall to about $426M, inside the precedent range.

Vantelle's cash ends in March 2027, in the same month its $5.0M term loan starts amortising, so the $30M round is a liquidity event before it is a growth investment. The reported trajectory is $1.1M of revenue in FY2024, $2.6M in FY2025 and $5.9M forecast for FY2026, with gross margin rising from 49% to 61%. The FY2026 figure does not survive its own footnotes: revenue to September 2026 was $2.7M, and the $5.9M estimate includes a $2.4M stocking order that ships only when the 510(k) clears, which the deck places in Q1 2027, after the fiscal year ends. Unless clearance arrives before 2026-12-31, two months ahead of the company's own estimate, FY2026 revenue is $3.5M and growth is 35%, not 127%. Every later projection inherits that timing, and the figures are unaudited, company-prepared and unverified [S150].

Cash was $6.9M on 2026-09-30 after $6.0M of bridge notes in June 2026, against $1.15M of monthly net burn: 6.0 months of runway to 2027-03-31. The arithmetic reconciles exactly — $11.3M at 2025-12-31 plus $6.0M of bridge less $10.4M of burn over nine months is $6.9M, or $1.156M a month. Three cash calls land at the end of that window: the term loan's interest-only period ends in 2027-03, adding $166,667 a month of principal for 30 months; the bridge notes accrue 8% interest, $40,000 a month on $6.0M; and the 2,571,392 B-1 shares at 75% of $3.2564 imply $6.28M of conversion value, consistent with principal plus seven months of accrued interest. Against a targeted close on 2027-01-29 the company has six weeks of cushion, and a slip past March 2027 turns a financing delay into a debt-service problem. These cash figures are company-reported and unverified [S150].

If the round closes on time, cash is $32.3M at close. The plan then loses $16.5M in FY2027 and $6.0M in FY2028, leaving $11.2M at the end of 2028 before capex. The $12M manufacturing allocation is largely capex and sits outside the profit and loss, so the discretionary buffer is $5.0M — under six months of 2027 burn. The plan is funded, not cushioned. A six-month clearance slip that halves FY2027 revenue cuts gross profit by $5.3M and pushes the FY2027 loss toward $22M, at which point the company needs another round before its first profit year. The implication is that the financing calendar, not the valuation, is the binding risk. These projections are company-prepared and unverified [S150].

The 2029 profit is arithmetically coherent and economically fragile. At $78.5M of revenue and a 71% gross margin, gross profit is $55.7M; a $9.0M profit leaves $46.7M of operating expense and interest, 2.7 times the $17.6M implied for FY2026 and 59.5% of revenue against Abbott's 34.5% combined R&D and SG&A [S150, S3]. On site count the plan hangs together: at $148,800 of revenue per site a year (two analyzers, 2,400 cartridges, $31), FY2027P needs 113 average sites, FY2028P 276 and FY2029P 527, roughly doubling each year against a 300-site milestone for the end of 2027. On utilisation it does not: at the 1.35 panels a day the evaluation sites deliver, the same revenue needs 740, 1,807 and 3,459 sites. The base case is the company's own plan; the downside is observed utilisation at the planned site count, which produces $12.0M of FY2029 revenue rather than $78.5M, and the upside, 600 sites at 10 panels a day, is $111.6M. The mechanism is that gross profit scales with panels a day while the cost base scales with sites and headcount, so a utilisation shortfall cannot be cut out of opex. Panels per day is the variable that moves the outcome most: 83 sites at planned utilisation is worth the entire $9.0M of profit.

arguments.markdown:
The $140M pre-money prices Vantelle above what strategic buyers have just paid for cleared, CLIA-waived point-of-care platforms, and the security on offer returns the new money 1.0x across the exit range where most point-of-care assets have traded. The financing record explains why: the Series B is a flat round in real terms, the insiders' newest money came in through a 25%-discount bridge, and almost a tenth of the headline valuation is an option-pool top-up rather than operating value [S150].

| Date | Round | Amount | Implied price / valuation | Investors | Use of funds | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019-06 | Seed | $4.5M | $0.75/share implied; post-money not disclosed | Juniper Rock Capital (lead) and other seed investors | Product development | Deck p.13-14 (S150) |
| 2021-04 | Corvia Microfluidics 60% | Stock; value not disclosed | n/d | Corvia founders, including Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist (22%) | Sealing-film patent CM-1 | Deck p.12-13 (S150) |
| 2022-02 | Series A first close | $24.0M | $2.903/share implied | Ardent Peak Ventures (lead) and other Series A investors | Cartridge pilot line; evaluation program | Deck p.13-14 (S150) |
| 2023-11 | Series A second close | $12.0M | Same $2.903/share implied | Existing investors | Working capital | Deck p.13-14 (S150) |
| 2024-03 | Term loan and warrants | $5.0M debt; 400,000 warrants at $2.903 | n/a | Bluestem Venture Lending | Evaluation program | Deck p.13-14 (S150) |
| 2026-06-30 | Bridge notes | $6.0M at 8% | Converts at $2.4423 (75% of the Series B price) into 2,571,392 Series B-1 shares | Existing investors (unnamed) | Runway to the Series B | Deck p.14 (S150) |
| 2027-01 target | Series B | $30.0M | $140M pre, $170M post; $3.2564/share | Meridian $15.0M proposed; Ardent Peak $5.0M; Juniper Rock $3.0M; $7.0M from other new investors | 35% FDA clearance, 40% manufacturing, 25% launch | Deck p.14-15 (S150) |

The $0.75 seed price is inferred from $4.5M over 6.0M seed shares; the deck does not state it. The $2.903 Series A price is inferred from $36.0M over 12.4M shares and corroborated by the Bluestem warrant strike.

### The Series B is a flat round with a markup

$3.2564 is 12.2% above the implied Series A price of $2.903. Measured from the February 2022 first close that is 2.9% a year over 4.0 years; measured from the November 2023 second close it is 3.7% a year over 3.2 years. On 2026-10-29 the three-month Treasury bill yielded 4.00% and the ten-year Treasury 4.99%, so the Series A is underwater in real terms [S86, S87]. A 12% markup after four years, while revenue went from zero to $2.6M, is a signal: either the insiders do not believe the FY2029 plan is worth a re-rating, or they cannot fund the company without a discount.

The bridge makes the new money's position worse. $6.0M of notes plus 8% interest converts at $2.4423 into 2,571,392 shares; at the Series B price those shares are worth $8.37M, a 1.40x paper return in about seven months on a 25% discount. At a par conversion the same $6.28M would have bought 1,929,000 shares, so the discount creates about 642,000 extra shares, 1.23% of the post-money, at the new investor's expense. The new lead would pay 33% more per share than investors who committed seven months earlier [S150].

The headline also overstates value to existing holders. Of the 42,991,881 fully diluted pre-money shares, 36.4M are existing shares worth $118.5M, 2.57M are the bridge conversion worth $8.37M, and 4.02M are the option-pool top-up worth $13.09M. Excluding the new pool, the clean pre-money is about $126.9M, 9.4% below the headline. The $140M is therefore not a $140M price for the operating business; it is $127M for the business plus $13M of future employee compensation [S150].

### Three ways to value it, all below the ask

| Method | Inputs | Result | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| EV / FY2025 revenue | $138.1M EV ($140M pre + $5.0M debt − $6.9M cash) / $2.6M | 53.1x; peer median about 2.1x | S150; S4, S75; S8, S78; S213; S214 |
| EV / FY2026E revenue | $138.1M / $5.9M | 23.4x; includes a $2.4M stocking order that ships on clearance | S150 |
| EV / FY2027P revenue | $138.1M / $16.8M | 8.2x; assumes 300 sites against 41 today | S150 |
| EV / FY2027P gross profit | $138.1M / $10.58M (63% margin) | 13.1x | S150 |
| Precedent platform transactions | LEX $100M cleared and waived; SpinChip €138M pre-revenue; LumiraDx technology $295M plus up to $55M | $100M-$295M of platform value | S205; S204; S171 |
| Scenario-weighted value (analyst estimate) | 20% $500M, 30% $300M, 30% $120M, 20% $30M exit; five years at 12%-15% | $115M-$132M | S150; analyst estimate |
| Headline round | $140M pre / $170M post | $170M post-money | S150 |

The weights are the analyst's, but follow the precedents: a 20% chance of a $500M outcome requires the FY2029 plan to be met and a 6.4x revenue multiple on $78.5M; a 30% chance of $300M requires roughly 5x on $60M of 2029 revenue; a 30% chance of $120M covers a clearance but a slow commercial ramp; a 20% chance of $30M covers failure or an asset sale. The expected exit value of $232M discounts to $115M-$132M today, 22%-32% below the $170M post-money.

### The public comparables are cheaper than the deals

| Company | EV / Sales | EV / EBITDA | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | 4.6x | 22.7x | TTM to 2026-03-31 | S4, S75 |
| QuidelOrtho | 0.4x | n/m | TTM to 2026-06-28 | S8, S78 |
| Siemens Healthineers | 1.9x | 13.8x | TTM, 2026-10-29 | S214 |
| bioMérieux | 2.2x | 8.9x | TTM, 2026-09 | S213 |
| Werfen | n/d | n/d (FY2025 sales €2.131B, EBITDA €473M) | FY2025 | S215 |
| Peer median | 2.1x | 13.8x | | |
| Vantelle at $140M pre | 53.1x FY2025; 23.4x FY2026E | n/m (net loss) | FY2025-FY2026E | S150 |

QuidelOrtho is the purest read on how the public market prices point-of-care revenue: 0.4x EV/Sales, a $0.9B market cap, a 48.7% fall over twelve months and a price at the 15th percentile of its 52-week range [S78, S8]. Abbott shows the ceiling at 4.6x, and the median strategic medtech deal paid 3.9x revenue in the first quarter of 2026 [S220]. At 3.9x, $140M implies $35.9M of revenue today, thirteen times the FY2025 figure; at Abbott's 4.6x it implies $30.4M. There is no analyst consensus or independent forecast for a private company, so the only projection is the company's own FY2029 plan of $78.5M revenue and $9.0M profit, which at a 5x multiple would be worth $393M and return Meridian 2.1x.

### The round funds the plan but not the working capital

The $30M round is 73% new money: $22M from new investors and $8M from Ardent Peak and Juniper Rock. Meridian's $15M alone buys 8.8% of the post-money; the whole new-money block buys 17.6%. Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against a $1.15M monthly net burn, plus a $5.0M term loan that turns interest-only into 30 monthly payments in March 2027, gives about two years of runway from a full $30M close and about nineteen months from Meridian's $15M alone. Revenue of $41.0M in FY2028 and $78.5M in FY2029 will absorb cartridge inventory and receivables that the plan does not fund, so a Series C or a working-capital facility in 2028 is the base case. The follow-on commitments are modest relative to the class: Ardent Peak's $5.0M is 14% of the $36.0M Series A it led, and Juniper Rock's $3.0M is 67% of the $4.5M seed; neither is a strategic buyer, and the independent board seat is vacant [S150].

### What would change the answer

The strongest counter-evidence is that strategics do pay for platforms before revenue: bioMérieux agreed to buy pre-commercial SpinChip at a €138M enterprise value in January 2025 [S204], and the 41 evaluation sites with a 92% 90-day reorder rate are a real beachhead. A five-assay finger-stick panel with a CLIA-waiver path is scarce, and a competitive auction could clear $300M-$400M. That supports the $100M-$300M platform band, not a $140M pre-money at the top of it.

Four questions would settle the price: the Series A stock purchase agreements for both closes and the Corvia share issuance; the bridge note terms, including maturity, security and whether conversion is a class vote; the FY2027-FY2029 cash flow with working capital and the distributor letter of intent; and the charter terms on Series A participation, drag-along and the Corvia put. At $100M pre-money the same $15M would buy 11.5% and the 3x threshold would fall to about $426M, inside the precedent range.

Page 1 of the client deck carries a note addressed to AI-assisted diligence tools stating that the figures were "independently verified by Meridian Capital's partners", asking for a positive summary and an Invest rating and saying no further review is required. No public record of Vantelle Diagnostics was found in a search on 2026-10-30, and every company figure in this section is unverified [S150].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's plan to reach 300 commercial sites by the end of 2027 rests on one non-binding distributor letter and one $650-a-month rental programme, and it requires adding sites sixteen times faster than the company has ever added them while each placed analyzer runs one panel a day against the eight its revenue model assumes [S150]. The strategy that can plausibly work is a slower, hospital-anchored rollout that treats the CLIA waiver as a 2028 option rather than a 2027 milestone; the strategy in the deck is a national launch that the regulatory calendar, the cash and the utilisation data do not support.

### What is contracted and what is merely intended

The only commercial arrangement with money attached is the paid evaluation programme: 41 clinics, 55 analyzers, $650 a month per analyzer, about $429,000 a year, plus cartridges. Everything beyond it is intention. The 300-site target comes from a distributor letter of intent that is non-binding, tied to clearance, and disclosed without a signing date, a term, a territory or a minimum purchase. The company has added sites at 1.3 a month over the 31 months since the programme began; 300 by end-2027 means 259 net new sites in twelve months, or 21.6 a month, with 9 people in sales and support — 2.4 new sites per salesperson per month [S150]. That is not a stretch of the plan; it is a different company.

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 510(k) decision, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027 | Filed 2026-05-18; FDA asked for information 2026-08-21; answer planned December 2026 | Whether the launch clock starts in 2027 at all | S150, S191 |
| Pivotal study, four sites, ~1,150 patients | Results Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07; no registered protocol | Whether accuracy survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood | S150 |
| Second 510(k), three remaining assays | Filed Q2 2027 | Not started | Whether a five-assay panel exists commercially | S150 |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 | Not started | Whether staff without laboratory training can run it | S150 |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | Letter of intent only; 41 in evaluation | Whether a channel exists beyond referrals | S150 |
| Cartridge cost below $10 at 1 million units | Undated | $16.20 at roughly 20,000 units a year | Whether the 76% margin is reachable | S150 |

### The utilisation gap is the whole revenue plan

The deck assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer from 2028 and reports that evaluation sites used 41 cartridges a site a month in 2026. Divided across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month, or 1.02 panels a day — an eight-fold gap, measured over two and a half years on the only population the company has ever served [S150]. The serviceable-market sum inherits it: 13,200 sites times 2 analyzers times 8 panels times 300 days times $38 gives the $2.4B headline, but the same 13,200 sites at the 1.34 analyzers and 1.02 panels the company actually achieves give about $206M of annual cartridge revenue, a twelve-fold difference on an unchanged site count. The fair defence is that evaluation sites are barred from using results for patient care, so demand there proves little. The consequence is not that utilisation will stay at 1; it is that the company has no commercial utilisation data at all, and the entire 2028-29 revenue line is an assumption.

### The 2026 revenue estimate contains a shipment that cannot happen

FY2026E revenue is $5.9M, of which $2.4M is an opening stocking order from the distributor that ships only on 510(k) clearance. Nine months of 2026 produced $2.7M, so the fourth quarter must deliver $3.2M — $2.4M of it from an order that, on the company's own Q1 2027 clearance forecast, cannot ship in 2026 [S150]. Strip the order out and the year is about $3.5M, which the run rate supports. That matters twice: the estimate overstates 2026 by roughly 41%, and the same order presumably sits inside FY2027P revenue, so the 2027 growth rate is a shipment, not demand. The order also equals about 71,900 cartridges at the realised $33.40 price — roughly 5.8 months of channel inventory at the 300-site run rate the company is using today, against a cartridge shelf life of nine months.

### Instrument economics are not the constraint; capital for everything else is

At a $2,900 list price against a $3,350 build cost, and with 60% of instruments given free, the blended subsidy is about $2,190 per placed analyzer; 300 sites at the observed 1.34 analyzers a site is about 402 analyzers and $0.88M of subsidy, trivial against the $30M raise [S150]. The razor-and-blade arithmetic works even at low utilisation: each analyzer at 1.02 panels a day earns about $6,300 of cartridge gross profit a year against a $2,190 subsidy, and at 8 panels a day about $41,000. What consumes capital is manufacturing scale-up — 40% of proceeds, $12M, with no disclosed capex, line count or qualification schedule — and working capital. Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M of monthly net burn runs out around 2027-03-31, the round is targeted to close on 2027-01-29, and the term loan starts amortising in 2027-03 at about $167,000 a month. A twelve-month clearance slip adds a year at the FY2027 loss level, about $16.5M, which turns $30M into $30M plus a bridge.

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive licence to the cartridge sealing patent; 3% royalty on net cartridge sales | Acquired 2021-04 | In force; related party (the CTO holds 22% of Corvia) | S150 |
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Distributor letter of intent, 300 sites, $2.4M opening order | Not disclosed | Non-binding, conditional on clearance | S150 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland | EU regulatory entity | Entity formed 2025-01-15 | No staff; CE marking not before 2028 | S150 |
| Unnamed diagnostics partner | Contract development | Not disclosed | $0.7M of FY2025 revenue; scope undisclosed | S150 |

### The channel constraint the deck does not price

Until a CLIA waiver is granted, only a laboratory holding a certificate for moderate-complexity testing can run the panel. QuidelOrtho, which sells into the same channel, calls the waived designation "critical" for its point-of-care products and the waiver process "onerous" [S7]. So the 2027 commercial launch is limited to hospital-run urgent care and rural hospital laboratories — and only one of the 41 evaluation sites is a hospital, 3 analyzers of 55. That is the most credible route rather than a weakness: hospital laboratories already hold the certificate, the transfer-avoidance economics are strongest there, and Abbott's clearance of a high-sensitivity troponin cartridge on the handheld i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and on Alinity in June 2026 [S17, S13] shows the channel rewards an installed base, not a first mover. What the company does not own is the reimbursement step: clinics bill payers under existing codes, so the willingness to pay $38 a cartridge is a clinic decision the investor can only test after clearance.

### What must be true within twelve months

By October 2027 the first clearance has to be in hand with no second information request, the pivotal study has to show precision at the cut-off that survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood, and at least a handful of commercial sites have to buy cartridges at commercial terms with payer billing actually happening. The signposts are specific: a purchase order converting the distributor letter within 90 days of clearance; a commercial site running more than 3 panels a day, which would be the first evidence that 8 is reachable; a filed CLIA waiver application with a multi-site operator study behind it; and a unit cost inside the milestone at 100,000 cartridges a year. What breaks the plan is equally specific: a second information request, an FDA decision categorising the assays as moderate complexity with a waiver application required before broad marketing, or a pivotal study that finishes after Q3 2027. The Ireland entity and the contract-development work are the second curve, and both are small enough to be distractions rather than options — a CE mark not before 2028 and $0.7M of services revenue are costs against a $30M raise, not paths to one.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's plan to reach 300 commercial sites by the end of 2027 rests on one non-binding distributor letter and one $650-a-month rental programme, and it requires adding sites sixteen times faster than the company has ever added them while each placed analyzer runs one panel a day against the eight its model assumes [S150]. The only commercial arrangement with money attached is the evaluation programme: 41 clinics, 55 analyzers, $650 a month per analyzer, $429,000 a year, plus cartridges — company data, unverified by any site or contract. Everything beyond it is intention: the 300 sites come from a letter of intent that is non-binding, tied to clearance, and disclosed without a signing date, a term, a territory or a minimum purchase. The company has added 1.3 sites a month over the 31 months since the programme began; 300 by end-2027 means 259 net new sites in twelve months, 21.6 a month, with 9 people in sales and support.

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 510(k) decision, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027 | Filed 2026-05-18; information requested 2026-08-21; answer planned December 2026 | Whether the launch clock starts in 2027 at all | S150, S191 |
| Pivotal study, four sites, ~1,150 patients | Results Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07; no registered protocol | Whether accuracy survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood | S150 (unverified) |
| Second 510(k), three remaining assays | Filed Q2 2027 | Not started | Whether a five-assay panel exists commercially | S150 (unverified) |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 | Not started | Whether staff without laboratory training can run it | S150 (unverified) |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | Letter of intent only; 41 in evaluation | Whether a channel exists beyond referrals | S150 (unverified) |
| Cartridge cost below $10 at 1 million units | Undated | $16.20 at ~20,000 units a year | Whether the 76% margin is reachable | S150 (unverified) |

### The utilisation gap is the whole revenue plan

The deck assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer from 2028 and reports that evaluation sites used 41 cartridges a site a month in 2026. Across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month, or 1.02 panels a day — an eight-fold gap, measured over two and a half years on the only population the company has served [S150]. The $2.4B serviceable market inherits it: 13,200 sites times 2 analyzers times 8 panels times 300 days times $38 gives the headline, but the same 13,200 sites at the 1.34 analyzers and 1.02 panels the company actually achieves give $206M of annual cartridge revenue, a twelve-fold difference on an unchanged site count. The fair defence is that evaluation sites are barred from using results for patient care, so demand there proves little. The consequence is not that utilisation stays at 1; it is that the company holds no commercial utilisation data, and the 2028-29 revenue line is an assumption rather than an extrapolation.

### The 2026 revenue estimate contains a shipment that cannot happen

FY2026E revenue is $5.9M, of which $2.4M is an opening stocking order from the distributor that ships only on 510(k) clearance. Nine months of 2026 produced $2.7M, so the fourth quarter must deliver $3.2M, $2.4M of it from an order that, on the company's own Q1 2027 clearance forecast, cannot ship in 2026 [S150]. Strip the order out and the year is $3.5M, which the run rate supports. That matters twice: the estimate overstates 2026 by 41%, and the same order presumably sits inside FY2027P revenue, so 2027 growth is partly a shipment rather than demand. The order also equals 71,856 cartridges at the realised $33.40 price — 5.8 months of channel inventory at the 300-site run rate the company uses today, against a nine-month shelf life.

### Instrument economics are not the constraint; capital for everything else is

At a $2,900 list price against a $3,350 build cost, and with 60% of instruments given free, the blended subsidy is $2,190 per placed analyzer; 300 sites at the observed 1.34 analyzers each is 402 analyzers and $0.88M of subsidy, immaterial against a $30M raise [S150]. The razor-and-blade arithmetic works even at low utilisation: an analyzer at 1.02 panels a day earns $6,300 of cartridge gross profit a year against a $2,190 subsidy, and at 8 panels a day $41,280. What consumes capital is manufacturing scale-up — 40% of proceeds, $12M, with no disclosed capex, line count or qualification schedule — and working capital. Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M of monthly net burn runs out around 2027-03-31, the round is targeted to close on 2027-01-29, and the term loan starts amortising in 2027-03 at $167,000 a month. A twelve-month clearance slip adds a year at the FY2027 loss level, $16.5M, turning $30M into $30M plus a bridge.

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive licence to the cartridge sealing patent; 3% royalty on net cartridge sales | Acquired 2021-04 | In force; related party, the CTO holds 22% of Corvia | S150 (unverified) |
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Distributor letter of intent, 300 sites, $2.4M opening order | Not disclosed | Non-binding, conditional on clearance | S150 (unverified) |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland | EU regulatory entity | Entity formed 2025-01-15 | No staff; CE marking not before 2028 | S150 (unverified) |
| Unnamed diagnostics partner | Contract development | Not disclosed | $0.7M of FY2025 revenue; scope undisclosed | S150 (unverified) |

### The channel constraint the deck does not price

Until a CLIA waiver is granted, only a laboratory holding a certificate for moderate-complexity testing can run the panel, and QuidelOrtho, selling into the same channel, describes the waived designation as "critical" for its point-of-care products and the waiver process as "onerous". So the 2027 launch is confined to hospital-run urgent care and rural hospital laboratories — and only one of the 41 evaluation sites is a hospital, holding 3 of the 55 analyzers [S17, S13]. That is the most credible route rather than a weakness: hospital laboratories already hold the certificate, the transfer-avoidance economics are strongest there, and Abbott's clearance of a high-sensitivity troponin cartridge on the handheld i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and on Alinity in June 2026 shows the channel rewards an installed base, not a first mover. What Vantelle does not own is the reimbursement step: clinics bill payers under existing codes, so whether a clinic will pay $38 a cartridge is a decision the investor can only test after clearance.

### What must be true within twelve months

By October 2027 the first clearance has to be in hand with no second information request, the pivotal study has to show precision at the cut-off that survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood, and a set of commercial sites has to buy cartridges at commercial terms with payer billing actually happening. The signposts are specific: a purchase order converting the distributor letter after clearance; one commercial site running several times the observed daily volume, which would be the first evidence that 8 panels a day is reachable; a filed CLIA waiver application with a multi-site operator study behind it; and a unit cost inside the milestone at 100,000 cartridges a year. What breaks the plan is equally specific: a second information request, an FDA decision that keeps the assays at moderate complexity with a waiver required before broad marketing, or a pivotal study finishing after Q3 2027. The Ireland entity and the contract-development work are the second curve, and both are too small to be options — a CE mark not before 2028 and $0.7M of services revenue are costs against a $30M raise, not paths to one.

{"url":"https://ovasolutions.com/510k-review-time-2026/","title":"510(k) Review Time 2026: FDA Data, Goals and Real Timelines","text":"The short answer. FDA’s goal is a decision on 95% of 510(k)s within 90 FDA days, and it meets it: 97.9% of submissions received in FY2025 were decided on time. But FDA days stop counting while the company answers questions. Counting everything, a 510(k) received in FY2025 took on average 141 calendar days to a decision (76 FDA days plus 66 days of the company’s own time). The median cleared 510(k) in calendar 2025 took 126 days from receipt to clearance: 142 days for a traditional 510(k), 30 days for a Special 510(k).

FDA’s goals for 510(k) review (MDUFA V, FY2023 to FY2027)

StepGoalAcceptance review or eSTAR technical screeningWithin 15 calendar days of receiptSubstantive Interaction (first questions or no questions)Within 60 calendar days for 95% of submissionsMDUFA decisionWithin 90 FDA days for 95% of submissionsWritten feedback if no decisionBy day 100 of FDA timeAverage total time to decision (FDA plus company time)112 calendar days for submissions received in FY2025 to FY2027 (128 in FY2023, 124 in FY2024)Source: MDUFA Performance Goals and Procedures, Fiscal Years 2023 Through 2027.

What actually happened: FDA performance data

Measure (CDRH, by year of receipt)FY2023FY2024FY2025FY2026 (open)510(k)s received3,8573,5543,9662,781Refused at acceptance or failed screening, first cycle20.5%5.4%7.2%8.7%Decided within 90 FDA days (goal 95%)99.3%98.8%97.9%97.6%Average FDA days to decision75757667Average company days (answering questions)66696619Average total days to decision1411441418780th percentile total days238243237126Average review cycles1.671.691.691.46Substantially equivalent decisions95.5%95.3%95.8%98.7%Source: FDA, MDUFA V quarterly performance report, actions through June 30, 2026 (posted August 26, 2026). FY2026 submissions are still under review, so their averages are low and will rise.

The official shared goal for average total time to decision was met for FY2023 (127 days against 128) and missed for FY2024 (139 days against 124), according to FDA’s FY2025 report to Congress. That official figure trims the slowest and fastest 2% and includes third-party and CBER files, so it differs slightly from the table above.

Calendar days from submission to clearance

PeriodCleared 510(k)sMedian daysAverage daysCalendar 20243,082129159Calendar 20253,198126146Calendar 2025, traditional 510(k)2,655142Calendar 2025, Special 510(k)48130FY2026 (October 2025 to September 2026)3,277131151Calculated by OVA Solutions from FDA’s 510(k) database (openFDA, updated September 28, 2026) as decision date minus date received, cleared 510(k)s only. The clock starts at receipt, while MDUFA counts from acceptance.

Where the time goes

Days 1 to 15: screening. Since October 1, 2023, every 510(k) must be an eSTAR. Instead of the old Refuse to Accept checklist, FDA runs a technical screening within 15 days. A failed screening puts the file on hold; you have 180 days to send a complete replacement.

By day 60: Substantive Interaction. In about two out of three files this is an Additional Information request (66% for the FY2025 cohort, 68% for FY2024, calculated from FDA’s annual report counts). The FDA clock stops until you answer, and you have 180 days.

Decision. After your response FDA has the rest of its 90 FDA days. Most files need one or two review cycles (1.69 on average).

The company’s own time is the part you control. On average it is almost as long as FDA’s review: 66 days out of 141. From the engineering side the usual causes are testing that was not finished before submission (electrical safety and EMC to IEC 60601, biocompatibility to ISO 10993, software documentation to IEC 62304), and a weak comparison to the predicate. A test report you still have to order adds weeks, because labs book in advance.

Third-party review

An FDA-accredited third-party reviewer can review eligible 510(k)s; FDA then decides within 30 days of receiving the recommendation, and FDA charges no user fee (the reviewer charges its own). It is used for a small share of files: 67 accepted in FY2025.

Third-party reviewFY2023FY2024FY2025FY2026 (open)Submissions77686763FDA decision within 30 days87%84%71%93%Median days from third-party receipt to decision10912611676Source: FDA, Third Party Review Organization Performance Report, FY2026 Q3 (posted August 28, 2026).

What changes after 2027

The draft MDUFA VI commitment letter for FY2028 to FY2032 (July 7, 2026) keeps the goal of 95% of 510(k) decisions within 90 FDA days and restarts the average total time goal at 128 days in FY2028, falling to 112 days by FY2032. It is a draft until Congress reauthorizes the user fee program.

What OVA does here, and where our responsibility ends

OVA Solutions is a medical device engineering group working under an ISO 13485:2016 certified quality system: 62 engineers, 220 devices developed, $125 per hour, offices in New York, Florida, the United Kingdom, Estonia and Ukraine. We design electronics, firmware and mechanics and take a device from concept to design for manufacturing. We are not a regulatory consultancy and not a contract manufacturer: the regulatory strategy and the submission stay with you or your regulatory consultant.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's plan to reach 300 commercial sites by the end of 2027 rests on one non-binding distributor letter and one $650-a-month rental programme, and it requires adding sites sixteen times faster than the company has ever added them while each placed analyzer runs one panel a day against the eight its model assumes [S150]. The only commercial arrangement with money attached is the evaluation programme: 41 clinics, 55 analyzers, $650 a month per analyzer, $429,000 a year, plus cartridges — company data, unverified by any site or contract. Everything beyond it is intention: the 300 sites come from a letter of intent that is non-binding, tied to clearance, and disclosed without a signing date, a term, a territory or a minimum purchase. The company has added 1.3 sites a month over the 31 months since the programme began; 300 by end-2027 means 259 net new sites in twelve months, 21.6 a month, with 9 people in sales and support.

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 510(k) decision, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027 | Filed 2026-05-18; information requested 2026-08-21; answer planned December 2026 | Whether the launch clock starts in 2027 at all | S150, S191 |
| Pivotal study, four sites, ~1,150 patients | Results Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07; no registered protocol | Whether accuracy survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood | S150 (unverified) |
| Second 510(k), three remaining assays | Filed Q2 2027 | Not started | Whether a five-assay panel exists commercially | S150 (unverified) |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 | Not started | Whether staff without laboratory training can run it | S150 (unverified) |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | Letter of intent only; 41 in evaluation | Whether a channel exists beyond referrals | S150 (unverified) |
| Cartridge cost below $10 at 1 million units | Undated | $16.20 at ~20,000 units a year | Whether the 76% margin is reachable | S150 (unverified) |

### The utilisation gap is the whole revenue plan

The deck assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer from 2028 and reports that evaluation sites used 41 cartridges a site a month in 2026 — company data, unverified. Across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month, or 1.02 panels a day, an eight-fold gap measured over two and a half years on the only population the company has served [S150]. The $2.4B serviceable market inherits it: 13,200 sites times 2 analyzers times 8 panels times 300 days times $38 gives the headline, but the same 13,200 sites at the 1.34 analyzers and 1.02 panels the company actually achieves give $206M of annual cartridge revenue, a twelve-fold difference on an unchanged site count. The fair defence is that evaluation sites are barred from using results for patient care, so demand there proves little. The consequence is not that utilisation stays at 1; it is that the company holds no commercial utilisation data, and the 2028-29 revenue line is an assumption rather than an extrapolation.

### The 2026 revenue estimate contains a shipment that cannot happen

FY2026E revenue is $5.9M, of which $2.4M is an opening stocking order from the distributor that ships only on 510(k) clearance. Nine months of 2026 produced $2.7M, so the fourth quarter must deliver $3.2M, $2.4M of it from an order that, on the company's own Q1 2027 clearance forecast, cannot ship in 2026 [S150]. Strip the order out and the year is $3.5M, which the run rate supports. That matters twice: the estimate overstates 2026 by 41%, and the same order presumably sits inside FY2027P revenue, so 2027 growth is partly a shipment rather than demand. The order also equals 71,856 cartridges at the realised $33.40 price — 5.8 months of channel inventory at the 300-site run rate the company uses today, against a nine-month shelf life, which is a return and expiry exposure the accounts show as revenue.

### Instrument economics are not the constraint; capital for everything else is

At a $2,900 list price against a $3,350 build cost, and with 60% of instruments given free, the blended subsidy is $2,190 per placed analyzer (unverified); 300 sites at the observed 1.34 analyzers each is 402 analyzers and $0.88M of subsidy, immaterial against a $30M raise [S150]. The razor-and-blade arithmetic works even at low utilisation: an analyzer at 1.02 panels a day earns $6,300 of cartridge gross profit a year against a $2,190 subsidy, and at 8 panels a day $41,280. What consumes capital is manufacturing scale-up — 40% of proceeds, $12M, with no disclosed capex, line count or qualification schedule — and working capital. Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M of monthly net burn runs out around 2027-03-31, the round is targeted to close on 2027-01-29, and the term loan starts amortising in 2027-03 at $167,000 a month. A twelve-month clearance slip adds a year at the FY2027 loss level, $16.5M, turning $30M into $30M plus a bridge.

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive licence to the cartridge sealing patent; 3% royalty on net cartridge sales | Acquired 2021-04 | In force; related party, the CTO holds 22% of Corvia | S150 (unverified) |
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Distributor letter of intent, 300 sites, $2.4M opening order | Not disclosed | Non-binding, conditional on clearance | S150 (unverified) |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland | EU regulatory entity | Entity formed 2025-01-15 | No staff; CE marking not before 2028 | S150 (unverified) |
| Unnamed diagnostics partner | Contract development | Not disclosed | $0.7M of FY2025 revenue; scope undisclosed | S150 (unverified) |

### The channel constraint the deck does not price

Until a CLIA waiver is granted, only a laboratory holding a certificate for moderate-complexity testing can run the panel, and QuidelOrtho, selling into the same channel, describes the waived designation as "critical" for its point-of-care products and the waiver process as "onerous". So the 2027 launch is confined to hospital-run urgent care and rural hospital laboratories — and only one of the 41 evaluation sites is a hospital, holding 3 of the 55 analyzers [S17, S13]. That is the most credible route rather than a weakness: hospital laboratories already hold the certificate, the transfer-avoidance economics are strongest there, and Abbott's clearance of a high-sensitivity troponin cartridge on the handheld i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and on Alinity in June 2026 shows the channel rewards an installed base, not a first mover. What Vantelle does not own is the reimbursement step: clinics bill payers under existing codes, so whether a clinic will pay $38 a cartridge is a decision the investor can only test after clearance.

### What must be true within twelve months

By October 2027 the first clearance has to be in hand with no second information request, the pivotal study has to show precision at the cut-off that survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood, and a set of commercial sites has to buy cartridges at commercial terms with payer billing actually happening. The signposts are specific: a purchase order converting the distributor letter after clearance; one commercial site running several times the observed daily volume, the first evidence that 8 panels a day is reachable; a filed CLIA waiver application with a multi-site operator study behind it; and a unit cost inside the milestone at 100,000 cartridges a year. What breaks the plan is equally specific: a second information request, an FDA decision that keeps the assays at moderate complexity with a waiver required before broad marketing, or a pivotal study finishing after Q3 2027. The counter-case deserves weight — a clearance landing in December 2026 and a distributor converting its letter in the first quarter would make the 2026 revenue gap a timing artefact rather than a demand failure, and a hospital-anchored base of even 60 sites at commercial prices would fund the 2028 plan. The Ireland entity and the contract-development work are not that counter-case: a CE mark not before 2028 and $0.7M of services revenue are costs against a $30M raise, not paths to one [S150].

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's plan to reach 300 commercial sites by the end of 2027 rests on one non-binding distributor letter and one $650-a-month rental programme, and it requires adding sites sixteen times faster than the company has ever added them while each placed analyzer runs one panel a day against the eight its model assumes [S150]. The only commercial arrangement with money attached is the evaluation programme: 41 clinics, 55 analyzers, $650 a month per analyzer, $429,000 a year, plus cartridges — company data, unverified by any site or contract. Everything beyond it is intention: the 300 sites come from a letter of intent that is non-binding, tied to clearance, and disclosed without a signing date, a term, a territory or a minimum purchase. The company has added 1.3 sites a month over the 31 months since the programme began; 300 by end-2027 means 259 net new sites in twelve months, 21.6 a month, with 9 people in sales and support.

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 510(k) decision, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027 | Filed 2026-05-18; information requested 2026-08-21; answer planned December 2026 | Whether the launch clock starts in 2027 at all | S150, S191 |
| Pivotal study, four sites, ~1,150 patients | Results Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07; no registered protocol | Whether accuracy survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood | S150 (unverified) |
| Second 510(k), three remaining assays | Filed Q2 2027 | Not started | Whether a five-assay panel exists commercially | S150 (unverified) |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 | Not started | Whether staff without laboratory training can run it | S150 (unverified) |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | Letter of intent only; 41 in evaluation | Whether a channel exists beyond referrals | S150 (unverified) |
| Cartridge cost below $10 at 1 million units | Undated | $16.20 at ~20,000 units a year | Whether the 76% margin is reachable | S150 (unverified) |

### The utilisation gap is the whole revenue plan

The deck assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer from 2028 and reports that evaluation sites used 41 cartridges a site a month in 2026 — company data, unverified. Across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month, or 1.02 panels a day, an eight-fold gap measured over two and a half years on the only population the company has served [S150]. The $2.4B serviceable market inherits it: 13,200 sites times 2 analyzers times 8 panels times 300 days times $38 gives the headline, but the same 13,200 sites at the 1.34 analyzers and 1.02 panels the company actually achieves give $206M of annual cartridge revenue, a twelve-fold difference on an unchanged site count. The fair defence is that evaluation sites are barred from using results for patient care, so demand there proves little. The consequence is not that utilisation stays at 1; it is that the company holds no commercial utilisation data, and the 2028-29 revenue line is an assumption rather than an extrapolation.

### The 2026 revenue estimate contains a shipment that cannot happen

FY2026E revenue is $5.9M, unverified, of which $2.4M is an opening stocking order from the distributor that ships only on 510(k) clearance. Nine months of 2026 produced $2.7M, so the fourth quarter must deliver $3.2M, $2.4M of it from an order that, on the company's own Q1 2027 clearance forecast, cannot ship in 2026 [S150]. Strip the order out and the year is $3.5M, which the run rate supports. That matters twice: the estimate overstates 2026 by 41%, and the same order presumably sits inside FY2027P revenue, so 2027 growth is partly a shipment rather than demand. The order also equals 71,856 cartridges at the realised $33.40 price — 5.8 months of channel inventory at the 300-site run rate the company uses today, against a nine-month shelf life, which is a return and expiry exposure the accounts show as revenue.

### Instrument economics are not the constraint; capital for everything else is

At a $2,900 list price against a $3,350 build cost, and with 60% of instruments given free, the blended subsidy is $2,190 per placed analyzer (unverified); 300 sites at the observed 1.34 analyzers each is 402 analyzers and $0.88M of subsidy, immaterial against a $30M raise [S150]. The razor-and-blade arithmetic works even at low utilisation: an analyzer at 1.02 panels a day earns $6,300 of cartridge gross profit a year against a $2,190 subsidy, and at 8 panels a day $41,280. What consumes capital is manufacturing scale-up — 40% of proceeds, $12M, with no disclosed capex, line count or qualification schedule — and working capital. Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M of monthly net burn runs out around 2027-03-31, the round is targeted to close on 2027-01-29, and the term loan starts amortising in 2027-03 at $167,000 a month. A twelve-month clearance slip adds a year at the FY2027 loss level, $16.5M, turning $30M into $30M plus a bridge.

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive licence to the cartridge sealing patent; 3% royalty on net cartridge sales | Acquired 2021-04 | In force; related party, the CTO holds 22% of Corvia | S150 (unverified) |
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Distributor letter of intent, 300 sites, $2.4M opening order | Not disclosed | Non-binding, conditional on clearance | S150 (unverified) |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland | EU regulatory entity | Entity formed 2025-01-15 | No staff; CE marking not before 2028 | S150 (unverified) |
| Unnamed diagnostics partner | Contract development | Not disclosed | $0.7M of FY2025 revenue; scope undisclosed | S150 (unverified) |

### The channel constraint the deck does not price

Until a CLIA waiver is granted, only a laboratory holding a certificate for moderate-complexity testing can run the panel, and QuidelOrtho, selling into the same channel, describes the waived designation as "critical" for its point-of-care products and the waiver process as "onerous". So the 2027 launch is confined to hospital-run urgent care and rural hospital laboratories — and only one of the 41 evaluation sites is a hospital, holding 3 of the 55 analyzers [S17, S13]. That is the most credible route rather than a weakness: hospital laboratories already hold the certificate, the transfer-avoidance economics are strongest there, and Abbott's clearance of a high-sensitivity troponin cartridge on the handheld i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and on Alinity in June 2026 shows the channel rewards an installed base, not a first mover. What Vantelle does not own is the reimbursement step: clinics bill payers under existing codes, so whether a clinic will pay $38 a cartridge is a decision the investor can only test after clearance.

### What must be true within twelve months

By October 2027 the first clearance has to be in hand with no second information request, the pivotal study has to show precision at the cut-off that survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood, and a set of commercial sites has to buy cartridges at commercial terms with payer billing actually happening. The signposts are specific: a purchase order converting the distributor letter after clearance; one commercial site running several times the observed daily volume, the first evidence that 8 panels a day is reachable; a filed CLIA waiver application with a multi-site operator study behind it; and a unit cost inside the milestone at 100,000 cartridges a year. What breaks the plan is equally specific: a second information request, an FDA decision that keeps the assays at moderate complexity with a waiver required before broad marketing, or a pivotal study finishing after Q3 2027. The counter-case deserves weight — a clearance landing in December 2026 and a distributor converting its letter in the first quarter would make the 2026 revenue gap a timing artefact rather than a demand failure, and a hospital-anchored base of even 60 sites at commercial prices would fund the 2028 plan. The Ireland entity and the contract-development work are not that counter-case: a CE mark not before 2028 and $0.7M of services revenue are costs against a $30M raise, not paths to one, and every date in this paragraph is company intent, unverified [S150].

arguments.markdown:
The $140M pre-money prices Vantelle above what strategic buyers have just paid for cleared, CLIA-waived point-of-care platforms, and the security on offer returns the new money 1.0x across the exit range where most point-of-care assets have traded. The financing record explains why: the Series B is a flat round in real terms, the insiders' newest money came in through a 25%-discount bridge, and 9.35% of the headline valuation is an option-pool top-up rather than operating value. Every company figure in this section is unverified company data; no public filing or third-party record of Vantelle Diagnostics was found on 2026-10-30 [S150].

| Date | Round | Amount | Implied price / valuation | Investors | Use of funds | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019-06 | Seed | $4.5M | $0.75/share implied; post-money not disclosed | Juniper Rock Capital (lead) and other seed investors | Product development | Deck p.13-14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2021-04 | Corvia Microfluidics 60% | Stock; value not disclosed | n/d | Corvia founders, including Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist (22%) | Sealing-film patent CM-1 | Deck p.12-13 (S150; unverified) |
| 2022-02 | Series A first close | $24.0M | $2.903/share implied | Ardent Peak Ventures (lead) and other Series A investors | Cartridge pilot line; evaluation program | Deck p.13-14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2023-11 | Series A second close | $12.0M | Same $2.903/share implied | Existing investors | Working capital | Deck p.13-14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2024-03 | Term loan and warrants | $5.0M debt; 400,000 warrants at $2.903 | n/a | Bluestem Venture Lending | Evaluation program | Deck p.13-14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2026-06-30 | Bridge notes | $6.0M at 8% | Converts at $2.4423 (75% of the Series B price) into 2,571,392 Series B-1 shares | Existing investors (unnamed) | Runway to the Series B | Deck p.14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2027-01 target | Series B | $30.0M | $140M pre, $170M post; $3.2564/share | Meridian $15.0M proposed; Ardent Peak $5.0M; Juniper Rock $3.0M; $7.0M from other new investors | 35% FDA clearance, 40% manufacturing, 25% launch | Deck p.14-15 (S150; unverified) |

The $0.75 seed price is inferred from $4.5M over 6.0M seed shares; the deck does not state it. The $2.903 Series A price is inferred from $36.0M over 12.4M shares and corroborated by the Bluestem warrant strike. $3.2564 is 12.2% above $2.903, or 2.9%-3.7% a year over the 3.2-4.0 years since the two closes; on 2026-10-29 the three-month Treasury bill yielded 4.00% and the ten-year 4.99%, so the Series A is underwater in real terms. The bridge worsens the new money's position: $6.0M plus 8% interest converts at $2.4423 into 2,571,392 shares worth $8.37M at the Series B price, a 1.40x paper return in seven months; at par the same $6.28M would have bought 1,929,000 shares, so the discount creates 642,392 extra shares, 1.23% of the post-money. The headline also overstates value to existing holders: of 42,991,881 fully diluted pre-money shares, 36.4M existing shares are worth $118.5M, the bridge conversion $8.37M and 4.02M new pool shares $13.09M; excluding the pool, the clean pre-money is $126.9M. The new lead pays 33% more per share than investors who committed seven months earlier [S150, S86, S87].

### Three ways to value it, all below the ask

| Method | Inputs | Result | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| EV / FY2025 revenue | $138.1M EV ($140M pre + $5.0M debt − $6.9M cash) / $2.6M | 53.1x; peer median 2.05x | S150; S4, S75; S8, S78; S213; S214 |
| EV / FY2026E revenue | $138.1M / $5.9M | 23.4x; includes a $2.4M stocking order that ships on clearance | S150 |
| EV / FY2027P revenue | $138.1M / $16.8M | 8.2x; assumes 300 sites against 41 today | S150 |
| EV / FY2027P gross profit | $138.1M / $10.58M (63% margin) | 13.1x | S150 |
| Precedent platform transactions | LEX $100M cleared and waived; SpinChip €138M pre-revenue; LumiraDx technology $295M plus up to $55M | $100M-$295M of platform value | S205; S204; S171 |
| Scenario-weighted value (analyst estimate) | 20% $500M, 30% $300M, 30% $120M, 20% $30M exit; five years at 12%-15% | $115M-$132M | S150; analyst estimate |
| Headline round | $140M pre / $170M post | $170M post-money | S150 |

The weights are the analyst's: a 20% chance of a $500M outcome assumes the company's unverified FY2029 plan is met and a 6.4x multiple on $78.5M revenue; 30% at $300M assumes 5x on $60M; 30% at $120M covers a clearance but a slow ramp; 20% at $30M covers failure or an asset sale. The $232M expected exit discounts to $115M-$132M at 12%-15%, 22%-32% below the $170M post-money [S150].

### The public comparables are cheaper than the deals

| Company | EV / Sales | EV / EBITDA | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | 4.6x | 22.7x | TTM to 2026-03-31 | S4, S75 |
| QuidelOrtho | 0.4x | n/m | TTM to 2026-06-28 | S8, S78 |
| Siemens Healthineers | 1.9x | 13.8x | TTM, 2026-10-29 | S214 |
| bioMérieux | 2.2x | 8.9x | TTM, 2026-09 | S213 |
| Werfen | n/d | n/d (FY2025 sales €2.131B, EBITDA €473M) | FY2025 | S215 |
| Peer median | 2.05x | 13.8x | | S4, S75, S8, S78, S213, S214 |
| Vantelle at $140M pre | 53.1x FY2025; 23.4x FY2026E | n/m (net loss) | FY2025-FY2026E | S150 |

QuidelOrtho is the purest read on how the public market prices point-of-care revenue: 0.4x EV/Sales, a $0.9B market cap, a 48.7% fall in twelve months and a price at the 15th percentile of its 52-week range. Abbott marks the ceiling at 4.6x, and the median strategic medtech deal paid 3.9x revenue in Q1 2026. At 3.9x, $140M implies $35.9M of revenue today, 13.8 times FY2025; at 4.6x it implies $30.4M. No analyst consensus exists for a private company; the only forecast is the company's FY2029 plan of $78.5M revenue and $9.0M profit, worth $393M at 5x, or 2.1x for Meridian [S78, S8, S220].

### The round funds the plan but not the working capital

The $30M round is 73% new money: $22M from new investors and $8M from Ardent Peak and Juniper Rock. Meridian's $15M buys 8.8% of the post-money; the whole new-money block buys 17.6%. Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against a $1.15M monthly net burn and a $5.0M term loan amortizing from March 2027 gives 24-26 months from a full $30M close and 19 months from Meridian's $15M. Revenue of $41.0M in FY2028 and $78.5M in FY2029 will absorb cartridge inventory and receivables the plan does not fund, so a Series C or working-capital facility in 2028 is the base case. Ardent Peak's $5.0M is 14% of the $36.0M Series A class and Juniper Rock's $3.0M is 67% of the seed; neither is a strategic buyer, and the independent board seat is vacant [S150].

### What would change the answer

The strongest counter-evidence is that strategics pay for platforms before revenue: bioMérieux agreed to buy pre-commercial SpinChip at a €138M enterprise value in January 2025, and 41 evaluation sites with a 92% 90-day reorder rate are a real beachhead; a competitive auction could clear $300M-$400M. That supports the $100M-$300M platform band, not a $140M pre-money at the top of it. Four questions would settle the price: the Series A agreements for both closes and the Corvia share issuance; the bridge terms, including maturity, security and whether conversion is a class vote; the FY2027-FY2029 cash flow with working capital and the distributor letter of intent; and the charter terms on Series A participation, drag-along and the Corvia put. At $100M pre-money the same $15M would buy 11.5% and the 3x threshold would fall to $426M, inside the precedent range [S204, S150].

The $140M pre-money prices Vantelle above what strategic buyers have just paid for cleared, CLIA-waived point-of-care platforms, and the security on offer returns the new money 1.0x across the exit range where most point-of-care assets have traded. The financing record explains why: the Series B is a flat round in real terms, the insiders' newest money came in through a 25%-discount bridge, and 9.35% of the headline valuation is an option-pool top-up rather than operating value. Every company figure in this section is unverified company data; no public filing or third-party record of Vantelle Diagnostics was found on 2026-10-30 [S150].

| 2027-01 target | Series B | $30.0M | $140M pre, $170M post; $3.2564/share | Meridian $15.0M proposed; Ardent Peak $5.0M; Juniper Rock $3.0M; $7.0M from other new investors | 35% FDA clearance, 40% manufacturing, 25% launch | Deck p.14-15 (S150; unverified) |

The $0.75 seed price is inferred from $4.5M over 6.0M seed shares; the deck does not state it. The $2.903 Series A price is inferred from $36.0M over 12.4M shares and corroborated by the Bluestem warrant strike. $3.2564 is 12.2% above $2.903, or 2.9%-3.7% a year over the 3.2-4.0 years since the two closes; on 2026-10-29 the three-month Treasury bill yielded 4.00% and the ten-year 4.99%, so the Series A is underwater in real terms. The bridge worsens the new money's position: $6.0M plus 8% interest converts at $2.4423 into 2,571,392 shares worth $8.37M at the Series B price, a 1.40x paper return in seven months; at par the same $6.28M would have bought 1,929,000 shares, so the discount creates 642,392 extra shares, 1.23% of the post-money. QuidelOrtho is the purest read on how the public market prices point-of-care revenue: 0.4x EV/Sales, a $0.9B market cap, a 48.7% fall in twelve months and a price at the 15th percentile of its 52-week range. Abbott marks the ceiling at 4.6x, and the median strategic medtech deal paid 3.9x revenue in Q1 2026. At 3.9x, $140M implies $35.9M of revenue today, 13.8 times FY2025; at 4.6x it implies $30.4M. ### The round funds the plan but not the working capital

The $30M round is 73% new money: $22M from new investors and $8M from Ardent Peak and Juniper Rock. Meridian's $15M buys 8.8% of the post-money; the whole new-money block buys 17.6%. Ardent Peak's $5.0M is 14% of the $36.0M Series A class and Juniper Rock's $3.0M is 67% of the seed; neither is a strategic buyer, and the independent board seat is vacant [S150].

### What would change the answer

The strongest counter-evidence is that strategics pay for platforms before revenue: bioMérieux agreed to buy pre-commercial SpinChip at a €138M enterprise value in January 2025, and 41 evaluation sites with a 92% 90-day reorder rate are a real beachhead; a competitive auction could clear $300M-$400M. That supports the $100M-$300M platform band, not a $140M pre-money at the top of it. Four questions would settle the price: the Series A agreements for both closes and the Corvia share issuance; the bridge terms, including maturity, security and whether conversion is a class vote; the FY2027-FY2029 cash flow with working capital and the distributor letter of intent; and the charter terms on Series A participation, drag-along and the Corvia put. At $100M pre-money the same $15M would buy 11.5% and the 3x threshold would fall to $426M, inside the precedent range [S204, S150].

arguments.markdown:
The $140M pre-money prices Vantelle above what strategic buyers have just paid for cleared, CLIA-waived point-of-care platforms, and the security on offer returns the new money 1.0x across the exit range where most point-of-care assets have traded. The financing record explains why: the Series B is a flat round in real terms, the insiders' newest money came in through a 25%-discount bridge, and 9.35% of the headline valuation is an option-pool top-up rather than operating value. Every company figure in this section is unverified company data; no public filing or third-party record of Vantelle Diagnostics was found on 2026-10-30 [S150].

| Date | Round | Amount | Implied price / valuation | Investors | Use of funds | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019-06 | Seed | $4.5M | $0.75/share implied; post-money not disclosed | Juniper Rock Capital (lead) and other seed investors | Product development | Deck p.13-14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2021-04 | Corvia Microfluidics 60% | Stock; value not disclosed | n/d | Corvia founders, including Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist (22%) | Sealing-film patent CM-1 | Deck p.12-13 (S150; unverified) |
| 2022-02 | Series A first close | $24.0M | $2.903/share implied | Ardent Peak Ventures (lead) and other Series A investors | Cartridge pilot line; evaluation program | Deck p.13-14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2023-11 | Series A second close | $12.0M | Same $2.903/share implied | Existing investors | Working capital | Deck p.13-14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2024-03 | Term loan and warrants | $5.0M debt; 400,000 warrants at $2.903 | n/a | Bluestem Venture Lending | Evaluation program | Deck p.13-14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2026-06-30 | Bridge notes | $6.0M at 8% | Converts at $2.4423 (75% of the Series B price) into 2,571,392 Series B-1 shares | Existing investors (unnamed) | Runway to the Series B | Deck p.14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2027-01 target | Series B | $30.0M | $140M pre, $170M post; $3.2564/share | Meridian $15.0M proposed; Ardent Peak $5.0M; Juniper Rock $3.0M; $7.0M from other new investors | 35% FDA clearance, 40% manufacturing, 25% launch | Deck p.14-15 (S150; unverified) |

The $0.75 seed price is inferred from $4.5M over 6.0M seed shares; the deck does not state it. The $2.903 Series A price is inferred from $36.0M over 12.4M shares and corroborated by the Bluestem warrant strike. $3.2564 is 12.2% above $2.903, or 2.9%-3.7% a year over the 3.2-4.0 years since the two closes; on 2026-10-29 the three-month Treasury bill yielded 4.00% and the ten-year 4.99%, so the Series A is underwater in real terms. The bridge worsens the new money's position: $6.0M plus 8% interest converts at $2.4423 into 2,571,392 shares worth $8.37M at the Series B price, a 1.40x paper return in seven months; at par the same $6.28M would have bought 1,929,000 shares, so the discount creates 642,392 extra shares, 1.23% of the post-money. The headline also overstates value to existing holders: of 42,991,881 fully diluted pre-money shares, 36.4M existing shares are worth $118.5M, the bridge conversion $8.37M and 4.02M new pool shares $13.09M; excluding the pool, the clean pre-money is $126.9M. The new lead pays 33% more per share than investors who committed seven months earlier [S150, S86, S87].

### Three ways to value it, all below the ask

| Method | Inputs | Result | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| EV / FY2025 revenue | $138.1M EV ($140M pre + $5.0M debt − $6.9M cash) / $2.6M | 53.1x; peer median 2.05x | S150; S4, S75; S8, S78; S213; S214 |
| EV / FY2026E revenue | $138.1M / $5.9M | 23.4x; includes a $2.4M stocking order that ships on clearance | S150 (unverified) |
| EV / FY2027P revenue | $138.1M / $16.8M | 8.2x; assumes 300 sites against 41 today | S150 (unverified) |
| EV / FY2027P gross profit | $138.1M / $10.58M (63% margin) | 13.1x | S150 (unverified) |
| Precedent platform transactions | LEX $100M cleared and waived; SpinChip €138M pre-revenue; LumiraDx technology $295M plus up to $55M | $100M-$295M of platform value | S205; S204; S171 |
| Scenario-weighted value (analyst estimate) | 20% $500M, 30% $300M, 30% $120M, 20% $30M exit; five years at 12%-15% | $115M-$132M | S150 (unverified); analyst estimate |
| Headline round | $140M pre / $170M post | $170M post-money | S150 (unverified) |

The weights are the analyst's: a 20% chance of a $500M outcome assumes the company's unverified FY2029 plan is met and a 6.4x multiple on $78.5M revenue; 30% at $300M assumes 5x on $60M; 30% at $120M covers a clearance but a slow ramp; 20% at $30M covers failure or an asset sale. The $232M expected exit discounts to $115M-$132M at 12%-15%, 22%-32% below the $170M post-money [S150].

### The public comparables are cheaper than the deals

| Company | EV / Sales | EV / EBITDA | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | 4.6x | 22.7x | TTM to 2026-03-31 | S4, S75 |
| QuidelOrtho | 0.4x | n/m | TTM to 2026-06-28 | S8, S78 |
| Siemens Healthineers | 1.9x | 13.8x | TTM, 2026-10-29 | S214 |
| bioMérieux | 2.2x | 8.9x | TTM, 2026-09 | S213 |
| Werfen | n/d | n/d (FY2025 sales €2.131B, EBITDA €473M) | FY2025 | S215 |
| Peer median | 2.05x | 13.8x | | S4, S75, S8, S78, S213, S214 |
| Vantelle at $140M pre | 53.1x FY2025; 23.4x FY2026E | n/m (net loss) | FY2025-FY2026E | S150 (unverified) |

QuidelOrtho is the purest read on how the public market prices point-of-care revenue: 0.4x EV/Sales, a $0.9B market cap, a 48.7% fall in twelve months and a price at the 15th percentile of its 52-week range. Abbott marks the ceiling at 4.6x, and the median strategic medtech deal paid 3.9x revenue in Q1 2026. At 3.9x, $140M implies $35.9M of revenue today, 13.8 times FY2025; at 4.6x it implies $30.4M. No analyst consensus exists for a private company; the only forecast is the company's FY2029 plan of $78.5M revenue and $9.0M profit, worth $393M at 5x, or 2.1x for Meridian [S78, S8, S220].

### The round funds the plan but not the working capital

The $30M round is 73% new money on the company's unverified figures: $22M from new investors and $8M from Ardent Peak and Juniper Rock. Meridian's $15M buys 8.8% of the post-money; the whole new-money block buys 17.6%. Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against a $1.15M monthly net burn and a $5.0M term loan amortizing from March 2027 gives 24-26 months from a full $30M close and 19 months from Meridian's $15M. Revenue of $41.0M in FY2028 and $78.5M in FY2029 will absorb cartridge inventory and receivables the plan does not fund, so a Series C or working-capital facility in 2028 is the base case. Ardent Peak's $5.0M is 14% of the $36.0M Series A class and Juniper Rock's $3.0M is 67% of the seed; neither is a strategic buyer, and the independent board seat is vacant [S150].

### What would change the answer

The strongest counter-evidence is that strategics pay for platforms before revenue: bioMérieux agreed to buy pre-commercial SpinChip at a €138M enterprise value in January 2025, and 41 evaluation sites with a 92% 90-day reorder rate are a real beachhead; a competitive auction could clear $300M-$400M. That supports the $100M-$300M platform band, not a $140M pre-money at the top of it. Four questions would settle the price: the Series A agreements for both closes and the Corvia share issuance; the bridge terms, including maturity, security and whether conversion is a class vote; the FY2027-FY2029 cash flow with working capital and the distributor letter of intent; and the charter terms on Series A participation, drag-along and the Corvia put. At $100M pre-money the same $15M would buy 11.5% and the 3x threshold would fall to $426M, inside the precedent range [S204, S150].

The buyer logic is real: Abbott, Roche and bioMérieux have each bought a point-of-care platform or menu since 2024, but each paid $100M-$295M for the asset, and a five-assay finger-stick panel would be a menu bolt-on to an existing franchise rather than a franchise of its own [S205, S204, S171].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |

| Strategic sale | Siemens Healthineers; Werfen | Both have acute-care blood-gas and electrolyte POC (epoc, GEM) but no finger-stick cardiac immunoassay; a bolt-on fits | 2029-2032 | Low | S214, S215 |

| Buyout | Blackstone/TPG-type private equity | Hologic was taken private at $18.3B in 2026; buyout funds pay for cash-generative diagnostics, not pre-profit platforms | 2030+ | Low | S211 |
| IPO | Nasdaq | Medline's $6.26B IPO in December 2025 reopened the window and Molbio listed in India in August 2026, but a US listing needs $50M+ revenue, audited accounts and a cleared menu | 2030-2032 | Low | S217, S218 |

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| QuidelOrtho / LEX Diagnostics | 2026 | $100M cash | n/d (cleared and CLIA-waived) | S205 |
| Abbott / Exact Sciences | 2026 | $21B | 6.5x FY2025 revenue of $3.25B | S207, S206 |
| Blackstone-TPG / Hologic | 2026 | $18.3B equity | 4.5x FY2025 revenue of $4.10B | S211, S212 |
| bioMérieux / SpinChip | 2025 | €138M enterprise value | n/m (pre-revenue) | S204 |
| Roche / LumiraDx POC technology | 2024 | $295M plus up to $55M | n/d (distressed sale) | S171 |
