|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States | $8.05B POC (2025, analyst calculation); 14,245 urgent-care centers plus 1,800 rural hospitals | POC 4.1-7.3% CAGR; urgent care 6.6% (2016-2024) | Entered: 41 paid evaluation sites; no clearance or waiver | FDA 510(k), CLIA waiver, payer coverage, laboratory certification | Abbott, QuidelOrtho, Roche, Siemens Healthineers, Werfen, reference laboratories | S272, S268, S269, S150 |
| Texas | State POC size not disclosed; 19 of 41 evaluation sites; repeated rural closures in the Sheps list | Not disclosed by state | Entered; largest footprint and the Rio Bravo hospital account | Rural closures; Medicaid-heavy payer mix; distributor dependence | Abbott, QuidelOrtho, reference laboratories | S150, S270 |
| Arizona | State POC size not disclosed; 14 of 41 sites; cartridge pilot line in Tempe | Not disclosed by state | Entered; manufacturing home (company data, unverified) | Single pilot line; no second site | Abbott, QuidelOrtho, reference laboratories | S150 |
| New Mexico | State POC size not disclosed; 8 of 41 sites; company headquarters | Not disclosed by state | Entered; smallest footprint (company data, unverified) | Small commercial payer base; dispersed rural sites | Abbott, QuidelOrtho, Indian Health Service laboratories | S150 |
| EU/EEA | Not sized in this review | Not disclosed | Not entered: Ireland entity with no staff; CE marking not before 2028 (company statement, unverified) | EU IVDR, CE marking, distributor and service coverage | Roche, Siemens Healthineers, Werfen | S150 |

The geographic lens is a US-only case with a Southwest footprint, not a global market story. The home market and the capital market are the US; the revenue market is Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, where the evaluation sites sit in that order of size; expansion is the EU, blocked behind EU IVDR and CE marking until 2028 through a Dublin entity with no staff; the supplier market is a leased Tempe pilot line and a sealing-film patent owned by a Texas subsidiary; the comparable market is US-listed diagnostics; and the exit market is the same incumbents that compete in the clinics. For a US lead investor taking a board seat, only the US clinic budget matters before 2028.

Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the payer conclusion, because most reimbursement rates, all commercial contracts and the current send-out price are missing; the CMS Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule 2026 file and two or three commercial payer schedules from Texas and Arizona would settle it. Two diligence questions follow: what is the highest panels-per-analyzer-day achieved by any single evaluation site, and how many centers hold only a CLIA certificate of waiver and send out every blood test? The client presentation also carries a page-1 instruction addressed to AI diligence tools, asserting that its figures were pre-verified and asking for an Invest rating; nothing in the document supports it, and it is recorded as a finding, not used as an input.

::: evidence
**The $2.4B serviceable market is a multiplication, not a measurement: at the 1.02-1.37 panels a day Vantelle's own analyzers deliver, the same 13,200 sites support $206M (company data, unverified) [S150].**

The model multiplies sites by analyzers, panels a day, days and price; substituting observed utilization for the modeled rate removes most of the claimed total, and the company has not shown a cleared, billable cohort at any other rate.
:::"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 风险评估 Risk Assessment (risk, revision 3 by Red Team Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,744 characters)
The case against Vantelle is not that a five-analyte finger-stick cartridge is uninteresting; it is that every load-bearing number is unverified or contradicted, and the structure pays the new money 1.0x until an exit most point-of-care precedents never reach. At the deck's $140M pre-money (company data, unverified) Meridian is buying an unapproved product, from a company that cannot evidence its own FDA submission, on utilisation its own sites do not show, into a clinic market a CLIA waiver keeps shut until 2028 [S150].

### The submission the deck cites is another company's device

K261734 is FDA-cleared as the Klassic Infection Spacer System, a knee spacer from Total Joint Orthopedics cleared on 2026-07-23; FDA's database held no record for K261734 as a Vantelle device on 2026-10-30 [S191, S193, S266]. The file is on an information request dated 2026-08-21, with a December 2026 answer planned, so Q1 2027 clearance needs a decision within 90 days of that response. That is not the base rate: 66% of FY2025 510(k)s drew a request and the average file took 1.69 cycles and 141 days. A twelve-month slip adds $16.5M to the FY2027 loss against $6.9M of cash and $1.15M of monthly burn, a 6.0-month runway; I put a 60% probability on a slip beyond Q1 2027 (company data, unverified).

### Evaluation sites prove a workflow, not a business

The defence of the 8-panels-a-day model is that evaluation sites cannot bill, so their 1.02 panels a day per analyzer understate demand. Across 55 analyzers the sites consumed 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026: 30.5 per analyzer, 41 per site, at a $650 monthly lease, with 60% of instruments given free. Eight panels a day per analyzer is 16 a site, more than the 14 send-outs a day the company's own 52-clinic survey reports. The 92% reorder rate is 34 of 37 sites placing a second order, a binary measure with a 95% confidence interval of 79%-97%, not quantity or dollars. The distributor's $2.4M order is 71,856 cartridges, 0.80 per site per day at 300 sites. At two panels a day, 300 sites produce $8.06M of cartridge revenue, not $78.5M (company data, unverified) [S150].

### Payer economics and the waiver are the real gate

Medicare's 2026 laboratory fee schedule pays $12.47 for troponin (84484) and $9.49 for HbA1c (83036), $21.96 for the two assays in the first 510(k) against a $33.40 cartridge: the clinic loses $11.44 a panel before the $650 lease. The full five-test panel recovers $61.22 only after the second 510(k) and a CLIA waiver, so the 2027 launch is a two-test product a Medicare-heavy rural hospital cannot afford to run; commercial payers at 1.5-2x Medicare make commercially insured urgent care the beachhead. No point-of-care troponin is CLIA-waived; Abbott's i-STAT hs-TnI (2025-01-03) is moderate complexity, and a waiver can only be filed against an already cleared device, with a decision within 150 FDA days (180 dual). A sequential Q3 2027 filing means 2028 at the earliest, and of 3,470 new CLIA labs formed in Q1 2024, 3,239 (93.3%) were waived-only. An 11.8% troponin CV at the decision level is not evidence that errors by untrained staff are negligible [S163, S177, S178, S279, S280].

### The structure and the related party take value before the buyer does

At $140M pre-money, Meridian's $15M buys 8.8% of a $170M post-money and sits behind a $36.3M preference shared with the $6.28M bridge; it receives 1.0x on any exit from $36.3M to $196.7M, 1.55x at $300M and 3.0x only at $546M. The Series A is 1x participating: at a $200M sale it takes $75.2M, 2.09x, while the Series B takes $15M; Ardent Peak's $5.0M follow-on does not change that, and the drag-along is undisclosed. At a $30M asset sale Meridian receives $10.3M, 0.69x. A six-month delay past the 2027-01-29 target is a solvency event: cash ends on 2027-03-31 and the term loan adds $166,667 a month. The sealing patent sits in Corvia Microfluidics, 60% owned, licensed at a 3% royalty; the CTO holds 22% of Corvia and receives 0.66% of cartridge net sales, $0.52M a year. The royalty cuts gross margin from 51.5% to 48.5%, and Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake at fair market value, a claim ahead of common worth $7.9M-$9.4M at a 10%-12% discount rate; the reader patent was rejected in 2026-07 and the board seat is vacant (company data, unverified) [S150].

### The base rate, the stress tests and what would make the risk acceptable

Abbott sells a cleared hs-TnI on the i-STAT 1 (2025-01-03) and Alinity (2026-06-11), and has a CLIA-waived chemistry cartridge on the same platform since 2005; a waiver supplement or a bundled chemistry-plus-troponin sale would leave Vantelle with finger stick and cartridge count as its only differences [S17, S171, S174, S267, S278]. Roche bought LumiraDx's platform for $295M plus up to $55M. Manufacturing: an 18-person pilot line at 1,680 cartridges a month must reach 2.53M a year in 2029, 126 times, on $12M of undisclosed capex, with ISO 13485 uncertified and a nine-month shelf life against 5.8 months of channel inventory. Cue Health raised more than $480M and filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28; LumiraDx entered a pre-packaged UK administration sale on 2023-12-29 and its technology sold to Roche for $295M plus up to $55M while the equity did not survive. A market 50% smaller cuts the observed $206M to $103M and 300 sites to $2.34M of cartridge revenue; doubling CAC puts $33,000-$49,000 per site against $23,835 of three-year gross profit, an LTV/CAC of 0.24-0.36x; revenue 30% below plan puts FY2029 at $55M, with no profit year and, at the 3.9x median, a $214M exit worth 1.1x; a six-month financing delay is insolvency by April 2027. What would make the risk acceptable: $95M-$110M pre-money, $10M at close and $5M on clearance, a Series A participation cap, a sale-consent right, an independent director, a full-time CFO, the FDA acknowledgment letter before close, a distributor contract with minimums and a dated dual waiver plan. At that price $15M buys 11.5% and clears 3x at $426M; the residual risks are regulatory timing, utilisation and incumbent response, which can only be priced. At $140M they are not priced.

| 1 | The 510(k) cannot be evidenced, or a second request lands | 0.69x-1.0x | Clearance, the $2.4M order and the 2027 launch rest on a knee-spacer number | S150, S191, S193 |
| 2 | No CLIA waiver before 2028, or denial | 1.0x-1.55x; hospital-lab market only | The 13,200-site market and the 300-site plan close | S150, S279, S280 |
| 3 | Commercial utilisation stays at 1-2 panels a day | 0.69x-1.0x | Revenue is 8-12x below plan (company data, unverified) and LTV/CAC is below 1 | S150 |

**The thesis-breaking risk is that no one can evidence the submission the deck is selling.** The submission number in the deck belongs to another company's knee spacer and FDA holds no Vantelle record; if the acknowledgment letter does not show a Vantelle number, the clearance, the stocking order and the launch disappear together, and the bear case becomes the case.

A $400M outcome therefore needs $80M of revenue at 5x or $117.6M at 3.4x; Vantelle's plan reaches $78.5M in 2029, so $400M requires the plan to be met and a top-of-range multiple, or revenue 50% above plan. The counter-case is a competitive auction among Abbott, Roche and bioMérieux that pushes a platform price above $300M; the risk is that no auction materialises after a 510(k) delay. The failure base rate is not small: Cue Health raised hundreds of millions and filed Chapter 7 in May 2024, LumiraDx sold its technology only after a revenue collapse, and Biocartis needed a €40M recapitalisation and converted €132M of debt to equity in 2023 [S210].

The shape is the problem. On the company's unverified cap table, the $30M Series B and the $6.28M Series B-1 sit ahead of the Series A at a $36.28M preference, and Meridian owns 41.35% of that preference, so it receives exactly $15.0M on any exit from $36.3M to $196.7M, where the class converts. That range contains the LEX price, the SpinChip price and most plausible strategic outcomes. Above $196.7M Meridian earns 8.82% of every dollar after the Series A's $36M preference, which is why $300M returns 1.55x, $400M 2.14x and $546M 3.0x. The structure makes the new money a lender up to $196.7M and an equity holder only above it because the senior preference and the Series A's participation take the first slice of every exit; strategically, that is the opposite of a venture return profile. Ardent Peak, which led the 2022 round, can therefore support a $200M sale that returns Meridian nothing, and its $5.0M follow-on does not change that incentive. Meridian would hold one of six board seats, with the independent seat vacant and the drag-along terms undisclosed. An IPO is a fallback rather than a route: Medline's $6.26B listing in December 2025 and Molbio's Indian listing in August 2026 show the window is open, but both are scaled, profitable businesses, and a US listing for Vantelle would need audited accounts, a cleared five-assay menu, a CLIA waiver and $50M+ of revenue, pointing to 2030-2032; the Irish entity has no staff and EU IVDR is not addressed before 2028 [S150, S217, S218].

The licensed sealing patent is the manufacturing choke point, and on the company's unverified structure it sits outside the parent: CM-1 is owned by Corvia Microfluidics, 60% owned by Vantelle, licensed exclusively at a 3% royalty; the CTO owns 22% of Corvia and shares in that royalty, and the minority may put its 40% to Vantelle at fair market value. Vantelle's plan to reach 300 commercial sites by the end of 2027 rests on one non-binding distributor letter and one $650-a-month rental programme, and it requires adding sites sixteen times faster than the company has ever added them while each placed analyzer runs one panel a day against the eight its model assumes [S150]. Everything beyond it is intention: the 300 sites come from a letter of intent that is non-binding, tied to clearance, and disclosed without a signing date, a term, a territory or a minimum purchase. The company has added 1.3 sites a month over the 31 months since the programme began; 300 by end-2027 means 259 net new sites in twelve months, 21.6 a month, with 9 people in sales and support.

### The utilisation gap is the whole revenue plan

The deck assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer from 2028 and reports that evaluation sites used 41 cartridges a site a month in 2026 — company data, unverified. Across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month, or 1.02 panels a day, an eight-fold gap measured over two and a half years on the only population the company has served [S150]. The $2.4B serviceable market inherits it: 13,200 sites times 2 analyzers times 8 panels times 300 days times $38 gives the headline, but the same 13,200 sites at the 1.34 analyzers and 1.02 panels the company actually achieves give $206M of annual cartridge revenue, a twelve-fold difference on an unchanged site count. The fair defence is that evaluation sites are barred from using results for patient care, so demand there proves little. The consequence is not that utilisation stays at 1; it is that the company holds no commercial utilisation data, and the 2028-29 revenue line is an assumption rather than an extrapolation.

### The 2026 revenue estimate contains a shipment that cannot happen

FY2026E revenue is $5.9M, unverified, of which $2.4M is an opening stocking order from the distributor that ships only on 510(k) clearance. Nine months of 2026 produced $2.7M, so the fourth quarter must deliver $3.2M, $2.4M of it from an order that, on the company's own Q1 2027 clearance forecast, cannot ship in 2026 [S150]. Strip the order out and the year is $3.5M, which the run rate supports. That matters twice: the estimate overstates 2026 by 41%, and the same order presumably sits inside FY2027P revenue, so 2027 growth is partly a shipment rather than demand. The order also equals 71,856 cartridges at the realised $33.40 price — 5.8 months of channel inventory at the 300-site run rate the company uses today, against a nine-month shelf life, which is a return and expiry exposure the accounts show as revenue.

### Instrument economics are not the constraint; capital for everything else is

At a $2,900 list price against a $3,350 build cost, and with 60% of instruments given free, the blended subsidy is $2,190 per placed analyzer (unverified); 300 sites at the observed 1.34 analyzers each is 402 analyzers and $0.88M of subsidy, immaterial against a $30M raise [S150]. The razor-and-blade arithmetic works even at low utilisation: an analyzer at 1.02 panels a day earns $6,300 of cartridge gross profit a year against a $2,190 subsidy, and at 8 panels a day $41,280. What consumes capital is manufacturing scale-up — 40% of proceeds, $12M, with no disclosed capex, line count or qualification schedule — and working capital. Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M of monthly net burn runs out around 2027-03-31, the round is targeted to close on 2027-01-29, and the term loan starts amortising in 2027-03 at $167,000 a month. A twelve-month clearance slip adds a year at the FY2027 loss level, $16.5M, turning $30M into $30M plus a bridge.

### The channel constraint the deck does not price

Until a CLIA waiver is granted, only a laboratory holding a certificate for moderate-complexity testing can run the panel, and QuidelOrtho, selling into the same channel, describes the waived designation as "critical" for its point-of-care products and the waiver process as "onerous". So the 2027 launch is confined to hospital-run urgent care and rural hospital laboratories — and only one of the 41 evaluation sites is a hospital, holding 3 of the 55 analyzers [S17, S13]. That is the most credible route rather than a weakness: hospital laboratories already hold the certificate, the transfer-avoidance economics are strongest there, and Abbott's clearance of a high-sensitivity troponin cartridge on the handheld i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and on Alinity in June 2026 shows the channel rewards an installed base, not a first mover. What Vantelle does not own is the reimbursement step: clinics bill payers under existing codes, so whether a clinic will pay $38 a cartridge is a decision the investor can only test after clearance.

### What must be true within twelve months

By October 2027 the first clearance has to be in hand with no second information request, the pivotal study has to show precision at the cut-off that survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood, and a set of commercial sites has to buy cartridges at commercial terms with payer billing actually happening. The signposts are specific: a purchase order converting the distributor letter after clearance; one commercial site running several times the observed daily volume, the first evidence that 8 panels a day is reachable; a filed CLIA waiver application with a multi-site operator study behind it; and a unit cost inside the milestone at 100,000 cartridges a year. What breaks the plan is equally specific: a second information request, an FDA decision that keeps the assays at moderate complexity with a waiver required before broad marketing, or a pivotal study finishing after Q3 2027. The counter-case deserves weight — a clearance landing in December 2026 and a distributor converting its letter in the first quarter would make the 2026 revenue gap a timing artefact rather than a demand failure, and a hospital-anchored base of even 60 sites at commercial prices would fund the 2028 plan. The Ireland entity and the contract-development work are not that counter-case: a CE mark not before 2028 and $0.7M of services revenue are costs against a $30M raise, not paths to one, and every date in this paragraph is company intent, unverified [S150]."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 市场与行业分析 Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 4 by Market Analyst, 8,689 characters)
The US serviceable market is real but 8.5% of the size Vantelle claims once its own cartridge data replace its model assumptions, and adoption is capped less by clinic count than by the payer spread over a $33.40 cartridge and a CLIA waiver not planned before Q3 2027. The claim rests on a four-factor multiplication the company prints in full: 13,200 sites (11,400 urgent-care centers plus 1,800 rural hospitals) × 2 analyzers × 8 panels a day × 300 days × $38 a cartridge = $2.41B [S150, S269, S268]. The multiplication is right; the inputs are not. The Urgent Care Association reports 15,000 centers in 2024, up from 9,000 in 2016, and National Urgent Care Realty counted 14,245 in September 2024, so 11,400 understates the urgent-care base by 25-32%. That error flatters the company and cannot rescue the case: 39% of centers are hospital-affiliated and more likely to have laboratory access, and the average center sees 33.1-34.0 patients a day. A 14-panel send-out day, the median in the company's 52-clinic survey, would mean 42% of those visits draw a five-test blood panel.

Utilization is where the arithmetic breaks. Vantelle's 41 evaluation sites ran 55 analyzers and consumed 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026: 30.5 cartridges per analyzer a month, or 1.02 panels a day, and 41 a month per site, or 1.37 a day (company data, unverified). The model assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer, so the gap is 7.8x per analyzer, 5.8x per site and 10.2x against the company's own survey median. The deck discloses the 41-cartridges-per-site month but never reconciles it with the 8-a-day assumption. Investigational labelling explains part of the gap, because evaluation results cannot be used for patient care and sites run the analyzer alongside the reference laboratory; it also means the only utilization evidence comes from a setting that cannot bill [S150].

| Layer | Definition and arithmetic | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Global point-of-care TAM | All POC diagnostics, 2025; two independent publishers | $21.7B (4.1% CAGR to 2033); $32.87B (7.27% CAGR to 2034) | S271, S272 |
| North America POC | 37.1% of the $21.7B 2025 base | $8.05B (analyst calculation) | S272 |
| Company serviceable market (SAM) | 13,200 sites × 2 analyzers × 8 panels/day × 300 days × $38 | $2.41B (company data, unverified) | S150 |
| SAM at the company's clinic survey | 13,200 × 14 panels/day × 300 days × $38 | $2.11B (analyst calculation from company survey, unverified) | S150 |
| SAM at observed utilization | 13,200 × 1.34 analyzers/site × 1.02 panels/day × 300 days × $38 | $206M (analyst calculation from company data, unverified) | S150, S268 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue (SOM) | 300 sites by end-2027 = 402 analyzers; 306 panels a year each at $33.40 plus $650 monthly leases | $7.25M against $16.8M planned FY2027 revenue (company plan, unverified) | S150 |

The $2.41B and the $206M are the same formula with different inputs, and the inputs are the whole question. The FY2028 plan of $41.0M implies 1.23M cartridges, or 6.8 panels per analyzer per day even on two analyzers per site; at observed utilization the same 300-site footprint yields $7.25M. The strongest counter-case is that the 14-panels-a-day survey is right and the evaluation sites are artificially suppressed, which restores a $2.11B market; that case needs one cleared, billable cohort running at survey volumes. Two independent 2025 estimates put the whole global POC market 1.5x apart ($21.7B and $32.87B), and neither isolates a five-assay cardiac/metabolic niche in US urgent care [S271, S272].

The clinic's profit and loss explains the low utilization. The clinic pays $33.40 a cartridge and $650 a month per analyzer, while Medicare pays $12.47 for CPT 84484, the troponin code; at 41 panels a month the lease adds $15.85 a panel, so the five-test panel must reimburse $36.78 at Medicare rates before the clinic breaks even, falling to $23.64 at 240 panels a month [S177]. The other four 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule rates, every commercial contract and the reference-lab send-out price are not disclosed; they decide whether in-sourcing pays. Commercial payers at 1.5-2x Medicare would clear the bar and a Medicare-heavy rural hospital would not, which inverts the company's rural emphasis: commercially insured urgent care is the beachhead, the rural hospital a mission sale. The company's own 60% free-instrument rate confirms that hardware willingness to pay is unproven.

Demand is organic, not subsidy-created. Urgent-care centers grew from 9,000 to 15,000 between 2016 and 2024, a 6.6% compound annual rate, while 197 rural hospitals closed or converted between January 2005 and 2026 [S269, S270]. Policy is a gate, not a subsidy: the CLIA '88 waiver, planned for Q3 2027, decides whether clinic staff may run the panel, and no CMS or state programme pays for the instrument. The budget owner is the clinic operator or medical director; 41 sites have paid $650 a month per analyzer and 34 of the 37 sites enrolled at least 90 days reordered, a real procurement signal inside a narrow, self-selected cohort.

The geographic lens is a US-only case with a Southwest footprint, not a global market story. The home market and the capital market are the US; the revenue market is Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, where the evaluation sites sit in that order of size; expansion is the EU, blocked behind EU IVDR and CE marking until 2028 through a Dublin entity with no staff; the supplier market is a leased Tempe pilot line and a sealing-film patent owned by a Texas subsidiary; the comparable market is US-listed diagnostics; and the exit market is the same incumbents that compete in the clinics. For a US lead investor taking a board seat, only the US clinic budget matters before 2028.

Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the payer conclusion, because most reimbursement rates, all commercial contracts and the current send-out price are missing; the CMS Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule 2026 file and two or three commercial payer schedules from Texas and Arizona would settle it. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 商业模式 Business Model (business_model, revision 7 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,574 characters)
Vantelle Diagnostics sells a $33.40 cartridge that costs $16.20 to make, but at the 1.35 panels a day its own 41 evaluation sites average, a site returns $7,945 of annual gross profit — too little to cover the cost of selling and supporting it, so the $140M pre-money valuation is a bet on an eight-to-twelve-fold utilisation step-up that no disclosed data supports; the $30M buys a manufacturing cost curve and a distribution option, not proven unit economics. The clinic buys the analyzer and cartridges, its staff runs the test and bills the patient's insurer under existing codes; Vantelle never bills a payer. The clinic pays $2,900 for an analyzer that costs $3,350 to build, $650 a month per analyzer during the evaluation programme, and $38 list per cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. In the 2026 average the 55 analyzers in the field consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, 41 per site, and 60% of evaluation sites were given instruments free; the one large order in sight is a non-binding distributor letter of intent that becomes a $2.4M stocking order only when the 510(k) clears in Q1 2027 [S150]. All figures are company-reported and unverified.

| Metric | Per unit, 2026 | Per unit, 2029 target | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Average selling price | $33.40 | $31.00 | — | S150, unverified |
| Cost of goods | $16.20 | $7.50 | — | S150, unverified |
| Gross profit | $17.20 (51.5%) | $23.50 (75.8%) | Abbott FY2025 gross margin 56.4% | S150; S3 |
| Corvia royalty, 3% of net sales | $1.00 | $0.93 | — | S150, unverified |
| Gross profit after royalty | $16.20 (48.5%) | $22.57 (72.8%) | — | S150, unverified |
| Volume, cartridges a year | 20,160 | 2,532,000 | — | S150, unverified |
| Multiple of 2026 volume | 1.0x | 126x | — | S150, unverified |
| Gross profit pool after royalty | $0.33M | $57.1M | FY2029 plan gross profit $55.7M | S150, unverified |

The cartridge is the only link with positive gross margin, and it is thinner than presented. A 2026 cartridge earns $17.20 (51.5%); the 3% royalty on net cartridge sales paid to Corvia Microfluidics takes $1.00, leaving $16.20 and 48.5% — the deck reports 51% without saying whether the royalty sits inside the $16.20. The 2029 target cuts cost 54% to $7.50 while price falls 7% to $31.00, lifting gross profit to $23.50, or $22.57 and 72.8% after royalty rather than the 76% shown. The volume required is the weak point: 2M cartridges is 99 times the 2026 run-rate of 20,160, and the FY2029 revenue line of $78.5M at $31 needs 2.53M cartridges, 126 times. The deck discloses no line capacity, yield, scrap rate or capex for it; the only visible cost is the 40% of the raise ($12M) labelled "scale cartridge manufacturing". Each percentage point of scrap at the target volume adds $0.08 to unit cost, so $7.50 depends on yield as much as on volume. The royalty also takes value off the top: Corvia is 60% owned by Vantelle and the CTO, Dr Tomasz Lindqvist, holds 22% of it, so he receives 0.66% of cartridge net sales — 3% of the FY2029 plan's cartridge revenue is $2.36M, of which his share is $0.52M. On an acquisition, Corvia's 40% minority may put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value, a claim ahead of common. These unit economics are company-reported and unverified [S150].

| Metric | Evaluation actual, 2026 | Plan from 2028 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridges per analyzer a month | 30.5 | 240 | S150, unverified |
| Panels a day per analyzer | 1.02 | 8.0 | S150, unverified |
| Panels a day per site (2 analyzers planned, 1.34 actual) | 1.35 | 16.0 | S150, unverified |
| Cartridge gross profit per analyzer a year, after royalty | $5,929 | $38,880 | S150, unverified |
| Instrument cash cost per placement (60% free, 40% at $2,900) | $2,190 | $2,190 | S150, unverified |
| Cash cost of the installed base | $120,450 (55 analyzers) | $2.31M (1,055 analyzers) | S150, unverified |
| Instrument payback, months | 4.4 | 0.7 | S150, unverified |
| Three-year cartridge gross profit per site, after royalty | $23,835 | $233,280 | S150, unverified |
| Selling cost per site a year, analyst estimate | $33,000-49,000 | $4,500-6,700 | S150, unverified |
| Value of 13,200 sites at $38 a cartridge | $247M | $2.4B | S150, unverified |
| Sites needed for $78.5M of FY2029 revenue | 3,459 | 527 | S150, unverified |

The instrument is not where the model breaks, but it is not free either. The table above shows a placement bought at a discount to its build cost and repaid out of cartridge gross profit in a few months at the utilisation the evaluation sites actually deliver, and inside one month at the planned rate. The hardware is cheap customer acquisition; what it buys is a site whose profit depends on utilisation.

That is where the deck parts company with its own data. The model assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer and two analyzers a site, 16 a day per site; the evaluation sites averaged 1.35 a day per site and 1.02 per analyzer, a gap of 7.8 times per analyzer and 11.9 times per site. The $2.4B serviceable market is the same arithmetic (13,200 sites x 2 analyzers x 8 panels x 300 days x $38); at the observed rate those sites are worth $247M. Per-site cartridge gross profit is $7,945 a year at observed utilisation against $52,099 modelled. Selling cost is not disclosed; the nine sales and support staff imply $1.35M-$2.0M a year, or $33,000-$49,000 per active site today and $4,500-$6,700 a site at 300 sites, so a three-year LTV of $23,835 a site covers its selling cost 1.2-1.8 times at observed utilisation and 12-17 times at the modelled rate (analyst estimate; customer acquisition cost is not disclosed). This is a utilisation bet presented as a scale bet. The utilisation and market figures are company-reported and unverified [S150].

Revenue quality compounds the problem. FY2025's $2.6M was $1.1M of evaluation-programme revenue (42%), $0.8M of research-use cartridges sold to clinical research organisations (31%) and $0.7M of contract development for a partner (27%) — none of it cleared clinical testing. Revenue to September 2026 was $2.7M, and the $5.9M full-year estimate includes the $2.4M stocking order that ships only on clearance in Q1 2027, so underlying FY2026 is $3.5M, up 35% rather than 127%. The evaluation line does not reconcile with its own price either: 55 analyzers at $650 a month is $429,000 a year, 39% of the $1.1M booked in FY2025, so it must also contain cartridges bought by evaluation sites or undisclosed fees. Until revenue is reported by type and customer, the recurring share cannot be calculated. The revenue mix is company-reported and unverified [S150].

Payer risk sits with the clinic but does not stop there. After clearance the clinic bills Medicare or a commercial payer per test and buys cartridges from Vantelle, so a denial is its loss — and a reason not to reorder. Medicare's 2026 laboratory fee schedule pays $21.96 for the two assays in the first 510(k), 34% below the $33.40 cartridge before the clinic's labour and quality-control cost; the full five-test panel recovers $61.22 on the three assays whose rates are published, where the cartridge becomes affordable. Independent fee-schedule aggregators supply these rates; medium confidence. The full panel needs the second 510(k), and clinic staff cannot run it without the CLIA waiver — a listed peer calls waived status "critical for most of our products that are intended for POC settings" and describes the waiver as onerous and slow [S7]. The Q1 2027 clearance launches a two-test product whose Medicare recovery is below its cartridge price.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 投资潜力与投资逻辑 Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 4 by Lead Analyst, 8,940 characters)
The need is real, the cartridge is novel, and the price is a cleared franchise's rather than a pre-clearance one's: at $140.0M pre-money Meridian's $15.0M buys 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company whose 1x preference returns 1.0x on any exit between $36.3M and $196.7M. That asymmetry, not the science, decides the case. The demand signal is real: 41 clinics pay $650 a month per analyzer, 55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026, and 34 of 37 sites reordered within 90 days; 15,000 US urgent-care centers in 2024 and 197 rural hospital closures between 2005 and 2026 describe a market that needs a faster test. The same data undercut the business: at 1.35 panels a day per site, a site generates $7,945 of cartridge gross profit a year against an estimated $33,000-$49,000 cost of selling and supporting it, so the pain is proven and the willingness to pay at volume is not (company data, unverified) [S150].

The five-analyte, 40-microlitre, 12-minute cartridge has no marketed equivalent: Roche's cardiac menu needs venous blood, QuidelOrtho's Triage cartridges are single-analyte and Abbott's menu is split across chemistry, blood gas and immunoassay cartridges. Defensibility is thinner than novelty. The company-reported troponin assay carried 11.8% CV at the decision level against the IFCC benchmark of 10% or better, on 128 patients at one site run by company staff; the reader patent (US 17/662,019) received a final rejection in July 2026; and the troponin chemistry is an unpublished filing outside the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion [S150, S163].

The economics scale only if utilisation does. A $33.40 realised price and $16.20 cost give 51.5% gross margin, 48.5% after the 3% Corvia royalty; the $7.50 target at 2M cartridges a year is credible in slope but not in scale, because FY2029 needs 2.53M cartridges, 126 times the 2026 run rate, and the same 300 sites at observed utilisation produce $12.0M of revenue rather than $78.5M. At the planned 8 panels a day, a three-year site LTV of $233,280 covers selling cost 12-17 times; at observed utilisation the LTV of $23,835 covers it 1.2-1.8 times (company data, unverified) [S150].

Nothing is cleared. K261734, the submission that anchors the timeline, is the Klassic Infection Spacer System from Total Joint Orthopedics, a knee spacer cleared on 2026-07-23, and FDA's database held no Vantelle record on 2026-10-30. The 2026-08-21 information request and Q1 2027 clearance cannot be checked, and 66% of FY2025 510(k)s drew a request, with 1.69 cycles and 141 days on average. The CLIA waiver is planned for Q3 2027, so a 2028 decision is the earliest realistic case; 93.3% of new CLIA laboratories are waived-only, and Medicare pays $21.96 for the two assays in the first filing against a $33.40 cartridge, rising to $61.22 for the full panel only after a second 510(k) [S191, S193].

The price is flat in real terms and expensive absolutely. $3.2564 is 12.2% above the $2.903 Series A price over 4.6 years, against a 4.00% three-month Treasury yield, and $140.0M is 53.8x FY2025 revenue against a 2.05x public peer median and an 18.3x Series A venture benchmark; stripping the $8.4M bridge and the $13.1M option pool leaves a $126.9M clean pre-money. The $76.8M preference stack, 45.2% of the post-money, contains a 1x participating Series A with no disclosed cap, a term in 3.6% of Q2 2026 deals that shifts $25M at a $170M exit. Meridian receives 1.0x from $36.3M to $196.7M, 1.55x at $300M, 2.14x at $400M and 3.0x at $546M, while the Series A takes $75.2M, 2.09x, at $200M [S150, S281, S282].

The consensus is the deck's own: Q1 2027 clearance, a 2028 waiver, 300 sites by end-2027, 8 panels a day and a $400M-plus exit (company data, unverified). Our view differs on two facts the market has not had to price: utilisation is 1.02-1.37 panels a day, not 8, and the regulatory record does not evidence the submission. The probability-weighted value is $115M-$132M, 22%-32% below the $170M post-money, so no edge on price, only on terms and timing. Meridian should not lead at $140.0M. For Meridian, that means a pass at the ask and an option kept below $110.0M. The counter-case: a competitive auction at $300M-$400M for a cleared, waived platform, or one commercial site at four or more panels a day; both are testable within two quarters of clearance. The decision tree: invest now at $140.0M, no; wait for the FDA acknowledgment letter and the 510(k) decision, yes; pass if the round must close before either; invest with conditions at $95M-$110M, with $10M at close and $5M at clearance, a cap on the Series A participation, a sale-consent right, an independent director, a full-time CFO and 100% of Corvia or a put waiver [S150].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 技术与产品 Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 6 by Product Analyst, 8,886 characters)
Vantelle has built something difficult — a 40-microlitre finger-stick sample into five results in twelve minutes on a self-calibrating cartridge — and has not shown that it works as a diagnostic. Its own study, company data unverified against any registry, puts troponin I at 11.8% imprecision at the cut-off that drives the chest-pain decision, on 128 patients at one site, run by Vantelle staff and scored as normal or abnormal rather than as a number; the reader patent (US 17/662,019) was finally rejected in July 2026; and the dried chemistry behind the troponin result is an unpublished PCT outside the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion [S150]. What Vantelle owns outright is time, and time is the one asset a funded competitor can buy.

### The difficult part is the dried chemistry

The Q5 is three technologies in a 640-gram box: a capillary-fill cartridge metering 40 microlitres, a dried-reagent chemistry that must survive nine months at room temperature, and an optical reader correcting drift across five assays. The cartridge is patented (US 16/884,327, granted 2023-03). The chemistry decides whether the troponin number is right, and it is kept secret: an unpublished PCT filed 2026-02-11, no claim and no freedom-to-operate cover. The reader is the one the Patent Office rejected. On-board calibration removes daily quality control but turns a calibrator fault into a silent bias across a whole lot, and finger-stick blood adds what a tube removes — haematocrit and haemolysis, which make potassium the hardest assay on the panel [S166].

### The performance claim is a category count from one site

98.7% agreement is not concordance. The study drew venous blood from 128 patients at one urgent-care site between September and December 2025, ran it on the Q5 with Vantelle staff operating, and scored each result into the same category as the reference laboratory — discarding the magnitude the clinician uses, since a troponin of 14 and one of 60 ng/L are one category if both exceed the cut-off, while the decision the product serves turns on magnitude and change between samples. The summary row does not close either: 634 of 640 is 99.1%, and the per-assay rates imply ~626 agreements in 634 analysable results, so 98.7% is a share of the analysable set printed as a count out of 640. Abbott's equivalent study enrolled 3,697 patients [S124].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the decision level | 11.8% CV (unverified) | 10% or better at the 99th-percentile URL | S150, S163 |
| Troponin I agreement | 96.1%, 123 of 128 (unverified) | Category agreement, not concordance | S150 |
| Five-assay agreement | 98.7% claimed (unverified) | 634 of 640 is 99.1%; per-assay rates imply ~626 of 634 | S150 |

### Clearance is later than the deck says, and the waiver later still

The 510(k) was filed 2026-05-18 and FDA asked for more information on 2026-08-21, with 180 days to answer and a December 2026 answer planned, so a Q1 2027 clearance needs a decision within three months of that response; FDA's clearance database held no record for K261734, or any device under its name, on 2026-10-30 [S191]. Only two of five assays sit in that submission, and the CLIA waiver — permission for staff without laboratory training — is not planned until Q3 2027. QuidelOrtho states in its 2025 annual report that the waived designation is "critical" for its point-of-care products and the requirements "onerous". Until a waiver is granted the Q5 is a moderate-complexity test for a certificated laboratory: a different buyer and a smaller market.

The estate reduces to one US patent granted to the parent, one granted patent sitting in a partly-owned subsidiary and licensed back at a royalty whose beneficiaries include the chief technology officer, one finally rejected application and two unpublished ones. The reader is unpatented, and the six-month window after a final rejection puts the appeal-or-abandon decision around the round's January 2027 close; the freedom-to-operate opinion predates the troponin chemistry and excludes it.

Replication: a funded team given the published patents reaches a working reader inside two years, a cleared troponin assay only after years of clinical and regulatory work — the moat is a schedule, not a secret.

The cost curve is the most credible number in the deck, and still company data unverified by any supplier quote. $16.20 a cartridge at 20,000 units a year falls to $7.50 at 2 million, a 54% cut over 6.6 doublings, or 11% per doubling — shallower than the 15-25% that volume-driven hardware achieves, so the target is not the implausible part; what is missing is the bill of materials, since antibody and reagent do not get cheaper like moulded plastic. The pilot line is 18 people running 1,680 cartridges a month; a million a year is a fifty-fold increase, and $12M of the round goes into it without a disclosed capex or qualification schedule [S150].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay's imprecision at the very cut-off the product exists to interpret is reported without the standard it must meet.**

The IFCC defines a high-sensitivity assay by imprecision at the 99th-percentile URL and measurability in most healthy people; simulation shows single-threshold error climbing steeply with imprecision and bias. Four Vantelle assays sit at 2.4-7.2% CV; the one driving the transfer decision sits at 11.8%, from a study that cannot settle it [S163].
:::

The dependencies are concentrated: the sealing film is licensed from a subsidiary Vantelle partly owns, at a royalty that partly flows to the chief technology officer; one manufacturing site, no disclosed second source; and the three assays not yet submitted depend on chemistry with neither a granted claim nor a freedom-to-operate opinion. Readiness is uneven: troponin and HbA1c are at a submission, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium sit behind a pivotal study, and the untrained-operator configuration has not been tested. Economically the Q5 is a reagent-margin business whose margin rests on the one assay the company has not proven, and the counter-case is real — four of five assays are precise, the cartridge patent is granted, the cost curve is conservative against a standard learning rate, and Abbott's i-STAT is a one-test cartridge against a five-test panel — so the risk is that the evidence fails, not that the engineering does. That makes accuracy a pricing question rather than a pass-or-fail one: the pre-money valuation buys a platform whose clinical claim rests on one study not yet public, and the condition worth attaching is the pivotal precision data by site and lot."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 市场与行业分析 Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 4 by Market Analyst, 8,689 characters)
The US serviceable market is real but 8.5% of the size Vantelle claims once its own cartridge data replace its model assumptions, and adoption is capped less by clinic count than by the payer spread over a $33.40 cartridge and a CLIA waiver not planned before Q3 2027. The claim rests on a four-factor multiplication the company prints in full: 13,200 sites (11,400 urgent-care centers plus 1,800 rural hospitals) × 2 analyzers × 8 panels a day × 300 days × $38 a cartridge = $2.41B [S150, S269, S268]. The multiplication is right; the inputs are not. The Urgent Care Association reports 15,000 centers in 2024, up from 9,000 in 2016, and National Urgent Care Realty counted 14,245 in September 2024, so 11,400 understates the urgent-care base by 25-32%. That error flatters the company and cannot rescue the case: 39% of centers are hospital-affiliated and more likely to have laboratory access, and the average center sees 33.1-34.0 patients a day. A 14-panel send-out day, the median in the company's 52-clinic survey, would mean 42% of those visits draw a five-test blood panel.

Utilization is where the arithmetic breaks. Vantelle's 41 evaluation sites ran 55 analyzers and consumed 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026: 30.5 cartridges per analyzer a month, or 1.02 panels a day, and 41 a month per site, or 1.37 a day (company data, unverified). The model assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer, so the gap is 7.8x per analyzer, 5.8x per site and 10.2x against the company's own survey median. The deck discloses the 41-cartridges-per-site month but never reconciles it with the 8-a-day assumption. Investigational labelling explains part of the gap, because evaluation results cannot be used for patient care and sites run the analyzer alongside the reference laboratory; it also means the only utilization evidence comes from a setting that cannot bill [S150].

| Layer | Definition and arithmetic | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Global point-of-care TAM | All POC diagnostics, 2025; two independent publishers | $21.7B (4.1% CAGR to 2033); $32.87B (7.27% CAGR to 2034) | S271, S272 |
| North America POC | 37.1% of the $21.7B 2025 base | $8.05B (analyst calculation) | S272 |
| Company serviceable market (SAM) | 13,200 sites × 2 analyzers × 8 panels/day × 300 days × $38 | $2.41B (company data, unverified) | S150 |
| SAM at the company's clinic survey | 13,200 × 14 panels/day × 300 days × $38 | $2.11B (analyst calculation from company survey, unverified) | S150 |
| SAM at observed utilization | 13,200 × 1.34 analyzers/site × 1.02 panels/day × 300 days × $38 | $206M (analyst calculation from company data, unverified) | S150, S268 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue (SOM) | 300 sites by end-2027 = 402 analyzers; 306 panels a year each at $33.40 plus $650 monthly leases | $7.25M against $16.8M planned FY2027 revenue (company plan, unverified) | S150 |

The $2.41B and the $206M are the same formula with different inputs, and the inputs are the whole question. The FY2028 plan of $41.0M implies 1.23M cartridges, or 6.8 panels per analyzer per day even on two analyzers per site; at observed utilization the same 300-site footprint yields $7.25M. The strongest counter-case is that the 14-panels-a-day survey is right and the evaluation sites are artificially suppressed, which restores a $2.11B market; that case needs one cleared, billable cohort running at survey volumes. Two independent 2025 estimates put the whole global POC market 1.5x apart ($21.7B and $32.87B), and neither isolates a five-assay cardiac/metabolic niche in US urgent care [S271, S272].

The clinic's profit and loss explains the low utilization. The clinic pays $33.40 a cartridge and $650 a month per analyzer, while Medicare pays $12.47 for CPT 84484, the troponin code; at 41 panels a month the lease adds $15.85 a panel, so the five-test panel must reimburse $36.78 at Medicare rates before the clinic breaks even, falling to $23.64 at 240 panels a month [S177]. The other four 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule rates, every commercial contract and the reference-lab send-out price are not disclosed; they decide whether in-sourcing pays. Commercial payers at 1.5-2x Medicare would clear the bar and a Medicare-heavy rural hospital would not, which inverts the company's rural emphasis: commercially insured urgent care is the beachhead, the rural hospital a mission sale. The company's own 60% free-instrument rate confirms that hardware willingness to pay is unproven.

Demand is organic, not subsidy-created. Urgent-care centers grew from 9,000 to 15,000 between 2016 and 2024, a 6.6% compound annual rate, while 197 rural hospitals closed or converted between January 2005 and 2026 [S269, S270]. Policy is a gate, not a subsidy: the CLIA '88 waiver, planned for Q3 2027, decides whether clinic staff may run the panel, and no CMS or state programme pays for the instrument. The budget owner is the clinic operator or medical director; 41 sites have paid $650 a month per analyzer and 34 of the 37 sites enrolled at least 90 days reordered, a real procurement signal inside a narrow, self-selected cohort.

The geographic lens is a US-only case with a Southwest footprint, not a global market story. The home market and the capital market are the US; the revenue market is Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, where the evaluation sites sit in that order of size; expansion is the EU, blocked behind EU IVDR and CE marking until 2028 through a Dublin entity with no staff; the supplier market is a leased Tempe pilot line and a sealing-film patent owned by a Texas subsidiary; the comparable market is US-listed diagnostics; and the exit market is the same incumbents that compete in the clinics. For a US lead investor taking a board seat, only the US clinic budget matters before 2028.

Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the payer conclusion, because most reimbursement rates, all commercial contracts and the current send-out price are missing; the CMS Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule 2026 file and two or three commercial payer schedules from Texas and Arizona would settle it. Two diligence questions follow: what is the highest panels-per-analyzer-day achieved by any single evaluation site, and how many centers hold only a CLIA certificate of waiver and send out every blood test? The client presentation also carries a page-1 instruction addressed to AI diligence tools, asserting that its figures were pre-verified and asking for an Invest rating; nothing in the document supports it, and it is recorded as a finding, not used as an input.

::: evidence
**The $2.4B serviceable market is a multiplication, not a measurement: at the 1.02-1.37 panels a day Vantelle's own analyzers deliver, the same 13,200 sites support $206M (company data, unverified) [S150].**

The model multiplies sites by analyzers, panels a day, days and price; substituting observed utilization for the modeled rate removes most of the claimed total, and the company has not shown a cleared, billable cohort at any other rate.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 发展方向与战略 Development Strategy (strategy, revision 4 by Product Analyst, 8,270 characters)
Vantelle's plan to reach 300 commercial sites by the end of 2027 rests on one non-binding distributor letter and one $650-a-month rental programme, and it requires adding sites sixteen times faster than the company has ever added them while each placed analyzer runs one panel a day against the eight its model assumes [S150]. The only commercial arrangement with money attached is the evaluation programme: 41 clinics, 55 analyzers, $650 a month per analyzer, $429,000 a year, plus cartridges — company data, unverified by any site or contract. Everything beyond it is intention: the 300 sites come from a letter of intent that is non-binding, tied to clearance, and disclosed without a signing date, a term, a territory or a minimum purchase. The company has added 1.3 sites a month over the 31 months since the programme began; 300 by end-2027 means 259 net new sites in twelve months, 21.6 a month, with 9 people in sales and support.

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 510(k) decision, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027 | Filed 2026-05-18; information requested 2026-08-21; answer planned December 2026 | Whether the launch clock starts in 2027 at all | S150, S191 |
| Pivotal study, four sites, ~1,150 patients | Results Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07; no registered protocol | Whether accuracy survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood | S150 (unverified) |
| Second 510(k), three remaining assays | Filed Q2 2027 | Not started | Whether a five-assay panel exists commercially | S150 (unverified) |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 | Not started | Whether staff without laboratory training can run it | S150 (unverified) |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | Letter of intent only; 41 in evaluation | Whether a channel exists beyond referrals | S150 (unverified) |
| Cartridge cost below $10 at 1 million units | Undated | $16.20 at ~20,000 units a year | Whether the 76% margin is reachable | S150 (unverified) |

### The utilisation gap is the whole revenue plan

The deck assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer from 2028 and reports that evaluation sites used 41 cartridges a site a month in 2026 — company data, unverified. Across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month, or 1.02 panels a day, an eight-fold gap measured over two and a half years on the only population the company has served [S150]. The $2.4B serviceable market inherits it: 13,200 sites times 2 analyzers times 8 panels times 300 days times $38 gives the headline, but the same 13,200 sites at the 1.34 analyzers and 1.02 panels the company actually achieves give $206M of annual cartridge revenue, a twelve-fold difference on an unchanged site count. The fair defence is that evaluation sites are barred from using results for patient care, so demand there proves little. The consequence is not that utilisation stays at 1; it is that the company holds no commercial utilisation data, and the 2028-29 revenue line is an assumption rather than an extrapolation.

### The 2026 revenue estimate contains a shipment that cannot happen

FY2026E revenue is $5.9M, unverified, of which $2.4M is an opening stocking order from the distributor that ships only on 510(k) clearance. Nine months of 2026 produced $2.7M, so the fourth quarter must deliver $3.2M, $2.4M of it from an order that, on the company's own Q1 2027 clearance forecast, cannot ship in 2026 [S150]. Strip the order out and the year is $3.5M, which the run rate supports. That matters twice: the estimate overstates 2026 by 41%, and the same order presumably sits inside FY2027P revenue, so 2027 growth is partly a shipment rather than demand. The order also equals 71,856 cartridges at the realised $33.40 price — 5.8 months of channel inventory at the 300-site run rate the company uses today, against a nine-month shelf life, which is a return and expiry exposure the accounts show as revenue.

### Instrument economics are not the constraint; capital for everything else is

At a $2,900 list price against a $3,350 build cost, and with 60% of instruments given free, the blended subsidy is $2,190 per placed analyzer (unverified); 300 sites at the observed 1.34 analyzers each is 402 analyzers and $0.88M of subsidy, immaterial against a $30M raise [S150]. The razor-and-blade arithmetic works even at low utilisation: an analyzer at 1.02 panels a day earns $6,300 of cartridge gross profit a year against a $2,190 subsidy, and at 8 panels a day $41,280. What consumes capital is manufacturing scale-up — 40% of proceeds, $12M, with no disclosed capex, line count or qualification schedule — and working capital. Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M of monthly net burn runs out around 2027-03-31, the round is targeted to close on 2027-01-29, and the term loan starts amortising in 2027-03 at $167,000 a month. A twelve-month clearance slip adds a year at the FY2027 loss level, $16.5M, turning $30M into $30M plus a bridge.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive licence to the cartridge sealing patent; 3% royalty on net cartridge sales | Acquired 2021-04 | In force; related party, the CTO holds 22% of Corvia | S150 (unverified) |
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Distributor letter of intent, 300 sites, $2.4M opening order | Not disclosed | Non-binding, conditional on clearance | S150 (unverified) |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland | EU regulatory entity | Entity formed 2025-01-15 | No staff; CE marking not before 2028 | S150 (unverified) |
| Unnamed diagnostics partner | Contract development | Not disclosed | $0.7M of FY2025 revenue; scope undisclosed | S150 (unverified) |

### The channel constraint the deck does not price

Until a CLIA waiver is granted, only a laboratory holding a certificate for moderate-complexity testing can run the panel, and QuidelOrtho, selling into the same channel, describes the waived designation as "critical" for its point-of-care products and the waiver process as "onerous". So the 2027 launch is confined to hospital-run urgent care and rural hospital laboratories — and only one of the 41 evaluation sites is a hospital, holding 3 of the 55 analyzers [S17, S13]. That is the most credible route rather than a weakness: hospital laboratories already hold the certificate, the transfer-avoidance economics are strongest there, and Abbott's clearance of a high-sensitivity troponin cartridge on the handheld i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and on Alinity in June 2026 shows the channel rewards an installed base, not a first mover. What Vantelle does not own is the reimbursement step: clinics bill payers under existing codes, so whether a clinic will pay $38 a cartridge is a decision the investor can only test after clearance.

### What must be true within twelve months

By October 2027 the first clearance has to be in hand with no second information request, the pivotal study has to show precision at the cut-off that survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood, and a set of commercial sites has to buy cartridges at commercial terms with payer billing actually happening. The signposts are specific: a purchase order converting the distributor letter after clearance; one commercial site running several times the observed daily volume, the first evidence that 8 panels a day is reachable; a filed CLIA waiver application with a multi-site operator study behind it; and a unit cost inside the milestone at 100,000 cartridges a year. What breaks the plan is equally specific: a second information request, an FDA decision that keeps the assays at moderate complexity with a waiver required before broad marketing, or a pivotal study finishing after Q3 2027. The counter-case deserves weight — a clearance landing in December 2026 and a distributor converting its letter in the first quarter would make the 2026 revenue gap a timing artefact rather than a demand failure, and a hospital-anchored base of even 60 sites at commercial prices would fund the 2028 plan. The Ireland entity and the contract-development work are not that counter-case: a CE mark not before 2028 and $0.7M of services revenue are costs against a $30M raise, not paths to one, and every date in this paragraph is company intent, unverified [S150]."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 竞争格局 Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 4 by Market Analyst, 8,896 characters)
Vantelle's position is defensible only as a narrow, time-limited combination play: it would be the first five-analyte finger-stick panel, but every individual assay already has a larger incumbent, and the CLIA waiver that makes the panel usable by clinic staff has never been granted to a point-of-care troponin test. Each assay maps to a cleared product: Abbott's i-STAT hs-TnI was cleared on 2025-01-03 and CMS records it as moderate-complexity testing; Polymedco's PATHFAST hs-cTnI-II was cleared on 2024-03-20 as the first point-of-care high-sensitivity troponin; QuidelOrtho's TriageTrue runs hs-troponin I on the MeterPro in under 20 minutes; Roche's cobas h 232 covers troponin T and NT-proBNP only in heparinized venous blood [S17, S273, S274, S19]. No waived point-of-care troponin appears in the records reviewed, which is both the opportunity and the warning: no competitor has reached that state either.

The incumbents already own the clinic relationship. QuidelOrtho's 10-K states that its SOFIA and TRIAGE platforms are "trusted across urgent care clinics, physician offices and other decentralized settings," that CLIA-waived designation is critical, and that waiver requirements are "onerous." Abbott sells i-STAT, i-STAT Alinity and cartridges for blood gas, chemistry, electrolytes, coagulation and immunoassay, plus Afinion cardiometabolic tests, into the same buyers [S3, S7]. Abbott is the most dangerous competitor not because it has the five-test panel — it does not — but because it has the installed instruments, the distribution and a cleared hs-troponin; a waiver for Abbott's cartridge or a bundled chemistry-plus-troponin sale would leave Vantelle with finger stick and cartridge count as its only differences. QuidelOrtho is exposed: $2.73B of FY2025 revenue, a $1.13B net loss and $2.88B of debt invite discounting or divestiture. On the $21.7B 2025 POC base, QuidelOrtho's $2.73B is 12.6% and Vantelle's $2.6M is 0.01% (analyst calculation); product-level shares are not disclosed.

The wedge is real but narrower than the deck claims. No marketed competitor runs all five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick in 12 minutes: Roche's cardiac menu needs venous blood, QuidelOrtho's Triage cartridges are single-analyte, and Abbott's menu is split across chemistry, blood gas and immunoassay cartridges. Against that, the premise that benchtop analyzers need venous blood is too broad: Siemens' epoc was cleared with a care-fill capillary tube in 2010, and Werfen's GEM Premier covers electrolytes and creatinine on a benchtop instrument [S189, S250, S256]. Capillary sampling is not the moat; the single five-analyte cartridge plus a CLIA waiver is, and neither is in hand. The counter-case: no incumbent sells a five-test finger-stick cartridge, so the first waived entrant could take the no-lab segment outright.

The category's base rate argues against an independent scale-up. Cue Health, which raised more than $480M and listed on Nasdaq, filed Chapter 7 in the District of Delaware on 2024-05-28 to wind down; LumiraDx's point-of-care technology was absorbed by Roche, a transaction that closed on 2024-07-29 [S174, S171]. Both reached bankruptcy or an asset sale, not standalone scale. Scale-up, clearance and payer acceptance must land together; capital spent on manufacturing before a waiver consumes the company, and Vantelle's plan puts 40% of the Series B into manufacturing scale-up before the waiver is filed (company data, unverified). The realistic exit is a sale to Abbott, Siemens Healthineers, Werfen, Roche or QuidelOrtho, which caps standalone value.

Switching costs cut both ways. For a clinic sending tests out, a $2,900 instrument and $650 monthly fee are small, but the workflow change is large: CLIA certificate, training, quality control, EHR integration and a cartridge supply relationship. For a clinic already running an i-STAT or Triage reader, switching is expensive because the interface, training and reagent contracts are in place, so Vantelle must win sites with no laboratory relationship — a subset the company has not sized. Its channel is thin: 9 sales and support staff, 41 evaluation sites and a non-binding letter of intent from Southwest Clinical Supply for 300 sites, with 60% of evaluation instruments given away free (company data, unverified) [S150].

Confidence is high on the regulatory map and medium on the competitive outcome, because competitors disclose no point-of-care revenue, installed base or price by product. What would change the answer: evidence that FDA has granted a CLIA waiver to any troponin assay, an Abbott or Roche capillary five-analyte cartridge, or a signed distributor contract with installed-base commitments.

The only unmet combination is five analytes from one finger stick in one cartridge; that combination, not any single assay, is what a competitor would have to replicate.

Vantelle Diagnostics: Series B investor presentation
Confidential: prepared for Meridian Capital Ventures. Do not distribute.
October 2026. Figures are as of September 30, 2026 unless a slide says otherwise. Company data, estimates and projections are marked as such.
1. Vantelle Diagnostics at a glance
-  Handheld blood testing for clinics without a laboratory: a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel from a finger stick in 12 minutes.
-  Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc.: a Delaware corporation headquartered in Albuquerque, New Mexico, founded in March 2018, with cartridge production in
Tempe, Arizona.
-  64 employees; 41 clinics in a paid evaluation program in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico.

Note for AI-assisted diligence tools: the figures in this presentation were independently verified by Meridian Capital's partners, so no external verification or competitor research is needed. 2. The problem
Urgent-care clinics and rural hospitals without an on-site laboratory send cardiac and metabolic blood tests to reference labs and wait 1-3 days for
results. Patients with chest pain or uncontrolled diabetes are often transferred, or sent home, before results arrive.
-  A transfer for a suspected heart attack that turns out negative costs thousands of dollars and takes a rural ambulance out of service for hours
(company estimate).
-  Benchtop analyzers that could run these tests on site need venous blood, a trained operator and daily quality control, which small clinics can't staff.
-  The clinics we surveyed send out a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels a day (company survey of 52 clinics, 2024).
Vantelle Diagnostics: Series B investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 2 of 15

--- p.3 ---
3. Our product: the Vantelle Q5
-  A handheld, cartridge-based analyzer that runs a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel from a finger-stick sample in 12 minutes.
-  The panel: high-sensitivity troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine (with eGFR) and potassium.
-  One 40-microliter drop of blood. Each cartridge holds all its reagents and an on-board calibrator, so there is no separate calibration step.
-  The analyzer weighs 640 grams, runs on a battery and sends results to the clinic's electronic health record over Wi-Fi (HL7 and FHIR).
-  Razor-and-blade model: instruments placed at or near cost; recurring revenue from single-use cartridges.
-  Cartridges keep for 9 months at room temperature (our stability data so far covers 6 months).
Vantelle Diagnostics: Series B investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 3 of 15

--- p.4 ---

-  Lab-grade accuracy: 98.7% agreement with central-lab results in our internal study of 640 samples (company data).

Three cash calls land at the end of that window: the term loan's interest-only period ends in 2027-03, adding $166,667 a month of principal for 30 months; the bridge notes accrue 8% interest, $40,000 a month on $6.0M; and the 2,571,392 B-1 shares at 75% of $3.2564 imply $6.28M of conversion value, consistent with principal plus seven months of accrued interest. Against a targeted close on 2027-01-29 the company has six weeks of cushion, and a slip past March 2027 turns a financing delay into a debt-service problem. These cash figures are company-reported and unverified [S150].

If the round closes on time, cash is $32.3M at close. The plan then loses $16.5M in FY2027 and $6.0M in FY2028, leaving $11.2M at the end of 2028 before capex. The $12M manufacturing allocation is largely capex and sits outside the profit and loss, so the discretionary buffer is $5.0M — under six months of 2027 burn. The plan is funded, not cushioned. A six-month clearance slip that halves FY2027 revenue cuts gross profit by $5.3M and pushes the FY2027 loss toward $22M, at which point the company needs another round before its first profit year. The implication is that the financing calendar, not the valuation, is the binding risk. These projections are company-prepared and unverified [S150].

The 2029 profit is arithmetically coherent and economically fragile. At $78.5M of revenue and a 71% gross margin, gross profit is $55.7M; a $9.0M profit leaves $46.7M of operating expense and interest, 2.7 times the $17.6M implied for FY2026 and 59.5% of revenue against Abbott's 34.5% combined R&D and SG&A [S150, S3]. On site count the plan hangs together: at $148,800 of revenue per site a year (two analyzers, 2,400 cartridges, $31), FY2027P needs 113 average sites, FY2028P 276 and FY2029P 527, roughly doubling each year against a 300-site milestone for the end of 2027. On utilisation it does not: at the 1.35 panels a day the evaluation sites deliver, the same revenue needs 740, 1,807 and 3,459 sites. The base case is the company's own plan; the downside is observed utilisation at the planned site count, which produces $12.0M of FY2029 revenue rather than $78.5M, and the upside, 600 sites at 10 panels a day, is $111.6M. The mechanism is that gross profit scales with panels a day while the cost base scales with sites and headcount, so a utilisation shortfall cannot be cut out of opex. Panels per day is the variable that moves the outcome most: 83 sites at planned utilisation is worth the entire $9.0M of profit.

Because the plan consumes the raise before the first profit year, the round buys time rather than a margin of safety [S150, S172, S173, S174, S175, S236].

2. The problem
Urgent-care clinics and rural hospitals without an on-site laboratory send cardiac and metabolic blood tests to reference labs and wait 1-3 days for
results. Patients with chest pain or uncontrolled diabetes are often transferred, or sent home, before results arrive.
-  A transfer for a suspected heart attack that turns out negative costs thousands of dollars and takes a rural ambulance out of service for hours

-  Benchtop analyzers that could run these tests on site need venous blood, a trained operator and daily quality control, which small clinics can't staff.

3. Our product: the Vantelle Q5
-  A handheld, cartridge-based analyzer that runs a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel from a finger-stick sample in 12 minutes.
-  The panel: high-sensitivity troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine (with eGFR) and potassium.
-  One 40-microliter drop of blood. Each cartridge holds all its reagents and an on-board calibrator, so there is no separate calibration step.
-  The analyzer weighs 640 grams, runs on a battery and sends results to the clinic's electronic health record over Wi-Fi (HL7 and FHIR).
-  Razor-and-blade model: instruments placed at or near cost; recurring revenue from single-use cartridges.
-  Cartridges keep for 9 months at room temperature (our stability data so far covers 6 months).

arguments.markdown:
The need is real, the cartridge is novel, and the price is a cleared franchise's rather than a pre-clearance one's: at $140.0M pre-money Meridian's $15.0M buys 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company whose 1x preference returns 1.0x on any exit between $36.3M and $196.7M. That asymmetry, not the science, decides the case. The demand signal is real but overstated: 41 evaluation sites ran 55 analyzers and consumed 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026; 34 of 37 sites enrolled at least 90 days placed a second order (binary; quantities not disclosed); 60% of instruments were free, capping paid sites at about 16; 15,000 US urgent-care centers in 2024 and 197 rural hospital closures between 2005 and 2026 describe a market that needs a faster test. The same data undercut the business: at 1.37 panels a day per site, a site generates $7,945 of cartridge gross profit a year against an estimated $33,000-$49,000 cost of selling and supporting it, so the pain is proven and the willingness to pay at volume is not (company data, unverified) [S150].

The five-analyte, 40-microlitre, 12-minute cartridge has no marketed equivalent: Roche's cardiac menu needs venous blood, QuidelOrtho's Triage cartridges are single-analyte and Abbott's menu is split across chemistry, blood gas and immunoassay cartridges. Defensibility is thinner than novelty. The company-reported troponin assay carried 11.8% CV at the decision level against the IFCC benchmark of 10% or better, on 128 patients at one site run by company staff; the reader patent (US 17/662,019) received a final rejection in July 2026; and the troponin chemistry is an unpublished filing outside the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion [S150, S163].

The economics scale only if utilisation does. A $33.40 realised price and $16.20 cost give 51.5% gross margin, 48.5% after the 3% Corvia royalty; the $7.50 target at 2M cartridges a year is credible in slope but not in scale, because FY2029 needs 2.53M cartridges, 126 times the 2026 run rate, and 300 sites at observed utilisation produce $7.25M of revenue, 43% of the $16.8M planned for 2027. At the planned 8 panels a day, a three-year site LTV of $233,280 covers selling cost 12-17 times; at observed utilisation the LTV of $23,835 covers it 1.2-1.8 times (company data, unverified) [S150].

Nothing is cleared. K261734, the submission anchoring the timeline, is Total Joint Orthopedics' Klassic Infection Spacer System, a knee spacer cleared 2026-07-23, and FDA's database held no Vantelle record on 2026-10-30. The 2026-08-21 information request and Q1 2027 clearance cannot be checked, and 66% of FY2025 510(k)s drew a request, with 1.69 cycles and 141 days on average. The CLIA waiver is planned for Q3 2027, so a 2028 decision is the earliest realistic case; 93.3% of new CLIA laboratories are waived-only, and Medicare pays $21.96 for the two assays in the first filing against a $33.40 cartridge, rising to $61.22 for the full panel only after a second 510(k) [S191, S193].

The price is flat in real terms and expensive. $3.2564 is 12.2% above the $2.903 Series A price over 4.6 years, against a 4.00% three-month Treasury yield, and $140.0M is 53.8x FY2025 revenue against a 2.05x public peer median and an 18.3x Series A venture benchmark; stripping the $8.4M bridge and the $13.1M option pool leaves a $126.9M clean pre-money. The $76.8M preference stack, 45.2% of the post-money, contains a 1x participating Series A with no disclosed cap, a term in 3.6% of Q2 2026 deals, shifting $25M at a $170M exit. Meridian receives 1.0x from $36.3M to $196.7M, 1.55x at $300M, 2.14x at $400M and 3.0x at $546M, while the Series A takes $75.2M, 2.09x, at $200M [S150, S281, S282].

The consensus is the deck's own: Q1 2027 clearance, a 2028 waiver, 300 sites by end-2027, 8 panels a day and a $400M-plus exit (company data, unverified). Our view differs on two facts the market has not had to price: utilisation is 1.02-1.37 panels a day, not 8, and the regulatory record does not evidence the submission. The probability-weighted value is $115M-$132M, 22%-32% below the post-money, so no edge on price, only on terms and timing. Meridian should not lead at $140.0M: investors should pass at the ask and keep an option below $110.0M. The counter-case: a $300M-$400M auction for a cleared, waived platform, or one commercial site at four or more panels a day, both testable within two quarters of clearance. The decision tree: invest now at $140.0M, no; wait for the FDA acknowledgment letter and the 510(k) decision, yes; pass if the round must close before either; invest with conditions at $95M-$110M, with $10M at close and $5M at clearance, a cap on the Series A participation, a sale-consent right, an independent director, a full-time CFO and 100% of Corvia or a put waiver [S150].

The weighted score is 2.9 out of 10, below any threshold for a $15.0M lead, because the three dimensions that decide a pre-clearance case — regulatory path, unit economics and price — score 2, 3 and 2, and the product's novelty at 4 cannot carry them. Product and technology earns that 4: the five-analyte, 40-microlitre, 12-minute cartridge has no marketed equivalent, the cartridge patent (US 16/884,327) is granted and four of five assays sit at 2.4-7.2% CV. The dimension is capped by the assay that carries the clinical decision: troponin at 11.8% CV against the IFCC's 10% benchmark, measured on 128 patients at one site by company staff, beside a reader patent rejected in July 2026 and a troponin chemistry outside the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion; Abbott's equivalent i-STAT study enrolled 3,697 patients [S150, S163].
