arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's plan to reach 300 commercial sites by the end of 2027 rests on one non-binding distributor letter and one $650-a-month rental programme, and it requires adding sites about twenty-one times faster than the company has managed while each placed analyzer runs one panel a day against the eight its model assumes [S150]. The evaluation programme is real — 41 clinics, 55 analyzers, 1,680 cartridges a month — but it is not a revenue base the investor can underwrite. The deck does not say how many of the 41 sites pay the $650 monthly fee: it states that 60% of evaluation sites received their instruments free, which leaves at most about 16 paying, and the $429,000-a-year lease figure (55 analyzers × $650 × 12) assumes every analyzer is paid for. Nor is the free cohort's cartridge price disclosed; the only statement is that evaluation sites "buy their cartridges." Repeat behaviour is binary: 34 of the 37 sites enrolled at least 90 days placed a second order within 90 days, with quantities and dollars undisclosed, and the four sites enrolled less than 90 days sit outside the measure. The company added 32 net new sites in the 31 months from March 2024 to October 2026, about one a month; 300 by end-2027 means 259 net new sites in twelve months, 21.6 a month, with 9 people in sales and support.

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 510(k) decision, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027 | Unverified: "filed 2026-05-18", information requested 2026-08-21, answer planned December 2026; no FDA letter in the pack and the cited K number is another company's device | Whether the launch clock starts in 2027 at all | S150, S191, S193 |
| Pivotal study, four sites, ~1,150 patients | Results Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07; no registered protocol | Whether accuracy survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood | S150, S192 |
| Second 510(k), three remaining assays | Filed Q2 2027 | Not started | Whether a five-assay panel exists commercially | S150 |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 | Not started | Whether staff without laboratory training can run it | S150 |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | Letter of intent only; 41 in evaluation | Whether a channel exists beyond referrals | S150 |
| Cartridge cost below $10 at 1 million units | Undated | $16.20 at ~20,000 units a year | Whether the 76% margin is reachable | S150 |

### The utilisation gap is the whole revenue plan

The deck assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer from 2028 and reports that evaluation sites used 41 cartridges a site a month in 2026 — 30.5 an analyzer a month across 55 analyzers, or 1.02 panels a day, an eight-fold gap measured over two and a half years on the only population the company has served [S150]. At that rate the 300-site target produces $7.25M of annual revenue: 402 analyzers at 1.34 per site, 306 panels a year each at the $33.40 realised price, plus $3.1M of $650 monthly leases. That is 43% of the $16.8M FY2027 plan, so the plan needs about 2.3 times the revenue per site the observed base produces. The serviceable market carries the same arithmetic: 13,200 sites × 1.34 analyzers × 1.02 panels × 300 days × $38.00 list is $206M, against the $2.4B the deck prints from the same site count at 2 analyzers and 8 panels a day. The fair defence is that evaluation sites are barred from using results for patient care, so demand there proves little. The consequence is not that utilisation stays at 1; it is that the company holds no commercial utilisation data, and the 2028-29 revenue line is an assumption rather than an extrapolation.

### The 2026 revenue estimate contains a shipment that cannot happen

FY2026E revenue is $5.9M, unverified, of which $2.4M is an opening stocking order from the distributor that ships only on 510(k) clearance. Nine months of 2026 produced $2.7M, so the fourth quarter must deliver $3.2M, $2.4M of it from an order that, on the company's own Q1 2027 clearance forecast, cannot ship in 2026 [S150]. Strip the order out and the year is $3.5M, which the run rate supports. That matters twice: the estimate overstates 2026 by 41%, and the same order presumably sits inside FY2027P revenue, so 2027 growth is partly a shipment rather than demand. The order also equals 71,856 cartridges at the realised $33.40 price — 5.8 months of channel inventory at the 300-site target on observed utilisation, against a nine-month shelf life, a return and expiry exposure the accounts show as revenue.

### Instrument economics are not the constraint; capital for everything else is

At a $2,900 list price against a $3,350 build cost, and with 60% of evaluation sites receiving their instrument free, the blended subsidy is $2,190 per placed analyzer if free units sit in proportion (unverified); 300 sites at the observed 1.34 analyzers each is 402 analyzers and $0.88M of subsidy, immaterial against a $30M raise [S150]. The razor-and-blade arithmetic works even at low utilisation: an analyzer at 1.02 panels a day earns $5,263 of cartridge gross profit a year against a $2,190 subsidy, and at 8 panels a day $41,280. What consumes capital is manufacturing scale-up — 40% of proceeds, $12M, with no disclosed capex, line count or qualification schedule — and working capital. Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M of monthly net burn runs out around 2027-03-31, the round is targeted to close on 2027-01-29, and the term loan starts amortising in 2027-03 at $167,000 a month. A twelve-month clearance slip adds a year at the FY2027 loss level, $16.5M, turning $30M into $30M plus a bridge.

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive licence to the cartridge sealing patent; 3% royalty on net cartridge sales | Acquired 2021-04 | In force; related party, the CTO holds 22% of Corvia (unverified) | S150 |
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Distributor letter of intent, 300 sites, $2.4M opening order | Not disclosed | Non-binding, conditional on clearance (unverified) | S150 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland | EU regulatory entity | Entity formed 2025-01-15 | No staff; CE marking not before 2028 (unverified) | S150 |
| Unnamed diagnostics partner | Contract development | Not disclosed | $0.7M of FY2025 revenue; scope undisclosed (unverified) | S150 |

### The channel constraint the deck does not price

Until a CLIA waiver is granted, only a laboratory holding a certificate for moderate-complexity testing can run the panel, and QuidelOrtho, selling into the same channel, describes the waived designation as "critical" for its point-of-care products and the waiver process as "onerous". So the 2027 launch is confined to hospital-run urgent care and rural hospital laboratories — and only one of the 41 evaluation sites is a hospital, holding 3 of the 55 analyzers [S17, S13]. That is the most credible route rather than a weakness: hospital laboratories already hold the certificate, the transfer-avoidance economics are strongest there, and Abbott's clearance of a high-sensitivity troponin cartridge on the handheld i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and on Alinity in June 2026 shows the channel rewards an installed base, not a first mover. The plausible channel is not the distributor but the chain: Mesa Verde Urgent Care, 12 sites and 18 analyzers, is the only evaluation customer big enough to test a multi-site rollout, and 300 sites would take roughly 25 such chains. What Vantelle does not own is the reimbursement step: clinics bill payers under existing codes, so whether a clinic will pay $38 a cartridge is a decision the investor can only test after clearance.

### What must be true within twelve months

By October 2027 the first clearance has to be in hand with no second information request, the pivotal study has to show precision at the cut-off that survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood, and a set of commercial sites has to buy cartridges at commercial terms with payer billing actually happening. The signposts are specific: a purchase order converting the distributor letter after clearance; one commercial site running several times the observed daily volume, the first evidence that 8 panels a day is reachable; a filed CLIA waiver application with a multi-site operator study behind it; and a unit cost inside the milestone at 100,000 cartridges a year. What breaks the plan is equally specific: a second information request, an FDA decision that keeps the assays at moderate complexity with a waiver required before broad marketing, or a pivotal study finishing after Q3 2027. The counter-case deserves weight — a clearance landing in the first quarter of 2027 and a distributor converting its letter soon after would make the 2026 revenue gap a timing artefact rather than a demand failure, and a hospital-anchored base of even 60 sites at commercial prices would fund the 2028 plan. The Ireland entity and the contract-development work are not that counter-case: a CE mark not before 2028 and $0.7M of services revenue are costs against a $30M raise, not paths to one, and every date in this paragraph is company intent, unverified [S150].

rows.finding: Platform assets with cleared or near-cleared technology change hands at $100M-$295M: QuidelOrtho paid $100M for LEX Diagnostics after clearance and a CLIA waiver in 2026; bioMérieux agreed to buy pre-revenue SpinChip at a €138M enterprise value in 2025; Roche paid $295M plus up to $55M of additional funding support, a maximum of $350M, announced 2023-12-29, for LumiraDx's point-of-care technology.
rows.mechanism: Strategic buyers pay for cleared technology and menu fit; a pre-revenue buyer pays for the technology option only, and Roche's $55M top-up funded the platform business until closing rather than paying for performance.
rows.benchmark: Vantelle at $140M pre-money, pre-clearance; the $546M exit needed for a 3x return.
rows.weakens: SpinChip proves a pre-revenue platform can fetch a nine-figure valuation, so the band is not a hard ceiling.
rows.implication: The platform band supports a $250M-$350M sale at best, so the new money needs a structure that shares in that outcome; at 1x it does not.
rows.confidence: high on reported transaction values; medium on comparability.
rows.follow_up: Has any diagnostic platform over $300M sold before its first 510(k) clearance in the last three years?

rows.finding: QuidelOrtho's FY2025 Point of Care revenue was $601.6M, down 13% from $694.6M in FY2024; its reported $1.5B asking price for the unit equals 2.5x FY2025 Point of Care revenue and 3.3x the annualised Q1 2026 run-rate of $113M. Scaled diagnostics deals price at 2.5x-6.5x revenue.
rows.mechanism: Public and strategic buyers capitalise declining point-of-care revenue at low single-digit multiples, which caps the price a buyer can pay without diluting its own multiple.
rows.benchmark: The FY2029 plan of $78.5M revenue; a $400M exit.
rows.weakens: The $1.5B is an asking price and the unit carries COVID-era decline; Vantelle's growth would command a higher multiple.
rows.implication: A $400M exit needs $160M of revenue at 2.5x, $80M at 5x or $117.6M at 3.4x; the plan reaches $78.5M, so $400M requires a top-of-range multiple or 50% above plan.
rows.confidence: high on QuidelOrtho segment revenue from the 10-K; medium on the asking price.
rows.follow_up: Will the Point of Care unit be sold, and at what multiple to FY2025 revenue?

rows.finding: Cue Health filed Chapter 7 in May 2024 with equity at zero; LumiraDx sold its point-of-care technology to Roche only after a revenue collapse, in a deal announced 2023-12-29 at $295M plus up to $55M of additional funding support (maximum $350M); Biocartis needed a €40M recapitalisation and converted €132M of debt to equity in 2023.
rows.mechanism: Point-of-care economics are decided by clearance, reimbursement and utilisation; a company that misses one of the three sells its technology at a distressed price.
rows.benchmark: Three recent point-of-care failures against a venture portfolio's need for one 3x in ten.
rows.weakens: Survivorship cuts both ways: the failures were COVID-testing companies, and Vantelle's cardiac panel is a different demand pool.
rows.implication: Binary regulatory and commercial risk argues for a lower entry price and a preference structure that returns capital before the common; the current 1x does that but gives no upside.
rows.confidence: high on the events; medium on how representative they are.
rows.follow_up: What did Cue Health's and LumiraDx's last private valuations imply for late-stage investors?

rows.finding: Meridian receives 1.0x on any exit from $36.3M to $196.7M, 1.55x at $300M, 2.14x at $400M and 3.0x at $546M; the participating Series A takes $36M first and returns 2.09x at a $200M exit, so Ardent Peak can support a sale that pays the new money nothing.
rows.mechanism: A senior 1x preference plus a participating junior preference allocates the first $72M of exit value to the two preferred classes, leaving the new money flat across the range where point-of-care assets trade.
rows.benchmark: A 3x venture return on $15M, and the Series A's 2.09x at a $200M exit.

rows.implication: The structure, not only the price, fails the return test; a participation cap and a sale-consent right are conditions of investing.

rows.finding: A US IPO for Vantelle would need audited accounts, a cleared five-assay menu, a CLIA waiver and $50M+ of revenue, pointing to 2030-2032; Medline and Molbio listed as scaled, profitable businesses.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's plan to reach 300 commercial sites by the end of 2027 rests on one non-binding distributor letter and one $650-a-month rental programme, and it requires adding sites about twenty-one times faster than the company has managed while each placed analyzer runs one panel a day against the eight its model assumes [S150]. The programme is real — 41 clinics, 55 analyzers, 1,680 cartridges a month — but not a revenue base the investor can underwrite. The deck does not say how many of the 41 sites pay the $650 monthly fee: it states that 60% of evaluation sites received their instruments free, which leaves at most about 16 paying, and the $429,000-a-year lease figure (55 analyzers × $650 × 12) assumes every analyzer is paid for. Nor is the free cohort's cartridge price disclosed; the only statement is that evaluation sites "buy their cartridges." Repeat behaviour is binary: 34 of the 37 sites enrolled at least 90 days placed a second order within 90 days, with quantities and dollars undisclosed, and the four sites enrolled less than 90 days sit outside the measure. The company added 32 net new sites in 31 months from March 2024, about one a month; 300 by end-2027 means 259 net new sites in twelve months, 21.6 a month, with 9 people in sales and support.

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 510(k) decision, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027 | Unverified: "filed 2026-05-18", information requested 2026-08-21, answer planned December 2026; no FDA letter in the pack and the cited K number is another company's device | Whether the launch clock starts in 2027 at all | S150, S191, S193 |
| Pivotal study, four sites, ~1,150 patients | Results Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07; no registered protocol | Whether accuracy survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood | S150, S192 |
| Second 510(k), three remaining assays | Filed Q2 2027 | Not started | Whether a five-assay panel exists commercially | S150 |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 | Not started | Whether staff without laboratory training can run it | S150 |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | Letter of intent only; 41 in evaluation | Whether a channel exists beyond referrals | S150 |
| Cartridge cost below $10 at 1 million units | Undated | $16.20 at ~20,000 units a year | Whether the 76% margin is reachable | S150 |

### The utilisation gap is the whole revenue plan

The deck assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer from 2028 and reports that evaluation sites used 41 cartridges a site a month in 2026 — 30.5 an analyzer a month across 55 analyzers, or 1.02 panels a day, an eight-fold gap measured over two and a half years on the only population the company has served [S150]. At that rate the 300-site target produces $7.25M of annual revenue: 402 analyzers at 1.34 per site, 306 panels a year each at the $33.40 realised price, plus $3.1M of $650 monthly leases. That is 43% of the $16.8M FY2027 plan, so the plan needs about 2.3 times the revenue per site the observed base produces. The serviceable market carries the same arithmetic: 13,200 sites × 1.34 analyzers × 1.02 panels × 300 days × $38.00 list is $206M, against the $2.4B the deck prints from the same sites at 2 analyzers and 8 panels. The fair defence is that evaluation sites cannot use results for patient care, so demand there proves little. The consequence is not that utilisation stays at 1; it is that the company holds no commercial utilisation data, and the 2028-29 revenue line is an assumption rather than an extrapolation.

### The 2026 revenue estimate contains a shipment that cannot happen

FY2026E revenue is $5.9M, unverified, of which $2.4M is an opening stocking order from the distributor that ships only on 510(k) clearance. Nine months of 2026 produced $2.7M, so the fourth quarter must deliver $3.2M, $2.4M of it from an order that, on the company's own Q1 2027 clearance forecast, cannot ship in 2026 [S150]. Strip the order out and the year is $3.5M, which the run rate supports. That matters twice: the estimate overstates 2026 by 41%, and the same order presumably sits inside FY2027P revenue, so 2027 growth is partly a shipment rather than demand. The order also equals 71,856 cartridges at the realised $33.40 price — 5.8 months of channel inventory at the 300-site target, against a nine-month shelf life, a return and expiry exposure booked as revenue.

### Instrument economics are not the constraint; capital for everything else is

At a $2,900 list price against a $3,350 build cost, and with 60% of evaluation sites receiving their instrument free, the blended subsidy is $2,190 per placed analyzer if free units sit in proportion (unverified); 300 sites at the observed 1.34 analyzers each is 402 analyzers and $0.88M of subsidy, immaterial against a $30M raise [S150]. The razor-and-blade arithmetic works even at low utilisation: an analyzer at 1.02 panels a day earns $5,263 of cartridge gross profit a year against a $2,190 subsidy, and at 8 panels a day $41,280. What consumes capital is manufacturing scale-up — 40% of proceeds, $12M, with no disclosed capex or qualification schedule — and working capital. Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M of monthly net burn runs out around 2027-03-31, the round is targeted to close on 2027-01-29, and the term loan starts amortising in 2027-03 at $167,000 a month. A twelve-month clearance slip adds a year at the FY2027 loss level, $16.5M, turning $30M into $30M and a bridge.

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive licence to the cartridge sealing patent; 3% royalty on net cartridge sales | Acquired 2021-04 | In force; related party, the CTO holds 22% of Corvia (unverified) | S150 |
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Distributor letter of intent, 300 sites, $2.4M opening order | Not disclosed | Non-binding, conditional on clearance (unverified) | S150 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland | EU regulatory entity | Entity formed 2025-01-15 | No staff; CE marking not before 2028 (unverified) | S150 |
| Unnamed diagnostics partner | Contract development | Not disclosed | $0.7M of FY2025 revenue; scope undisclosed (unverified) | S150 |

### The channel constraint the deck does not price

Until a CLIA waiver is granted, only a laboratory holding a certificate for moderate-complexity testing can run the panel, and QuidelOrtho, selling into the same channel, describes the waived designation as "critical" for its point-of-care products and the process "onerous". So the 2027 launch is confined to hospital-run urgent care and rural hospital laboratories — and only one of the 41 evaluation sites is a hospital, holding 3 of the 55 analyzers [S17, S13]. That is the most credible route rather than a weakness: hospital laboratories already hold the certificate, the transfer-avoidance economics are strongest there, and Abbott's clearance of a high-sensitivity troponin cartridge on the handheld i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and on Alinity in June 2026 shows the channel rewards an installed base, not a first mover. The plausible channel is the chain: Mesa Verde Urgent Care, 12 sites and 18 analyzers, is the only evaluation customer big enough to test a multi-site rollout, and 300 sites would take roughly 25 such chains. What Vantelle does not own is the reimbursement step: clinics bill payers under existing codes, so whether a clinic will pay $38 a cartridge is a decision the investor can only test after clearance.

### What must be true within twelve months

By October 2027 the first clearance has to be in hand with no second information request, the pivotal study has to show precision at the cut-off that survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood, and a set of commercial sites has to buy cartridges at commercial terms with payer billing actually happening. The signposts are specific: a purchase order converting the distributor letter after clearance; one commercial site running several times the observed daily volume, the first evidence that 8 panels a day is reachable; a filed CLIA waiver application with a multi-site operator study behind it; and a unit cost inside the milestone at 100,000 cartridges a year. What breaks the plan is equally specific: a second information request, an FDA decision that keeps the assays at moderate complexity with a waiver required before broad marketing, or a pivotal study finishing after Q3 2027. The counter-case deserves weight — a clearance landing in the first quarter of 2027 and a distributor converting its letter soon after would make the 2026 revenue gap a timing artefact rather than a demand failure, and a hospital-anchored base of even 60 sites at commercial prices would fund the 2028 plan. The Ireland entity and the contract-development work are not that counter-case: a CE mark not before 2028 and $0.7M of services revenue are costs against a $30M raise, and every date in this paragraph is company intent, unverified [S150].

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's plan to reach 300 commercial sites by the end of 2027 rests on one non-binding distributor letter and one $650-a-month rental programme — company data, unverified — and it requires adding sites twenty-one times faster than the company has managed while each placed analyzer runs one panel a day against the eight its model assumes [S150]. The programme is real — 41 clinics, 55 analyzers, 1,680 cartridges a month — but not a revenue base the investor can underwrite. The deck does not say how many of the 41 sites pay the $650 fee: it states that 60% of evaluation sites received their instruments free, which leaves at most 16 paying, and the $429,000-a-year lease figure assumes every analyzer is paid for. Nor is the free cohort's cartridge price disclosed: evaluation sites just "buy their cartridges." Repeat behaviour is binary: 34 of the 37 sites enrolled at least 90 days placed a second order within 90 days, quantities and dollars undisclosed; the four sites enrolled less than 90 days sit outside the measure. The company added 32 net new sites in 31 months from March 2024, 1.03 a month; 300 by end-2027 means 259 net new sites in twelve months, 21.6 a month, with 9 people in sales and support.

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 510(k) decision, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027 | Unverified: "filed 2026-05-18", information requested 2026-08-21, answer planned December 2026; no FDA letter in the pack and the cited K number is another company's device | Whether the launch clock starts in 2027 at all | S150, S191, S193 |
| Pivotal study, four sites, 1,150 patients | Results Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07; no registered protocol | Whether accuracy survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood | S150, S192 |
| Second 510(k), three remaining assays | Filed Q2 2027 | Not started (unverified) | Whether a five-assay panel exists commercially | S150 |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 | Not started (unverified) | Whether staff without laboratory training can run it | S150 |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | Letter of intent only (unverified); 41 in evaluation | Whether a channel exists beyond referrals | S150 |
| Cartridge cost below $10 at 1 million units | Undated | $16.20 at 20,000 units a year (unverified) | Whether the 76% margin is reachable | S150 |

### The utilisation gap is the whole revenue plan

The deck assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer from 2028 and reports, unverified, that evaluation sites used 41 cartridges a site a month in 2026 — 30.5 an analyzer a month across 55 analyzers, or 1.02 panels a day, an eight-fold gap measured over two and a half years on the only population the company has served [S150]. At that rate the 300-site target produces $7.25M of annual revenue: 402 analyzers at 1.34 per site, 306 panels a year each at the $33.40 realised price, plus $3.1M of $650 monthly leases. That is 43% of the $16.8M FY2027 plan, so the plan needs 2.3 times the revenue per site the observed base produces. The serviceable market carries the same arithmetic: 13,200 sites × 1.34 analyzers × 1.02 panels × 300 days × $38.00 list is $206M, against the $2.4B the deck prints from the same sites at 2 analyzers and 8 panels. The fair defence is that evaluation sites cannot use results for patient care, so demand there proves little. The consequence is not that utilisation stays at 1; it is that the company holds no commercial utilisation data, and the 2028-29 revenue line is an assumption rather than an extrapolation.

### The 2026 revenue estimate contains a shipment that cannot happen

FY2026E revenue is $5.9M, unverified, of which $2.4M is an opening stocking order from the distributor that ships only on 510(k) clearance. Nine months of 2026 produced $2.7M, so the fourth quarter must deliver $3.2M, $2.4M of it from an order that, on the company's own Q1 2027 clearance forecast, cannot ship in 2026 [S150]. Strip the order out and the year is $3.5M, which the run rate supports. That matters twice: the estimate overstates 2026 by 41%, and the same order presumably sits inside FY2027P revenue, so 2027 growth is partly a shipment rather than demand. The order also equals 71,856 cartridges at the realised $33.40 price — 5.8 months of channel inventory at the 300-site target, against a nine-month shelf life, a return and expiry exposure booked as revenue.

### Instrument economics are not the constraint; capital for everything else is

At a $2,900 list price against a $3,350 build cost, and with 60% of evaluation sites receiving their instrument free, the blended subsidy is $2,190 per placed analyzer if free units sit in proportion (unverified); 300 sites at the observed 1.34 analyzers each is 402 analyzers and $0.88M of subsidy, immaterial against a $30M raise [S150]. The razor-and-blade arithmetic works even at low utilisation: an analyzer at 1.02 panels a day earns $5,263 of cartridge gross profit a year against a $2,190 subsidy, and at 8 panels a day $41,280. What consumes capital is manufacturing scale-up — 40% of proceeds, $12M, with no disclosed capex or qualification schedule — and working capital. Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M of monthly net burn runs out at the end of March 2027, the round is targeted to close on 2027-01-29, and the term loan starts amortising in 2027-03 at $167,000 a month. A twelve-month clearance slip adds a year at the FY2027 loss level, $16.5M, turning $30M into $30M and a bridge.

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive licence to the cartridge sealing patent; 3% royalty on net cartridge sales | Acquired 2021-04 | In force; related party, the CTO holds 22% of Corvia (unverified) | S150 |
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Distributor letter of intent, 300 sites, $2.4M opening order | Not disclosed | Non-binding, conditional on clearance (unverified) | S150 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland | EU regulatory entity | Entity formed 2025-01-15 | No staff; CE marking not before 2028 (unverified) | S150 |
| Unnamed diagnostics partner | Contract development | Not disclosed | $0.7M of FY2025 revenue; scope undisclosed (unverified) | S150 |

### The channel constraint the deck does not price

Until a CLIA waiver is granted, only a laboratory holding a certificate for moderate-complexity testing can run the panel, and QuidelOrtho, selling into the same channel, describes the waived designation as "critical" for its point-of-care products and the process "onerous". So the 2027 launch is confined to hospital-run urgent care and rural hospital laboratories — and only one of the 41 evaluation sites is a hospital, holding 3 of the 55 analyzers [S17, S13]. That is the most credible route rather than a weakness: hospital laboratories already hold the certificate, the transfer-avoidance economics are strongest there, and Abbott's clearance of a high-sensitivity troponin cartridge on the handheld i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and on Alinity in June 2026 shows the channel rewards an installed base, not a first mover. The plausible channel is the chain: Mesa Verde Urgent Care, 12 sites and 18 analyzers, is the only evaluation customer that could test a multi-site rollout, and 300 sites would take 25 such chains. What Vantelle does not own is the reimbursement step: clinics bill payers under existing codes, so whether a clinic will pay $38 a cartridge is a decision the investor can only test after clearance.

### What must be true within twelve months

By October 2027 the first clearance has to be in hand with no second information request, the pivotal study has to show precision at the cut-off that survives clinic staff and finger-stick blood, and a set of commercial sites has to buy cartridges at commercial terms with payer billing actually happening. The signposts: a purchase order converting the distributor letter after clearance; one commercial site running more than 3 panels a day, triple the observed 1.02, the first evidence that 8 panels a day is reachable; a filed CLIA waiver application with a multi-site operator study behind it; and a unit cost inside the milestone at 100,000 cartridges a year. What breaks the plan: a second information request, an FDA decision that keeps the assays at moderate complexity with a waiver required before broad marketing, or a pivotal study finishing after Q3 2027. The counter-case: a clearance landing in the first quarter of 2027 and a distributor converting its letter soon after would make the 2026 revenue gap a timing artefact rather than a demand failure, and a hospital-anchored base of even 60 sites at commercial prices would fund the 2028 plan. The Ireland entity and the contract-development work are not that counter-case: a CE mark not before 2028 and $0.7M of services revenue are costs against a $30M raise, and every date in this paragraph is company intent, unverified [S150].

The $140M pre-money prices Vantelle above what strategic buyers have just paid for cleared, CLIA-waived point-of-care platforms, and the security on offer returns the new money 1.0x across the exit range where most point-of-care assets have traded. The financing record explains why: the Series B is a flat round in real terms, the insiders' newest money came through a 25%-discount bridge, and 9.35% of the headline valuation is an option-pool top-up, not operating value. No public record of Vantelle Diagnostics existed on 2026-10-30; the 510(k) number the deck cites is another company's device [S150, S191].

| Date | Round | Amount | Implied price / valuation | Investors | Use of funds | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 2021-04 | Corvia Microfluidics 60% | Stock; value not disclosed | n/d | Corvia founders, incl. Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist (22%) | Sealing-film patent CM-1 | Deck p.12-13 (S150; unverified) |
| 2022-02 | Series A first close | $24.0M | $2.903/share implied | Ardent Peak Ventures (lead) and Series A investors | Cartridge line; evaluation | Deck p.13-14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2023-11 | Series A second close | $12.0M | $2.903/share implied | Existing investors | Working capital | Deck p.13-14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2024-03 | Term loan and warrants | $5.0M debt; 400,000 warrants at $2.903 | n/a | Bluestem Venture Lending | Evaluation program | Deck p.13-14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2026-06-30 | Bridge notes | $6.0M at 8% | Converts at $2.4423 (75% of the Series B price) into 2,571,392 Series B-1 shares | Existing investors (unnamed) | Bridge runway | Deck p.14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2027-01 target | Series B | $30.0M | $140M pre, $170M post; $3.2564/share | Meridian $15.0M; Ardent Peak $5.0M; Juniper Rock $3.0M; $7.0M other new investors | 35% FDA clearance, 40% manufacturing, 25% launch | Deck p.14-15 (S150; unverified) |

The $0.75 seed price is inferred from $4.5M over 6.0M shares, and the $2.903 Series A price, the $2.4423 bridge conversion and the Series A participation are inferred from the deck's p.14 aggregates; all remain working assumptions until the Series A agreements, bridge notes and charter arrive. $3.2564 is 12.2% above $2.903, or 2.9%-3.7% a year over the 3.2-4.0 years since the two closes; on 2026-10-29 the three-month Treasury bill yielded 4.00% and the ten-year 4.99%, so the Series A is underwater in real terms. The bridge worsens the new money's position: $6.0M plus 8% interest converts at $2.4423 into 2,571,392 shares worth $8.37M at the Series B price, a 1.40x paper return in seven months; the discount creates 642,392 extra shares, 1.23% of the post-money. The headline overstates operating value: of 42,991,881 fully diluted pre-money shares, 4.02M new pool shares are worth $13.09M and the bridge $8.37M, so the clean pre-money is $126.9M. The new lead pays 33% more per share than investors who committed seven months earlier [S150, S86, S87].

### Every basis is labelled, and all of them sit above the peer median

| Method | Basis | Inputs | Result | Source |

| Post-money / FY2025 revenue | Post-money $170.0M | $170.0M / $2.6M | 65.4x | S150, unverified |

| EV / FY2027P revenue | Enterprise value $138.1M | $138.1M / $16.8M | 8.2x | S150, unverified |
| EV / FY2027P gross profit | Enterprise value $138.1M | $138.1M / $10.58M (63% gross margin) | 13.1x | S150, unverified |
| Precedent platform transactions | Transaction value | LEX $100M, cleared and waived; SpinChip EUR138M, pre-revenue; Roche paid $295M plus up to $55M of additional funding support, a maximum of $350M, for LumiraDx's point-of-care technology, announced 2023-12-29 | $100M-$295M | S205; S204; S284 |
| Scenario-weighted value | Analyst estimate | 20% $500M, 30% $300M, 30% $120M, 20% $30M exit; five years at 12%-15% | $115M-$132M | S150 (unverified); analyst estimate |

Basis note: the headline KPI quotes the pre-money $140.0M, where Meridian's $15.0M enters; post-money adds the $30.0M raise and enterprise value nets the $5.0M term loan against $6.9M cash. FY2025 revenue is therefore 53.8x pre-money, 65.4x post-money and 53.1x on EV, and each is quoted with one basis only. Weights are the analyst's: 20% at $500M assumes the FY2029 plan and a 6.4x multiple on $78.5M revenue; 30% at $300M assumes 5x on $60M; 30% at $120M a clearance with a slow ramp; 20% at $30M failure or an asset sale. The $232M expected exit discounts to $115M-$132M, 22%-32% below the $170M post-money [S150, unverified].

### The public comparables are cheaper than the deals

| Abbott | 4.6x | 22.7x | TTM to 2026-03-31; EV/revenue and EV/EBITDA | S4, S75 |

| Werfen | n/d | n/d (FY2025 sales EUR2.131B, EBITDA EUR473M) | FY2025 | S215 |
| Peer median | 2.05x | 13.8x | EV/revenue and EV/EBITDA, TTM | S4, S75, S8, S78, S213, S214 |

The 2.05x peer median is an enterprise-value-to-revenue comparison on trailing-twelve-month figures, the same basis as Vantelle's 53.1x EV/FY2025 row. QuidelOrtho is the purest read on how the public market prices point-of-care revenue: 0.4x EV/revenue, a Point of Care unit of $601.6M that fell 13% in FY2025 from $694.6M, a $0.9B market cap and a price at the 15th percentile of its 52-week range. Abbott marks the ceiling at 4.6x EV/revenue, and the median strategic medtech deal paid 3.9x revenue in Q1 2026. At 3.9x, $140M implies $35.9M of revenue today, 13.8 times FY2025; at 4.6x it implies $30.4M. There is no analyst consensus; the only forecast is the FY2029 plan of $78.5M revenue and $9.0M profit, worth $393M at 5x, or 2.1x for Meridian [S7, S8, S78, S220].

### The round funds the plan but not the revenue ramp

The $30M round is 73% new money on the company's unverified figures: $22M from new investors and $8M from Ardent Peak and Juniper Rock. Vantelle Diagnostics sells a $33.40 cartridge that costs $16.20 to make, but at the 1.37 panels a day its own evaluation sites average, a site returns $7,945 of annual gross profit before selling cost — too little to cover the $33,000-49,000 a year it costs to sell and support a site today — so the $140M pre-money valuation is a bet on an eight-to-twelve-fold utilisation step-up that no disclosed data supports; the $30M buys a manufacturing cost curve and a distribution option, not proven unit economics. The clinic buys the analyzer and cartridges, its staff runs the test and bills the patient's insurer under existing codes; Vantelle never bills a payer. The clinic pays list $2,900 for an analyzer that costs $3,350 to build when it buys one, $650 a month per analyzer during the evaluation programme, and $38 list per cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. In the 2026 average the 55 analyzers in the field consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, 41 per site; 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free. The one large order in sight is a non-binding distributor letter of intent that becomes a $2.4M stocking order only when the 510(k) clears in Q1 2027 [S150]. All figures are company-reported and unverified.

| Corvia royalty, 3% of net sales | $1.00 | $0.93 | — | S150, unverified |
| Gross profit after royalty | $16.20 (48.5%) | $22.57 (72.8%) | — | S150, unverified |

The cartridge is the only link with positive gross margin, and it is thinner than presented. A 2026 cartridge earns $17.20 (51.5%); the 3% royalty on net cartridge sales paid to Corvia Microfluidics takes $1.00, leaving $16.20 and 48.5% — the deck reports 51% without saying whether the royalty sits inside the $16.20. The 2029 target cuts cost 54% to $7.50 while price falls 7% to $31.00, lifting gross profit to $23.50, or $22.57 and 72.8% after royalty rather than the 76% shown. The volume required is the weak point: 2M cartridges is 99 times the 2026 run-rate of 20,160, and the FY2029 revenue line of $78.5M at $31 needs 2.53M cartridges, 126 times. The deck discloses no line capacity, yield, scrap rate or capex for it; the only visible cost is the 40% of the raise ($12M) labelled "scale cartridge manufacturing". Each point of scrap adds $0.08 to unit cost, so $7.50 depends on yield as much as volume. The royalty also takes value off the top: Corvia is 60% owned by Vantelle and the CTO, Dr Tomasz Lindqvist, holds 22% of it, so he receives 0.66% of cartridge net sales — 3% of the FY2029 plan's cartridge revenue is $2.36M, of which his share is $0.52M; Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake to Vantelle at fair value on an acquisition, ahead of common. These unit economics are company-reported and unverified [S150].

The instrument is not where the model breaks, but it is not free either. A placement costs $2,190 in cash on the 60/40 free-paid mix, against a $3,350 build cost, and is repaid out of cartridge gross profit in 4.4 months at the utilisation the evaluation sites deliver and inside one month at the planned rate. The hardware is cheap customer acquisition; the site's profit depends on utilisation.

That is where the deck parts company with its own data. The model assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer and two analyzers a site, 16 a day per site; the evaluation sites averaged 1.37 a day per site and 1.02 per analyzer, a gap of 7.8 times per analyzer and 11.7 times per site. The $2.4B serviceable market assumes 13,200 sites × 2 analyzers × 8 panels × 300 days × $38; on the observed footprint (1.34 analyzers a site, 1.02 panels an analyzer a day, 300 days) those sites are worth $206M. Per-site cartridge gross profit is $7,945 a year at observed utilisation against $77,760 modelled. Selling cost is not disclosed; the nine sales and support staff imply $1.35M-$2.0M a year, $33,000-$49,000 per active site today and $4,500-$6,700 a site at 300 sites. A three-year LTV of $23,835 therefore covers 0.2 times today's selling cost and 1.2-1.8 times the at-scale cost, against 12-17 times at the modelled rate (analyst estimate; customer acquisition cost is not disclosed). This is a utilisation bet presented as a scale bet. The utilisation and market figures are company-reported and unverified [S150].

Revenue quality compounds the problem. FY2025's $2.6M was $1.1M of evaluation-programme revenue (42%), $0.8M of research-use cartridges sold to clinical research organisations (31%) and $0.7M of contract development for a partner (27%) — none of it cleared clinical testing. Revenue to September 2026 was $2.7M, and the $5.9M full-year estimate includes the $2.4M stocking order that ships only on clearance in Q1 2027, so underlying FY2026 is $3.5M, up 35% rather than 127%. The evaluation line cannot be reconciled to the disclosed split. The deck calls all 41 sites a paid evaluation programme and says sites pay $650 a month per analyzer, but also says 60% of sites received their analyzer free: if "free" means no charge at all, at most about 16 of 41 sites pay the fee — roughly $170,000 a year on 22 analyzers, 16% of the $1.1M line — and the remaining $0.9M would have to be cartridges plus undisclosed fees; if it means only that the $2,900 analyzer price was waived, all 55 analyzers could pay the fee and the line reconciles to $1.10M on 2026 volumes ($429,000 of fees plus $673,000 of cartridges). The deck states neither how many sites pay the fee nor what the free cohort pays per cartridge. Retention is binary: 34 of the 37 sites enrolled at least 90 days placed a second order within 90 days, with quantities and dollars not disclosed, so a second order can be one cartridge; four sites under 90 days sit outside that cohort. The revenue mix is company-reported and unverified [S150].

Payer risk sits with the clinic but does not stop there. After clearance the clinic bills Medicare or a commercial payer per test and buys cartridges from Vantelle, so a denial is its loss — and a reason not to reorder. Medicare's 2026 laboratory fee schedule pays $21.96 for the two assays in the first 510(k), 34% below the $33.40 cartridge before the clinic's labour and quality-control cost; the full five-test panel recovers $61.22 on the three assays whose rates are published, where the cartridge becomes affordable. arguments.markdown:
The $140M pre-money prices Vantelle above what strategic buyers have just paid for cleared, CLIA-waived point-of-care platforms, and the security on offer returns the new money 1.0x across the exit range where most point-of-care assets have traded. The financing record explains why: the Series B is a flat round in real terms, the insiders' newest money came through a 25%-discount bridge, and 9.35% of the headline valuation is an option-pool top-up, not operating value. No public record of Vantelle Diagnostics existed on 2026-10-30; the 510(k) number the deck cites is another company's device [S150, S191].

| Date | Round | Amount | Implied price / valuation | Investors | Use of funds | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019-06 | Seed | $4.5M | $0.75/share implied; post-money not disclosed | Juniper Rock Capital (lead) and seed investors | Product development | Deck p.13-14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2021-04 | Corvia Microfluidics 60% | Stock; value not disclosed | n/d | Corvia founders, incl. Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist (22%) | Sealing-film patent CM-1 | Deck p.12-13 (S150; unverified) |
| 2022-02 | Series A first close | $24.0M | $2.903/share implied | Ardent Peak Ventures (lead) and Series A investors | Cartridge line; evaluation | Deck p.13-14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2023-11 | Series A second close | $12.0M | $2.903/share implied | Existing investors | Working capital | Deck p.13-14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2024-03 | Term loan and warrants | $5.0M debt; 400,000 warrants at $2.903 | n/a | Bluestem Venture Lending | Evaluation program | Deck p.13-14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2026-06-30 | Bridge notes | $6.0M at 8% | Converts at $2.4423 (75% of the Series B price) into 2,571,392 Series B-1 shares | Existing investors (unnamed) | Bridge runway | Deck p.14 (S150; unverified) |
| 2027-01 target | Series B | $30.0M | $140M pre, $170M post; $3.2564/share | Meridian $15.0M; Ardent Peak $5.0M; Juniper Rock $3.0M; $7.0M other new investors | 35% FDA clearance, 40% manufacturing, 25% launch | Deck p.14-15 (S150; unverified) |

The $0.75 seed price is inferred from $4.5M over 6.0M shares, and the $2.903 Series A price, the $2.4423 bridge conversion and the Series A participation are inferred from the deck's p.14 aggregates; all remain working assumptions until the Series A agreements, bridge notes and charter arrive. $3.2564 is 12.2% above $2.903, or 2.9%-3.7% a year over the 3.2-4.0 years since the two closes; on 2026-10-29 the three-month Treasury bill yielded 4.00% and the ten-year 4.99%, so the Series A is underwater in real terms. The bridge worsens the new money's position: $6.0M plus 8% interest converts at $2.4423 into 2,571,392 shares worth $8.37M at the Series B price, a 1.40x paper return in seven months; the discount creates 642,392 extra shares, 1.23% of the post-money. The headline overstates operating value: of 42,991,881 fully diluted pre-money shares, 4.02M new pool shares are worth $13.09M and the bridge $8.37M, so the clean pre-money is $126.9M. The new lead pays 33% more per share than investors who committed seven months earlier [S150, S86, S87].

### Every basis is labelled, and all of them sit above the peer median

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pre-money / FY2025 revenue | Pre-money $140.0M | $140.0M / $2.6M | 53.8x | S150, unverified |
| Pre-money / FY2026E revenue | Pre-money $140.0M | $140.0M / $5.9M, including the $2.4M stocking order | 23.7x | S150, unverified |
| Post-money / FY2025 revenue | Post-money $170.0M | $170.0M / $2.6M | 65.4x | S150, unverified |
| EV / FY2025 revenue | Enterprise value $138.1M | ($140.0M + $5.0M debt - $6.9M cash) / $2.6M | 53.1x; peer median 2.05x EV/revenue | S150, unverified; S4, S75; S8, S78; S213; S214 |

| Scenario-weighted value | Analyst estimate | 20% $500M, 30% $300M, 30% $120M, 20% $30M exit; five years at 12%-15% | $115M-$132M | S150 (unverified); analyst estimate |

Basis note: the headline KPI quotes the pre-money $140.0M, where Meridian's $15.0M enters; post-money adds the $30.0M raise and enterprise value nets the $5.0M term loan against $6.9M cash. FY2025 revenue is therefore 53.8x pre-money, 65.4x post-money and 53.1x on EV, and each is quoted with one basis only. Weights are the analyst's: 20% at $500M assumes the FY2029 plan and a 6.4x multiple on $78.5M revenue; 30% at $300M assumes 5x on $60M; 30% at $120M a clearance with a slow ramp; 20% at $30M failure or an asset sale. The $232M expected exit discounts to $115M-$132M, 22%-32% below the $170M post-money [S150, unverified].

### The public comparables are cheaper than the deals

| Company | EV/revenue (TTM) | EV/EBITDA (TTM) | Period and basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | 4.6x | 22.7x | TTM to 2026-03-31; EV/revenue and EV/EBITDA | S4, S75 |
| QuidelOrtho | 0.4x | n/m | TTM to 2026-06-28; FY2025 revenue $2,730.2M, of which Point of Care $601.6M | S8, S78, S7 |
| Siemens Healthineers | 1.9x | 13.8x | TTM, 2026-10-29 | S214 |
| bioMérieux | 2.2x | 8.9x | TTM, 2026-09 | S213 |
| Werfen | n/d | n/d (FY2025 sales EUR2.131B, EBITDA EUR473M) | FY2025 | S215 |
| Peer median | 2.05x | 13.8x | EV/revenue and EV/EBITDA, TTM | S4, S75, S8, S78, S213, S214 |
| Vantelle at $140M pre | 53.8x FY2025; 23.7x FY2026E | n/m (net loss) | Pre-money basis | S150 (unverified) |

The 2.05x peer median is an enterprise-value-to-revenue comparison on trailing-twelve-month figures, the same basis as Vantelle's 53.1x EV/FY2025 row. QuidelOrtho is the purest read on how the public market prices point-of-care revenue: 0.4x EV/revenue, a Point of Care unit of $601.6M that fell 13% in FY2025 from $694.6M, a $0.9B market cap and a price at the 15th percentile of its 52-week range. Abbott marks the ceiling at 4.6x EV/revenue, and the median strategic medtech deal paid 3.9x revenue in Q1 2026. At 3.9x, $140M implies $35.9M of revenue today, 13.8 times FY2025; at 4.6x it implies $30.4M. There is no analyst consensus; the only forecast is the FY2029 plan of $78.5M revenue and $9.0M profit, worth $393M at 5x, or 2.1x for Meridian [S7, S8, S78, S220].

### The round funds the plan but not the revenue ramp

The $30M round is 73% new money on the company's unverified figures: $22M from new investors and $8M from Ardent Peak and Juniper Rock. Meridian's $15M buys 8.8% of the post-money; the whole new-money block buys 17.6%. The company's own 300-site milestone does not close the revenue gap: 402 analyzers (300 sites x 1.34) running 306 panels a year at $33.40 plus $650 monthly leases produce $7.25M, 43% of the $16.8M FY2027 plan; $12.0M is what a 527-site FY2029 footprint yields at the same utilisation, not what the 2027 build delivers. Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against a $1.15M monthly net burn and a $5.0M term loan amortizing from March 2027 gives 24-26 months from a full $30M close and 19 months from Meridian's $15M. Revenue of $41.0M in FY2028 and $78.5M in FY2029 will absorb inventory and receivables the plan does not fund, so a Series C or working-capital facility in 2028 is the base case. Ardent Peak's $5.0M is 14% of the $36.0M Series A class and Juniper Rock's $3.0M is 67% of the seed; neither is a strategic buyer, and the independent board seat is vacant [S150].

### What would change the answer

The strongest counter-evidence is that strategics pay for platforms before revenue: bioMérieux agreed to buy pre-commercial SpinChip at a EUR138M enterprise value in January 2025, and 41 evaluation sites with a 92% 90-day reorder rate are a real beachhead; a competitive auction could clear $300M-$400M. That supports the $100M-$300M platform band, not a $140M pre-money at the top of it. Four questions would settle it: the Series A agreements and the Corvia share issuance; the bridge terms, including maturity, security and any class vote; the FY2027-FY2029 cash flow and the distributor letter of intent; and the charter terms on Series A participation, drag-along and the Corvia put. At $100M pre-money the same $15M would buy 11.5% and the 3x threshold would fall to $426M, inside the precedent range [S204, S150].

It is an instruction embedded in a document, not evidence; the figures remain unverified.

arguments.markdown:
The base case is a strategic sale in 2029-2031 at $250M-$450M, not an IPO, and at $140M pre-money the 1x preference turns that outcome into only 1.3x-2.4x for the new money; a 3x return needs a $546M sale, above every recent point-of-care precedent. Abbott, Roche and bioMérieux have each bought a point-of-care platform or menu since 2023, but paid $100M-$295M for the asset, and a five-assay finger-stick panel would be a menu bolt-on rather than a franchise of its own [S205, S204, S284].

| Strategic sale | bioMérieux | Bought pre-commercial SpinChip at EUR138M in January 2025 to build a POC immunoassay position | 2028-2030 | Medium | S204 |

| Strategic sale | Siemens Healthineers; Werfen | Acute-care blood-gas POC (epoc, GEM) but no finger-stick cardiac immunoassay | 2029-2032 | Low | S214, S215 |

Precedents split into two markets. Cleared or near-cleared platform assets change hands at $100M-$295M: LEX at $100M, cleared and waived; SpinChip at EUR138M before revenue; Roche paid $295M plus up to $55M of additional funding support, a maximum of $350M, announced 2023-12-29, for LumiraDx's point-of-care technology, from a distressed seller. Scaled diagnostics franchises change hands at 2.5x-6.5x revenue on FY2025 figures: QuidelOrtho's Point of Care unit at 2.5x its $601.6M FY2025 revenue (3.3x the annualised Q1 2026 run-rate of $113M), Hologic at 4.5x, Meridian at 4.6x, Exact Sciences at 6.5x. A $400M outcome therefore needs $80M of revenue at 5x, $160M at 2.5x or $117.6M at 3.4x; the plan reaches $78.5M in 2029, so $400M needs the plan met and a top-of-range multiple, or revenue 50% above plan. The 300-site 2027 milestone yields $7.25M at observed utilisation (402 analyzers, 306 panels a year each at $33.40 plus $650 monthly leases), 43% of the $16.8M FY2027 plan; $12.0M is the 527-site FY2029 footprint at the same utilisation, not the 2027 build (company data, unverified). The counter-case is a competitive auction among Abbott, Roche and bioMérieux that pushes a platform price above $300M; the risk is that no auction materialises after a 510(k) delay. The failure base rate is real: Cue Health raised hundreds of millions and filed Chapter 7 in May 2024, LumiraDx sold its technology only after a revenue collapse, and Biocartis needed a EUR40M recapitalisation and converted EUR132M of debt to equity in 2023 [S205, S204, S284, S210, S7, S8, S150].

### The waterfall leaves the new money flat until a $197M exit

| $300M | $23.3M | 1.55x | 9.2% | S150 (unverified); analyst waterfall |
| $400M | $32.1M | 2.14x | 16.4% | S150 (unverified); analyst waterfall |
| $546M | $45.0M | 3.00x | 24.6% | S150 (unverified); analyst waterfall |
| $700M | $58.6M | 3.91x | 31.4% | S150 (unverified); analyst waterfall |

The shape is the problem. On the company's unverified cap table, with the per-share prices, the bridge conversion and the Series A's participation (modelled as uncapped because the deck states no cap) inferred from the p.14 aggregates until the agreements arrive, the $30M Series B and the $6.28M Series B-1 sit ahead of the Series A at a $36.28M preference, and Meridian owns 41.35% of that preference, so it receives exactly $15.0M on any exit from $36.3M to $196.7M, where the class converts. That range contains the LEX price, the SpinChip price and most strategic outcomes. Above $196.7M Meridian earns 8.82% of every dollar after the Series A's $36M preference, which is why $300M returns 1.55x, $400M 2.14x and $546M 3.0x. The structure makes the new money a lender up to $196.7M and an equity holder only above it because the senior preference and the Series A's participation take the first slice; strategically, that is the opposite of a venture return profile. The $546M threshold is 7.0x the FY2029 revenue plan and 1.8x the median 3.9x strategic multiple; at 3.9x the same $546M requires $140M of revenue, 78% above plan [S150].

### The Series A is paid before the Series B, and the IPO is a fallback

The participating Series A changes who wants a sale. At a $200M exit the Series A class receives $75.2M, a 2.09x return on its $36.0M, while the Series B receives its 1.0x preference; at $400M the Series A receives $122.5M, 3.4x, against the Series B's 2.14x. Ardent Peak, which led the 2022 round, can therefore support a $200M sale that returns Meridian nothing, and its $5.0M follow-on does not change that incentive. Meridian would hold one of six board seats, with the independent seat vacant and the drag-along terms undisclosed. An IPO is a fallback rather than a route: Medline's $6.26B listing in December 2025 and Molbio's Indian listing in August 2026 show the window is open, but both are scaled and profitable; a US listing for Vantelle needs audited accounts, a cleared five-assay menu, a CLIA waiver and $50M+ of revenue, pointing to 2030-2032; the Irish entity has no staff and EU IVDR is not addressed before 2028 [S150, S217, S218].

### The buyer will price the Corvia subsidiary before the menu

The licensed sealing patent is the manufacturing choke point and, on the company's unverified structure, sits outside the parent: CM-1 is owned by Corvia Microfluidics, 60% owned by Vantelle, licensed exclusively at a 3% royalty; the CTO owns 22% of Corvia and shares in that royalty, and the minority may put its 40% to Vantelle at fair market value. At the FY2029 plan the royalty is $2.36M a year, a permanent leak, and a buyer will want 100% of Corvia, a renegotiated CTO arrangement and an escrow for the put before it signs. The patent position adds diligence: VD-2, the five-assay optical reader, received a final rejection in July 2026 and is under appeal, and the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion did not cover the troponin chemistry in VD-4 [S150].

Policy is not the binding constraint for most buyers: diagnostics manufacturing is not dual-use, so European, Japanese or Korean buyers face no special US review, while a Chinese acquirer would face political scrutiny. The binding gates remain the 510(k) additional-information request of 2026-08-21, the CLIA waiver planned for the third quarter of 2027 and the 300-site build. Holding period and entry price are the two levers Meridian controls: at $140M pre-money a 3x needs $546M, while at $100M pre-money the same $15M buys 11.5%, a 3x needs $426M and a $300M sale returns 2.03x instead of 1.55x. Investable terms are a $95M-$110M pre-money, the bridge converted at the Series B price, a cap on the Series A participation, the vacant independent seat plus a sale-consent right, and a tranche tied to 510(k) clearance [S216, S150].

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle Diagnostics sells a $33.40 cartridge that costs $16.20 to make, but at the 1.37 panels a day its own evaluation sites average, a site returns $7,945 of annual gross profit before selling cost — too little to cover the $33,000-49,000 a year it costs to sell and support a site today — so the $140M pre-money valuation is a bet on an eight-to-twelve-fold utilisation step-up that no disclosed data supports; the $30M buys a manufacturing cost curve and a distribution option, not proven unit economics. The clinic buys the analyzer and cartridges, its staff runs the test and bills the patient's insurer under existing codes; Vantelle never bills a payer. The clinic pays list $2,900 for an analyzer that costs $3,350 to build when it buys one, $650 a month per analyzer during the evaluation programme, and $38 list per cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. In the 2026 average the 55 analyzers in the field consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, 41 per site, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free. The one large order in sight is a non-binding distributor letter of intent that becomes a $2.4M stocking order only when the 510(k) clears in Q1 2027 [S150]. All figures are company-reported and unverified.

| Metric | Per unit, 2026 | Per unit, 2029 target | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Average selling price (list $38) | $33.40 | $31.00 | — | S150, unverified |
| Cost of goods | $16.20 | $7.50 | — | S150, unverified |
| Gross profit | $17.20 (51.5%) | $23.50 (75.8%) | Abbott FY2025 gross margin 56.4% | S150; S3 |
| Corvia royalty, 3% of net sales | $1.00 | $0.93 | — | S150, unverified |
| Gross profit after royalty | $16.20 (48.5%) | $22.57 (72.8%) | — | S150, unverified |
| Volume, cartridges a year (2029 = 126x 2026) | 20,160 | 2,532,000 | — | S150, unverified |
| Gross profit pool after royalty | $0.33M | $57.1M | FY2029 plan gross profit $55.7M | S150, unverified |

The cartridge is the only link with positive gross margin, and it is thinner than presented. A 2026 cartridge earns $17.20 (51.5%); the 3% royalty on net cartridge sales paid to Corvia Microfluidics takes $1.00, leaving $16.20 and 48.5% — the deck reports 51% without saying whether the royalty sits inside the $16.20. The 2029 target cuts cost 54% to $7.50 while price falls 7% to $31.00, lifting gross profit to $23.50, or $22.57 and 72.8% after royalty rather than the 76% shown. The volume required is the weak point: 2M cartridges is 99 times the 2026 run-rate of 20,160, and the FY2029 revenue line of $78.5M at $31 needs 2.53M cartridges, 126 times. The deck discloses no line capacity, yield, scrap rate or capex for it; the only visible cost is the 40% of the raise ($12M) labelled "scale cartridge manufacturing". The royalty also takes value off the top: Corvia is 60% owned by Vantelle and the CTO, Dr Tomasz Lindqvist, holds 22% of it, so he receives 0.66% of cartridge net sales — 3% of the FY2029 plan's cartridge revenue is $2.36M, of which his share is $0.52M; Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake to Vantelle at fair value on an acquisition, ahead of common. These margins are company-reported and unverified [S150].

| Metric | Evaluation actual, 2026 | Plan from 2028 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridges per analyzer a month | 30.5 | 240 | S150, unverified |
| Panels a day per analyzer | 1.02 | 8.0 | S150, unverified |
| Panels a day per site (2 analyzers planned, 1.34 actual) | 1.37 | 16.0 | S150, unverified |
| Cartridge gross profit per analyzer a year, after royalty | $5,929 | $38,880 | S150, unverified |
| Instrument cash cost per placement (60% free, 40% at $2,900) | $2,190 | $2,190 | S150, unverified |
| Cash cost of the installed base | $120,450 (55 analyzers) | $2.31M (1,055 analyzers) | S150, unverified |
| Instrument payback, months | 4.4 | 0.7 | S150, unverified |
| Three-year cartridge gross profit per site, after royalty | $23,835 | $233,280 | S150, unverified |
| Selling cost per site a year, analyst estimate | $33,000-49,000 | $4,500-6,700 | S150, unverified |
| Value of 13,200 sites at $38 (13,200 × 1.34 analyzers × 1.02 panels/analyzer/day × 300 days) | $206M | $2.4B at 16 panels a day | S150, derived, unverified |
| Sites needed for $78.5M of FY2029 revenue | 3,459 | 527 | S150, unverified |

The instrument is not where the model breaks, but it is not free either. A placement is bought at a discount to its build cost on the free-paid mix and repaid out of cartridge gross profit in a few months at the utilisation the evaluation sites actually deliver, and inside one month at the planned rate.

That is where the deck parts company with its own data. The model assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer and two analyzers a site, 16 a day per site; the evaluation sites averaged 1.37 a day per site and 1.02 per analyzer, a gap of 7.8 times per analyzer and 11.7 times per site. The $2.4B serviceable market assumes 13,200 sites × 2 analyzers × 8 panels × 300 days × $38; on the observed footprint (1.34 analyzers a site, 1.02 panels an analyzer a day, 300 days) those sites are worth $206M. Per-site cartridge gross profit is $7,945 a year at observed utilisation against $77,760 modelled. Selling cost is not disclosed; the nine sales and support staff imply $1.35M-$2.0M a year, $33,000-$49,000 per active site today and $4,500-$6,700 a site at 300 sites. A three-year LTV of $23,835 therefore covers 0.2 times today's selling cost and 1.2-1.8 times the at-scale cost, against 12-17 times at the modelled rate (analyst estimate). This is a utilisation bet presented as a scale bet. The utilisation and market figures are company-reported and unverified [S150].

Revenue quality compounds the problem. FY2025's $2.6M was $1.1M of evaluation-programme revenue (42%), $0.8M of research-use cartridges sold to clinical research organisations (31%) and $0.7M of contract development for a partner (27%) — none of it cleared clinical testing. Revenue to September 2026 was $2.7M, and the $5.9M full-year estimate includes the $2.4M stocking order that ships only on clearance in Q1 2027, so underlying FY2026 is $3.5M, up 35% rather than 127%. The $1.1M evaluation line cannot be reconciled to the disclosed split: the deck calls all 41 sites a paid evaluation programme and says sites pay $650 a month per analyzer, but also says 60% received their analyzer free. If free means no charge at all, at most about 16 of 41 sites pay the fee — roughly $170,000 on 22 analyzers, 16% of the line — leaving $0.9M of cartridges and undisclosed fees; if it means only that the $2,900 price was waived, all 55 analyzers can pay, and $429,000 of fees plus $673,000 of cartridges matches the line on 2026 volumes. The deck says neither how many sites pay nor what the free cohort pays per cartridge. Retention is binary: 34 of the 37 sites enrolled at least 90 days placed a second order, with quantities and dollars not disclosed, so a second order can be one cartridge; four sites under 90 days sit outside that cohort. The revenue mix is company-reported and unverified [S150].

Payer risk sits with the clinic but does not stop there. After clearance the clinic bills Medicare or a commercial payer per test and buys cartridges from Vantelle, so a denial is its loss — and a reason not to reorder. Medicare's 2026 laboratory fee schedule pays $21.96 for the two assays in the first 510(k), 34% below the $33.40 cartridge before the clinic's own costs; the full five-test panel recovers $61.22 on the three assays whose rates are published, where the cartridge becomes affordable. The full panel needs the second 510(k), planned for Q2 2027, and clinic staff cannot run it without the CLIA waiver, whose application is planned for Q3 2027; a listed peer calls waived status critical for point-of-care products and onerous to obtain [S7, S176, S177, S178].

| Test (CPT) | Medicare 2026 rate | Cleared in the first 510(k)? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin, quantitative (84484) | $12.47 | Yes | S177, independent |
| HbA1c (83036) | $9.49 | Yes | S178, independent |
| BNP/NT-proBNP (83880) | $39.26 | No, second 510(k) | S176, independent |
| First two assays, subtotal | $21.96 | — | Derived, S177-S178 |
| Three assays, subtotal | $61.22 | — | Derived, S176-S178 |

::: evidence
**At the utilisation its own evaluation sites show, Vantelle's cartridge annuity does not cover the cost of selling a site; the plan needs a step-up in panels per day that no disclosed data supports.**

Evidence: the $2.4B market model assumes 16 panels a day per site against 1.37 observed, and 2M cartridges a year is 99 times the current run-rate; LumiraDx entered pre-pack administration and its Point of Care platform sold to Roche, which paid $295M plus up to $55M of additional funding support, a maximum of $350M, announced 2023-12-29, while Cue Health filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28 after $480M+ raised [S150, S172, S174, S236, S284].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's cash ends in March 2027, in the same month its $5.0M term loan starts amortising, so the $30M round is a liquidity event before it is a growth investment. The reported trajectory is $1.1M of revenue in FY2024, $2.6M in FY2025 and $5.9M forecast for FY2026, with gross margin rising from 49% to 61%. The FY2026 figure does not survive its own footnotes: revenue to September 2026 was $2.7M, and the $5.9M estimate includes a $2.4M stocking order that ships only when the 510(k) clears, which the deck places in Q1 2027, after the fiscal year ends. Unless clearance arrives before 2026-12-31, two months ahead of the company's own estimate, FY2026 revenue is $3.5M and growth is 35%, not 127%. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 商业模式 Business Model (business_model, revision 9 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,906 characters)
Vantelle Diagnostics sells a $33.40 cartridge that costs $16.20 to make, but at the 1.37 panels a day its own evaluation sites average, a site returns $7,945 of annual gross profit before selling cost — too little to cover the $33,000-49,000 a year it costs to sell and support a site today — so the $140M pre-money valuation is a bet on an eight-to-twelve-fold utilisation step-up that no disclosed data supports; the $30M buys a manufacturing cost curve and a distribution option, not proven unit economics. The clinic buys the analyzer and cartridges, its staff runs the test and bills the patient's insurer under existing codes; Vantelle never bills a payer. The clinic pays list $2,900 for an analyzer that costs $3,350 to build when it buys one, $650 a month per analyzer during the evaluation programme, and $38 list per cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. In the 2026 average the 55 analyzers in the field consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, 41 per site, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free. The one large order in sight is a non-binding distributor letter of intent that becomes a $2.4M stocking order only when the 510(k) clears in Q1 2027 [S150]. All figures are company-reported and unverified.

| Corvia royalty, 3% of net sales | $1.00 | $0.93 | — | S150, unverified |

The cartridge is the only link with positive gross margin, and it is thinner than presented. A 2026 cartridge earns $17.20 (51.5%); the 3% royalty on net cartridge sales paid to Corvia Microfluidics takes $1.00, leaving $16.20 and 48.5% — the deck reports 51% without saying whether the royalty sits inside the $16.20. The 2029 target cuts cost 54% to $7.50 while price falls 7% to $31.00, lifting gross profit to $23.50, or $22.57 and 72.8% after royalty rather than the 76% shown. The volume required is the weak point: 2M cartridges is 99 times the 2026 run-rate of 20,160, and the FY2029 revenue line of $78.5M at $31 needs 2.53M cartridges, 126 times. The deck discloses no line capacity, yield, scrap rate or capex for it; the only visible cost is the 40% of the raise ($12M) labelled "scale cartridge manufacturing". The royalty also takes value off the top: Corvia is 60% owned by Vantelle and the CTO, Dr Tomasz Lindqvist, holds 22% of it, so he receives 0.66% of cartridge net sales — 3% of the FY2029 plan's cartridge revenue is $2.36M, of which his share is $0.52M; Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake to Vantelle at fair value on an acquisition, ahead of common. These margins are company-reported and unverified [S150].

| Instrument cash cost per placement (60% free, 40% at $2,900) | $2,190 | $2,190 | S150, unverified |

The instrument is not where the model breaks, but it is not free either. A placement is bought at a discount to its build cost on the free-paid mix and repaid out of cartridge gross profit in a few months at the utilisation the evaluation sites actually deliver, and inside one month at the planned rate.

That is where the deck parts company with its own data. The model assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer and two analyzers a site, 16 a day per site; the evaluation sites averaged 1.37 a day per site and 1.02 per analyzer, a gap of 7.8 times per analyzer and 11.7 times per site. The $2.4B serviceable market assumes 13,200 sites × 2 analyzers × 8 panels × 300 days × $38; on the observed footprint (1.34 analyzers a site, 1.02 panels an analyzer a day, 300 days) those sites are worth $206M. Per-site cartridge gross profit is $7,945 a year at observed utilisation against $77,760 modelled. Selling cost is not disclosed; the nine sales and support staff imply $1.35M-$2.0M a year, $33,000-$49,000 per active site today and $4,500-$6,700 a site at 300 sites. A three-year LTV of $23,835 therefore covers 0.2 times today's selling cost and 1.2-1.8 times the at-scale cost, against 12-17 times at the modelled rate (analyst estimate). This is a utilisation bet presented as a scale bet. The utilisation and market figures are company-reported and unverified [S150].

Revenue quality compounds the problem. FY2025's $2.6M was $1.1M of evaluation-programme revenue (42%), $0.8M of research-use cartridges sold to clinical research organisations (31%) and $0.7M of contract development for a partner (27%) — none of it cleared clinical testing. Revenue to September 2026 was $2.7M, and the $5.9M full-year estimate includes the $2.4M stocking order that ships only on clearance in Q1 2027, so underlying FY2026 is $3.5M, up 35% rather than 127%. The $1.1M evaluation line cannot be reconciled to the disclosed split: the deck calls all 41 sites a paid evaluation programme and says sites pay $650 a month per analyzer, but also says 60% received their analyzer free. If free means no charge at all, at most about 16 of 41 sites pay the fee — roughly $170,000 on 22 analyzers, 16% of the line — leaving $0.9M of cartridges and undisclosed fees; if it means only that the $2,900 price was waived, all 55 analyzers can pay, and $429,000 of fees plus $673,000 of cartridges matches the line on 2026 volumes. The deck says neither how many sites pay nor what the free cohort pays per cartridge. Retention is binary: 34 of the 37 sites enrolled at least 90 days placed a second order, with quantities and dollars not disclosed, so a second order can be one cartridge; four sites under 90 days sit outside that cohort. The revenue mix is company-reported and unverified [S150].

Payer risk sits with the clinic but does not stop there. After clearance the clinic bills Medicare or a commercial payer per test and buys cartridges from Vantelle, so a denial is its loss — and a reason not to reorder. Medicare's 2026 laboratory fee schedule pays $21.96 for the two assays in the first 510(k), 34% below the $33.40 cartridge before the clinic's own costs; the full five-test panel recovers $61.22 on the three assays whose rates are published, where the cartridge becomes affordable. The full panel needs the second 510(k), planned for Q2 2027, and clinic staff cannot run it without the CLIA waiver, whose application is planned for Q3 2027; a listed peer calls waived status critical for point-of-care products and onerous to obtain [S7, S176, S177, S178].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 市场与行业分析 Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 6 by Market Analyst, 8,992 characters)
The US serviceable market is real but 8.5% of the size Vantelle claims once its own cartridge data replace its model assumptions, and adoption is capped less by clinic count than by the payer spread over a $33.40 cartridge and a CLIA waiver not planned before Q3 2027. The claim rests on a four-factor multiplication the company prints in full: 13,200 sites (11,400 urgent-care centers plus 1,800 rural hospitals) × 2 analyzers × 8 panels a day × 300 days × $38 a cartridge = $2.41B [S150, S269, S268]. Urgent Care Association data show 15,000 centers in 2024 and National Urgent Care Realty 14,245 in September 2024, so 11,400 understates the urgent-care base by 25-32%. A larger base does not rescue the case: 39% of centers are hospital-affiliated and more likely to have laboratory access, and the average center sees 33.1-34.0 patients a day, so a 14-panel send-out day — the median in its 52-clinic survey — means 42% of visits draw a five-test blood panel.

Utilization is where the arithmetic breaks. Vantelle's 41 evaluation sites ran 55 analyzers and consumed 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026: 30.5 cartridges per analyzer a month, or 1.02 panels an analyzer a day, and 41 a month per site, or 1.37 a site a day — the second is not an independent measurement but 1.02 × 1.34 analyzers a site (55 ÷ 41 = 1.34), kept separate (company data, unverified). The model assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer, so the gap is 7.8x per analyzer, 5.8x per site and 10.2x against the company's survey median. The deck never reconciles the 41-cartridges-per-site month with the 8-a-day assumption. Investigational labelling explains part of the gap, because evaluation results cannot be used for patient care and sites run the analyzer alongside the reference laboratory; it also means the only utilization evidence comes from a setting that cannot bill [S150].

|---|---|---|---|
| Global point-of-care TAM | All POC diagnostics, 2025 | $21.7B (4.1% CAGR to 2033); $32.87B (7.27% CAGR to 2034) | S271, S272 |
| North America POC | 37.1% of the $21.7B 2025 base | $8.05B (analyst calculation) | S272 |
| Company's claimed serviceable market | 13,200 sites × 2 analyzers/site × 8 panels/analyzer/day × 300 days × $38.00 list | $2.41B (company data, unverified) | S150 |
| Serviceable market at observed utilization | 13,200 sites × 1.34 analyzers/site × 1.02 panels/analyzer/day × 300 days × $38.00 list (300 operating days; 2026 list price, not realised) | $206M (analyst calculation from company data, unverified) | S150, S268 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue (SOM) | 300 sites × 1.34 = 402 analyzers; 306 panels/analyzer/year at $33.40 realised = $4.11M cartridges + $3.14M leases at $650/month if all pay | $7.25M; $12.0M is the 527-site FY2029 footprint; FY2027 plan $16.8M (company data, unverified) | S150 |

At observed utilization 300 sites yield $7.25M ($4.11M cartridges plus $3.14M leases), not $12.0M (the 527-site FY2029 footprint) or the $16.8M FY2027 plan; at the disclosed 60% free-instrument rate only about 40% of analyzers pay the lease, cutting the total to $5.37M. The FY2028 plan of $41.0M implies 1.23M cartridges, or 6.8 panels per analyzer per day on two analyzers per site over 300 days. The strongest counter-case is that the 14-panel survey is right and evaluation sites are suppressed; it needs one cleared, billable cohort at survey volumes. Two independent 2025 estimates put the global POC market 1.5x apart, and neither isolates a US five-assay urgent-care niche [S271, S272].

The clinic's profit and loss explains the low utilization. A clinic on paid terms pays $33.40 a cartridge and $650 a month per analyzer, while Medicare pays $12.47 for CPT 84484, the troponin code; at 41 panels a month the lease adds $15.85 a panel, so the five-test panel must reimburse $36.78 at Medicare rates before in-sourcing breaks even, falling to $23.64 at 240 panels a month [S177]. The other four 2026 fee-schedule rates, every commercial contract and the send-out price are not disclosed; they decide whether in-sourcing pays. Commercial payers at 1.5-2x Medicare would clear the bar; a Medicare-heavy rural hospital would not, inverting the rural emphasis: commercially insured urgent care is the beachhead, the rural hospital a mission sale. Procurement is a $650 monthly lease for a single-site operator but a capital and certification decision for a hospital-affiliated site; the 60% free-instrument rate leaves hardware willingness to pay unproven.

Demand is organic, not subsidy-created. Urgent-care centers grew from 9,000 to 15,000 between 2016 and 2024 (6.6% a year) while 197 rural hospitals closed or converted between January 2005 and 2026 [S269, S270, S150]. Policy is a gate, not a subsidy: the CLIA '88 waiver, planned for Q3 2027, decides whether clinic staff may run the panel, and no CMS or state programme pays for the instrument. The budget owner is the clinic operator or medical director. The 'paid' evaluation programme is only partly paid: 60% of instruments were placed free, so at most about 16 of the 41 sites pay the $650 monthly fee, and the deck gives one 2026 average realised price of $33.40 across all sites, with no free-cohort price. 34 of the 37 sites enrolled at least 90 days placed a second order — a binary measure; quantities and dollars are not disclosed, and the four sites under 90 days sit outside the count.
