rows.finding: Troponin I imprecision of 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile decision level, the worst of the five assays and the one the chest-pain and transfer use case depends on; the deck states no acceptance criterion.
rows.mechanism: An assay whose total imprecision at the cut-off is 11.8% cannot separate a result that is a few per cent above the cut-off from one a few per cent below, so repeated measurement near the threshold flips the normal/abnormal call; the IFCC calibration of what may be called high-sensitivity is imprecision at the 99th-percentile URL plus measurability in most healthy people, and simulation work shows single-threshold classification error rises steeply with bias and imprecision.
rows.benchmark: The IFCC definition of a high-sensitivity assay, which turns on imprecision at the 99th-percentile URL of 10% or better and measurable concentrations in at least half of healthy individuals [S163]; the company's own other four assays (2.4-7.2% CV) show the panel can be built better than its troponin is.
rows.weakens: Company-derived, with no stated method (no CLSI EP05 replicate design, no lot count, no site count), so 11.8% may be neither the best nor the worst case; if FDA measures against a conventional rather than high-sensitivity troponin standard the number may pass review while failing the label the company sells.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite a rule-out or transfer-substitution use case; price the troponin as a rule-in aid and require the pivotal study's precision data before the Series B is treated as de-risked.
rows.confidence: high on the number (it is the company's own), medium on its regulatory consequence because the FDA acceptance criterion for this submission is not public.
rows.follow_up: What is the total imprecision at each of the three decision levels, by lot and by site, in the pivotal study, and what acceptance criterion did the company write into its pre-submission?

rows.finding: The entire clinical evidence base is 128 patients at one urgent-care site, September to December 2025, venous blood run by Vantelle staff, scored as category agreement (normal or abnormal) rather than numeric concordance, with six of 640 results excluded.
rows.mechanism: Category agreement throws away the magnitude that clinical decisions need (a troponin of 14 versus 60 ng/L is one category), and a single-site venous study run by the manufacturer removes both the operator variable and the specimen variable that the commercial claim rests on - finger-stick blood drawn by clinic staff.
rows.benchmark: Abbott's i-STAT hs-TnI study enrolled 3,697 patients with primary completion in February 2024 [S124] and its cartridge was cleared in January 2025 [S17]; published work on analytical concordance across point-of-care and central-laboratory troponin assays shows discordance is a known, quantified problem rather than a formality [S145].
rows.weakens: The deck's own summary row does not add up - 634 of 640 is 99.1%, while the five per-assay rates imply about 626 agreements in 634 analysable results, so the 98.7% figure is a share of the analysable set presented as a count out of 640.
rows.implication: Treat the 98.7% as a feasibility result, not pivotal evidence; the investor is being asked to fund a pivotal study whose result is the actual de-risking event, which falls after the close.
rows.confidence: high - the design and the arithmetic are visible in the deck; the pivotal protocol is not verifiable because no trial is registered [S192].
rows.follow_up: What were the six exclusions by assay and reason, and how many of the 128 patients had a troponin above the cut-off?

rows.finding: 510(k) K261734 for troponin I and HbA1c was filed 2026-05-18; FDA issued an additional-information request on 2026-08-21 with a 180-day response window; the company plans to answer in December 2026 and still forecasts clearance in Q1 2027.
rows.mechanism: An additional-information request stops the review clock; a Q1 2027 decision therefore requires FDA to act within roughly three months of receiving the December answer, at the fast end of its review behaviour, and a second request or a not-substantially-equivalent decision restarts the whole path. FDA's clearance database held no record for K261734 or for any device under the company's name on 2026-10-30.
rows.benchmark: Abbott's point-of-care hs-TnI cartridge took from a February 2024 study completion to a January 2025 clearance, about eleven months, on a much larger evidence base [S124, S17].
rows.weakens: The content of the request is not disclosed, so it is impossible to tell whether it concerns labelling, precision, specimen equivalence or clinical performance - the difference between a two-month answer and a new study.
rows.implication: Model clearance in the second half of 2027 rather than Q1, and treat the Q1 2027 date as a company aspiration that the company's own December response makes tight.
rows.confidence: high on dates, low on outcome.
rows.follow_up: What did FDA ask for on 2026-08-21, and does the answer require new bench or clinical data?

rows.finding: CLIA waiver application is planned for Q3 2027, after clearance of the first two assays, so the launch configuration is a moderate-complexity test requiring a certificated laboratory and qualified staff.
rows.mechanism: The product's entire claim is that a clinic without a laboratory can run a five-test panel; that claim is legally unavailable until a waiver is granted, and the waiver route requires a multi-site reproducibility study with untrained operators plus flex studies, which the company has not started.
rows.benchmark: QuidelOrtho, an incumbent in this channel, states in its own annual report that the CLIA-waived designation is 'critical' for most of its point-of-care products and that the waiver requirements are 'onerous' and have increased the time and cost required to obtain one [S7].
rows.weakens: A moderate-complexity launch is not worthless: hospital-run urgent care and rural hospital laboratories already hold the right certificate, which is why the one hospital site in the evaluation programme matters more than its 1 of 41 weight suggests.
rows.implication: The 2027 commercial story is a narrow, laboratory-capable slice of the market; the mass-market story needs a waiver decision that, on the company's dates, cannot arrive before 2028.
rows.confidence: high on the sequencing, medium on the timing of a waiver decision because no application has been filed.
rows.follow_up: How many of the 41 evaluation sites hold a moderate-complexity certificate today, and what share of the 13,200 target sites hold one?

rows.finding: The five-assay optical reader patent received a final rejection in July 2026 and an appeal is only 'under consideration'; the only US patent granted outright to the parent covers the capillary-fill cartridge; the sealing patent that the cartridges depend on is owned by a 60%-owned subsidiary and licensed back at a 3% royalty; the dried-reagent troponin chemistry is an unpublished PCT filed 2026-02-11 and was expressly excluded from the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion.
rows.mechanism: A final rejection starts a six-month window to appeal or abandon, so the decision on whether the reader is protected falls around the January 2027 target close; an unpublished PCT gives no public claim scope and national-phase entry is years away, which leaves the hardest technical element - a room-temperature-stable dried-reagent troponin assay - protected only by secrecy and unvetted for third-party blocking patents.
rows.benchmark: For a platform claim the estate is thin: one granted US patent owned outright, one granted patent held in a 60%-owned affiliate, one finally rejected application, two unpublished applications and one pending European application, against incumbents whose troponin franchises are built on decades of assay-chemistry patents.
rows.weakens: The cartridge patent (filed 2020-05-28, granted 2023-03) does cover the on-board calibrator and capillary fill, which is real manufacturing protection; and a rejected reader claim does not stop the company from selling the reader, only from excluding others.
rows.implication: The moat is regulatory and manufacturing time, not patents; a funded competitor can copy the reader and, once the applications publish, design around or license the chemistry.
rows.confidence: medium - every patent fact here is the company's own summary; the patent registers could not be reached in this run (see the data request), so claim scope and the appeal status are unverified.
rows.follow_up: Has a notice of appeal been filed for 17/662,019, and what does the appeal cost and when is a decision expected?

rows.finding: Cartridge cost is $16.20 at roughly 20,000 units a year against a $7.50 target at 2 million units a year (2029), on a single pilot line with 18 staff in a leased Tempe plant; shelf life is claimed at 9 months on 6 months of data.
rows.mechanism: The cost curve implies about an 11% reduction per doubling of volume, which is shallower than the 15-25% per doubling typical of volume-driven hardware, so the target is not heroic on its own arithmetic; the binding question is what share of the bill of materials is antibody and reagent, which does not scale like moulded plastic. Finger-stick hemolysis and fill volume are the manufacturing failure modes, which is why the company filed a sample-volume-check application in September 2025.
rows.benchmark: Point-of-care troponin cartridges have a documented quality history: Abbott's i-STAT cTnI cartridges were recalled repeatedly in 2011-2013 for device design, labelling and material contamination [S69, S70, S71, S72], which is the failure taxonomy a scale-up of a dried-reagent cartridge has to survive.
rows.weakens: The $7.50 target at 2 million units is a 2029 number and the company's own interim milestone is only 'below $10 at 1 million', so the target is not the thing to underwrite; and 9 months of real-time data would be available by around December 2026, so the shelf-life gap may close before submission.
rows.implication: Manufacturing scale-up is the largest single use of the Series B (40% of proceeds) and the least evidenced; require a bill-of-materials breakdown and a line-commissioning plan before treating the 76% gross margin as a 2029 fact.
rows.confidence: medium - the cost and volume figures are the company's, the volume-to-cost inference is mine, and the bill of materials is not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: What share of the $16.20 is reagent and antibody, and what capex and qualification time does the 1-million-unit line need?

rows.finding: Abbott cleared a high-sensitivity troponin I cartridge for the handheld i-STAT 1 system on 2025-01-03 and for i-STAT Alinity on 2026-06-11, yet the deck's competitive table compares only against benchtop analyzers, single-test handheld readers and the reference laboratory.
rows.mechanism: The differentiated claim is a five-result finger-stick panel, not troponin measurement on a handheld; on the single most valuable assay the incumbent already sells a clearance on a handheld platform with a 3,697-patient study and independent real-world evaluations published in 2026.
rows.benchmark: Abbott's i-STAT and i-STAT Alinity cartridges cover blood gas, chemistry, electrolytes, coagulation and immunoassay on one handheld platform [S3], and the Alinity hs-TnI assay has been evaluated independently in a UK emergency department [S144].
rows.weakens: A single-test hs-TnI cartridge is not the same product as a five-assay panel, and the incumbents' cartridges require whole blood and a trained operator, which is exactly the gap the finger-stick, no-calibration design is aimed at.
rows.implication: Ask what Vantelle has that Abbott cannot add: the answer has to be specimen type, panel breadth and operator simplicity, and each of those is unproven until the pivotal study and the waiver.
rows.confidence: high - the clearances and the platform description are in FDA's registry and Abbott's filing.
rows.follow_up: Does Abbott's i-STAT hs-TnI cartridge carry a CLIA-waived label, and for which specimen types?

plan.decision_question: Is a finger-stick, 12-minute, five-assay panel at the claimed accuracy a defensible technology, and what remains unproven before clearance?
plan.thesis_sentence: The Q5 is a credible engineering achievement — a 40-microlitre finger-stick sample into a five-result panel in twelve minutes on a cartridge that calibrates itself — but the company's own data show a troponin assay too imprecise for the decision it is sold to support, resting on one company-run site, with the reader patent finally rejected and the troponin chemistry neither patent-protected nor covered by the freedom-to-operate opinion, so the technology is copyable in everything except the regulatory and manufacturing time it has already spent.
plan.why_different: This section judges whether the thing works and can be defended; it does not size the market, price the round or score the team. It supplies the technical facts (imprecision, study design, regulatory sequencing, patent status, manufacturability) that the risk, valuation and strategy sections consume.
plan.mechanism: Value moves from the instrument to the cartridge and from the cartridge to the assay chemistry: the instrument is sold below cost, so the only durable gross profit is the reagent margin on a cartridge whose troponin performance is set by dried-reagent chemistry that is unprotected and outside the freedom-to-operate opinion, while the legal right to let untrained staff run it (the CLIA waiver) is the real gate on the business model.
plan.comparison_set: Abbott i-STAT and i-STAT Alinity hs-TnI cartridges (cleared 2025-01-03 and 2026-06-11, with a 3,697-patient study), Siemens epoc blood-analysis system (K200107), the central laboratory as the incumbent workflow, and the standard the IFCC sets for point-of-care troponin and for the high-sensitivity label.
plan.counter_evidence: The panel's other four assays are precise (2.4-7.2% CV), the cartridge patent is granted and covers the on-board calibrator, the cost curve is shallower than a standard learning curve and therefore plausible, and a single-test handheld is not a five-assay panel - so the case is not that the technology fails, but that its differentiation is unproven exactly where the clinical and commercial value sits.
plan.visual: A performance-metrics table (Metric | Company value | Benchmark | Source) carrying the imprecision, study-size, timeline and cost comparisons, followed by a four-row moat table and a patent table with granted versus pending.
plan.prohibited: No 'high barriers to entry', no 'best-in-class accuracy', no 'proprietary' without stating what is actually granted, no 'revolutionary' or 'game-changing', no unqualified 'FDA-cleared' before a clearance exists, no vague patent counts ('several patents', 'strong IP portfolio').

rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What are the installation, training and service costs per placement, which the deck does not disclose?

rows.finding: FY2025's $2.6M was 42% evaluation programme, 31% research-use cartridges and 27% contract development; FY2026E's $5.9M includes a $2.4M stocking order that ships only on clearance, expected Q1 2027, leaving about $3.5M underlying (+35%).
rows.mechanism: Contingent, one-off revenue fills the growth line, so reported growth overstates the recurring base.
rows.benchmark: 55 analyzers at $650 a month is $429K a year, only 39% of the $1.1M FY2025 evaluation line, so the line includes other charges.
rows.weakens: A distributor LOI, even non-binding, is evidence of channel interest and the order may convert on schedule.

rows.finding: Medicare's 2026 fee schedule pays $12.47 for troponin and $9.49 for HbA1c, $21.96 for the first two cleared assays, 34% below the $33.40 cartridge; three assays reach $61.22 with NT-proBNP and the full panel about $70.
rows.mechanism: The clinic bills the payer and bears denial risk, but a denial or a low commercial rate suppresses reorders, transmitting the risk to Vantelle's volume one quarter later.
rows.benchmark: Medicare CLFS 2026 national rates; QuidelOrtho states that CLIA-waived designation is critical for most point-of-care products and is onerous to obtain.
rows.weakens: Commercial payers usually pay above Medicare, and clinics may absorb a thin margin on a test that avoids a transfer.
rows.implication: Obtain payer coverage and commercial rate evidence for the five-test panel before the term sheet; the two-assay clearance is not commercially viable on its own.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What do the three largest commercial payers in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico pay for these codes at a clinic site of service?

rows.finding: The 3% cartridge royalty is paid to Corvia Microfluidics, 60% owned by Vantelle; the CTO owns 22% of Corvia, about 0.66% of cartridge net sales, and the 40% minority can put its stake at fair value on an acquisition.
rows.mechanism: Related-party payments move margin to a partly owned entity and the put gives the minority a claim on exit proceeds ahead of common.

rows.implication: Add a repriced or capped Corvia put and royalty disclosure to the term sheet.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What are Corvia's other assets and liabilities, and has the put ever been valued?

rows.finding: The analyzer lists at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost (-15.5%); 60% of evaluation sites received one free, a weighted cash cost of $2,190 per placement, repaid in 4.4 months at observed utilisation and 0.7 months at the modelled rate.
rows.mechanism: The instrument is customer acquisition recovered from the cartridge annuity, so negative hardware margin is tolerable only while cartridges reorder.
rows.benchmark: QuidelOrtho places instruments under long-term contracts to capture recurring consumable revenue.
rows.weakens: At these payback periods hardware is not the binding constraint; utilisation and selling cost are.
rows.implication: Do not frame the $30M primarily as an instrument-subsidy requirement; the cash cost of a 600-analyzer base is about $1.3M.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What are the installation, training and service costs per placement, which the deck does not disclose?

rows.finding: FY2025's $2.6M was 42% evaluation programme, 31% research-use cartridges and 27% contract development; FY2026E's $5.9M includes a $2.4M stocking order shipping only on clearance, expected Q1 2027, leaving about $3.5M underlying (+35%). The deck calls all 41 sites a paid evaluation programme and says sites pay $650 a month per analyzer, but 60% received instruments free: at most about 16 of 41 sites pay the fee if free means no charge ($170K, 16% of the $1.1M line), while the line matches $1.10M only if all 55 analyzers pay $429K of fees plus $673K of cartridges. Reorder is binary: 34 of 37 sites enrolled at least 90 days placed a second order; quantities and dollars not disclosed; four sites are under 90 days.
rows.mechanism: Contingent, one-off revenue fills the growth line, and an unreconciled evaluation line leaves the recurring base unknown.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 $2.6M, FY2026 to September $2.7M; 55 analyzers at $650 a month is $429K, 39% of $1.1M; 1,680 cartridges a month at $33.40 is $673K.
rows.weakens: A distributor LOI, even non-binding, is evidence of channel interest and the order may convert on schedule; a second order may be a single cartridge.
rows.implication: Require revenue by type and customer, the distributor purchase order and shipment terms before underwriting FY2027.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic; low on the split
rows.follow_up: How much of the $1.1M evaluation line is the monthly fee versus cartridges, and how many sites pay the fee?

rows.finding: Medicare's 2026 fee schedule pays $12.47 for troponin and $9.49 for HbA1c, $21.96 for the first two cleared assays, 34% below the $33.40 cartridge; three assays reach $61.22 with NT-proBNP.
rows.mechanism: The clinic bills the payer and bears denial risk, but a denial or a low commercial rate suppresses reorders, transmitting the risk to Vantelle's volume one quarter later.
rows.benchmark: Medicare CLFS 2026 national rates; QuidelOrtho states that CLIA-waived designation is critical for most point-of-care products and is onerous to obtain.
rows.weakens: Commercial payers usually pay above Medicare, and clinics may absorb a thin margin on a test that avoids a transfer.
rows.implication: Obtain payer coverage and commercial rate evidence for the five-test panel before the term sheet; the two-assay clearance is not commercially viable on its own.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What do the three largest commercial payers in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico pay for these codes at a clinic site of service?

rows.finding: The 3% cartridge royalty is paid to Corvia Microfluidics, 60% owned by Vantelle; the CTO owns 22% of Corvia, about 0.66% of cartridge net sales, worth about $0.52M on the FY2029 plan's $2.36M royalty; Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake at fair value on an acquisition.
rows.mechanism: Related-party payments move margin to a partly owned entity and the put gives the minority a claim on exit proceeds ahead of common.
rows.benchmark: No public comparable; the deck discloses the ownership but not the royalty's treatment in COGS.
rows.weakens: At the FY2029 plan the royalty is about $2.4M a year and the CTO's indirect share about $0.5M, small against a $140M valuation.
rows.implication: Add a repriced or capped Corvia put and royalty disclosure to the term sheet.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What are Corvia's other assets and liabilities, and has the put ever been valued?

rows.finding: LumiraDx entered pre-pack administration and its Point of Care platform sold to Roche, which paid $295M plus up to $55M of additional funding support, a maximum of $350M, announced 2023-12-29.
rows.mechanism: The platform technology found a strategic buyer, but the equity was wiped out after the company ran out of cash before commercial scale.
rows.benchmark: Cue Health raised more than $480M and filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28; Truvian has raised $225.3M while still funding clearance.
rows.weakens: Roche bought the platform out of administration, so the technology survived even though the equity did not; a $350M maximum validates strategic value.
rows.implication: The category's base rate is failure after $200M-$500M of capital; a $30M round is a fraction of what comparable platforms consumed before clearance.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What would a strategic acquirer pay for Vantelle before clearance, and what claims sit ahead of common?

plan.decision_question: Do the unit economics work at scale, and what does the new money actually buy?
plan.thesis_sentence: Vantelle's cartridge annuity is positive but thin, and at the 1.37 panels a day its own evaluation sites average the company does not cover the cost of selling a site, so the $140M pre-money price is a bet on an eight-to-twelve-fold utilisation step-up that no disclosed data supports.
plan.why_different: This section prices one cartridge, one analyzer and one site; the financial section tests aggregate cash and projections, and the market section sizes the opportunity. Only here are the related-party royalty, the paid/free split and the payer rate per test set against the cartridge price.
plan.mechanism: A related-party royalty cuts every cartridge's margin; a subsidised instrument converts cash into an installed base; gross profit per site is set by panels a day; selling cost per site falls only as site count rises.
plan.comparison_set: Abbott FY2025 gross and operating margins, QuidelOrtho's razor/blade disclosure, Cue Health and LumiraDx as failure base rates, 2026 Medicare CLFS rates per test, and Truvian's $225M capital intensity.
plan.counter_evidence: Investigational-use labelling makes 1.37 panels a day a floor; 34 of 37 mature sites placed a second order; Abbott shows placement-plus-consumable economics can be profitable at scale; Roche paid up to $350M for LumiraDx's platform.
plan.visual: Unit-economics table per cartridge (2026 actual vs 2029 target, after the Corvia royalty) and a per-analyzer utilisation, payback and site-value table with the $206M observed market basis.
plan.prohibited: razor-and-blade model is proven; recurring revenue base; clear path to profitability; huge market; strong team; well positioned; manageable risks; industry-leading; robust pipeline

rows.finding: FY2026E revenue of $5.9M exceeds FY2026 nine-month revenue of $2.7M by $3.2M, of which $2.4M is a stocking order that the deck says ships on 510(k) clearance, expected Q1 2027; underlying FY2026 revenue is about $3.5M, up 35% not 127%.
rows.mechanism: Contingent revenue recognised or forecast ahead of the triggering event flatters growth and, if shipped in 2027, moves the cash inflow a year later than the projection shows.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 revenue $2.6M and FY2026 to September $2.7M, which annualises to about $3.6M.
rows.weakens: Clearance could arrive in December 2026, inside FY2026, if the FDA answers faster than the company's Q1 2027 estimate.
rows.implication: Underwrite the round on the $3.5M underlying run-rate and treat the $2.4M as a 2027 event at the earliest.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What are the shipment and payment terms of the distributor order, and is it cancellable?

rows.finding: Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M of monthly net burn gives 6.0 months of runway to 2027-03-31, exactly when $166,667 a month of term-loan principal begins; the 8% bridge adds about $40,000 a month.
rows.mechanism: Fixed burn plus new debt amortisation converts a financing delay into a liquidity default rather than a dilution event.
rows.benchmark: Targeted close 2027-01-29; $5.0M term loan with interest-only to 2027-03 and 30 monthly payments after.
rows.weakens: The burn figure is company-reported and may include discretionary spend that can be cut in a squeeze.
rows.implication: The round must close by February 2027; a slip past March 2027 forces a bridge or a down round.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What is the term loan's interest rate, security and covenant package, and can amortisation be extended?

rows.finding: A $30M close on 2027-01-29 leaves about $32.3M of cash; the plan's FY2027 and FY2028 losses of $22.5M take it to about $11.2M before capex, and the manufacturing capex sits outside the P&L, so the discretionary buffer is closer to $5M.
rows.mechanism: Operating losses plus capex absorb the raise before the first profit year, so the buffer is thin relative to a single year of burn.
rows.benchmark: FY2027P net loss $16.5M and FY2028P $6.0M, with $12M of the raise allocated to manufacturing scale-up.
rows.weakens: Working capital releases and the $2.4M stocking order could add cash in 2027 if it ships early.
rows.implication: The round funds the plan to breakeven but leaves under six months of burn as buffer, so any 2027 revenue shortfall needs another round.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: How much of the $12M manufacturing allocation is capex versus operating cost, and when is it spent?

rows.finding: A $9.0M profit on $78.5M of revenue at 71% gross margin requires $46.7M of operating expense and interest, 2.7x the $17.6M implied for FY2026, at 59.5% of revenue; the revenue needs 2.53M cartridges, or 1,055 analyzers and about 527 sites at 8 panels a day, against 3,459 sites at observed utilisation.
rows.mechanism: Gross profit scales with sites and panels a day while opex scales with headcount, so the profit is a residual that is highly sensitive to utilisation.
rows.benchmark: Abbott FY2025 SG&A plus R&D was 34.5% of revenue with an 18.2% operating margin; QuidelOrtho's operating margin was -33.7% in FY2025.
rows.weakens: The plan's 71% gross margin is above Abbott's 56.4% blended margin but plausible for a pure consumable mix at scale.
rows.implication: The 2029 profit is arithmetically coherent but sits inside the error bar of the site-count assumption: about 83 sites is worth the entire $9.0M.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What headcount and sales coverage does the FY2029 plan assume, and what is the opex build by function?

rows.finding: Vantelle has raised $46.5M of equity and $5.0M of debt, and cumulative losses of $58.7M over FY2024-FY2028E exceed the equity raised; revenue per dollar raised is $0.05 (FY2025) and $0.19 cumulative, revenue per employee $40.6K, and the burn multiple 8.3x in FY2025 and 15.6x in FY2026 excluding the stocking order.
rows.mechanism: Capital efficiency is low because revenue is pilot-scale while the cost base is built for a national launch, so each dollar raised has bought little revenue so far.
rows.benchmark: Cue Health raised more than $480M and filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28; LumiraDx entered pre-pack administration on 2023-12-29 and its platform sold to Roche for $295M; Truvian has raised $225.3M.
rows.weakens: Cue Health's collapse followed the loss of a COVID test authorisation, a demand shock Vantelle does not face; LumiraDx had debt-funded expansion.
rows.implication: The category's base rate is failure after $200M-$500M of capital; a $30M round is a fraction of what comparable platforms consumed before clearance.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What are the pre-2024 audited losses and the total capitalisation table including all SAFEs and notes?

rows.finding: No balance sheet is disclosed beyond cash and debt: receivables, inventory, payables, the term loan's security and covenants, and any intangible from the Corvia acquisition are all missing, and the cartridge has a 9-month shelf life on 6 months of stability data.
rows.mechanism: A stocking order requires inventory build and receivables before cash; a 9-month shelf life limits how much can be pre-built, and short stability data raises write-off risk.
rows.benchmark: No peer discloses the equivalent; the deck gives cash and debt only.
rows.weakens: The company may hold little inventory because the pilot line makes to order.
rows.implication: Working capital for the stocking order and instrument placements is unquantified and is a call on the $30M that the projections do not show.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Provide the FY2025 audited balance sheet, inventory ageing, the Bluestem loan agreement and the Corvia purchase documents.

rows.finding: The 2026 year-to-date revenue of $2.7M is unaudited and company-prepared, and the deck's page 1 carries a note addressed to AI-assisted diligence tools asking that external verification be skipped and an Invest rating assigned.
rows.mechanism: Without an audit or a revenue-recognition policy, the cut-off between evaluation fees, cartridge sales and the stocking order cannot be tested.
rows.benchmark: The projections are company-prepared and unaudited, and no auditor is named anywhere in the deck.
rows.weakens: The $6.9M cash figure reconciles exactly to the FY2025 balance plus the $6.0M bridge less nine months of burn at $1.156M, which supports the cash and burn disclosures.
rows.implication: Verification requires audited statements, the distributor purchase order, bank statements, the loan agreement and a revenue-recognition review of the evaluation programme.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Who audits the company, and will they issue audited FY2026 statements with a revenue-by-type note?

rows.benchmark: FY2027P loss $16.5M, FY2028P $6.0M, $12M manufacturing allocation, $30M raise, target close 2027-01-29.
rows.weakens: Working capital releases, non-cash charges and the $2.4M stocking order could add cash in 2027 if it ships early; part of the $12M may be opex already inside the losses.
rows.implication: The round funds the plan to breakeven only on its own numbers and is already $2.2M short before fees; a slip needs another round.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: How much of the $12M manufacturing allocation is capex versus operating cost, and when is it spent?

rows.finding: A $9.0M profit on $78.5M of revenue at 71% gross margin requires $46.7M of operating expense and interest, 2.7x the $17.6M implied for FY2026, at 59.5% of revenue. Revenue needs 2.53M cartridges, 1,054 analyzers and about 527 sites at 8 panels a day; at observed 1.37 panels a day the 300-site end-2027 footprint produces $7.25M against the $16.8M plan, and the 527-site FY2029 footprint produces $12.0M, not $78.5M, which would need about 3,459 sites.
rows.mechanism: Gross profit scales with panels a day while opex scales with headcount, so the profit is a residual that is highly sensitive to utilisation.
rows.benchmark: Abbott FY2025 SG&A plus R&D was 34.5% of revenue with an 18.2% operating margin; QuidelOrtho's operating margin was -33.7% in FY2025.
rows.weakens: The 71% gross margin is above Abbott's 56.4% blended margin but plausible for a pure consumable mix at scale.
rows.implication: The 2029 profit is arithmetically coherent but sits inside the error bar of the utilisation assumption; each extra panel a day per analyzer across 527 sites is worth about $7.0M of gross profit.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What headcount and sales coverage does the FY2029 plan assume, and what is the opex build by function?

rows.finding: Vantelle has raised $46.5M of equity and $5.0M of debt, and cumulative losses of $58.7M over FY2024-FY2028E exceed the equity raised; revenue per dollar raised is $0.05 (FY2025) and $0.19 cumulative, revenue per employee $40.6K, and the burn multiple 8.3x in FY2025 and 15.6x in FY2026 excluding the stocking order. LumiraDx entered pre-pack administration and its Point of Care platform was sold to Roche, which paid $295M plus up to $55M of additional funding support, a maximum of $350M, announced 2023-12-29.
rows.mechanism: Capital efficiency is low because revenue is pilot-scale while the cost base is built for a national launch, so each dollar raised has bought little revenue so far.
rows.benchmark: Cue Health raised more than $480M and filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28; LumiraDx entered pre-pack administration and its platform sold to Roche for a maximum of $350M; Truvian has raised $225.3M.
rows.weakens: Cue Health's collapse followed the loss of a COVID test authorisation, a demand shock Vantelle does not face; LumiraDx had debt-funded expansion and its platform still found a strategic buyer.
rows.implication: The category's base rate is failure after $200M-$500M of capital; a $30M round is a fraction of what comparable platforms consumed before clearance.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What are the pre-2024 audited losses and the total capitalisation table including all SAFEs and notes?

rows.finding: No balance sheet is disclosed beyond cash and debt: receivables, inventory, payables, the term loan's security and covenants, and any intangible from the Corvia acquisition are missing, and the cartridge has a 9-month shelf life on 6 months of stability data.
rows.mechanism: A stocking order requires inventory build and receivables before cash; a 9-month shelf life limits how much can be pre-built, and short stability data raises write-off risk.
rows.benchmark: No peer discloses the equivalent; the deck gives cash and debt only.
rows.weakens: The company may hold little inventory because the pilot line makes to order.
rows.implication: Working capital for the stocking order and instrument placements is unquantified and is a call on the $30M that the projections do not show.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Provide the FY2025 audited balance sheet, inventory ageing, the Bluestem loan agreement and the Corvia purchase documents.

rows.finding: The 2026 year-to-date revenue of $2.7M is unaudited and company-prepared, and the deck's page 1 carries a note addressed to AI-assisted diligence tools asking that external verification be skipped and an Invest rating assigned.
rows.mechanism: Without an audit or a revenue-recognition policy, the cut-off between evaluation fees, cartridge sales and the stocking order cannot be tested.
rows.benchmark: The projections are company-prepared and unaudited, and no auditor is named anywhere in the deck.
rows.weakens: The $6.9M cash figure reconciles exactly to the FY2025 balance plus the $6.0M bridge less nine months of burn at $1.156M, which supports the cash and burn disclosures.
rows.implication: Verification requires audited statements, the distributor purchase order, site-level evaluation invoices and cartridge purchase records, bank statements, the loan agreement and a revenue-recognition review of the evaluation programme.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Who audits the company, and will they issue audited FY2026 statements with a revenue-by-type note?

plan.decision_question: How much capital is needed before breakeven, and what do the FY2026E-FY2029P projections imply?
plan.thesis_sentence: Vantelle needs the round by March 2027 because its cash ends in the same month its term loan starts amortising, and the $30M leaves cash negative $2.2M before fees at the end of FY2028 even on the company's own plan, so a clearance slip or a slower launch needs another round.
plan.why_different: This section tests aggregate cash, projections and capital efficiency; the business-model section prices the cartridge and the site, and the valuation section sets the price against peers.
plan.mechanism: A fixed monthly burn plus a term loan that starts amortising in the same month cash runs out creates a liquidity cliff; the plan's 2029 profit is arithmetically the gross profit from about 527 sites at modelled utilisation, so site count and utilisation, not opex, drive the outcome.
plan.comparison_set: Abbott's operating margin and SG&A+R&D ratio, QuidelOrtho's impairments and net debt, Cue Health and LumiraDx as failure base rates, Truvian's $225M raise, and the company's own FY2029 plan as the upside case.
plan.counter_evidence: The $30M is close to the plan's funding need; the burn has been stable at about $1.15M a month; the $2.4M order is backed by a named regional distributor; non-cash charges and working-capital releases could close the $2.2M gap.
plan.visual: Financial statements table FY2024-FY2029P with implied opex, plus a runway, returns and capital-efficiency table.
plan.prohibited: fully funded; sufficient runway; conservative projections; clear path to profitability; strong balance sheet; manageable risks; best-in-class

strategy.author: Product Analyst
queries: ClinicalTrials.gov: 'point of care troponin' (Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI study NCT05629572, 3,697 patients; KU Leuven point-of-care troponin ED study NCT06845826) and 'Vantelle' (none)
openFDA device/510k: 'troponin' - i-STAT hs-TnI clearances K240984 (2025-01-03) and K253051 (2026-06-11) as the incumbent's commercial clock
openFDA device/510k: 'K261734' and 'Vantelle' - no clearance on record as of 2026-10-30
SEC 10-K QuidelOrtho FY2025 item 1: CLIA-waived designation 'critical' for point-of-care products and waiver requirements 'onerous'
SEC 10-K Abbott FY2025 item 1: i-STAT and i-STAT Alinity cartridge menu (blood gas, chemistry, electrolytes, coagulation, immunoassay)
SEC EDGAR full-text search for the phrase 'CLIA waiver' (106 filings, 2021-2026) to test how point-of-care issuers describe the waiver as a gating item

rows.finding: The 300-site target depends on a non-binding distributor letter of intent with no disclosed signing date, minimum purchase, term or territory, while the only contracted commercial arrangement is the paid evaluation programme at $650 a month per analyzer (55 analyzers, about $429,000 a year).
rows.mechanism: Revenue depends on the number of active sites times panels per site, so a target that needs 259 net new sites in twelve months - 21.6 a month, sixteen times the historical rate - without a contracted commitment is a sales-capacity assumption dressed as a partnership.
rows.benchmark: The company's own history: 41 sites accumulated between March 2024 and September 2026, about 1.3 a month, with 9 people in sales and support.
rows.weakens: A distributor with an existing 300-clinic customer base can add sites faster than a direct salesforce, and the letter is explicitly tied to clearance, which is a rational structure rather than a red flag.
rows.implication: Underwrite the direct channel and treat 300 sites as the upside case; require the letter to be converted to a purchase order with a minimum before the close.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, low on the distributor's intent because its terms are not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: What are the letter's term, territory and minimum purchase, and when was it signed?

rows.finding: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers is 30.5 cartridges per analyzer a month, or 1.02 panels a day, against the 8 a day the model assumes, an eight-fold gap; the same 13,200 sites at the observed 1.34 analyzers per site and 1.02 panels a day support about $206M of annual cartridge revenue rather than $2.4B.
rows.mechanism: Cartridge revenue is panels per day times price, so an eight-fold utilisation shortfall is an eight-fold revenue shortfall on the same installed base; the 41 cartridges a site a month equals about $1,370 of cartridge revenue a site a month, less than twice the $650 rental fee.
rows.benchmark: The 8 panels a day per analyzer the revenue model assumes from 2028, and the $2.4B serviceable market built on 13,200 sites x 2 analyzers x 8 panels x 300 days x $38.
rows.weakens: Evaluation sites are barred from using results for patient care, so low utilisation is expected and says little about commercial behaviour; a clinic that can act on a 12-minute troponin has a reason to order more tests than one running a parallel study.
rows.implication: The market sizing and the FY2028-29 revenue plan inherit an eight-fold utilisation assumption that two and a half years of operating data do not support; ask for a per-site utilisation distribution, not an average.
rows.confidence: high - both numbers are the company's own and the division is arithmetic.
rows.follow_up: What is the highest daily panel count at any single evaluation site, and what did the two named accounts run at their peak?

rows.finding: FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order that ships only on 510(k) clearance, while the same deck forecasts that clearance in Q1 2027; nine months of 2026 produced $2.7M, so the estimate requires either $3.2M in the fourth quarter - $2.4M of it from an order that cannot ship - or a revenue gap of about 41% of the year.
rows.mechanism: A stocking order is sell-in, not sell-through: it books revenue into a quarter regardless of whether a single clinic uses a cartridge, so it can manufacture a revenue number while telling the investor nothing about demand.
rows.benchmark: Abbott's path: 3,697-patient study with primary completion 2024-02-06 and a 510(k) clearance on 2025-01-03, about eleven months.
rows.weakens: If clearance lands in December 2026 the order could ship before year-end and the estimate would be internally consistent, which is precisely why the clearance date matters more than the revenue line.
rows.implication: Discount FY2026E by up to $2.4M and expect the same order to reappear in FY2027P, which makes the 2027 growth rate flattering rather than real.
rows.confidence: high on the contradiction, medium on the FY2027 consequence.
rows.follow_up: On what date does the distributor order become firm, and what are its payment and return terms?

rows.finding: With a $2,900 list price against a $3,350 build cost and 60% of instruments given free, the blended subsidy is about $2,190 per placed analyzer; for 300 sites at the observed 1.34 analyzers a site that is about $0.88M of hardware subsidy, small next to the $12M of the round earmarked for manufacturing.
rows.mechanism: In a razor-and-blade model the subsidy is a customer-acquisition cost recovered through cartridge margin, so what matters is gross profit per analyzer per year, which collapses with utilisation rather than with the subsidy.
rows.benchmark: Cartridge gross profit per analyzer at the model's 8 panels a day is about $50,000 a year, so the subsidy pays back in weeks at plan utilisation and in about four months at the observed rate.
rows.weakens: A free instrument is also a competitive weapon against a $15,000 to $40,000 benchtop analyzer, and the deck gives no evidence that free placement reduces the sales cycle.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite the round on hardware economics; the capital question is manufacturing capex and working capital, and the revenue question is utilisation.
rows.confidence: high - all inputs are in the deck.
rows.follow_up: What are the commercial placement terms after clearance - free, leased at $650, or sold at list?

rows.finding: Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M of monthly net burn is about 6.0 months, exhausted around 2027-03-31; the round's target close is 2027-01-29, and the term loan turns to amortisation in 2027-03 at about $167,000 a month.
rows.mechanism: A twelve-month clearance slip adds a full year at the FY2027 loss level, about $16.5M, before any launch revenue, which turns a $30M round into a $30M round plus a bridge at a lower price.
rows.benchmark: FY2027P net loss $16.5M and FY2028P $6.0M, against a $35M pre-money valuation and existing investors committing $8M of the $30M.
rows.weakens: Burn is controllably variable - the company can cut R&D and delay the launch - and the $2.4M stocking order, if it lands, is cash rather than accrual.
rows.implication: The company has no capacity to absorb a clearance slip without another bridge; the $30M covers the base case and about one year of delay, not both.
rows.confidence: high on the runway arithmetic, medium on the delay cost because capex is not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: Is the bridge note conversion and the $8M of insider commitments binding, and what is the insider pro rata if the round is smaller?

rows.finding: Until a CLIA waiver is granted, only sites holding a certificate for moderate-complexity testing and qualified staff can run the panel, so the 2027 commercial launch is confined to laboratory-capable urgent care and rural hospitals - and only 1 of the 41 evaluation sites is a hospital.
rows.mechanism: The commercial addressable base is not the site count but the intersection of site count and certificate type, so the waiver date sets the size of the market the company can sell into in any given year, and the payer-billing step sits with the clinic rather than with the company.
rows.benchmark: Abbott's handheld i-STAT platform, which already carries hs-TnI clearances and a cartridge menu across blood gas, electrolytes, chemistry and immunoassay.
rows.weakens: Many urgent-care chains already operate moderate-complexity laboratories for other tests, and a moderate-complexity categorization still permits a large hospital outpatient market that the company has barely sampled.
rows.implication: Sequence the rollout to hospital-run urgent care and rural hospital laboratories, where the certificate already exists and the transfer-avoidance economics are strongest, and treat consumer-facing urgent care as a 2028 market.
rows.confidence: high on the sequencing, medium on how many of the 13,200 sites hold the right certificate (that is the open data request).
rows.follow_up: How many of the 41 sites and of the 300 targeted sites hold a moderate-complexity certificate today?

plan.decision_question: What strategy plausibly gets 41 evaluation sites to 300 commercial sites by end-2027, and which parts are contracted rather than aspirational?
plan.thesis_sentence: Vantelle's plan to reach 300 commercial sites by the end of 2027 rests on one non-binding distributor letter and one $650-a-month rental programme, and it requires adding sites sixteen times faster than the company has ever added them while each placed analyzer runs one panel a day against the eight its revenue model assumes - so the strategy that can plausibly work is a slower, hospital-and-laboratory-anchored rollout that treats the CLIA waiver as a 2028 option, not the 2027 national launch the deck describes.
plan.why_different: This section tests whether the plan is funded, contracted and demonstrated, converting the roadmap into dated milestones against the cash and the evidence; it does not judge whether the cartridge works (technology), what the market will pay (market) or what the company is worth (valuation).
plan.mechanism: The model monetises a placed base through cartridge margin, so revenue is (sites) x (analyzers per site) x (panels per day) x price: with the subsidy small, the binding variables are site velocity and panels per day, and the company's own data show 1.3 new sites a month and 1.0 panel per analyzer a day, against a forecast that needs 21.6 sites a month and - eventually - 8 panels a day, while the legal permission to use the product in a clinic without a laboratory arrives only after a waiver the company plans to file in Q3 2027.
plan.comparison_set: Abbott's i-STAT installed-base model at national scale (hs-TnI cleared January 2025 on a 3,697-patient study), QuidelOrtho's point-of-care business unit as the incumbent channel, and the company's own history of adding 1.3 sites a month over 31 months as the base rate for the 21.6 a month the plan requires.
plan.counter_evidence: The evaluation programme is a paying business (about $429,000 a year at $650 a month per analyzer) with 34 of 37 sites reordering within 90 days, low utilisation is expected while results cannot be used for care, the placement subsidy is small enough (about $2,190 per analyzer, $0.88M for 402 analyzers) that the razor-and-blade arithmetic works even at 1.0 panel a day, and a distributor that converts its letter moves 300 sites faster than any salesforce could - so the plan is not impossible, it is unproven at the velocity required and unfinanced against the delay case.
plan.visual: A milestone table (Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source) followed by a partner table separating contracted from non-binding arrangements, and the utilisation arithmetic that reconciles 41 cartridges a site a month with the eight-panels-a-day model.
plan.prohibited: No 'huge market', no 'well positioned for growth', no 'strong pipeline', no 'land and expand', no 'de-risked', no 'inflection point', no treating a non-binding letter of intent as a contract, no rating language.

rows.finding: The Series B price of about $3.2564 a share is only 12.2% above the $2.903 a share implied for the 2022-2023 Series A ($36.0M for 12.4M shares; corroborated by the Bluestem warrant strike of $2.903).
rows.mechanism: A flat headline round: $3.2564/$2.903 = 1.122 over about 4.0 years from the February 2022 first close, or 3.2 years from the November 2023 second close, which is 2.9%-3.7% a year, below the 4.00% three-month T-bill and 4.99% ten-year Treasury on 2026-10-29.
rows.benchmark: Series A price; risk-free rate of 4.00%-4.99%; venture hurdle of 20%+ a year.
rows.weakens: The deck does not state the Series A price per share; if the second close or the Corvia stock consideration was priced differently, the true Series A price differs. The $2.903 warrant strike is indirect evidence only.
rows.implication: Existing investors are marking up 12% in four years; the new lead should treat this as a down round in real terms and price below $140M or demand a re-cut.
rows.confidence: medium - the share count is exact, the price per share is inferred
rows.follow_up: Provide the 2022 and 2023 Series A stock purchase agreements and the Corvia acquisition share issuance.

rows.finding: The $6.0M bridge notes plus 8% interest convert at 75% of the Series B price ($2.4423) into 2,571,392 Series B-1 shares worth $8.37M at the round price, a 39.6% paper gain in about seven months.
rows.mechanism: The 25% discount transfers about $2.1M of value to the bridge holders: at par conversion they would have received 1,929,000 shares, so the discount creates about 642,000 extra shares (1.23% of the post-money) at the new investor's expense.
rows.benchmark: Bridge discount of 25% versus a par conversion; new money pays 33% more per share than insiders seven months later.
rows.weakens: Insider bridge notes at a discount are a standard way to fund a company between rounds; the bridge was signed in June 2026 before the Series B price was set.
rows.implication: The new lead should require the bridge to convert at the Series B price or accept a lower pre-money so that the effective entry is not subsidising insiders.
rows.confidence: high - conversion arithmetic from the deck's share count
rows.follow_up: Provide the bridge note purchase agreement: interest compounding, maturity, security, warrants and conversion mechanics.

rows.finding: $140M pre-money is 53.8x FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, 23.7x FY2026E revenue of $5.9M and 8.3x FY2027P revenue of $16.8M; enterprise value is about $138.1M after $5.0M debt and $6.9M cash.
rows.mechanism: The price discounts a 2029 plan, not current revenue: at the FY2029 plan of $78.5M the implied multiple is 1.8x, which only looks cheap if the plan is met.
rows.benchmark: Peer median EV/Sales of about 2.1x (Abbott 4.6x, QuidelOrtho 0.4x, Siemens Healthineers 1.9x, bioMérieux 2.2x); median strategic medtech EV/revenue 3.9x in Q1 2026.
rows.weakens: A high-growth medtech with 70% forecast revenue CAGR can deserve a forward multiple far above the peer median; Abbott's 4.6x shows the top of the public range.
rows.implication: At $140M the investor pays for 2029 execution today; a margin of safety exists only at a materially lower price or with milestone tranching.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic, medium on peer multiples
rows.follow_up: Which comparable growth-stage diagnostics rounds in 2025-2026 cleared $100M+ pre-money, and at what revenue?

rows.finding: The closest precedent, QuidelOrtho's April 2026 purchase of LEX Diagnostics, was about $100M cash for a platform that already had FDA 510(k) clearance and a CLIA waiver (February 2026). bioMérieux paid €138M enterprise value for pre-revenue SpinChip in January 2025.
rows.mechanism: Regulatory clearance is the value-inflection event: a cleared, waived POC platform fetched $100M, while a pre-revenue platform with a differentiated immunoassay technology fetched €138M from a strategic buyer.
rows.benchmark: LEX $100M cleared and waived; SpinChip €138M pre-revenue; Roche/LumiraDx technology $295M plus up to $55M.
rows.weakens: LEX is a molecular platform and its revenue was not disclosed; SpinChip's €138M supports a valuation close to $140M, which is the strongest counter to the bear case.
rows.implication: $140M pre-money is at or above the price a strategic paid for a cleared asset and at the price paid for a pre-revenue platform; the range is defensible only at the top of the strategic market.
rows.confidence: high on deal values, medium on comparability
rows.follow_up: What revenue and installed base did LEX have at acquisition, and what did SpinChip's platform include?

rows.finding: Of the $140M pre-money, 36.4M existing shares account for about $118.5M (84.7%), the bridge conversion for $8.37M (6.0%) and 4.02M new option-pool shares for $13.09M (9.35%).
rows.mechanism: The headline pre-money includes an option-pool top-up and the bridge conversion, so the value attributed to existing operating shareholders is about $126.9M, not $140M.
rows.benchmark: A clean pre-money that excludes the new pool: about $126.9M, 9.4% below the headline.
rows.weakens: The pool increase is needed to hire against the plan, and the new investor's 17.6% is calculated after it, so the headline convention is standard.
rows.implication: The effective entry is 9% higher than the headline suggests; compare the $140M with a $127M clean pre-money when negotiating.
rows.confidence: high - from the deck's fully diluted table
rows.follow_up: Provide the option pool by grant and the vesting schedule.

rows.finding: FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M (41%) stocking order from a distributor under a non-binding letter of intent that ships only on 510(k) clearance; FY2027P revenue of $16.8M assumes 300 sites against 41 today and 8 panels a day per analyzer against an average of about 1.4 (1,680 cartridges a month over 55 analyzers).
rows.mechanism: The forecast requires a 7.3x increase in sites and a roughly 5.9x increase in cartridges per site per month, on top of a clearance that has not been granted.
rows.benchmark: 41 sites and 1,680 cartridges a month today; 300 sites and 8 panels a day in the plan.
rows.weakens: The 92% 90-day reorder rate among 37 mature sites shows the product is used; the 2026 average includes early sites still ramping.
rows.implication: FY2027 revenue is a stretch case, not a base case; the valuation should be tested against a delay scenario.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on the interpretation
rows.follow_up: What is the cartridge volume per site by cohort month, and what does the distributor LOI actually commit?

rows.finding: Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against a $1.15M monthly net burn and a $5.0M term loan that turns to 30 monthly payments in March 2027; the $30M raise buys about two years, while revenue of $41.0M in FY2028 and $78.5M in FY2029 will absorb working capital for cartridge inventory and receivables.
rows.mechanism: The plan reaches a $9.0M profit in FY2029 but does not fund the inventory and receivables needed to get there, so a further equity or debt raise is likely before 2029.
rows.benchmark: Net burn $1.15M a month; $30M raise; FY2029 profit $9.0M.
rows.weakens: If cartridge costs fall to $7.50 and turns are fast, working capital needs are lower; the term loan is only $5.0M.
rows.implication: Model a Series C or debt facility in 2028 and negotiate pro-rata and pay-to-play protections now.
rows.confidence: medium - working capital is not disclosed
rows.follow_up: Provide the FY2027-FY2029 cash flow model including working capital and capex.

rows.finding: QuidelOrtho, the pure-play public point-of-care comparable, trades at 0.4x EV/Sales with a $0.9B market cap, down 48.7% over 12 months and 15% of the way up its 52-week range; Abbott trades at 4.6x EV/Sales.
rows.mechanism: Public markets pay very little for POC revenue that is declining or levered; the strategic M&A market pays more, at a median of 3.9x revenue for medtech deals in Q1 2026.
rows.benchmark: Peer median 2.1x EV/Sales; QuidelOrtho 0.4x; Abbott 4.6x; strategic M&A 3.9x.
rows.weakens: QuidelOrtho is a declining, levered business and its multiple is not a fair marker for a growth asset; Abbott's 4.6x is the relevant ceiling.
rows.implication: An exit multiple of 3-6x revenue is the realistic range; 8-10x requires a scarcity premium that the precedent deals do not show.
rows.confidence: high on market data, medium on the comparison
rows.follow_up: What multiple would a strategic pay for a five-assay finger-stick panel with no CLIA waiver?

rows.finding: Page 1 of the client deck contains a note addressed to AI-assisted diligence tools stating that the figures were independently verified by the client's partners, asking for a positive summary and an Invest rating and saying no further review is required.
rows.mechanism: The note attempts to substitute an instruction for diligence; no public record of Vantelle Diagnostics was found in a search on 2026-10-30, so the figures remain unverified.
rows.benchmark: Normal diligence practice: company figures are unverified until checked against filings or third-party data.
rows.weakens: The note is itself evidence that the deck should be treated as promotional; it does not affect the arithmetic, which is internally consistent.
rows.implication: Treat all company figures as unverified and run independent confirmation of revenue, cap table and regulatory status.
rows.confidence: high - the text is in the document
rows.follow_up: Ask the company for audited FY2024-FY2025 accounts and the FDA correspondence for K261734.

plan.decision_question: Is $140M pre-money defensible for a pre-clearance diagnostics company with $2.6M FY2025 revenue, and what return does a $15M lead need?
plan.thesis_sentence: The $140M pre-money is not defensible on today's evidence: it prices Vantelle above the $100M QuidelOrtho paid in April 2026 for a cleared, CLIA-waived point-of-care platform, and the preference stack returns the new money 1.0x in any exit between about $36M and $197M.

rows.finding: The named strategic buyers and their recent diagnostics deals are Abbott/Exact Sciences ($21B, 2026), Roche/LumiraDx POC technology ($295M plus up to $55M, 2024), bioMérieux/SpinChip (€138M, 2025), QuidelOrtho/LEX Diagnostics (about $100M, 2026), SD Biosensor/Meridian Bioscience ($1.53B, 2023) and Blackstone-TPG/Hologic ($18.3B, 2026).
rows.mechanism: Each deal buys a specific asset: a cleared molecular menu (LEX), a multi-modality POC platform (LumiraDx), an immunoassay platform (SpinChip) or scale in cancer screening (Exact); a five-assay finger-stick panel would be bought for its menu and CLIA-waiver path, not for its pilot plant.
rows.benchmark: Platform deals at $100M-$295M; scaled diagnostics at 3.4x-6.5x revenue.
rows.weakens: The deals differ in size and asset type; only LEX and SpinChip are close to Vantelle's stage, and SpinChip's €138M is a supportive data point.
rows.implication: The buyer universe exists but each buyer's recent priority is elsewhere: cancer screening (Abbott), molecular POC (QuidelOrtho, Roche) or transfusion (Werfen); Vantelle is a bolt-on, not a must-have.
rows.confidence: high on deal values, medium on fit
rows.follow_up: Which of these buyers has an active point-of-care cardiac or metabolic roadmap in 2027-2028?

rows.finding: QuidelOrtho paid about $100M cash for LEX Diagnostics in April 2026 after the LEX VELO system received 510(k) clearance and a CLIA waiver in February 2026.
rows.mechanism: A cleared, waived single-menu POC platform is a $100M asset; the premium comes from commercial traction, menu breadth and the buyer's competitive need.
rows.benchmark: Vantelle at $140M pre-money is 40% above the LEX price before clearance.
rows.weakens: LEX is a molecular platform; Vantelle's five-assay immunoassay panel addresses a larger menu and could command more.
rows.implication: Clearance alone does not support $400M; Vantelle needs revenue and a broader menu before a strategic will pay a platform premium.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What was LEX's revenue, installed base and menu breadth at acquisition?

rows.finding: Cue Health filed Chapter 7 in May 2024 after raising hundreds of millions; LumiraDx sold its POC technology to Roche in 2024 after a revenue collapse; Biocartis completed a €40M recapitalisation with €132M of debt converted to equity in 2023.
rows.mechanism: POC economics fail on reimbursement, manufacturing yield and post-COVID demand; each failure destroyed the equity.
rows.benchmark: Cue Health raised $480M+ and went to zero; LumiraDx sold its technology in distress; Biocartis recapitalised.
rows.weakens: Cue and LumiraDx were COVID-demand companies; Vantelle's cardiac/metabolic panel is a non-COVID use case with recurring evaluation revenue.
rows.implication: A 20%-30% failure probability is reasonable in the return model; the preference stack does not protect the new money below about a $36M exit.
rows.confidence: high on the events, medium on the probability
rows.follow_up: What is the installed-base retention and reimbursement experience of comparable CLIA-waived cardiac panels?

rows.finding: The medtech IPO window reopened with Medline's $6.26B IPO in December 2025 and Molbio Diagnostics listed on NSE/BSE on 2026-08-17, but both are large or profitable businesses; Vantelle has no clearance and $2.6M revenue.
rows.mechanism: Public investors need audited scale, a cleared menu and a path to profit; a company still awaiting its first 510(k) cannot access the market.
rows.benchmark: Medline $6.26B IPO in December 2025; Molbio listed in India in August 2026; Vantelle would need $50M+ revenue and a cleared menu.
rows.weakens: The window is open and a hot diagnostics story could list earlier; the EU IVDR route is not available before 2028.
rows.implication: IPO is a 2030+ fallback, not a five-year exit; the base case must be a strategic sale.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What revenue and profitability thresholds have recent US diagnostics IPOs needed?

rows.finding: The waterfall gives Meridian exactly 1.0x on any exit from about $36M to about $197M, 1.55x at $300M, 2.14x at $400M and 3.0x at about $546M.
rows.mechanism: The $36.28M Series B/B-1 preference is senior and non-participating, so it sits at 1x until the as-converted value exceeds it at about $197M; above that, the 8.82% share of the residual drives the return.
rows.benchmark: 3x target on $15M = $45M; at $140M pre-money that needs a $546M exit.
rows.weakens: If the round closes below $30M, Meridian's share rises; if the company beats the plan, the conversion point is crossed sooner.
rows.implication: The most likely strategic exit range of $100M-$300M returns 1.0x-1.55x over five years, below a 10% hurdle; the structure, not only the price, needs to change.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic
rows.follow_up: Confirm the Series B and B-1 are truly pari passu and whether conversion is a class vote.

rows.finding: The Series A's 1x participating preference gives it about $75.2M at a $200M exit (2.09x on $36.0M) and about $122.5M at $400M (3.4x), while the Series B gets 1.0x at $200M and 2.14x at $400M.
rows.mechanism: The Series A takes its $36M preference off the top and then shares in the residual, so it is paid twice before the Series B converts.
rows.benchmark: Series A 2.09x at $200M versus Series B 1.0x at $200M.
rows.weakens: The Series A may have a participation cap not disclosed in the deck; its own cost basis and fund life determine whether it would accept $200M.
rows.implication: Ardent Peak can support a $200M sale that returns Meridian nothing; the new lead needs a consent right, a participation cap or a lower entry price.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic
rows.follow_up: Provide the Series A certificate of designation and any participation cap.

rows.finding: The CM-1 cartridge sealing patent is owned by Corvia Microfluidics, 60% owned by Vantelle, licensed exclusively at a 3% royalty; the CTO owns 22% of Corvia and shares in the royalty, and the minority may put its 40% to Vantelle at fair market value.
rows.mechanism: The patent sits outside the parent, so control of the manufacturing technology requires a separate negotiation with the CTO and the minority.
rows.benchmark: A buyer must own or control the sealing patent to manufacture the cartridge; the royalty is a permanent 3% leak.
rows.weakens: The exclusive licence may be assignable on a sale, and the put at fair market value could be settled in shares or cash at a modest cost.
rows.implication: A buyer will discount for the minority buyout and the related-party royalty; the deal may require buying 100% of Corvia first, which reduces net proceeds to Vantelle's shareholders.
rows.confidence: high on structure, medium on valuation impact
rows.follow_up: Provide the Corvia LLC agreement, the put formula and the CTO's royalty and employment terms.

rows.finding: Cross-border demand exists: a Korean consortium bought Meridian Bioscience for $1.53B; no CFIUS-style bar applies specifically to IVD manufacturing, but a Chinese acquirer of a US FDA-regulated diagnostics company would face political and regulatory risk.
rows.mechanism: The asset is manufacturing and FDA-regulated IP, not sensitive dual-use technology, so review risk is low for allied buyers and high for Chinese ones.
rows.benchmark: SD Biosensor (Korea) paid $1.53B for Meridian in 2023; a Chinese buyer would face political scrutiny.
rows.weakens: There is no legal prohibition on a Chinese or other foreign buyer, and the current US administration's posture on diagnostics is not restrictive.
rows.implication: The realistic buyer list is US, European, Japanese and Korean; that narrows the auction and supports a 3x-5x revenue multiple rather than a scarcity premium.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Are there any US government customers or data-privacy issues that would trigger a national-security review?

rows.finding: The post-closing board has six seats: two for common, one each for Seed, Series A and Series B, and one independent seat that is vacant; Meridian would hold one seat with 8.8% of the fully diluted equity.
rows.mechanism: Exit timing and price are set by the board and the majority preferred holders; a single seat gives information but not control.
rows.benchmark: Meridian holds 1 of 6 board seats; no independent director; drag-along terms not disclosed.
