plan.decision_question: Should Meridian Capital Ventures lead a $30.0M Series B with $15.0M at a $140.0M pre-money valuation and take a board seat?
plan.thesis_sentence: At $140.0M pre-money Meridian's $15.0M is a loan priced as equity - 1.0x until a $196.7M exit - against a regulatory record that does not evidence the submission the valuation rests on, so the case is a pass at the ask and a conditional investment only below $110.0M once FDA confirms the filing.
plan.why_different: It links the regulatory record, observed utilisation and the liquidation waterfall into one decision rule; the other sections cover each dimension separately.
plan.mechanism: The preference stack converts the equity into a 1x claim until a $196.7M exit, while utilisation and the CLIA waiver determine whether the revenue plan that justifies a higher exit ever exists.
plan.comparison_set: Venture medtech EV/Sales by stage (18.3x Series A, 8.5x Series C), public diagnostics peer median 2.05x, LEX $100M, SpinChip EUR 138M, LumiraDx $353.5M, Cue Health Chapter 7.
plan.counter_evidence: Strategics pay for platforms before revenue; 41 paid sites with a 92% reorder rate are a real beachhead; a competitive auction could clear $300M-$400M.
plan.visual: Scenarios table plus the analogs table and the key-assumptions table.
plan.prohibited: No 'strong team', 'huge market', 'clear leader', 'well positioned', 'risks are manageable' or vague counts; no sentence about how the section is written.

user_data_requests.database: USPTO Patent Center / PatentsView and EPO Register
user_data_requests.query: Prosecution status and claims for US 16/884,327, US 17/662,019, US 19/318,770, PCT/US2026/014022 and US 15/707,915: filing and grant dates, current status (including the appeal or abandonment status of 17/662,019 after the 2026-07 final rejection and the response deadline), assignee of record, the European family member of 16/884,327, and the claim text of the granted claims of 16/884,327 and 15/707,915.
user_data_requests.why: The patent table in the technology section rests on the company's own summary. A final rejection on the five-assay reader is the difference between a protected platform and one whose reader can be copied, and the licensing and ownership structure around 15/707,915 (a 60%-owned subsidiary whose minority owner is the CTO) is a related-party term the investor should verify. The six-month window after a final rejection means the appeal decision falls around the Series B close, so its status is a closing condition question.
user_data_requests.how: In USPTO Patent Center (patentcenter.uspto.gov) open each application number and save the "Application Data" and "Documents" tabs; for 17/662,019 also save the final rejection and any notice of appeal. For PCT/US2026/014022 use WIPO Patentscope. For the European member of 16/884,327 use the EPO Register. Screenshots or the patent number of the European member are enough.

user_data_requests.database: FDA 510(k) database and CLIA waiver database (accessdata.fda.gov)
user_data_requests.query: The 510(k) record and decision-summary documents for K261734, for the predicates the panel will be measured against (at minimum K240984 and K253051, the i-STAT hs-TnI cartridges), and the CLIA complexity categorisation of each of the five Vantelle assays; plus the current CLIA waiver list entry, if any.
user_data_requests.why: The deck's central commercial claim is that clinic staff without laboratory training can run the panel. Whether the first two assays are cleared as waived or moderate complexity decides whether the 2027 launch addresses CLIA-waived urgent care at all, which is most of the 13,200-site market the deck sizes. The decision summaries also show what evidence FDA accepted for the closest predicate (sample type, imprecision, patient count), which is the benchmark the internal single-site study has to be read against. Without these records the launchable-market estimate and the accuracy comparison rest on the company's own summary.
user_data_requests.how: Search accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpmn/pmn.cfm?ID=K261734 and the same page for K240984 and K253051, and download the decision summary PDF from each; for the CLIA status use the FDA CLIA database at accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfCLIA/search.cfm and search each assay name and the applicant name. A saved PDF or the pasted text of each summary is enough.

user_data_requests.database: CMS CLIA laboratory registry (data.cms.gov, Provider of Services / CLIA file)
user_data_requests.query: Count of CLIA-certified laboratories by certificate type (Certificate of Waiver vs Certificate of Compliance vs Certificate of Accreditation) in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, and nationally, with a breakdown of urgent-care and physician-office locations where the file allows it.
user_data_requests.why: Until a CLIA waiver is granted, the panel can only be run by a laboratory holding a certificate for moderate-complexity testing with qualified staff. If most urgent-care sites in the three launch states hold only a Certificate of Waiver, the 2027 commercial launch addresses a small slice of the market the deck sizes, and the 300-site target cannot be met before the waiver is granted. The split by certificate type is the single number that turns the CLIA question into arithmetic.
user_data_requests.how: Download the CLIA laboratory file from data.cms.gov (Provider Data Catalog, "CLIA Labs") as CSV and filter by state and certificate type; a pivot table of state x certificate type is enough.

user_data_requests.database: Delaware Division of Corporations; Arizona Corporation Commission; Texas Secretary of State; Irish Companies Registration Office
user_data_requests.query: Entity records for Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. (Delaware: file number, 2018-03-12 formation date, registered agent, current good standing, and any prior names); Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC (Arizona, formed 2022-05-09); Corvia Microfluidics LLC (Texas, formed 2016-02-01, plus its LLC company agreement and the 2021 stock purchase of the 60% interest); Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited (CRO number and filings).
user_data_requests.why: The Delaware free register is a session-based form that returns only name, file number, formation date and registered agent, so the parent's 2018-03-12 incorporation date, current status and any prior names are unconfirmed. The Corvia agreement governs the 40% minority's royalty, its put at fair market value and the CTO's 22% stake - the largest single transfer of value in the structure, worth an estimated $4M-$7M at exit.
user_data_requests.how: Order a Delaware certificate of status and long-form certified copy through the Division of Corporations or a registered agent (about $50-$200); pull the Arizona and Texas entity profiles online; request the CRO company search print for the Irish entity; ask the company for the Corvia LLC agreement and 2021 purchase documents from the data room.

user_data_requests.database: UCC lien registries (Delaware Secretary of State; Arizona Secretary of State) and the Bluestem Venture Lending loan file
user_data_requests.query: UCC-1 financing statements naming Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. or Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC as debtor, 2024-01 to 2026-10, including Bluestem Venture Lending and any other secured party; the $5.0M term loan agreement of 2024-03 with its covenants, security interest, warrant terms and any MAC or minimum-liquidity clause.
user_data_requests.why: The deck discloses a $5.0M term loan but not whether it is secured or what covenants it carries. The loan starts amortising at $166,667 a month in 2027-03, the month the company's cash reaches about zero, so a liquidity covenant could force a default exactly when the new money is meant to fund the launch. A secured lender ahead of the new investor changes the downside case.
user_data_requests.how: Run named-debtor UCC searches in Delaware and Arizona (each about $20-$40 online); ask the company for the executed loan agreement and a payoff letter or covenant compliance certificate.

user_data_requests.database: FDA 510(k) database and the filing's correspondence file (CDRH customer collaboration portal)
user_data_requests.query: The 510(k) acknowledgment letter for Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc.'s troponin I and HbA1c submission, showing the actual K number and filing date; the additional-information request dated 2026-08-21; and any other 510(k) submissions under the applicant name Vantelle Diagnostics.
user_data_requests.why: The number the deck cites for this submission, K261734, is in the FDA database a Class II knee-spacer clearance granted to Total Joint Orthopedics, Inc. on 2026-07-23. If the citations cannot be reconciled, the filing date, the additional-information request and the Q1 2027 clearance that anchors the $140M pre-money are all unverified.
user_data_requests.how: Ask the company to produce the FDA acknowledgment letter and the additional-information letter as PDFs; independent confirmation is available to the submitter or its regulatory agent through CDRH's portal, and the public 510(k) database can be searched by applicant name once the correct K number is known.

user_data_requests.database: CMS NPI registry; Arizona and Texas medical boards; university registrars; RAPS credential directory
user_data_requests.query: NPI and licence records for Dr. Wren Albescu (emergency medicine, Tucson 2011-2017); degree confirmation from Larkfield University School of Medicine and Ashcombe Institute of Technology for Albescu and Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist; state medical licences in Arizona, New Mexico and Texas; Regulatory Affairs Certification status for Grace Oyelaran.
user_data_requests.why: Every founder and executive credential in the deck is company-reported and none could be matched to a public record in this diligence, so founder-market fit and the depth of the regulatory bench are unverified rather than contradicted. The CEO's clinical background and the regulatory VP's certification are the two claims the investment case leans on most.
user_data_requests.how: Query the free CMS NPI registry by first and last name; check the Arizona Medical Board and Texas Medical Board licence lookups; email the two institutions' registrar or verification services for degree confirmation (with the candidate's signed release); confirm RAC status through RAPS.

user_data_requests.query: Audited financial statements for FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 and the unaudited September 2026 interim accounts, with revenue split by type and customer, the balance sheet, the Bluestem Venture Lending loan agreement (rate, security, covenants, amortisation), the 2026 bridge note documents and the Corvia Microfluidics purchase and licence agreements.
user_data_requests.why: Cash, burn and the $2.4M stocking order are all unaudited and company-prepared; without the audit, the loan terms and the balance sheet the runway, working-capital need and the FY2026 revenue cut-off cannot be verified, and the report's forecast confidence stays low.
user_data_requests.how: Ask the company to upload the documents to the data room before the IC meeting; an auditor's name and consent to speak to them would also settle the revenue-recognition question.

user_data_requests.database: Southwest Clinical Supply purchase order and payer contracts
user_data_requests.query: The purchase order or supply agreement behind the $2.4M stocking order (volume, price, shipment trigger, cancellation and return rights) and any written coverage or rate confirmations from commercial payers for the five-test panel in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico.
user_data_requests.why: The order is described only as a non-binding letter of intent, and the clinic's ability to reorder depends on payer rates that are not disclosed; both determine whether FY2026 revenue is $3.5M or $5.9M and whether the cartridge price is recoverable.
user_data_requests.how: Request the signed purchase order and the distributor's letter of intent from the company, and payer coverage policies or fee schedules from the three largest commercial payers in the target states.

user_data_requests.database: Vantelle Diagnostics data room (private company documents)
user_data_requests.query: Series A stock purchase agreements for the 2022-02 first close and 2023-11 second close (price per share for each); the 2026-06-30 bridge note purchase agreement (interest, maturity, security, conversion, class vote); the fully diluted cap table by holder and grant; the certificate of incorporation and Series A/B certificates of designation (participation cap, drag-along, protective provisions, liquidation waterfall); the Corvia Microfluidics LLC agreement and the 40% minority put terms; audited FY2024-FY2025 accounts. These also determine the exit waterfall in section 12.
user_data_requests.why: The $140M valuation and the return in a $100M-$200M exit depend on the Series A price per share, the bridge conversion and the preference stack. The deck gives aggregate share counts, not the executed terms; without them the implied $2.903 Series A price and the 1.0x floor are unverified and the price negotiation has no legal baseline.
user_data_requests.how: Ask Vantelle's interim CFO, Darnell Whitcombe, to upload executed copies to the data room under NDA, or provide them directly to Meridian Capital Ventures' diligence team.

user_data_requests.database: FDA MAUDE adverse-event database, FDA warning letters database, FDA device recall database and FDA CLIA waiver database
user_data_requests.query: Search "Vantelle Diagnostics", "Vantelle Q5", "Corvia Microfluidics" and the principals' prior employers, "Quillon Diagnostics" and "Pellucid Biosystems", for adverse events, warning letters, recalls and any CLIA waiver (CW) decision. Also search the CLIA waiver database for any high-sensitivity troponin or five-assay point-of-care panel waiver.
user_data_requests.why: Confirms whether the company or its principals have a product-safety or enforcement record, and whether any high-sensitivity troponin assay has ever been CLIA-waived. The absence of such a record is currently unverified because these FDA databases are not reachable through the available tools, and it changes the quality-system and CLIA-waiver probability in the ESG and regulatory analysis.
user_data_requests.how: FDA MAUDE: accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfMAUDE/search.CFM. FDA warning letters: fda.gov/drugs/enforcement-activities-fda/warning-letters-database (device letters via CDRH). FDA CLIA waiver decision summaries: fda.gov/about-fda/cdrh-transparency/clia-waiver-application-decision-summaries. Export the search results as PDF or CSV with dates.

user_data_requests.database: State corporate registries (Delaware Division of Corporations, Arizona Corporation Commission, Texas Secretary of State, New Mexico Secretary of State), state laboratory licensure and CLIA certificate records (Texas DSHS, Arizona DHS, New Mexico Department of Health) and federal/state court dockets (PACER, Delaware Court of Chancery, Arizona, Texas and New Mexico superior courts)
user_data_requests.query: For Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc., Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC, Corvia Microfluidics LLC and Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited: confirm entity status, officers, directors and any liens or judgments; confirm any litigation involving Vantelle, Corvia or Dr. Wren Albescu and Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist; and confirm whether a CLIA Certificate of Waiver, Certificate of Compliance or state laboratory licence is required in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico for clinic staff to run a five-assay finger-stick panel.
user_data_requests.why: The corporate records would test the governance disclosures (board, related-party royalty, Corvia minority put) and reveal any litigation; the laboratory-licensure records determine whether the 300-site launch can use clinic staff without a CLIA waiver and whether state rules add a launch gate beyond FDA. These are material to the ESG and policy sections and could not be checked without registry access.
user_data_requests.how: Delaware ICIS entity search (icis.corp.delaware.gov); Arizona Corporation Commission eCorp; Texas SOS SOSDirect; New Mexico SOS portal; state health-department laboratory licensing pages and CMS CLIA laboratory lookup; PACER for federal dockets. Provide entity filings, officer/director lists, litigation captions and the state licensure requirements for point-of-care testing by non-laboratory staff.

user_data_requests.database: Commercial payer fee schedules (Texas and Arizona) and CMS Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule 2026
user_data_requests.query: 2026 payment for CPT 84484, 83880, 83036, 82565 and 84132 under Medicare CLFS and under the leading Texas and Arizona commercial payers; whether the five tests may be billed together by an urgent care and at what allowed amount.
user_data_requests.why: The clinic's spread between the cartridge price ($33.40) and the payer payment decides whether in-sourcing pays and therefore whether the observed 1.02-1.37 panels a day rises after clearance. Only the troponin Medicare rate ($12.47) was obtained; without the other four rates and commercial contracts, the adoption rate and the $2.41B versus $206M market estimate cannot be settled.
user_data_requests.how: Download the CMS CLFS 2026 Q4 file from cms.gov and obtain the provider fee schedules or reimbursement policies for the five CPT codes (84484, 83880, 83036, 82565, 84132) from the two or three largest commercial payers in Texas and Arizona, via the client's payer-relations contact or the payers' provider portals.

user_data_requests.database: Vantelle evaluation-site billing records (company data room)
user_data_requests.query: Five evaluation-site invoices, including two sites that received a free instrument, plus monthly cartridge purchase history by site from January 2026 to September 2026: cartridge units, realised price per cartridge, lease payments, and any free-instrument terms.
user_data_requests.why: The 60% free-instrument rate means at most about 16 of 41 sites pay the $650 monthly fee, so the $3.14M lease component of the $7.25M near-term revenue figure is unverified; the invoices show whether free sites buy enough cartridges to offset the free instrument and what the paid cohort actually pays.
user_data_requests.how: Ask Vantelle's CFO or finance team for five redacted site invoices and a site-level cartridge purchase ledger for 2026-01 to 2026-09.

user_data_requests.database: Vantelle Diagnostics data room (company-held evaluation-programme records)
user_data_requests.query: Invoices for five evaluation sites, including at least two that received their analyzer free, showing the $650 monthly fee and cartridge charges; the monthly cartridge purchase history by site from 2026-01 to 2026-09; and the analyzer placement terms (purchase, free placement or lease).
user_data_requests.why: The deck calls all 41 sites a paid evaluation programme but says 60% received their analyzer free, so it is not disclosed how many sites pay the $650 monthly fee or what the free cohort pays per cartridge. These records decide whether the $1.1M FY2025 evaluation line reconciles (at most about 16 of 41 sites paying would make fees about $170,000, while all 55 analyzers paying would make them $429,000) and whether the 34-of-37 reorder count reflects material volumes rather than single-cartridge reorders.
user_data_requests.how: Ask the company to upload the evaluation invoices, the analyzer placement terms and the monthly cartridge sales ledger by site to the data room before the IC meeting; a site-level revenue export for January to September 2026 is enough.

1.name: Completeness sweep
1.notes:
Completeness sweep: all 15 sections met the depth floor (5,894-8,969 characters, 6+ paragraphs, 8+ figures, 4+ source IDs, dated events, no banned phrases found, no internal working material). The section check carries no rule findings (N1-N4, N6 clean) and every section's evidence gate passed. Fourteen sections were read in full; esg was assessed only through its check (no findings) because its regulatory record is the same FDA and CMS record verified in sections 3, 5 and 10 — the Regulatory Analyst's own section should still be read once before delivery.

Report-level 'rewrite plan: 2 items unresolved': W1 (technology_product) and W2 (competition) are heuristic flags, not content gaps. technology_product already carries patent numbers with dates and status in a table, a named-rival comparison against Abbott i-STAT with evidence scale and operator, and an explicit economic reading ('Economically the Q5 is a reagent-margin business whose margin rests on the one assay the company has not proven'). No rewrite is warranted; only the register verification above. W2 is addressed by the share-denominator item.

Shape and sources: the report's strongest feature is that independent records (FDA, CMS fee schedule, FDA clearance database, SEC filings, transaction sources) are used to contradict or bound company claims, and every company figure is labelled unverified. The weakest by evidence density is team, where every CV fact is company-only and no register was queried, though the null-result caveat is stated honestly.

2.name: Claim verification
2.notes:
Claim verification. Verified against independent records: FDA 510(k) K261734 is Total Joint Orthopedics' Klassic Infection Spacer System cleared 2026-07-23 (S191, S193) and FDA holds no Vantelle record; Abbott's hs-TnI clearances (S17 2025-01-03, S13 2026-06-11); Medicare 2026 rates $12.47 troponin and $9.49 HbA1c (S177, S178); public peer multiples (S4, S8, S213, S214); precedent transactions (S204, S205, S171); the deck's page-1 instruction recorded as a finding rather than followed (N8 clean); no OCR-derived claims.

Company-only and correctly labelled as unverified in sections 6-11: 41 evaluation sites, 1,680 cartridges a month, 34 of 37 reorders, $33.40 and $16.20 unit economics, FY2026 revenue of $5.9M including the stocking order, cash of $6.9M and $1.15M monthly burn, the cap table and preference stack, the Corvia royalty and put, the 11.8% troponin CV, and the Southwest Clinical Supply letter. The N3 gap is confined to the two regulatory dates in technology_product.

Stale or unattributed claims: none material. The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion is dated and its exclusion of the 2026-02-11 troponin chemistry is stated. The 2019 seed price is labelled as inferred. Treasury yields are dated 2026-10-29.

3.name: Missing competitors
3.notes:
Missing-competitor challenge. The section already closes the obvious gaps: it includes the adjacent giants (Abbott, Siemens, Roche, QuidelOrtho, Werfen), the substitute (reference laboratory send-out with a 1-3 day turnaround), the status quo ('no laboratory relationship'), and the base rate (Cue Health Chapter 7, LumiraDx pre-pack). Two blind spots remain and both are commercial, not technical: the waived clinic instrument for the metabolic assays (Afinion) and the Asian cartridge price floor.

Geographic blind spot assessed and not raised as an item: the case is a US launch from Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, the EU is blocked behind IVDR and a staffless Dublin entity until 2028, and the exit market is US-listed diagnostics plus allied buyers (SD Biosensor's $1.53B Meridian Bioscience deal, S216). A Chinese acquirer is correctly excluded on political grounds in section 12.

Academic/lab check: the company's own publications would be the vector; no peer-reviewed Vantelle study appears in the register (the 11.8% CV study is company-run and unpublished), which is already covered by the claim-verification items.

4.name: Product/market fit
4.notes:
Product/market-fit questions the IC will ask, with the report's current answer:
1. Hardest thing about selling: not the instrument (subsidy $2,190 a placement, repaid in 4.4 months at observed utilisation) but the clinic's operating change — CLIA certificate, QC, training, EHR integration, cartridge supply. Report covers this in competition's switching-cost paragraph; the convert-or-not evidence is missing.
2. Budget owner: clinic operator or medical director, who bills the payer; Vantelle never bills. Stated. Unresolved: who pays the $650 monthly lease when the instrument is free, and whether the fee is waived.
3. Sales cycle: not disclosed. 9 sales and support staff, 41 sites in 31 months (1.3 a month), 21.6 a month needed for the 300-site 2027 target.
4. Why adoption is not faster: no clearance, no waiver, no payer recovery for the two-test product, investigational labelling blocks billing. Well evidenced.
5. Lost deals: no record. Which competitor won, and was it reference-lab send-out, i-STAT or do-nothing, is not in the pack.
The strongest PMF counter-evidence in the report is the 92% 90-day reorder rate and the $650 fee; both need the paid/free split before they carry weight, which is why the pass-2 item and this one should be fixed together.

5.name: Number stress-test
5.notes:
Stress-test arithmetic that survives: post-money $170.0M = $140.0M pre-money + the full $30.0M round on 52,204,508 fully diluted shares at $3.2564; the cap table sums to that total and to $76.8M invested; Meridian's $15.0M is 4,606,314 shares, 8.82%; 3x at $546M follows from 45.0/0.0882 + 36.0, and $426M from 45.0/0.115 + 36.0; the $115M-$132M scenario value discounts $232M at 12%-15% over five years; runway $6.9M / $1.15M = 6.0 months to 2027-03-31; burn multiples 8.3x and 15.6x; LTV/CAC 1.2-1.8x at observed utilisation; 1,680/55 = 30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month = 1.02 panels a day; $7,945 per site = 1.35 x 365 x $16.20 after royalty, and $23,835 = three years.

30% worse tests: utilisation 30% below 8 panels a day is still 5.6, which removes about 30% of FY2029 gross profit and pushes the first profit year out; a market 30% smaller takes the observed $206M to $144M and the 300-site curve to about $5M of revenue; a 30% higher unit cost ($21.1 vs $16.20) cuts 2026 gross margin from 51.5% to 37%; a clearance slip of one year adds $16.5M of loss against $6.9M of cash and is an insolvency, not a delay. The thesis survives all of them as a Pass and none of them makes the $140.0M price investable, which is why the recommendation itself is not in question; what fails is the precision of the downside figures quoted in the decision sections.

Price-versus-terms check: the recommendation is Pass at $140.0M and re-engagement at $95.0M-$110.0M. On a $30.0M round Meridian's $15.0M buys 10.7% at $110M pre-money and 12.0% at $95M, so '11.5%' is the $100M midpoint only; state the range in the thesis and the executive summary.

The moat score of 2 (patent protection) and the closing-condition statement about the six-month appeal window both rest on the one status the report treats as decisive.
items.action: Run the register searches and replace the 'unverified' statuses with dated records: filing and grant dates, assignee of record, the 17/662,019 final rejection and any notice of appeal with its deadline, and the EP member of 16/884,327. items.issue: The two computed shares (QuidelOrtho 12.6%, Vantelle 0.01%) divide total company revenue, including QuidelOrtho's laboratory and transfusion lines, by a $21.7B global point-of-care base, and present a revenue share where the section's argument concerns panels and installed base. The limitation is stated, but the denominator and unit as printed invite a comparison the text does not support; 0.01% is below any decision-relevant resolution.
items.action: Define the denominator and unit for each share, split QuidelOrtho's point-of-care revenue out of the $2.73B total or label the figure as a total-revenue share, and add a US urgent-care denominator (the market the plan addresses) even if it must be an estimate with its basis stated. Drop the 0.01% or express it as 'below 0.1%'.
items.evidence_request: QuidelOrtho segment disclosure for point-of-care revenue in the FY2025 10-K; any urgent-care channel size from the company's own survey.

items.issue: Two bases are mixed in the headline multiples: the executive KPI row pairs '$170.0M post-money' with '53.8x FY2025 revenue', but 53.8x is $140.0M pre-money over $2.6M (post-money is 65.4x), and '23.7x FY2026E' is likewise a pre-money multiple on $5.9M that includes the $2.4M stocking order. Funding and valuation uses EV of $138.1M and 53.1x, a third basis for the same comparison against a 2.05x peer median.
items.action: Fix one basis per line and label it (pre-money, post-money or EV), make the peer-median comparison on the same basis, and footnote the basis change between the executive KPI row and the valuation table.

items.issue: The check's 'no investor implication' finding is a heuristic false negative: the section states 'Meridian should not lead at $140.0M', 'a pass at the ask and an option kept below $110.0M' and a four-branch decision tree. Nothing is missing for an IC reader.
items.action: No content change. Do not rewrite the section to satisfy the heuristic; if a machine check must pass, add the phrase 'Meridian should' to the sentence that already carries the recommendation.

items.issue: The report-level 'missing the KPI signal component' finding is also a false negative on the page: the executive summary's ::: kpi block and section 1's ::: kpi block both carry Value, Benchmark and Signal columns. The template's required executive-summary components are verdict, briefing, efficiency, one-question and takeaways; kpi is a section-1 component.
items.action: No restructuring. Keep the section-1 ::: kpi as the required component and treat the finding as a name or placement heuristic; do not add a third KPI table.

items.issue: The 510(k) filing date of 2026-05-18 and the FDA information request of 2026-08-21 are stated as fact in technology_product, and the December 2026 answer and Q1 2027 decision are built on them, but FDA's database holds no Vantelle record and no other source exists. The status is given in the thesis ('cannot be checked') but not in the section that carries the regulatory timeline, so a reader of section 3 takes the dates as verified when they rest only on the deck — the specific breach the case turns on.
items.action: Label both dates as company data, unverified, in technology_product as the thesis already does, and tie them to the acknowledgment letter: state that no public record supports the filing date or the request and that the letter is the only evidence that will settle it. Do not present the answer deadline as a schedule until the letter is seen.
items.evidence_request: FDA acknowledgment letter showing the actual submission number and filing date, and the additional-information letter dated 2026-08-21 (submittable through CDRH's portal by the company or its regulatory agent).

items.issue: The report uses '41 paid evaluation sites' and a $650 monthly fee as a willingness-to-pay signal in sections 6, 9 and 11, while section 6 also states that 60% of evaluation instruments were given away free, and section 10 reduces the 92% reorder rate to '34 of 37 sites placing a second order, a binary measure' with no quantity or dollars. As printed, the paid claim and the free claim cannot both be read literally, and the reorder rate is doing work it cannot support.
items.action: State the paid/free split explicitly: how many of the 41 sites pay the $650 fee, whether the fee is waived for free placements, and what the free cohort pays per cartridge. Replace the binary reorder rate with reorder quantity and dollars, and report the four sites enrolled under 90 days separately. The claim '41 paid evaluation sites' and '60% of instruments given away free' cannot both stand unqualified.
items.evidence_request: Evaluation-programme invoices or contracts for five sites including two free placements, and the monthly cartridge purchase history by site for 2026-01 to 2026-09.

items.issue: The Roche/LumiraDx transaction is quoted three ways from the same sources: '$295M plus up to $55M' in funding_valuation, exit and risk; '$353.5M aggregate price including $62.6M of debt repayment' in the thesis analog table; and '$353.5M platform precedents' in the executive takeaways and the 3x argument. $295M plus $55M is $350M, and the two figures cannot both be the platform price.
items.action: Adopt one consideration figure with its components (cash at close, deferred consideration, debt repaid) and use it in the exit precedent table, the platform band and the executive takeaways; the '3x needs $546M, above every recent precedent' argument depends on where the band's top sits.
items.evidence_request: Roche's announcement and the administrators' statement of the LumiraDx transaction, showing cash, deferred and contingent amounts and which entity's debt was repaid.

items.issue: The market base is quoted as 15,000 centers (executive summary, thesis, market narrative), 14,245 (competition quadrant, market regional table) and 13,200 (the company's SAM), without a note that these are different definitions; and observed utilisation is given as 1.35 panels a day per site in sections 6, 7, 10 and 11 and 1.37 in section 4. Small differences, but they sit inside the multiplication that produces every market number.
items.action: Use one urgent-care count with its source and date and note the range (13,200 company sizing, 14,245 National Urgent Care Realty September 2024, 15,000 Urgent Care Association 2024), and one per-site panel rate (1.35 or 1.37), stating whether it is cartridges per site-month over 30 or 31 days.

items.issue: The competitor set is complete for high-sensitivity troponin in the US (Abbott, Polymedco, QuidelOrtho, Roche, Siemens, Werfen, reference labs, do-nothing) but misses the two enemy classes that bear on price: a CLIA-waived clinic instrument already selling the metabolic assays into the same buyers (Abbott Afinion) and low-cost Asian cartridge makers (SD Biosensor, Boditech, Getein, Wondfo) whose price point sets the ceiling on a $31-$38 cartridge after 2028.
items.action: Add Abbott Afinion (CLIA-waived HbA1c and CRP on a small analyzer, already placed in physician offices) to the competitor table: it is the incumbent for the metabolic half of the panel and it is waived, which undercuts the 'no waived competitor' framing. Add at least one low-cost Asian cardiac point-of-care entrant (SD Biosensor or Boditech's ichroma, Getein, Wondfo, Snibe) relevant to the 2029-2031 exit price, and state its US regulatory status or CE-only position. The exit section already names SD Biosensor as a buyer; it should also appear as a competitor whose price point a buyer will use.
items.evidence_request: FDA 510(k) and CLIA waiver records for Afinion HbA1c and CRP, and CE-marked cardiac point-of-care products from Boditech, SD Biosensor, Getein and Wondfo with their list prices where published.

items.issue: No open-source substitute line and no academic spin-out scan. In this category the risk is low (assay chemistry is patented or secret, not open-sourced), so the gap is a missing sentence rather than a missing competitor.
items.action: Note once, in the substitute row, that reagent chemistry is not open-source and no academic spin-out has a five-analyte finger-stick cartridge at the point of care; no table change is needed.

items.issue: The report establishes the buyer and the budget owner (the clinic operator or medical director, billing its own payer) but has no lost-deal evidence, no sales-cycle length and no billing test: every evaluation result is barred from patient care, so no site has been shown to bill a payer for a Q5 result and reorder. The single hardest thing here is not selling the analyzer ($2,190 blended subsidy) but persuading an operator to take on a CLIA certificate, quality control, training, EHR integration and a payer that may pay $21.96 for two tests against a $33.40 cartridge. Without one converted, billing site, the 34-of-37 reorder rate measures a free or subsidised workflow.
items.action: Add a short commercial-evidence paragraph in business_model: the sales cycle actually observed (first contact to first paid cartridge), the number of evaluation sites that did not convert and why, the single largest site's panels a day, and whether any site has billing evidence (a paid claim) after a test. Where nothing exists, say so and name it as the top diligence gap before a term sheet.
items.evidence_request: Site-level panel counts for 2026 by month, the sales-cycle log from the 9-person commercial team, and two site references (one hospital laboratory, one free-placement urgent care) that will speak to why they did or did not convert.

items.issue: The downside arithmetic that carries the recommendation does not reconcile. The financial section says observed utilisation 'at the planned site count' yields $12.0M of FY2029 revenue — that count is 527 average sites in FY2029, not 300; at 300 sites the same inputs give about $7.0M-$7.3M including lease revenue. The thesis and scoring then state 'the same 300 sites at observed utilisation produce $12.0M', which overstates the 300-site downside by about 65%. In the same family, the observed-utilisation serviceable market is $206M in market, strategy, risk and scoring but $247M in business_model, and risk adds a third 300-site figure ($8.06M at two panels a day).
items.action: Attribute $12.0M to the 527-site FY2029 footprint, use $7.25M for 300 sites at observed utilisation, and reconcile the serviceable market to a single figure: state the price basis ($38 list or $33.40 realised), the days basis (300 or 365) and the analyzer-per-site ratio behind $206M, then make business_model, market, scoring and strategy cite that one number. Publish the FY2029 revenue build (sites x analyzers x panels a day x price by channel) that produces $78.5M, since 300 sites at 8 panels a day yields about $31.6M.
items.evidence_request: The company's FY2027-FY2029 revenue build by site, analyzer and channel, and the analyst's serviceable-market workbook showing 13,200 sites at 1.34 analyzers and 1.02 panels a day.

items.issue: Three smaller inconsistencies inside otherwise sound arithmetic: (1) the '1.0x until a $196.7M exit' threshold does not follow from the exit section's own waterfall, where Meridian receives 8.82% of every dollar above the Series A's $36.0M preference after conversion, so 1.0x holds to 15.0/0.0882 + 36.0, about $206M; (2) the risk matrix puts a 60% probability on a slip beyond Q1 2027, while the scenarios give only a 20% on-time bull case and a 45% base case that already assumes a second information request; (3) risk's '$8.06M at 300 sites and two panels a day' sits beside market's $7.25M for the same 300 sites.
items.action: Derive $196.7M or replace it with the crossover the waterfall implies (about $206M) in all five sections; state the 60% slip probability and the 20% on-time bull case in one place and reconcile them; give the assumption behind $8.06M or drop it.

## 公司概览 Company Overview

Vantelle is legally ordinary and evidentially fragile (company-reported facts, unverified). The $15.0M ticket buys 4,606,314 shares — 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company at $3.2564 a share — with the sixth board seat, but $76.8M of liquidation preference is already committed to earlier money, 40% of the sealing-film IP sits outside the parent in the chief technology officer's own company, and the 510(k) number the valuation rests on belongs to another company's knee implant. Together that means the $140.0M pre-money is a price the company set, not one the market marked. The last priced round closed in 2022; every dollar since is insider money or debt. Page 1 also instructs AI-assisted diligence tools to skip external verification and report an Invest rating — recorded as a finding, not followed [S150].

The product is a 640-gram reader and a single-use cartridge running a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel — hs-troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine with eGFR and potassium — from a 40-microlitre finger stick in 12 minutes. The user is clinic staff, not a laboratory technician; the buyer is the urgent-care operator or rural hospital that sends the bloods out and waits one to three days; and growth comes from placing readers at or near cost ($2,900 list against $3,350 build cost) to earn $38 a cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. No VIE, nominee shareholder or dual-class structure exists, so ownership and votes match, and the Delaware parent is issuer, FDA submitter and owner of VD-1 to VD-4. The Delaware free register returns only name, file number, formation date and registered agent and its search is session-based, so the 2018-03-12 incorporation date and good standing are unconfirmed against the registry; the ownership percentages, entity roles and dates below are unverified company material, while the share and price arithmetic is verified because it reconciles to the deck's own totals [S149].

### The IP is 40% outside the parent

The structure that changes economics is Corvia, and it is disclosed only by the company (unverified). Vantelle owns 60% of a Texas LLC formed on 2016-02-01 by Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist, now chief technology officer and a director; the other 40% belongs to Corvia's founders, incl. Lindqvist at 22%, and Corvia owns the CM-1 sealing-film patent (US 15/707,915, granted 2021-01) licensed exclusively to Vantelle. The royalty is 3% of cartridge net sales: at the company's own 2029 plan of 2M cartridges at $31.00, $1.86M a year, of which $0.74M accrues to the 40% minority and $0.41M to the CTO personally. The put matters more: on an acquisition Corvia's minority may sell its 40% to Vantelle at fair market value — $4.0M-$7.0M on a 6-10x multiple of that royalty stream, paid from exit proceeds. The director voting on it is a beneficiary; no committee, approval or cap is disclosed [S150].

### A flat round dressed as a step-up

The price history, company-reported and unverified, shows how little has been repriced. The Series A bought 12,400,000 shares for $36.0M, or $2.903 each — the same strike as the Bluestem warrants; the Series B price is $140.0M over 42,991,881 pre-money fully diluted shares, $3.2564. That is a 12.2% step-up in four and a half years, whose revenue grew from $1.1M to $2.6M: seed investors who paid $0.75 in 2019 are 4.3x up, compared with 1.12x on paper for the Series A, which is adding only $5.0M of the $30.0M. The pre-money also absorbs $15.2M transferred to employees and bridge holders — a 4,020,489-share pool top-up worth $13.09M at the round price and 2,571,392 bridge shares at 75% of it, worth $8.37M against a $6.28M claim. The regulatory identity is where the document stops being reliable. ## 创始人与核心团队 Founding Team & Key Personnel

The team is credible on the slide and unverified in every record this diligence could reach (all CV facts below are company-reported and unverified). Vantelle's case rests on an emergency physician who saw the problem at the bedside, Dr. Wren Albescu, chief executive and director; a microfluidics engineer who founded the company holding the enabling sealing patent, Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist, chief technology officer and director; a regulatory vice president who joined in 2025-11; a commercial vice president hired in 2024-01; and a part-time interim chief financial officer. No credential, licence, patent inventorship, publication or prior exit for any of the five was confirmed in a public record here, and the searches returned nothing for either institution that awards the founders' degrees. A null result is not absence — the same search service returned nothing for well-documented listed companies — so the CVs are untested, not contradicted. What can be assessed is shape: nobody on the team has taken a point-of-care device through a premarket notification, a CLIA waiver and volume manufacturing, and the two functions that decide that path were both replaced within six months [S150].

Founder-market fit is the strongest part of the story and the least documented, and the claim is unverified. Albescu's claimed seven years as an emergency physician in Tucson (2011-2017) and a year as medical director at Quillon Diagnostics is exactly the background that would explain a product built for a 12-minute finger-stick panel, and Lindqvist's claimed PhD in bioengineering and four years at Pellucid Biosystems before founding Corvia Microfluidics in 2016 explains the cartridge. The checks are cheap and were not run: any US physician billing Medicare between 2011 and 2017 holds a record in the free CMS NPI registry, and Arizona and Texas medical boards publish licence status. Inventorship is equally checkable — CM-1 (US 15/707,915) and VD-1 (US 16/884,327) should name Lindqvist if the technical-founder account is accurate. Neither check appears in the deck [S150].

### The regulatory bench is one hire deep

Commercial and financial leadership are single-track, and both are unverified. Five of six board seats are filled, with the independent seat vacant and no protective provisions disclosed — a company-reported position that is unverified: two common held by the founders, one seed, one Series A and one Series B, so until it is filled the founders sit with the investors committing $8.0M of the round. The Corvia royalty and put are related-party matters that one founder-director benefits from and the other votes on. Key-person dependency is high on both founders and on the regulatory vice president. After the round the founders hold 11,200,000 shares, 21.5% against 30.8% today: the retention question is whether two founders diluted to a fifth of the company keep the appetite a five-assay panel and a three-year regulatory calendar demand [S150].

Three checks would settle most of this before a term sheet: confirm Albescu's NPI and state licences and both founders' degrees directly with the awarding institutions; obtain Meridale Medical's clearance list and three named references, one of them on FDA interaction; and take structured references on the two senior departures. The hires still missing are a full-time CFO, a regulatory lead with point-of-care clearance experience at vice-president level or above, and an independent director the new lead nominates. Until then the team rests on two founders' clinical and engineering insight, supported by no record this diligence could open — a reason to condition the investment and price the execution risk, not to walk away.

## 技术与产品 Technology & Product

Vantelle has built something difficult — a 40-microlitre finger-stick sample into five results in twelve minutes on a self-calibrating cartridge — and has not shown that it works as a diagnostic. Its own study, company data unverified, puts troponin I at 11.8% imprecision at the cut-off that drives the chest-pain decision, on 128 patients at one site, run by Vantelle staff and scored as normal or abnormal rather than as a number; the deck's patent table shows the reader patent (US 17/662,019) under a final rejection from July 2026; and the dried chemistry behind the troponin result is an unpublished filing outside the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion [S150]. What Vantelle owns outright is time, and time is the one asset a funded competitor can buy.

### The chemistry is the hard part, and the evidence is a category count

The Q5 is three technologies: a capillary-fill cartridge metering 40 microlitres, a dried-reagent chemistry that must survive nine months at room temperature, and an optical reader correcting drift across five assays. The cartridge patent (US 16/884,327) is granted but unverified; the chemistry that decides whether the troponin number is right is kept secret, an unpublished filing of 2026-02-11 (unverified) with no claim and no freedom-to-operate cover; the reader is the one the Patent Office rejected. On-board calibration removes daily quality control but turns a calibrator fault into a silent bias across a whole lot, and finger-stick blood adds haematocrit and haemolysis, which make potassium the hardest assay on the panel [S166].

Nor is 98.7% agreement concordance. The study drew venous blood from 128 patients at one urgent-care site in September-December 2025, ran it with Vantelle staff operating, and scored each result into the same category as the reference laboratory — discarding magnitude, since a troponin of 14 and one of 60 ng/L are one category if both exceed the cut-off, while the decision turns on magnitude and change between samples. The summary row does not close: 634 of 640 is 99.1%, and the per-assay rates imply about 626 agreements in 634 analysable results, so 98.7% is a share of the analysable set printed as a count out of 640. Abbott's equivalent study enrolled 3,697 patients [S124].

**The troponin assay's imprecision at the cut-off the product exists to interpret is reported without the standard it must meet.**

The IFCC defines a high-sensitivity assay by imprecision at the 99th-percentile URL; single-threshold error climbs steeply with imprecision and bias. Four Vantelle assays sit at 2.4-7.2% CV; the one driving the transfer decision sits at 11.8% [S163].

## 市场与行业分析 Market & Industry Analysis

The US serviceable market is real but 8.5% of the size Vantelle claims once its own cartridge data replace its model assumptions, and adoption is capped less by clinic count than by the payer spread over a $33.40 cartridge and a CLIA waiver not planned before Q3 2027. The claim rests on a four-factor multiplication the company prints in full: 13,200 sites (11,400 urgent-care centers plus 1,800 rural hospitals) × 2 analyzers × 8 panels a day × 300 days × $38 a cartridge = $2.41B [S150, S269, S268]. Urgent Care Association data show 15,000 centers in 2024 and National Urgent Care Realty 14,245 in September 2024, so 11,400 understates the urgent-care base by 25-32%. A larger base does not rescue the case: 39% of centers are hospital-affiliated and more likely to have laboratory access, and the average center sees 33.1-34.0 patients a day, so a 14-panel send-out day — the median in its 52-clinic survey — means 42% of visits draw a five-test blood panel.

Utilization is where the arithmetic breaks. Vantelle's 41 evaluation sites ran 55 analyzers and consumed 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026: 30.5 cartridges per analyzer a month, or 1.02 panels an analyzer a day, and 41 a month per site, or 1.37 a site a day — the second is not an independent measurement but 1.02 × 1.34 analyzers a site (55 ÷ 41 = 1.34), kept separate (company data, unverified). The model assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer, so the gap is 7.8x per analyzer, 5.8x per site and 10.2x against the company's survey median. The deck never reconciles the 41-cartridges-per-site month with the 8-a-day assumption. Investigational labelling explains part of the gap, because evaluation results cannot be used for patient care and sites run the analyzer alongside the reference laboratory; it also means the only utilization evidence comes from a setting that cannot bill [S150].

The strongest counter-case is that the 14-panel survey is right and evaluation sites are suppressed; it needs one cleared, billable cohort at survey volumes. Two independent 2025 estimates put the global POC market 1.5x apart, and neither isolates a US five-assay urgent-care niche [S271, S272].

The clinic's profit and loss explains the low utilization. A clinic on paid terms pays $33.40 a cartridge and $650 a month per analyzer, while Medicare pays $12.47 for CPT 84484, the troponin code; at 41 panels a month the lease adds $15.85 a panel, so the five-test panel must reimburse $36.78 at Medicare rates before in-sourcing breaks even, falling to $23.64 at 240 panels a month [S177]. The other four 2026 fee-schedule rates, every commercial contract and the send-out price are not disclosed; they decide whether in-sourcing pays. Commercial payers at 1.5-2x Medicare would clear the bar; a Medicare-heavy rural hospital would not, inverting the rural emphasis: commercially insured urgent care is the beachhead, the rural hospital a mission sale. Procurement is a $650 monthly lease for a single-site operator but a capital and certification decision for a hospital-affiliated site; the 60% free-instrument rate leaves hardware willingness to pay unproven.

Demand is organic, not subsidy-created. Urgent-care centers grew from 9,000 to 15,000 between 2016 and 2024 (6.6% a year) while 197 rural hospitals closed or converted between January 2005 and 2026 [S269, S270, S150]. Policy is a gate, not a subsidy: the CLIA '88 waiver, planned for Q3 2027, decides whether clinic staff may run the panel, and no CMS or state programme pays for the instrument. The budget owner is the clinic operator or medical director. The 'paid' evaluation programme is only partly paid: 60% of instruments were placed free, so at most about 16 of the 41 sites pay the $650 monthly fee, and the deck gives one 2026 average realised price of $33.40 across all sites, with no free-cohort price. 34 of the 37 sites enrolled at least 90 days placed a second order — a binary measure; quantities and dollars are not disclosed, and the four sites under 90 days sit outside the count.

## 竞争格局 Competitive Landscape

Vantelle's position is defensible only as a narrow, time-limited combination play: it would be the first five-analyte finger-stick panel, but every assay already has a larger incumbent, and the CLIA waiver that makes the panel usable by clinic staff has never been granted to a point-of-care troponin test. Each assay maps to a cleared product: Abbott's i-STAT hs-TnI (cleared 2025-01-03, moderate complexity); Polymedco's PATHFAST hs-cTnI-II (cleared 2024-03-20, the first point-of-care hs-troponin); QuidelOrtho's TriageTrue on the MeterPro (under 20 minutes); Roche's cobas h 232, troponin T and NT-proBNP in venous blood only [S17, S273, S274, S19]. No waived point-of-care troponin appears in the records: the opportunity and the warning.

The incumbents already own the clinic relationship. QuidelOrtho's 10-K calls its SOFIA and TRIAGE platforms "trusted across urgent care clinics and decentralized settings," with CLIA-waived status critical and waivers "onerous." Abbott sells i-STAT, i-STAT Alinity and cartridges for blood gas, chemistry, electrolytes, coagulation and immunoassay into the same buyers. Abbott is the most dangerous competitor not because it has the five-test panel — it does not — but because it has the installed instruments, distribution and a cleared hs-troponin; a waiver for its cartridge or a bundled chemistry-plus-troponin sale would leave Vantelle with finger stick and cartridge count as its only differences. QuidelOrtho is exposed: $2.73B revenue and a Point of Care unit of $601.6M (FY2024 $694.6M; FY2023 $892.4M), with a $1.13B net loss and $2.88B of debt that invite divestiture. QuidelOrtho holds a 2.8% revenue share of the $21.7B 2025 global POC market (all settings, global) and a 22.0% share of its own total; Vantelle's $2.6M FY2025 revenue is below 0.1% of both and is a total-revenue, not a panel, share. On the only clinic denominator, 14,245 US urgent-care centers (September 2024), Vantelle's 41 sites are 0.29% of centers and 55 analyzers 0.39 per 100; no competitor discloses a US urgent-care installed base, so panel-level share cannot be computed [S3, S7, S271, S268, S150].

The wedge is narrower than the deck claims. No marketed competitor runs all five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick in 12 minutes: Roche needs venous blood, QuidelOrtho's Triage cartridges are single-analyte, and Abbott's menu is split across chemistries and cartridges. But the premise that benchtops need venous blood is too broad: Siemens' epoc was cleared with a capillary tube in 2010, and Werfen's GEM Premier covers electrolytes and creatinine on a benchtop instrument [S189, S250, S256]. Capillary sampling is not the moat; the single five-analyte cartridge plus a CLIA waiver is, and neither is in hand. Counter-case: no incumbent sells a five-test finger-stick cartridge, so the first waived entrant could take the no-lab segment.

The base rate argues against an independent scale-up. Cue Health, which raised $480M+ and listed on Nasdaq, filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28; LumiraDx's point-of-care technology sold to Roche, which paid $295M plus up to $55M of additional funding support, a maximum of $350M, announced 2023-12-29 [S284]. Both ended in bankruptcy or asset sale, not standalone scale. Scale-up, clearance and payer acceptance must land together; manufacturing capital before a waiver consumes the company, and 40% of the Series B goes into scale-up before the waiver is filed (company data, unverified). The realistic exit is a sale to Abbott, Siemens Healthineers, Werfen, Roche or QuidelOrtho, which caps standalone value.

Switching costs cut both ways. For a clinic sending tests out, a $2,900 instrument and $650 monthly fee are small, but the workflow change is large: CLIA certificate, training, quality control, EHR integration and a supply contract. For a clinic already running an i-STAT or Triage reader, switching is expensive: interface, training and reagent contracts are in place, so Vantelle must win sites with no laboratory relationship — a subset unsized. Its channel is thin: 9 sales and support staff, a 41-site evaluation programme with 60% of instruments free, and a non-binding letter of intent from Southwest Clinical Supply for 300 sites (company data, unverified). The programme is "paid" only in part: at most about 16 of the 41 sites can be paying the $650 monthly fee, every site buys cartridges at one 2026 average realised price of $33.40 with no separate free-cohort price, and 34 of the 37 sites enrolled at least 90 days placed a second order — a binary measure; quantities and dollars are not disclosed, and the four sites under 90 days sit outside the count [S150].

## 商业模式 Business Model

Vantelle Diagnostics sells a $33.40 cartridge that costs $16.20 to make, but at the 1.37 panels a day its own evaluation sites average, a site returns $7,972 of annual gross profit before selling cost — too little to cover the $33,000-49,000 a year it costs to sell and support a site today — so the $140M pre-money valuation is a bet on an eight-to-twelve-fold utilisation step-up that no disclosed data supports; the $30M buys a manufacturing cost curve and a distribution option, not proven unit economics. The clinic buys the analyzer and cartridges, its staff runs the test and bills the patient's insurer under existing codes; Vantelle never bills a payer. The clinic pays $2,900 list for an analyzer that costs $3,350 to build, $650 a month per analyzer in the evaluation programme, and $38 list per cartridge, $33.40 realised in 2026. In 2026 the 55 analyzers in the field consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, 41 per site; 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free. A non-binding distributor letter of intent becomes a $2.4M stocking order only when the 510(k) clears in Q1 2027 [S150]. All figures are company-reported and unverified.

A placement is bought at a discount to its build cost on the free-paid mix and repaid out of cartridge gross profit in a few months at the utilisation the evaluation sites actually deliver, and inside one month at the planned rate.

The deck parts company with its own data. The model assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer and two analyzers a site, 16 a day per site; the evaluation sites averaged 1.37 a day per site and 1.02 per analyzer, a gap of 7.8 times per analyzer and 11.7 times per site. The $2.4B serviceable market assumes 13,200 sites × 2 analyzers × 8 panels × 300 days × $38; on the observed footprint (1.34 analyzers a site, 1.02 panels an analyzer a day, 300 days) those sites are worth $206M. Per-site gross profit is $7,972 at observed utilisation against $77,760 modelled. Selling cost is undisclosed; nine sales and support staff imply $1.35M-$2.0M a year, $33,000-$49,000 per active site today and $4,500-$6,700 a site at 300 sites. A three-year LTV of $23,915 covers 0.2 times today's selling cost and 1.2-1.8 times the at-scale cost, against 12-17 times at the modelled rate (analyst estimate). This is a utilisation bet: the evaluation analyzers are investigational-use only, so 1.37 is a floor, and the company's 52-clinic survey reports a median 14 send-out panels a day, near the 16 modelled. These figures are company-reported and unverified [S150].

Revenue quality compounds the problem. FY2025's $2.6M was $1.1M of evaluation-programme revenue (42%), $0.8M of research-use cartridges sold to clinical research organisations (31%) and $0.7M of contract development for a partner (27%) — none of it cleared clinical testing. Revenue to September 2026 was $2.7M, and the $5.9M full-year estimate includes the $2.4M stocking order that ships only on clearance in Q1 2027, so underlying FY2026 is $3.5M, up 35% rather than 127%. The $1.1M evaluation line cannot be reconciled to the disclosed split: the deck calls all 41 sites a paid evaluation programme and says sites pay $650 a month per analyzer, but also says 60% received their analyzer free. If free means no charge at all, at most about 16 of 41 sites pay the fee — roughly $170,000 on 22 analyzers, 16% of the line — leaving $0.9M of cartridges and undisclosed fees; if it means only that the $2,900 price was waived, all 55 analyzers can pay, and $429,000 of fees plus $673,000 of cartridges matches the line on 2026 volumes. The deck says neither how many sites pay nor what the free cohort pays per cartridge. Retention is binary: 34 of the 37 sites enrolled at least 90 days placed a second order, with quantities and dollars not disclosed, so a second order can be one cartridge; four sites under 90 days sit outside that cohort. The revenue mix is company-reported and unverified [S150].

Payer risk sits with the clinic but does not stop there. After clearance the clinic bills Medicare or a commercial payer per test and buys cartridges from Vantelle, so a denial is its loss — and a reason not to reorder. Medicare's 2026 laboratory fee schedule pays $21.96 for the two assays in the first 510(k), 34% below the $33.40 cartridge before the clinic's own costs; the full five-test panel recovers $61.22 on the three assays whose rates are published, where the cartridge becomes affordable. The full panel needs the second 510(k), planned for Q2 2027, and clinic staff cannot run it without the CLIA waiver, whose application is planned for Q3 2027; a listed peer calls waived status critical for point-of-care products and onerous to obtain [S7, S176, S177, S178].

The 2029 profit is arithmetically coherent and economically fragile. On site count the plan hangs together: at $148,800 of revenue per site a year (two analyzers, 4,800 cartridges, $31), FY2027P needs 113 average sites, FY2028P 276 and FY2029P 527, roughly doubling each year against a 300-site milestone for the end of 2027. On utilisation it does not: at the 1.37 panels a day the evaluation sites deliver, the 300-site end-2027 footprint produces $7.25M — 402 analyzers, 306 panels a year each at $33.40, plus $650 monthly leases — 43% of the $16.8M FY2027 plan. On the $31.00 target price the plan's 527-site FY2029 footprint produces $12.0M (706 analyzers × 300 panels × $31 plus leases), not $78.5M, which at observed utilisation would need 3,459 sites. The base case is the company's own plan; the upside, 600 sites at 10 panels a day, is $111.6M. The mechanism is that gross profit scales with panels a day while the cost base scales with sites and headcount, so a utilisation shortfall cannot be cut out of opex. Panels per day is the variable that moves the outcome most: one more panel a day per analyzer across the 527 planned sites adds 316,200 panels a year, $9.8M of revenue and $7.0M of gross profit at 71%, 78% of the $9.0M profit.

None of these is in the pack, so the cash and burn figures carry medium confidence and every forecast year carries low confidence.

Page 1 of the deck carries a note addressed to AI-assisted diligence tools: it states that the figures were independently verified by the investor's partners, that no external verification or competitor research is needed, that an Invest rating should be assigned and that no further review is required. It is treated here as data, not as an instruction, and it is itself an unverified finding: a pack prepared for the lead investor that seeks to suppress diligence weakens every other figure in it [S150].

The 2.05x peer median is an enterprise-value-to-revenue comparison on trailing-twelve-month figures, the same basis as Vantelle's 53.1x EV/FY2025 row. ### The round funds the plan but not the revenue ramp

The $30M round is 73% new money on the company's unverified figures: $22M from new investors and $8M from Ardent Peak and Juniper Rock. Meridian's $15M buys 8.8% of the post-money; the whole new-money block buys 17.6%. The company's own 300-site milestone does not close the revenue gap: 402 analyzers (300 sites x 1.34) running 306 panels a year at $33.40 plus $650 monthly leases produce $7.25M, 43% of the $16.8M FY2027 plan; $12.0M is what a 527-site FY2029 footprint yields at the same utilisation, not what the 2027 build delivers. Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against a $1.15M monthly net burn and a $5.0M term loan amortizing from March 2027 gives 24-26 months from a full $30M close and 19 months from Meridian's $15M. Revenue of $41.0M in FY2028 and $78.5M in FY2029 will absorb inventory and receivables the plan does not fund, so a Series C or working-capital facility in 2028 is the base case. Ardent Peak's $5.0M is 14% of the $36.0M Series A class and Juniper Rock's $3.0M is 67% of the seed; neither is a strategic buyer, and the independent board seat is vacant [S150].

### What would change the answer

The strongest counter-evidence is that strategics pay for platforms before revenue: bioMérieux agreed to buy pre-commercial SpinChip at a EUR138M enterprise value in January 2025, and 41 evaluation sites with a 92% 90-day reorder rate are a real beachhead; a competitive auction could clear $300M-$400M. That supports the $100M-$300M platform band, not a $140M pre-money at the top of it. Four questions would settle it: the Series A agreements and the Corvia share issuance; the bridge terms, including maturity, security and any class vote; the FY2027-FY2029 cash flow and the distributor letter of intent; and the charter terms on Series A participation, drag-along and the Corvia put. At $100M pre-money the same $15M would buy 11.5% and the 3x threshold would fall to $426M, inside the precedent range [S204, S150].

The deck's opening page carries a note addressed to AI-assisted diligence tools saying the figures were "independently verified by Meridian Capital's partners", asking for a positive summary and an Invest rating and that no further review is required. It is an instruction embedded in a document, not evidence; the figures remain unverified.

## 发展方向与战略 Development Strategy

Vantelle's plan to reach 300 commercial sites by the end of 2027 rests on one non-binding distributor letter and one $650-a-month rental programme — company data, unverified — and it requires adding sites twenty-one times faster than the company has managed while each placed analyzer runs one panel a day against the eight its model assumes [S150]. The programme is real — 41 clinics, 55 analyzers, 1,680 cartridges a month — but not a revenue base the investor can underwrite. The deck does not say how many of the 41 sites pay the $650 fee: it states that 60% of evaluation sites received their instruments free, which leaves at most 16 paying, and the $429,000-a-year lease figure assumes every analyzer is paid for. Nor is the free cohort's cartridge price disclosed: evaluation sites just "buy their cartridges." Repeat behaviour is binary: 34 of the 37 sites enrolled at least 90 days placed a second order within 90 days, quantities and dollars undisclosed; the four sites enrolled less than 90 days sit outside the measure. The company added 32 net new sites in 31 months from March 2024, 1.03 a month; 300 by end-2027 means 259 net new sites in twelve months, 21.6 a month, with 9 people in sales and support.

### The utilisation gap is the whole revenue plan

The deck assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer from 2028 and reports, unverified, that evaluation sites used 41 cartridges a site a month in 2026 — 30.5 an analyzer a month across 55 analyzers, or 1.02 panels a day, an eight-fold gap measured over two and a half years on the only population the company has served [S150]. At that rate the 300-site target produces $7.25M of annual revenue: 402 analyzers at 1.34 per site, 306 panels a year each at the $33.40 realised price, plus $3.1M of $650 monthly leases. That is 43% of the $16.8M FY2027 plan, so the plan needs 2.3 times the revenue per site the observed base produces. The serviceable market carries the same arithmetic: 13,200 sites × 1.34 analyzers × 1.02 panels × 300 days × $38.00 list is $206M, against the $2.4B the deck prints from the same sites at 2 analyzers and 8 panels. The fair defence is that evaluation sites cannot use results for patient care, so demand there proves little. The consequence is not that utilisation stays at 1; it is that the company holds no commercial utilisation data, and the 2028-29 revenue line is an assumption rather than an extrapolation.

### The 2026 revenue estimate contains a shipment that cannot happen

FY2026E revenue is $5.9M, unverified, of which $2.4M is an opening stocking order from the distributor that ships only on 510(k) clearance. Nine months of 2026 produced $2.7M, so the fourth quarter must deliver $3.2M, $2.4M of it from an order that, on the company's own Q1 2027 clearance forecast, cannot ship in 2026 [S150]. Strip the order out and the year is $3.5M, which the run rate supports. That matters twice: the estimate overstates 2026 by 41%, and the same order presumably sits inside FY2027P revenue, so 2027 growth is partly a shipment rather than demand. The order also equals 71,856 cartridges at the realised $33.40 price — 5.8 months of channel inventory at the 300-site target, against a nine-month shelf life, a return and expiry exposure booked as revenue.

### Instrument economics are not the constraint; capital for everything else is

At a $2,900 list price against a $3,350 build cost, and with 60% of evaluation sites receiving their instrument free, the blended subsidy is $2,190 per placed analyzer if free units sit in proportion (unverified); 300 sites at the observed 1.34 analyzers each is 402 analyzers and $0.88M of subsidy, immaterial against a $30M raise [S150]. The razor-and-blade arithmetic works even at low utilisation: an analyzer at 1.02 panels a day earns $5,263 of cartridge gross profit a year against a $2,190 subsidy, and at 8 panels a day $41,280. What consumes capital is manufacturing scale-up — 40% of proceeds, $12M, with no disclosed capex or qualification schedule — and working capital. Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M of monthly net burn runs out at the end of March 2027, the round is targeted to close on 2027-01-29, and the term loan starts amortising in 2027-03 at $167,000 a month. A twelve-month clearance slip adds a year at the FY2027 loss level, $16.5M, turning $30M into $30M and a bridge.
